Steve Votier

Audio from seabirds fitted with mini recordin…
items.feedText: Many large vessels are now legally required to carry automatic identification systems broadcasting their identity and location at regular intervals. Although this has allowed interactions between animals and fisheries to be studied at scale, there are enormous gaps in coverage. In fact, recent research suggests that three-quarters of industrial fishing vessels don’t use the technology, says Jonathan Rutter at the University of Oxford. This is partly because regulations on the types of vessels that are required t…
items.body:
A northern gannet ( *Morus bassanus* ) tagged with biologging devices on its back and tail

Steve Votier

Audio from seabirds fitted with mini recording devices and GPS trackers has been used by researchers to show that marine life can record encounters with vessels that are otherwise difficult to track.

Many large vessels are now legally required to carry automatic identification systems broadcasting their identity and location at regular intervals. Although this has allowed interactions between animals and fisheries to be studied at scale, there are enormous gaps in coverage.

In fact, recent research suggests that [three-quarters of industrial fishing vessels](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06825-8) don’t use the technology, says [Jonathan Rutter](https://www.biology.ox.ac.uk/people/jonathan-rutter) at the University of Oxford. This is partly because regulations on the types of vessels that are required to share data vary by country. Large satellite ‘blind spots’ also contribute to the problem, he says, and so does subterfuge for the purpose of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU).

[Read more Most large fishing boats go untracked as ‘dark vessels’](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2410541-most-large-fishing-boats-go-untracked-as-dark-vessels/)

Rutter says that being caught as bycatch in fishing is one of the greatest risks to seabird populations, but if fishing vessels are only tracked “with conventional methods, such footprints of risk may be strikingly incomplete”.

The team analysed audio collected from devices attached to seven northern gannets ( *Morus bassanus* ) and found that one third of the audio detections couldn’t be matched with vessel tracking data – mostly off the UK coast.

Overall, 12 per cent of the vessel detections made by the four critically endangered Balearic shearwaters ( *Puffinus mauretanicus* ) included in the study couldn’t be matched to public data. But given the high vessel density where they were – off the Catalan coast – the researchers estimated that up to 20 per cent of the vessels detected by the four birds weren’t broadcasting their identity.

[Tammy Davies](https://www.birdlife.org/global-science-team/) at BirdLife International – a global partnership of non-governmental organisations – who wasn’t involved in the study, says the research could “give us a more complete picture of the risks seabirds face at sea” and “ultimately, this could contribute to better assessments of bycatch risk and help identify fisheries and areas where conservation measures are most needed”.

[Peter Ejbye-Ernst](https://nscr.nl/en/medewerker/peter-ejbye-ernst-msc/) at the Netherlands Institute for the Study of Crime and Law Enforcement (NSCR), describes the study as “fascinating” from a green criminology point of view, too.

A tagged northern gannet coming in to land in Wales

Steve Votier

“What this study is somewhat proposing is that we can also look outside of humans for witnesses too,” he says, which overcomes a key barrier in observing crime at sea.

In terms of its applications for cracking down on IUU, he says: “There’s a fine line between trying to understand something better and document it and then trying to control it and surveil it.”

There are caveats, as the study has a small sample size and records both false-negatives and false-positives. It also gives very little information on the type of activity vessels were carrying out. But, while the research isn’t a solution to the problem of IUU, it is “part of the toolbox” for understanding what is happening at sea, says Ejbye-Ernst.

The study didn’t differentiate between the size of vessels, but Rutter and his colleagues say this would be a good area for future research.

[Powerful images show dark side of South-East Asia’s fishing industry Photographer Nicole Tung captures the tough world facing South-East Asia’s fishers and their families in this series of images, which won her the Carmignac Photojournalism Award for fieldwork](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2495209-powerful-images-show-dark-side-of-south-east-asias-fishing-industry/)

“Animal-borne audio recorders could potentially be used to investigate other ecological interactions and human activities that are difficult to observe directly, particularly in the marine environment,” says team member [Ana Bertoldi Carneiro](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=KpYB2rYAAAAJ&hl=en), also at BirdLife International.

[Hugo Tagholm](https://oceana.org/people-partners/hugo-tagholm/) at the charity Oceana says it is shocking that so many of the interactions were with unseen vessels, but he is concerned about attaching devices to seabirds on a broader scale to track this.

“Seabirds are already grappling with the harm caused by overfishing and climate breakdown, we don’t want to put them at even greater risk from vessel operators acting illegally,” he says.

“What we need is mandatory remote electronic monitoring across all fishing vessels, clear and effective laws and catch limits to protect and restore our seas, and truly deterrent sanctions for those breaking the law.”

**Journal Reference:**

*Science Advances*
[DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh2224](https://dx.doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeh2224)

items.body:
# Eine neue Plattform von Universal Audio - was versteckt sich hinter UA Universe?

## UA Universe Plattform für eigene DAW-Tools

## Neue Plattform von Universal Audio

UA Universe Plattform für eigene DAW-Tools

Das Thema KI und das damit zusammenhängende Vibe-Coding ist aktuell in aller Munde, schließlich öffnen nach und nach viele Hersteller ihr Firmwares für die Öffentlichkeit. Auch wir berichten regelmäßig über dieses Thema. Mit UA Universe stellt nun überraschenderweise auch Universal Audio eine neue Plattform vor, mit der Nutzer eigene Add-Ons für die DAW entwickeln können.

## UA Universe

Gerade bei der Entwicklung von Software und Plug-ins nimmt Künstliche Intelligenz immer mehr eine größere Rolle ein. Universal Audio geht mit seiner neuen Plattform nun in die Offensive und stellt damit eine Möglichkeit vor, sich Add-ons wie Plug-ins selbst zu gestalten.

Universal Audio stellt hierfür das passende SDK/Framework zur Verfügung, die Programmierung erfolgt danach mit üblichen KI-Agenten wie bspw. Claude oder Codex. Basis der ganzen Sache ist die DAW LUNA , die Universal Audio kürzlich in der dritten Version vorgestellt hat.

In der Praxis funktioniert die Plattform wie folgt: Zunächst wird LUNA auf dem eigenen Rechner installiert und mit den LUNA Builder Tools verknüpft. Mit Hilfe von Text-Prompts lässt sich dann ein Add-On erstellen und der KI-Agent erzeugt damit das passende Tool, fertig. Klingt kinderleicht!

Von ganz einfachen Aufgaben wie „Erzeuge mir ein Button, um die Tracks 1-4 stummzuschalten“ bis hin zu „Ich benötige eine Effekt-Kette für die Bearbeitung meiner Drums-Aufnahme“ soll vieles möglich sein.

Und da alle Kreationen direkt mit der UAD-Community geteilt werden können, könnte schnell ein großes Portfolio an Add-Ons, Tools und Plug-ins entstehen. Bereits jetzt zeigt Universal Audio auf seiner Discover-Seite was möglich ist und von anderen Nutzern erstellt wurde:

- UA Universe – Discover
Es wird spannend sein zu sehen, wie sich das Projekt UA Universe in den nächsten Monaten entwickelt. Was ist eure Meinung dazu?

# The gentle sounds of a tiny acoustic piano from Denmark - CDM Create Digital Music

## The gentle sounds of a tiny acoustic piano from Denmark

In northern Europe, it’s that time of year that disappears under a thick blanket of cloud, and the hours of daylight seem to melt away into cinder gray. That calls for some cozy comforts. And look at this: some new acoustic instrument engineering, and a tiny acoustic piano.

This is not a toy piano — which is a lovely instrument, just in fact, I’d argue not a piano at all. Toy pianos, with metal (or sometimes glass or xylphone) bars, are essentially their own class of percussion instrument that happens to have a piano-style keyboard manual.

No, this is a wonderfully scaled-down acoustic piano, as in, honey I shrunk the spinet. (To this day, my favorite instrument of all time was the childhood Everett spinet, a friendly US-built model.

Helsinki-based pianist Antti Kujanpää recorded this beautiful demo, which has every right to go a bit viral at this moment on Earth. (He didn’t even do a thumbnail looking surprised pointing at anything! See? )

They really did manage to make it small. The Danish-built Keybird L1, supporting by a crowdfunding campaign of all things, is only 39 kg, 70x115x55 cm, but still has four octaves and you can play it with even-softer felt engaged, and it comes with a tuning key. It’s clearly a piano you would have a very different relationship with than the 19th century monster we’ve inherited. It’s a piano you can tune. It’s a piano you can carry around . I’m intrigued by the phrase “one of the smallest acoustic pianos on the market.” It’s the smallest I’ve seen.

Optional add-ons give it MIDI capabilities and Helpinstill pickups , plus the usual accoutrements like a tuning kit and road case.

Some outlets picked this up earlier this year, but the appearance of this video indicates that they are now starting to ship, as promised, this quarter.

Antti’ has this lovely solo album, too. Listen, let me tell you, I like music. Sometimes I like it to sound like a swarm of alien bees set to tear out your eardrums, and sometimes I like it to sound like this.

That being said, I do hope there’s some angular, dissonant music composed for it, too! I imagine that could be fragile and strange, like a snowflake on a moon of Jupiter. Uh, if anyone has one and wants a composer, I volunteer.

If you want one yourself, it’s €3.750,00 incl. VAT — but expect some time to get one.

Over ten years ago, I wrote an extended feature on another new acoustic piano — the Una Corda, now positively enormous at 100 kg.

> Acoustic Revelation: Inside the Una Corda, the 100kg, 21st Century Piano Built for Nils Frahm

But here as now, even as someone who’s spent long hours at the desk of a Steinway grand, I am absolutely overjoyed to see the tyranny of the Steinway Model D-274 finally seeing some resistance. (Even competing models from Yamaha and others are closely related in design.) We’ll always have the Model D. It’s long past time to have something else, too.

Keybird Instruments L1

## What I’m thankful for, literarily.

– Weird and in person celebrations of books.

– Listening to a poem while doing my little stretches. The Library of Congress and Poetry Archive collections, to be specific.

– And I’m thankful in advance to the programmer who builds me a little widget or website that streams a random poem from these archives.

– The new Marlon James . I’m late to the party, but damn.

– Finding something cool in a pile of books someone is giving away.

– The major book awards no longer being afraid of support for Palestine, and Paradiso 17 and Huna winning NBAs.

– A really good pen. I’ve had two instances recently where I had a small bookstore coupon that I spent on luxe pens. Highly recommend treating yourself to a fine writing instrument.

– Funny novels with funny first person narrators.

– The tide continuing to turn against AI. I’m thankful we may see AI’s high water mark very soon.

– Getting to interview Adam Peterson for the release of his story collection.

– Booksellers, who are in the middle of their most hectic season. I’m thankful for everyone who treats them reasonably this time of year.

– Peanuts, a Perfect Snack For Reading.

– Librarians, who are always in the middle of hectic season.

– Flaming Hydra , and especially Luke O’Neil’s recent New England Week which I’m revisiting as I pack up to go to Boston for the holiday.

– Connecting with a stranger over a book, especially that thing where someone points at your book from a distance, and you close it and hold up the cover, and they give you a thumbs up. Really good stuff.

– Small presses, and all the cool and weird things they’re taking a chance on.

– Marilynne Robinson . Her middle name is Summers, but she’s an autumn writer.

– My sweet seven month old showing preferences for books. And I also chew on the books that I like, so I’m thankful that he inherited that trait from me.

– Trying to explain Gene Wolfe ’s deal to someone for the first time.

– A small book you can read in an afternoon. Also having an afternoon free to read.

– Olga Ravn’s gift guide , which includes Ibuprofen and haunted dolls.

– Reading an author who is really going for it and trying something new. I appreciate someone taking a risk, regardless of the outcome. (Usually.)

– A friend asking for a book recommendation, and then actually reading your recommendation, and then telling you they liked your recommendation. No better feeling in the world.

# Bill Kaulitz stellt Sachbearbeiter an den Pranger und lässt ihn ausbuhen – Stadt Leipzig kündigt juristische Prüfung an

## Bill Kaulitz vs. Ordnungsamt Leipzig : Eine Entschuldigung wäre angebracht

Kommentar von

Es ist das Markenzeichen der Kaulitz-Brüder, arrogant und abgehoben und doch irgendwie charmant zu sein. Aber der Vorfall in Leipzig war eins drüber.

25.11.2026

19:54 Uhr

teilen

Diesen Artikel teilen

Feuerwerk Fanboy: Bill Kaulitz Foto: Breuel-Bild/imago

A ls Bill Kaulitz einmal gefragt wurde, ob er nicht Lust hätte bei der Datingshow „The Bachelor“ mitzumachen, verneinte er. Die ausgefallenen Dates mit Helikopterflügen seien vielleicht für die Kandidaten etwas Besonderes, aber für ihn sei das Alltag, erklärte er sinngemäß. Ein anderes Mal sagt er im Podcast „Kaulitz Hills“ zu seinem Bruder Tom, dass er es ekelig fände, wenn jemand nicht konsequent jede Woche seine Bettwäsche wechsele. Dass die meisten Menschen aber keine Haushaltshilfe haben, die das mal eben übernimmt, schien er in dem Moment nicht mitzudenken.

Bill Kaulitz ist arrogant und abgehoben. Und genau das macht seinen Charme aus. Während man es anderen Superreichen missgönnt, wenn sie im Überfluss leben, freuen sich die Fans für den Tokio-Hotel-Sänger. Der fliegt im Heli durch die Welt, badet mit Champagnerglas im neu angelegten Pool in Los Angeles und lässt sich von Assistent Daniel die Hermès-Taschen durch die Stadt schleppen. Mit Bodenständigkeit hat das nichts mehr zu tun.

Seine Fangemeinde stört das nicht – im Gegenteil. Vielleicht, weil man den Kaulitz-Brüdern, die in finanziell schwierigeren Verhältnissen in einem Dorf in Sachsen-Anhalt aufgewachsen sind, den Reichtum gönnt. Vielleicht, weil sie nicht wie Kanzler Merz so tun, als seien sie Teil der Mittelschicht, sondern einfach zugeben können, dass sie reich sind und verdammt gerne Geld ausgeben. Oder vielleicht macht es einfach Spaß, ihnen im Podcast, ihrer Netflix-Show und bei Instagram dabei zuzusehen, wie sie ein abgedrehtes Leben führen.

Sicherlich ist die Antwort eine Mischung aus allen drei Vermutungen. Feststeht: Bill und Tom Kaulitz wissen, wie man unterhält. Dass es wichtig ist, sich über andere lustig zu machen und noch wichtiger, dass man über sich selbst lachen kann. Im Regelfall funktioniert die Gratwanderung des guten Geschmacks bei den Brüdern gut, sie stellen nur die in die Öffentlichkeit, die eh schon da sind. Bis jetzt – bei der Tokio-Hotel-Arena-Tour durch Europa haben sie einen Menschen an den Pranger gestellt, der es nicht verdient hat und keine Person des öffentlichen Lebens ist.

## Wer ist hier der Spielverderber

Es war beim Konzert in Leipzig als Bill Kaulitz einen Sachbearbeiter des Ordnungsamtes namentlich genannt und ausbuhen lassen hat. Er machte ihn dafür verantwortlich, dass die Band einen Teil ihrer Pyrotechnik nicht abbrennen lassen durfte. Schon okay, sich darüber zu ärgern, wenn Special Effekts, wie eine sprühende Feuerwerksfontäne aus Tom Kaulitz Gitarre, verboten sind.

Weniger verständlich ist es, dass der Frontsänger vor 10.000 Fans einen Sachbearbeiter in die Öffentlichkeit zieht, ihm unterstellt er habe ein Scheißleben und solle besser seinen Job verlieren. So viel Verständnis für die Lebensrealität der anderen erwartet man dann auch von einem Superstar. Dass er anerkennt, was es für Konsequenzen für einen einzelnen Menschen haben kann, wenn sein Job und sein Ruf öffentlich angegriffen werden.

Die Stadt Leipzig reagierte prompt, Bürgermeister Burkhard Jung verurteilte die „Grenzverletzung“ durch Bill Kaulitz stark und forderte mehr Rückhalt für Beschäftigte im öffentlichen Dienst. Die Stadt kündigte eine umfassende juristische Prüfung an. Und auch in den Medien ist die Empörung groß.

Manches wird dabei etwas aufgebauscht. Bislang hat die Stadt Leipzig weder wie angekündigt Kontakt zum Management von Tokio Hotel aufgenommen noch Anzeige erstattet. Und auch über einen Shitstorm gegen den Sachbearbeiter, wie manch einer es suggeriert, ist nichts bekannt. Das sagte die Stadt der taz auf Anfrage.

Ernsthafte Konsequenzen wird Bill Kaulitz Auftritt wohl also nicht haben. Eine echte Entschuldigung wäre trotz allem angebracht. Bislang passiert eher das Gegenteil. In der aktuellen Podcast-Folge von „Kaulitz Hills“ treten die Brüder nach und ziehen noch einmal namentlich über den Sachbearbeiter her. Vielleicht warten sie mit ihrer Entschuldigung aber auf die ganz große Bühne: Als Moderatorenduo bei „Wetten, dass..“ nächste Woche. Wie man einen großen Auftritt hinlegt, wissen die beiden ja.

Carolina Schwarz Ressortleiterin taz zwei

items.body:
# Where scientists draw the line on AI agents

## a]:hidden"> Where scientists draw the line on AI agents

📄 Tech Report

Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work.

These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings.

To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies.

Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used.

One of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of scientific trust : validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. These are matters of responsible conduct of research.

Another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized.

A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge.

## Helping researchers check the work

For many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing new ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually.

But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs.

Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis.

But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way.

Our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows.

These examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks.

These evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like.

## Keep scientific judgment in the loop

Verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process?

An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?”

# The Iowa Lead Detonation Happened. Now the Real Work Begins to Study It

On Wednesday morning, the US Army detonated nearly five tons of degraded lead azide outside of Middletown, Iowa.

Environmental Protection Administration chief Lee Zeldin told CNN shortly after the explosion that preliminary monitoring from the site detected no lead in the air around the site .

But the full extent of the fallout may not be certain for at least a few days. A barrage of government, university, and citizen monitoring and testing projects are underway. Air, soil, and water samples they’ve collected will determine the extent of lead exposure, if any, in Middletown and the surrounding area.

The lead azide has been on the base near Middletown for decades, but recently the Army deemed it unstable and too dangerous to move and remediate. Poor communication between the Army and towns in the path of the fallout led to a public uproar. While the federal government stepped up its mitigation measures—the Army dug a dam around the detonation site, while NASA stepped in with research jets and satellites for monitoring—universities had already been swinging into action due to the chaotic rollout.

Several departments at the University of Iowa kicked into gear to begin to set up air and soil monitoring stations late last week. “Initially we did not know that [the] EPA or Army or anybody else was going to be doing anything,” says Peter Thorne, a professor of environmental health at the university.

Scientists at Purdue University, nearly 300 miles away, also put out a call for soil samples from Middletown.

“We learned about the detonation late last week; once we learned of the initial delay in detonation date we decided to put forth the call,” says Ellen Wells, a professor of public health at Purdue who is helping lead the testing.

Surrounding towns were notified in late October that the Army wanted to conduct pre- and post-detonation soil sampling for “an intentional, controlled detonation” of a “quantity of lead azide”—seemingly the only notification that many towns in the initial modeled path of the fallout say they received before a press release issued by the Army days before the planned explosion.

The lack of communication has, understandably, instilled a lot of public distrust in the federal government, including agencies’ monitoring programs. Thorne says that efforts like the University of Iowa’s are not meant to displace federal monitoring, but rather to supplement and support it—and hopefully reassure the public.

“We and the EPA are doing similar exposure assessment efforts. If they agree, they can give us some confidence,” he says. “For people who might be concerned about the veracity of what the government tells them, if their findings are in alignment with ours, then I think that helps quell some of those concerns.”

Thorne says that the soil samples the University of Iowa scientists had measured before the detonation had low levels of lead. “If I saw something like a 10 fold increase in the amount of lead in the soil 20 miles downwind, I’d be concerned with that,” he says.

Some soil testing can be done instantaneously with devices that can image the soil’s surface, using a gun device that fires X-ray beams into a sample and measures the specific electromagnetic signature of lead atoms that bounce back. While Wells and her team don’t have those instruments in the field, they are planning on using them to analyze the samples they receive. More sensitive lab equipment can provide even more granular data, though Thorne estimates those results could take about a week.

In addition to monitoring being done by the Army and the EPA, which is maintaining a live website of air quality results, University of Iowa scientists are monitoring the plume to figure out where the highest concentration of lead may settle. They’re also collecting data on particulate matter in the air around the detonation site for analysis, sending air filters to the lab for more detailed results.

“As these data are compiled over the holiday week to the early next week, I think we'll start to have a bigger picture of roughly how much loading we have of the soil at various places downwind and what we can expect from that,” says Thorne.

A lot of concern online has centered around how additional lead in the soil may impact crops in Iowa, one of the central agricultural hubs for soybeans and corn. Jeffrey Catalano, a professor of earth and environmental sciences at Washington University in Saint Louis, says that there’s a large amount of research showing that plants like corn are actually pretty bad at absorbing lead.

“The hazard is more like, if soil with lead in it gets stuck to leaves, and you eat leaves that have lead-rich soil on them,” he says. “If you take some corn crops next year versus this year and measure their lead content, I don’t think you would see anything other than random variations. I’m not worried about food produced in Iowa.”

Municipal drinking water is also unlikely to be affected because most treatment plants are designed to remove lead from water supplies, says Patrick McNamara, a professor of environmental engineering at Marquette University. It’s more worrisome for private wells or streams on people’s property where livestock may drink. McNamara suggests that owners use at-home lead water tests for safety.

While the detonation and haphazard announcements leading up to it raised alarm bells, both Thorne and Catalano say that there are communities dealing with legacy pollution around the country that are exposed to dangerous levels of lead every day that deserve attention—and remediation.

“I've done work in places like East Chicago, Indiana, where they built a housing project and a school on the grounds of a former lead smelting plant—we were seeing soil lead levels that are roughly 10,000-fold higher than what we've measured in Iowa this week,” Thorne says. “There are a lot of places around the country where there's a much greater lead hazard than I'm going to anticipate what we’ll end up with here. I don't want to over-sell this one when we recognize that there are places where people are really suffering, and need to be remediated for the health of their children.”

Service outages, like the ones we've seen take down everything from airlines to email, seem to be coming faster than ever. items.body:
**Das brandneue** **Elektron Tonverk 1.5-** **Update bringt den Performance-Sampler auf das nächste Level.** **Einen ganzen Stapel von neuen Features erwarten die User. Laut Elektron ist dies das bisher größte Update, das die Schweden bisher abgeliefert haben.**

## Alles über die Updates für Elektron Tonverk

- Das Elektron Tonverk 1.5-Update ist da Zwei neue Maschinen
- Neue Effekte
- Weitere Neuheiten im 1.5-Update für Elektron Tonverk
- Verfügbarkeit und Preis
- Weitere Infos

## Das Elektron Tonverk 1.5-Update ist da

Elektron Tonverk · Quelle: Elektron

Neue Maschinen, neue Effekte, verbesserter Workflow und erweiterte MIDI-Funktionen. Das alles steckt in dem 1.5-Update für Elektron Tonverk, das ab sofort verfügbar ist. Gehen wir mal die Neuheiten durch.

Kurzer Rückblick: Mit 1.0.1 gab es die ersten Bugfixes. 1.1.0 brachte mit Grainer und Shape Granular-Synthese und neue Filterparameter. 1.2.0 lieferte einen neuen Reverb und den Filter-Folder für neue Klangfarben. Wavetables zogen mit dem 1.3-Update ein und dazu ein paar weitere Optimierungen. 1.4 erfreute mit der langerwarteten Overbridge-Integration (die immer noch nicht ganz ausgreift ist) sowie neuen Möglichkeiten für Modulation und ein paar weiteren Verbesserungen.

Jetzt steht 1.5 an und damit wird Elektron Tonverk an vielen Stellen um Funktionen erweitert.

### Zwei neue Maschinen

Zwei Maschinen gibt es jetzt. Stretcher bringt Time-Stretching in den Performance-Sampler und kombiniert das mit Pitch-Shifting. Samples und Loops können so nicht nur einfacher angepasst, sondern auch im Sound verändert werden. Dafür stehen diverse Parameter und verschiedene Algorithmen bereit. Sehr cool! Elektron feiert das mit neuen kostenlosen Samples, die zeitnah erscheinen sollen.

Waveswarmer bringt eine Art von Super-Saw in den Sampler. Aber eben etwas anders! Ein Cluster von verstimmten Wavetables erzeugt den „Schwarm“ und natürlich können Position und Bewegung der Wavetables gesteuert werden. Phase-Modulation, zusätzliches Rauschen und weitere Goodies machen daraus eine schöne neue Engine.

### Neue Effekte

Neue Effekte bekommt Elektron Tonverk ebenfalls mit dem Update. Pulse Gate FX erzeugen Effekte, die einige als Trance-Gate bezeichnen. Über sequenzierte Hüllkurven wird Audio rhythmisch zerhackt.

Für mehr Punch oder Körper sorgen die Transient Control FX – dahinter steckt also ein Transient Shaper. Auch sehr willkommen! Zwei neue EQs gehören ebenso zu dem Update: Einer für den Channel oder auch Busse und Mixe, Parametric EQ bietet mehr chirurgische Eingeriffe.

### Weitere Neuheiten im 1.5-Update für Elektron Tonverk

Die Subtracks Machine bietet jetzt die Möglichkeit, einem einzelnen Subtrack einen eigenen Signalweg zuweisen und Send- sowie Insert-Effekte individuell einsetzen. So kannst du beispielsweise die Snare mit Reverb versehen, während die Kickdrum trocken bleibt.

Praktisch ist auch der neue Multisample-Editor, um Samples komfortabler direkt am Elektron Tonverk zu editieren. Der Hersteller verspricht dafür aber auch zusätzlich eine browserbasierte Version – einfach weil der Bildschirm an der Hardware dann doch etwas zu klein für solche Aufgaben ist. Dieser Editor soll dann als erste Erweiterung von Elektron Labb erscheinen. Demnächst!

Tonverk kann jetzt als MIDI-Host fungieren! USB-MIDI-Geräte können direkt angeschlossen und mit Storm (bis zu 500 mA bei 5 V) versorgt werden, ohne einen Rechner dazwischengeschaltet zu haben.

Als weitere Neuheiten bietet das Update: Unison mit Detune und Panorama-Spreading, Send-Tracks mit Arpeggiator-, Transpose- und MIDI-Funktionalität (!), einen Wavetable-Generator und ein paar weitere Verbesserungen.

Ein echt starkes Update, das ab sofort kostenlos zur Verfügung steht. Hier auf der [Website von Elektron](https://www.elektronauts.com/news/639) findest du weitere Infos.

## Verfügbarkeit und Preis

Das Update ist ab sofort [hier bei Elektron](https://www.elektron.se/support-downloads/tonverk#resources) erhältlich. Elektron Tonverk bekommst du [hier bei Thomann](https://www.thomann.de/de/elektron_tonverk.htm?offid=1&affid=84)*.

items.body:
As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth. Such crop variety can help with menus in deep space, something top of mind this week as the nation celebrates Thanksgiving.

Strawberries grown in the Space Life Sciences Lab’s controlled environment chamber. Cucumbers are grown in a controlled environment chamber at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Lemon basil is growing in chambers on the International Space Station.

NASA

Recent testing points to strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers. Space crops can absorb carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, and recycle water. These capabilities will become increasingly important as crewed missions extend farther from our home planet.

While space crop research advances on Earth, capabilities are also expanding in space. A [new investigation](https://science.nasa.gov/biological-physical-investigations-ohalo-iii/) from [NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division](https://science.nasa.gov/biological-physical/) is set to launch to the International Space Station, where the first-of-its-kind prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing crop production systems that could grow crops like these for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions.

## Sweet space strawberries

Strawberries are among the few sweet fruits under consideration for spaceflight and are nutritious, aromatic, and self-pollinating.

Researchers at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida are growing strawberries in flight-like growth chambers to evaluate the potential space crop, and NASA partners at [The Australian Research Council Centre for Excellence in Plants for Space](https://plants4space.com/) also are helping expand knowledge of space strawberries.

Researchers at NASA Kennedy, the University of Melbourne, and the University of Western Australia recently tested a wild strawberry against NASA’s leading strawberry candidate, ‘Delizz,’ to see which thrived better under simulated space conditions.

Delizz and the wild strawberry produced very different fruits, according to a [study](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2214552426000982?via%3Dihub) published in September in the journal Life Sciences in Space Research. Delizz grew large, red fruit, while the wild strawberry produced small, yellow fruit due to a recessive genetic mutation.

But looks are not everything. When grown from a seed, the wild strawberry produced twice as many buds, flowers, and fruit as Delizz. Ultimately, however, NASA’s pick kept its top spot, as the wild strawberry grew too many runners that would take up valuable room aboard a spacecraft.

## Cucumbers show promise

Many crops have been grown in space, but none so far have come from the gourd family. Cucumbers could be the first.

Before crops like cucumbers can be grown and eaten in space, they must undergo extensive testing. NASA-funded researchers recently evaluated cucumbers for their growth, yield, and nutrition under spaceflight conditions.

The researchers found that while the plants showed some signs of enlarged leaves, they produced a steady stream of edible fruit, according to a [study](https://journals.ashs.org/view/journals/hortsci/61/9/article-p2104.xml) published in August in the journal HortScience.

Offering a variety of crops, such as cucumbers, not only benefits astronauts’ diets and mental well-being, but it also increases plant biodiversity, which can improve the likelihood of crop success on long-duration missions.

## Spicing up spaceflight

Herbs can spice up life in space, turning a bland meal into a bold one.

Lemon basil, an edible herb with a citrus scent and taste, is making strides in testing at NASA Kennedy.

Researchers report that lemon basil passed its preliminary round of space crop testing and successfully underwent seed sanitization, which is required before spaceflight to remove microorganisms from the seeds. Lemon basil’s next steps include assessing its growth in plant pillows, which can house plants aboard the space station.

Menu fatigue can quickly become a problem for astronauts, but fresh herbs like lemon basil help transform packaged meals into something new and satisfying, supporting human health and performance in space.

## Biological & Physical Sciences Division

- [NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division](https://science.nasa.gov/biological-physical) pioneers scientific discovery and enables exploration by using space environments to conduct investigations not possible on Earth. Studying biological and physical phenomena under extreme conditions allows researchers to advance the fundamental scientific knowledge required to go farther and stay longer in space, while also benefitting life on Earth.

# iZotope’s Nectar 5 brings lyrics-based editing to its vocal production suite

Featured Deal

## iZotope’s Nectar 5 brings lyrics-based editing to its vocal production suite

The vocal plugin suite adds a transcription-driven effects tool, plus a new Serial Compressor and a retuned Vocal Assistant.

iZotope has launched Nectar 5, the latest edition of its vocal production suite. It introduces Moments, an ARA plugin that transcribes a vocal into lyrics in dozens of languages and lets users apply effects to selected words and phrases.

Once the vocal is transcribed, producers can add effects such as reverb throws, doubling and formant shifts to specific words and phrases rather than drawing the automation by hand. iZotope calls it an industry first for ARA-compatible DAWs.

### Two new modules and a retuned Vocal Assistant

Nectar 5 also adds two new modules. Serial Compressor lets you stack up to three compressors at once, to tame peaks while reinforcing the body of your vocal. This keeps the vocal upfront in the mix without over-compressing. It defaults to a FET-into-Opto setup which iZotope says professional engineers love. Vocal stabilizer is an adaptive EQ with two modes: Shape moves a vocal towards a more polished tonal balance, while Cut tames unwanted resonances. It also offers multiband control, with per-band Amount settings and adjustable crossover.

The Vocal Assistant, which builds a vocal chain in a single click, has been retuned to offer a better starting point. A new Custom Flow option gives users more control over the result. They can set the style, register, key, modules, Intensity and Atmosphere, or load an acapella reference for vocal matching.

An Overview page also joins the line-up, offering key controls for Nectar’s core processors with shortcuts to each module for finer adjustments.

Micro Pitch Shift gains a Dimension mode, which spreads and subtly detunes a vocal to add width and weight. Reverb, Delay and Dimension now have a Wet Level control and 3-band filters, plus easy ducking for Reverb and Delay.

The full suite includes 12 full modules and two mini-modules along with Moments, Breath Control, Melodyne Essential, the Mothership channel-strip plugin and more than 400 presets. It also includes 14 component plugins that can be used in other vocal chains.

### Pricing

Nectar 5 is currently on Cyber Sale for £175, down from £239, with the sale running until December 7. Existing iZotope customers can see crossgrade and upgrade pricing by logging in to the iZotope website.

For more information, or to purchase Nectar 5 visit iZotope.com .

items.body:
# Spuren des Einschlags: Hera entdeckt riesigen Krater auf Dimorphos - Spektrum der Wissenschaft

## Spuren des Einschlags: Hera entdeckt riesigen Krater auf Dimorphos

Startseite Astronomie Aktuelle Seite: Spuren des Einschlags: Hera entdeckt riesigen Krater auf Dimorphos © ESA / Hera reveals stadium-sized asteroid crater from spacecraft impact (Ausschnitt) Durch den gezielten Beschuss mit der NASA-Raumsonde DART am 26. September 2026 entstand ein im Vergleich zum 151 Meter großen Asteroiden Dimorphos (kleineres Objekt oben links) riesiger Krater, der etwa ein Drittel bis zur Hälfte der getroffenen Hemisphäre einnimmt. Dadurch wurden die Form und die Bahn des Himmelskörpers beträchtlich verändert. Vor etwas mehr als vier Jahren, am 26. September 2022, schlug die NASA-Raumsonde DART , der Double Asteroid Redirection Test, gezielt mit rund sechs Kilometern pro Sekunde wie ein Projektil auf Dimorphos ein. Dieser ist der kleinere Begleiter des Asteroiden Didymos; gemeinsam bilden sie ein gravitativ gebundenes System. Beim Impakt wurden große Mengen an Felsbrocken und Staub aus dem nur 151 Meter großen Asteroidenmond herausgeschleudert. Sie bildeten einen Schweif, der auch von der Erde aus verfolgt werden konnte. Am Abend des 25. November 2026 stellte die Europäische Raumfahrtagentur ESA erstmals Bilder vor, welche die Folgen des Einschlags der rund eine halbe Tonne schweren Sonde zeigen. Auf Dimorphos ist ein im Verhältnis zum Himmelskörper riesiger Einschlagkrater entstanden, der rund ein Drittel bis zur Hälfte der getroffenen Hemisphäre einnimmt (siehe »Dimorphos vor und nach dem Treffer von DART«). Die ESA vergleicht ihn mit der Größe eines Stadions. © NASA/Johns Hopkins APL (links); ESA (rechts) / Hera reveals stadium-sized asteroid crater from spacecraft impact (Ausschnitt) Dimorphos vor und nach dem Treffer von DART | Mehr als vier Jahre liegen zwischen dem Bild der NASA-Raumsonde DART (links) vom 26. September 2022 und dem Bild der europäischen Sonde Hera von Mitte November 2026 (rechts). Auf dem Mond Dimorphos (kleineres Objekt links vom Hauptkörper Didymos) entstand durch den gezielten Einschlag der Raumsonde DART ein im Verhältnis zum 151 Meter großen Dimorphos riesiger Krater, der die Form des Himmelskörpers drastisch veränderte. In der Mitte des Kraters lässt sich auch eine zigarrenförmige Zentralerhebung erkennen. Vor den Aufnahmen der Raumsonde Hera war unklar , welche Folgen der Einschlag von DART auf Dimorphos hatte. Die Bandbreite der Vermutungen erstreckte sich von kaum sichtbar bis zu einem riesigen Loch, wobei Letzteres eindrucksvoll bestätigt wurde. Beim Aufprall wurde DART innerhalb von Sekundenbruchteilen vollständig zerstört. Lediglich eine zuvor ausgesetzte Subsonde von der Größe eines Schuhkartons lieferte Aufnahmen des Einschlags, allerdings aus einer Perspektive, von der aus die Einschlagnarbe nicht sichtbar war. Weite Aufnahmen von Hera zeigen zudem, dass die Region um den Doppelasteroiden Didymos/Dimorphos für Raumsonden sehr gefährlich ist, denn Hunderte von Felsbrocken von bis zu mehreren Metern Durchmesser treiben sich im Umfeld der beiden Himmelskörper herum (siehe »Gefährlicher Schwarm«). Sie wurden beim Einschlag von DART nicht ausreichend beschleunigt, um das schwache Schwerefeld von Didymos zu verlassen. Sie zeigen sich auf langbelichteten Aufnahmen. Somit hat Didymos mittlerweile nicht nur einen, sondern Hunderte von Monden. © ESA / Hera reveals stadium-sized asteroid crater from spacecraft impact (Ausschnitt) Gefährlicher Schwarm | Hunderte Felsbrocken unterschiedlicher Größe ziehen durch das Didymos/Dimorphos-System. Ihre Bewegungen sind in dieser zusammengesetzten Aufnahme als punktförmige Spuren zu erkennen. Das Bild vereint elf Langzeitbelichtungen, die mit der Hyperscout-H-Kamera am 6. November aus einer Entfernung von etwa 29,9 Kilometern aufgenommen wurden. Didymos und Dimorphos wurden aus der Darstellung herausgerechnet (große schwarze Flecken in der Bildmitte), damit die umliegenden Gesteinsbrocken besser zur Geltung kommen.

items.title: A Closer Look at Claude’s Mac “Apps”
items.subtitle: Yesterday, Anthropic announced a major new feature for artifacts, now available in beta for Mac and Windows: the ability for users to turn artifact…
items.feedText: Yesterday, Anthropic announced a major new feature for artifacts, now available in beta for Mac and Windows: the ability for users to turn artifacts into “apps” they can install on their computers. From the [company’s blog](https://claude.com/resources/articles/install-as-app): > Starting today, you can use Claude artifacts to create, run, and share desktop apps. The “Install as app” feature is rolling out in beta in Claude for Mac and Windows. > When an artifact is installed as a Mac or Windows app, it gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude. You can share it with others, and it needs your permission before it can interact with your computer. You choose how much to allow.
items.body:
Yesterday, Anthropic announced a major new feature for artifacts, now available in beta for Mac and Windows: the ability for users to turn artifacts into “apps” they can install on their computers. From the [company’s blog](https://claude.com/resources/articles/install-as-app):

> Starting today, you can use Claude artifacts to create, run, and share desktop apps. The “Install as app” feature is rolling out in beta in Claude for Mac and Windows.
> When an artifact is installed as a Mac or Windows app, it gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude. You can share it with others, and it needs your permission before it can interact with your computer. You choose how much to allow.
> Each app can use Claude and your connectors, and it updates automatically when the underlying artifact is edited. This simplifies the process for building and maintaining apps for both knowledge workers and developers. Requests the app makes to Claude count toward your plan’s usage limits.

If you’re an [AppStories](https://www.macstories.net/show/appstories) listener, you know that I’ve long thought it was only a matter of time until one of the big labs figured out how to turn their models’ frontier coding capabilities into a means to disrupt the App Store. This move feels like Anthropic’s first step in that direction.

Before I get into the technical details, let me say this upfront: if I were Apple, I’d be *very* concerned that Anthropic is now shipping a nicely packaged system for users to make whatever app they want and turn Apple’s ecosystem into **Claude’s ecosystem** of tools and mods on their computers.

Now, the way Anthropic made this happen can be debated, but I think the system is based on some clever engineering and savvy lock-in strategy. First, for these apps to work, you need the main Claude app to be installed and logged in with your account. These apps require the main Claude process to be running because every action they perform is actually handled by the Claude app behind the scenes, including permissions such as Full Disk Access. All apps made with Claude (either the ones you make, or the ones shared with you by other people) get installed at ~/Applications/Claude Apps, so they’re indexed by Spotlight and can be pinned to the macOS Dock. In fact, when you first create an app inside a Claude conversation (which can be a regular Claude session – you do not need to use Claude Code for these), there is a cute animation and install flow that puts an app directly in your Dock. It’s not too dissimilar from how the Shortcuts app can add individual shortcuts to your Mac’s Dock.

You can preview and install apps from Claude.

Crucially, these are **not** native apps created with Swift or SwiftUI: they’re HTML apps, wrapped inside an Electron shim, which is entirely managed by Claude’s Chromium process for Electron. It’s somewhat reminiscent of Raycast’s [Glaze](https://www.glaze.app/) product, which uses Vite/React web apps, rendered inside Apple’s [WKWebView](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/webkit/wkwebview), wrapped in a custom Swift shell. (Glaze also added the ability to [integrate native Swift modules](https://www.glaze.app/changelog/0-13-0-0) into their apps; I expect Anthropic to add this too.)

To test out this Claude feature, I wanted to create a disk analyzer utility with a menu bar companion for my Mac. The initial prompt was pure vibe coding:

> make me an artifact that analyzes disk space on my Mac with a stunning native Liquid Glass UI and install it in my dock

A few minutes later, Opus 5.5 made something that worked and installed it in my Dock, but it wasn’t great. So, I kept tweaking it. As Claude was working, I noticed that it kept editing a single index.html file:

How Claude makes “apps”.

When the app was done, I asked Claude Code to explain how the other Claude built the app. Here is the Claude Code explanation of it all:

> Storage Lens isn’t a traditional Mac app. Its 900 KB bundle holds no web code at all, just three pieces:
> A 51 KB Objective-C launcher, linked only against Cocoa and Foundation. It uses Electron’s “app shim” mechanism to find /Applications/Claude.app and load Claude’s copy of the Electron framework.
> An 80 KB notification helper built on UserNotifications. It won’t run unless it was launched by a signed Claude.app.
> An icon.
> What looks like a standalone app with its own Dock icon is really a Claude process in disguise.
> The app itself is a single HTML file, written by hand with no third-party frameworks: no React, no Tailwind, no D3. It’s plain JavaScript, with one state object and render() functions that rebuild the page. Everything visual is hand-made:
> The capacity ring is an SVG drawn with stroke-dasharray tricks.
> The treemap uses a hand-written squarified layout.
> The app icon is drawn on a <canvas> each time the app launches.
> The Liquid Glass look comes entirely from CSS: backdrop-filter, light-dark(), and color-mix(in oklab).
> The sliding toolbar highlight uses an SVG distortion filter whose map is generated pixel by pixel, so it bends the background like a real lens.
> The interesting part is how a web page gets to touch the file system. Storage Lens calls window.claude.use('desktop'), an API that closely mirrors Electron’s own: childProcess.spawn, fs.readdir, shell.trashItem, Menu.setApplicationMenu, app.dock.setBadge. With that, it runs the same command-line tools a power user would:
> df -kP and diskutil for volumes
> du -k -x -d 2 for folder sizes
> mdfind with a kMDItemFSSize query for large files
> It reads their output line by line as they run and caches the results in localStorage. Nothing leaves the Mac.

That pretty much says it all. Liquid Glass is faked with CSS (incredible), everything is designed in HTML (not a surprise, given how much Claude *loves* [pretty HTML artifacts](https://simonwillison.net/2026/May/8/unreasonable-effectiveness-of-html/)), and all code routes through Electron via the main Claude app.

Anyway, back to my Storage Lens app. In a follow-up prompt, I asked:

> menu bar works, segmented control still does not, and these overlapping elements are ugly. do better. follow Apple HIG.

A few minutes later, I ended up with this, which has all the makings of a web app putting on a native macOS trench coat, but which…also works:

Behind the scenes, this app asks Claude to run some Terminal commands to list my files and delete them.

I’ve been using the app on my Mac mini this morning to free up some storage. Since I’d already granted Full Disk Access to Claude, I didn’t have to go through a similar flow with the app again: after all, it’s just an HTML page asking Claude to run some shell commands in the background! I also took one of Anthropic’s official demos for a spin – [Vitals](https://claude.ai/artifact/NSkw2jaPZdkdqkrVfswSGc), their menu bar take on a simplified macOS Activity Monitor.

This also works.

…

items.title: Recent sinking of Russian vessels abroad shows the Russia-Ukraine war has officially gone global
items.subtitle: Ukraine has been executing a series of successful strikes against Russian assets around the world.
items.feedText: Ukrainian forces disabled a Russian cargo vessel off the coast of Finland, and sunk a Russian corvette, the Merkury, along with damaging another cargo vessel, in Libyan waters. These attacks, in the aftermath of Ukraine’s severe damage to the Kerch Strait Bridge in Russian-occupied Crimea, have created hope among Ukraine’s allies. The year 2026 hasn’t advanced Ukraine’s goal of ending the war. A stagnant battlefront, increased Russian aerial attacks and a recalcitrant American president have increased the burden…
items.body:
Ukraine has been executing a series of successful strikes against Russian assets around the world. Ukrainian forces [disabled a Russian cargo vessel](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/world/article-russian-cargo-ship-still-burning-off-finland-after-suspected-ukrainian/) off the coast of Finland, and [sunk a Russian corvette](https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/zelenskyy-confirms-ukrainian-naval-drones-072900157.html), the Merkury, along with damaging another cargo vessel, in Libyan waters.

These attacks, in the aftermath of Ukraine’s severe damage to the [Kerch Strait Bridge](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/17/ukraine-strikes-critical-damage-russia-kerch-bridge-crimea) in Russian-occupied Crimea, have created hope among Ukraine’s allies.

The year 2026 hasn’t advanced Ukraine’s goal of ending the war. A [stagnant battlefront](https://hfu.org/current-situation-in-ukraine-2026/), [increased Russian aerial attacks](https://www.cnn.com/2026/08/09/europe/russia-ukraine-escalation-aerial-strikes-intl-vis) and a [recalcitrant American president](https://apnews.com/article/russia-ukraine-war-trump-putin-diesel-228ccf74b2848c1ff0ac23f038b37512) have increased the burdens on Ukraine’s government and its people.

Russia hasn’t had a good year either. More than [400,000 Russians have been killed in the war](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/09/russians-killed-ukraine-war-leaked-data) — and potentially [as many as 700,000](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/world/europe/russia-ukraine-war-deaths.html).

For Ukraine to have any chance of winning, it must increase the pressure on Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s government. Making Russian assets vulnerable globally is one way to do it.

## The international dimension

Since its outset, the Russia-Ukraine conflict has had an international dimension. Ukraine’s allies, both [prior to](https://www.war.gov/News/Releases/Release/Article/3066864/fact-sheet-on-us-security-assistance-to-ukraine/) and [after](https://www.cfr.org/articles/how-much-us-aid-going-ukraine) Russia’s full-fledged invasion in 2022, rushed supplies to Ukraine in its moment of need.

Providing aid to Ukraine [has continued](https://www.defensenews.com/global/europe/2026/09/25/trump-administration-obligates-307m-for-military-aid-to-ukraine/) for the past four years, [despite disruptions](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2025/02/28/us/trump-news) caused by United States President Donald Trump’s involvement in the negotiation process.

The supplies provided by Ukraine’s allies are critical to its success. While the fighting is conducted by the Ukrainian people and Ukraine has increased [domestic arms production](https://thedefensepost.com/2026/07/03/ukraine-arms-exports/), outside supplies are crucial in a number of areas — notably, [air defence](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/22/zelenskyy-urges-us-to-release-patriot-missiles).

Equally important is the economic aid Ukraine’s allies [have and continue](https://www.kielinstitut.de/media/news/ukraine-aid-eu-support-is-crucial-but-harder-to-access/) to provide the country. Given the size differential between Russia and Ukraine and how hard the war [has hit the Ukrainian economy](https://ces.org.ua/en/tracker-economy-during-the-war/), economic aid allows Ukraine to provide basic services to its citizens.

Initially, Russia did not court outside support to the same extent as Ukraine, as it believed it would achieve a [rapid victory](https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-invasion-ukraine-intelligence-putin/31748594.html) over its adversary. Once the reality of the conflict became clear, Russia turned to the international community for support.

That support has taken many forms. [Iran and North Korea](https://thesoufancenter.org/intelbrief-2024-october-24/) have been among Russia’s top supporters, providing drones and soldiers.

Other countries, most notably China, have provided an [economic lifeline](https://www.dw.com/en/china-russia-economy-trade-sanctions-iran-strait-of-hormuz-technology-oil/a-77193402) to Russia, allowing it access to their markets in an effort to stave off the worst impacts of the economic sanctions Ukraine’s allies have imposed on the Russians.

Countries in [Central Asia](https://jamestown.org/central-asia-and-russia-sanctions/) and the [Middle East](https://www.reuters.com/world/us-allies-press-uae-over-russia-trade-sanctions-2024-05-01/) have also served Russia as important intermediaries for acquiring sanctioned materials.

## Targeting support

In a conflict that is increasingly [defined by attrition](https://doi.org/10.1080/13518046.2026.2714478), it’s been necessary for both Ukraine and Russia to rally their allies. The demands of [industrialized warfare](https://doi.org/10.1017/CHO9781139021203) and the production of necessary armaments means neither country can produce what’s needed on their own.

Because both sides are receiving critical support in this industrialized conflict, the war has [reached an equilibrium](https://www.newsweek.com/map-shows-how-ukraine-war-shifted-since-putin-said-its-coming-to-an-end-12700169). In their current states, neither side is likely to achieve a decisive breakthrough to rapidly end the fighting.

For both Ukraine and Russia, that means targeting their adversary’s international allies is necessary to win the conflict.

The least risky form of targeting enemy support, and among the most important, is [by constructing narratives while delegitimizing those of your opponent](https://doi.org/10.1080/03932729.2024.2327492).

Ukraine has [focused on Russia’s aggression and its violation of international norms and laws](https://www.chathamhouse.org/2022/02/ukraine-debunking-russias-legal-justifications). The focus on international law is particularly important for Ukraine given Russian accusations that [the West has flouted international norms](https://theconversation.com/western-countries-demand-russia-follows-international-law-so-why-dont-they-182659) for decades; Russia uses western association with Ukraine to gain support in the Global South.

Russia has put forward [several narratives](https://doi.org/10.1177/17506352241264436) to justify the war, ranging from defending itself from NATO imperialist expansion to its factually questionable [claims of the Ukrainian state’s genocide against ethnic Russians in Ukraine](https://www.themoscowtimes.com/2025/12/08/russian-prosecutors-accuse-dozens-of-top-ukrainian-officials-of-genocide-in-donbas-a91368).

Russia had some early successes from these narratives, making political gains [in Africa](https://www.cfr.org/backgrounders/russias-growing-footprint-africa) and earning support among [far-right](https://icct.nl/publication/russia-and-far-right-insights-ten-european-countries) European parties.

…

items.body:
[Via Marcin Wichary](https://unsung.aresluna.org/ive-spent-years-on-it-years-on-a-box/), who writes:

> Designer Pablo Stanley created [a really fun interactive exploration](https://composer.pablostanley.com/) of what it takes to create a seemingly simple
> “composer” (industry’s jargon for a more sophisticated input field
> or things like it). [...]
> Also, I am burying the lede: it’s a really enjoyable and
> well-crafted experience — don’t miss the sound and music! — and this unique way of talking about interface details could be
> inspiring in and of itself.
> You can also watch the entire thing [as a video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8q0pwh98qmU) with Stanley
> narrating, but I personally liked the interactive version more.

At first I enjoyed this a lot. I got maybe a quarter of the way through it before I thought it was too long — and then poked around and figured out that I wasn’t even halfway done with it yet. At first, yes, it brings to life just how many details a designer might have to think about. But after a bit it’s just interminable neuroticism. I drew this conclusion before I looked up [where Stanley works](https://www.linkedin.com/in/pablostanley1/), which I would have won a bet on. I wound up skipping over half of it, which makes this a rare exception — I almost never link to anything on DF which I skipped through.

At the point where I began wondering if this whole thing was a prank of some sort, all I could think was: this is why platforms need a HIG; why the HIG needs to be thorough, thoughtful, and good; and why designers ought to follow the platform’s HIG. It takes humility to defer to a standard platform reference, and humility is what is lacking in much of modern UI design in general, and Stanley’s interactive essay in particular.

And is it really industry jargon to call these “composers”? It’s a text box. It needs some buttons. It ought to look good. Its functionality ought to be obvious. It shouldn’t be needlessly distracting. Get to work. Build that. Move on. If you call these “composers” you might be in a segment of the industry where the life of a *designer* is so abstract and proudly navel-gazing that you don’t just lose the forest for the trees, but you lose the trees for endless rumination about the texture of bark. Real designers stay focused on helping users get through a delightful forest.

[★](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/25/the-life-of-a-composer)

items.title: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
items.subtitle: Data centers are fueling a natural-gas surge: Natural gas has essentially become America's default electricity solution to meet rising demand, incl…
items.feedText: Nearly half the capacity of new proposals in the country's largest grid came from gas plants. Big tech's emissions are climbing fast: Meta's greenhouse-gas emissions jumped 45% in a single year — outpacing Google, Amazon, and Microsoft — and the company is quietly reconsidering its 2030 net-zero commitment. Companies are building their own power plants: Unable to wait for grid connections, data center developers have proposed over 100 off-grid gas facilities since early 2025, with combined capacity more than dou…
items.body:
In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a [feature story](https://www.technologyreview.com/2025/05/20/1116272/ai-natural-gas-data-centers-energy-power-plants/) describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.

Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence.

Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to [10](https://www.eenews.net/articles/meta-plans-7-new-gas-plants-to-power-massive-louisiana-data-center/). And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own [off-grid gas power plants](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/24/1149622/data-centers-natural-gas/). How did we get here?

If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today.

But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator [announced](https://insidelines.pjm.com/over-700-new-generation-projects-accepted-into-first-cycle-of-reformed-interconnection-process/) that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants.

If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an [analysis by Kevin Kircher](https://kevinjkircher.com/what-energy-infrastructure-are-people-trying-to-build/), an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.

This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released [2026 Sustainability Report](https://sustainability.atmeta.com/blog/2026/11/19/meta-launches-2026-sustainability-report/). That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google ([18%](https://www.axios.com/2026/06/30/google-ai-boom-emissions-power-use)), Amazon ([16%](https://techcrunch.com/2026/07/02/a-warning-sign-about-ais-real-cost-courtesy-of-google-and-amazon/)), and Microsoft ([25%](https://www.esgdive.com/news/microsofts-data-center-expansion-drove-25-emissions-spike-2025-environmental-sustainability-report/825082/)). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there.

And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation.

This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead.

It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source.

But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025.

There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example. I’ve also written before about [demand flexibility](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/06/03/1138350/virtual-power-plants-data-centers/)—efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high.

Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom.

*This article is from The Spark,* MIT Technology Review *’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday,* *[sign up here](https://forms.technologyreview.com/newsletters/climate-energy-the-spark/).*

items.title: Liebe in Zeiten der Rackets
items.subtitle: Skrupelloses Machtstreben und grotesker US-Alltagswahnsinn bestimmen seit jeher die Welt von GTA.
items.feedText: In der langen Wartezeit auf den neuesten Teil hat die Wirklichkeit die Satire der Spiele in beiderlei Hinsicht längst eingeholt. GTA 6 reagiert darauf, indem es seiner zynischen Weltsicht eine Liebesgeschichte entgegensetzt.
items.body:
# Liebe in Zeiten der Rackets

## Liebe in Zeiten der Rackets

Skrupelloses Machtstreben und grotesker US-Alltagswahnsinn bestimmen seit jeher die Welt von GTA. In der langen Wartezeit auf den neuesten Teil hat die Wirklichkeit die Satire der Spiele in beiderlei Hinsicht längst eingeholt. GTA 6 reagiert darauf, indem es seiner zynischen Weltsicht eine Liebesgeschichte entgegensetzt.

„We got x before GTA 6“ – diese Formel hatte sich in den vergangenen Jahren als eines der populärsten Memes des Internets etabliert. Was auch immer sich an Unwahrscheinlichem in der Welt ereignete, es wurde zum nächsten Meilenstein des schier endlosen Wartens auf den neuesten Teil der erfolgreichen Videospielereihe. Wir hatten eine globale Pandemie vor Grand Theft Auto VI , zwei Trump-Präsidentschaften, Kriege in Europa und im Nahen Osten. Irgendwann schien es dann nur noch eine Frage der Zeit, bis auch der Dritte Weltkrieg oder die KI-Apokalypse auf dieser Liste landen würden: Würde die reale Welt untergehen, noch bevor wir endlich in die virtuelle flüchten durften? Wenn nicht, dann musste GTA 6 aber bitte schön mehr sein als ein Videospiel; es musste uns erlösen, zumindest vorübergehend, von den Zumutungen unserer polykrisengebeutelten Gegenwart.

Seit dem 19. November, 13 Jahre nach dem Erscheinen des Vorgängers, haben wir GTA 6; die Welt steht noch, und: Gemessen an den Verkaufsrekorden (erfolgreichster Verkaufsstart eines Unterhaltungsprodukts) und den euphorischen Kritiken (99 von 100 Punkten bei den Fachkritikern) wird das Spiel dem Hype tatsächlich gerecht. Die Memes und Schlagzeilen, die überlasteten Download-Server und auffällig vielen Krankmeldungen zum Release: Für ein langes Wochenende hat GTA 6 eine Erfahrung popkultureller Gleichzeitigkeit hergestellt, wie es sie in Zeiten algorithmisch fragmentierter Medienöffentlichkeiten kaum noch gibt. Und das Spiel selbst? Keine Revolution des Mediums, sehr wohl aber seine vorläufige Vollendung. Die Entwickler von Rockstar Games trumpfen mit einer Spielwelt von beispielloser Detailfülle und atmosphärischer Dichte auf, mit technischer Brillanz und einer Überfülle spielerischer Möglichkeiten. Allein die Open World – die künftig auch im Online-Modus spielbar sein dürfte – ist groß genug, um sich darin für die Dauer der nächsten ein, zwei Weltkrisen zu verlieren.

## Die Rackets sind los

Seit dem Debüt der Reihe 1997 folgt die Welt der GTA-Spiele einer Logik, die der Philosoph Max Horkheimer Anfang der 1940er-Jahre im US-Exil auf den Begriff des „Rackets“ brachte. Ursprünglich eine Slangbezeichnung für organisierte Kriminalität, insbesondere für Schutzgelderpressung, wurde der Begriff von Denkern der Frankfurter Schule auf die Herrschaftsverhältnisse der Gesellschaft im Allgemeinen übertragen. Horkheimer wollte damit den marxistischen Klassenbegriff erweitern: Der Kampf um Macht und Einfluss verläuft nicht ausschließlich entlang von Klassengrenzen, sondern auch zwischen bandenartig organisierten Interessengruppen, die Schutz und Privilegien gewähren gegen Loyalität und Gehorsam.

Bei GTA funktioniert alles nach diesem Racket-Prinzip: die zahlreichen Verbrecherbanden natürlich, aber auch Unternehmen, Polizei und Politik. Typisch für die Reihe ist außerdem, dass der Spieler selbst in die Rolle eines Racketeers schlüpft: Man beginnt meist als Kleinganove, knackt Autos oder treibt Schulden ein, erledigt die Drecksarbeit für immer mächtigere Gangsterbosse und arbeitet sich hoch in der kriminellen Hierarchie.

Das zweite Markenzeichen der Reihe ist ihre beißende Satire auf die amerikanische Gesellschaft: Die fiktiven Radiosender und grotesk überzeichneten Figuren nehmen Waffenwahn und Starkult, Pornografisierung und religiösen Fanatismus aufs Korn. Während der kriminelle Aufstieg in den frühen Spielen noch eher lustvoll zelebriert wurde, rechneten die späteren mit dem amerikanischen Traum ab.

Damit stand die Spielereihe zuletzt vor einem seit Trumps erstem Wahlsieg 2016 vielfach diagnostizierten Dilemma der politischen Satire: Die Wirklichkeit hat die Satire längst eingeholt. Bei GTA gilt das gleich in zweifacher Hinsicht: Nicht nur wirken die vulgären, moralisch enthemmten Charaktere angesichts der realen amerikanischen Politakteure und ihrer Entourage aus alternden Rockstars und exzentrischen Tech-Milliardären kaum noch überzeichnet. Auch die Racket-Logik hat sich längst in Washington breitgemacht, weshalb Horkheimers nie vollendeter Theorieansatz ausgerechnet seit Trumps Präsidentschaft wieder verstärkt Beachtung findet. Das Weiße Haus wird dieser Tage wie ein privates Firmenimperium geführt, in dem familiäre und geschäftliche Interessen, persönliche Loyalitäten und politischer Einfluss auf geradezu mafiöse Weise ineinandergreifen.

So boten die 13 Jahre seit dem letzten Teil unzählige Szenen jener GTA-haften Mischung aus Absurdität und Brutalität: den QAnon-Schamanen , der mit Büffelhörnern das Kapitol stürmte, Elon Musk, der auf der Bühne eine Kettensäge schwang, oder ICE-Beamte, die wie marodierende Banden durch die Straßen von Minneapolis zogen. Donald Trump selbst wirkt ohnehin wie aus einem GTA-Spiel entsprungen. Tatsächlich tauchte in gleich mehreren frühen Teilen mit dem skrupellosen Medien- und Immobilienmogul „Donald Love“ eine Trump-Karikatur auf.

## Liebe statt Satire

GTA 6 versucht nun nicht, die neue amerikanische Wirklichkeit durch immer schrillere Überzeichnungen zu überbieten. Ein Glück, denn es gibt heute kaum etwas Langweiligeres als Trump-Parodien. An satirischen Seitenhieben mangelt es freilich auch diesmal nicht – sie gelten nun auch der Influencer-Kultur und dem Kulturkampf –, doch sind sie ein Stück weit an die Peripherie gerückt.

Den erzählerischen Kern bildet diesmal eine überraschend einfühlsame Liebesgeschichte um Jason und Lucia, ein Ganovenpaar nach dem Vorbild von Bonnie und Clyde, das im fiktiven US-Bundesstaat Leonida nach einem missglückten Coup immer tiefer in eine weitgespannte Verschwörung gerät. Die beiden sind selbstverständlich keine Unschuldslämmer. Sie rauben, betrügen und töten, wie es sich für GTA-Protagonisten gehört, sind dabei jedoch immer wieder den Machenschaften mächtigerer Gangster ausgeliefert. Ihr eigentliches Ziel ist indes nicht der Aufstieg in der Unterwelt, sondern der Ausstieg daraus – ein Stück Normalität, familiäres Glück.

Das führt zu Missionen, wie man sie aus der Reihe bislang nicht kennt und die nicht bei allen Spielern auf Begeisterung stoßen. Während Lucia noch im Gefängnis sitzt, kann Jason das Haus auf Vordermann bringen, Blumen und Lebensmittel für ihre Rückkehr besorgen. Später gilt es, die Bewährungsauflagen einzuhalten, um das Sorgerecht für Lucias kleinen Sohn nicht zu gefährden, oder beim Versuch, ein gemeinsames Bankkonto zu eröffnen, nicht an der miserablen Bonität der beiden zu scheitern.
