items.title: Wie Wespen einander am Gesicht erkennen
items.subtitle: Ähnlich wie wir Menschen besitzen Wespen spezialisierte Neuronen, mit denen sie sich die Gesichter ihrer Artgenossen merken.
items.feedText: Unser menschliches Gehirn ist darauf spezialisiert, Gesichter zu erkennen. Das geht so weit, dass wir sogar dazu neigen, Gesichter in unbelebte Objekte wie Steckdosen, Autos oder Wolken hineinzuinterpretieren. Frühere Studien haben bereits gezeigt, dass spezielle Nervenzellen in unserem Gehirn, die sogenannten Gesichtszellen , detaillierte Merkmale von Gesichtern kodieren und uns damit ermöglichen, uns das Aussehen tausender Menschen zu merken . Doch auch soziale Insekten sind teils erstaunlich gut darin, ihre Artgenossen am Gesicht zu erkennen. „Ähnlich wie Primaten haben weibliche nordamerikanische Papierwespen (Polistes fuscates) die Fähigkeit zur individuellen Gesichtserkennung entwickelt, die sie nutzen, um Kooperationen und Konflikte innerhalb ihrer Gemeinschaften zu regeln“, berichtet ein Team um Christopher Jernigan von der Cornell University in New York. Unter anderem merken sich die Wespen, wer welche Position in der sozialen Hierarchie einnimmt.
items.body:
# Wie Wespen einander am Gesicht erkennen

Unser menschliches Gehirn ist darauf spezialisiert, Gesichter zu erkennen. Das geht so weit, dass wir sogar dazu neigen, Gesichter in unbelebte Objekte wie Steckdosen, Autos oder Wolken hineinzuinterpretieren. Frühere Studien haben bereits gezeigt, dass spezielle Nervenzellen in unserem Gehirn, die sogenannten Gesichtszellen , detaillierte Merkmale von Gesichtern kodieren und uns damit ermöglichen, uns das Aussehen tausender Menschen zu merken .

## Kleines Hirn, komplexes Sozialleben

Doch auch soziale Insekten sind teils erstaunlich gut darin, ihre Artgenossen am Gesicht zu erkennen. „Ähnlich wie Primaten haben weibliche nordamerikanische Papierwespen (Polistes fuscates) die Fähigkeit zur individuellen Gesichtserkennung entwickelt, die sie nutzen, um Kooperationen und Konflikte innerhalb ihrer Gemeinschaften zu regeln“, berichtet ein Team um Christopher Jernigan von der Cornell University in New York.

Unter anderem merken sich die Wespen, wer welche Position in der sozialen Hierarchie einnimmt. Das gilt sogar, wenn sie als unbeteiligte Zuschauerinnen Kämpfe zwischen Nestgenossinnen beobachten. „Bei einer erneuten Begegnung behandeln sie die Siegerin dieses Kampfes anders als die Verliererin“, sagt Jernigan. „Trotz ihrer kleinen Gehirne und ihres relativ einfachen Sehvermögens führen sie ein wirklich komplexes soziales Leben, das sich um diese spezielle Fähigkeit dreht, einander zu erkennen.“

## Spezialisierte Nervenzellen

Gemeinsam mit seinen Kollegen hat Jernigan nun erforscht, wie die Gesichtserkennung im Wespenhirn funktioniert. Dazu fingen sie wildlebende Wespen ein, machten sie durch Kälte weitgehend bewegungsunfähig, fixierten sie dann mit Wachs und platzierten Elektroden in ihrem Gehirn. Anschließend präsentierten die Forschenden den Tieren verschiedene Bilder als Stimuli, darunter Gesichter und seitliche Körperaufnahmen von Artgenossen, geometrische Formen sowie Aufnahmen von anderen Insekten, Blumen und Autos.

„Wir haben dabei eine lokalisierte Population von Neuronen gefunden, die analog zu den menschlichen Gesichtszellen sind und die wir als ‚Wespenzellen‘ bezeichnen“, berichtet das Forschungsteam. „Diese Neuronen feuern selektiv bei Bildern von Wespen, die deren Kopf von vorne zeigen.“ Weitere Versuche mit bearbeiteten Wespengesichtern in schwarz-weiß oder Farbe enthüllten, dass manche Nervenzellen im Wespenhirn auf Formmerkmale und Kontraste spezialisiert sind, während andere auf unterschiedliche Farbverteilungen reagieren.

## Parallelen zur menschlichen Gesichtserkennung

Obwohl das Gehirn der Wespen wesentlich weniger komplex aufgebaut ist als unseres, haben die sozialen Insekten offenbar evolutionär unabhängig einen ähnlichen Mechanismus zur Gesichtserkennung entwickelt. Die Forschenden betonen jedoch, dass die Wespenzellen unseren Gesichtszellen zwar ähneln, aber nicht mit ihnen gleichzusetzen sind. „Sie stellen eine einzigartige Lösung für ein ähnliches Problem dar“, erklären Jernigan und seine Kollegen.

Dennoch hoffen die Forschenden, dass die Einblicke ins Wespenhirn auch neue Erkenntnisse über die menschliche Gesichtserkennung ermöglichen. Gerade durch den einfacheren Aufbau könnten sich Grundprinzipien der visuellen Verarbeitung, die womöglich auch für den Menschen gelten, bei den Wespen besser identifizieren lassen. „Wenn wir die Verbindungen zwischen den Schaltkreisen sowie die Rolle von Erfahrungen bei der Entstehung der Identitätserkennung besser verstehen, kann uns das dabei helfen, unser eigenes Gehirn besser zu verstehen“, sagt Jernigan.

Quelle: Christopher Jernigan (Cornell University, Ithaca, New York, USA) et al., Cell, doi: 10.1016/j.cell.2026.10.052

items.feedText: # Abolish Lock Poisoning - Armin Ronacher 's Thoughts and Writings blog archive projects talks about Abolish Lock Poisoning written on November 25, 2026 Rust has a curious feature that I don’t think the language would land today, if it was not there for a long time: mutex poisoning. When some Rust code panics while holding a std::sync::Mutex , the mutex is poisoned . That means that any further call to lock() returns a PoisonError . The motivation for this feature is that an object might have some internal invariants that need to be upheld and panicking in the wrong moment might invalidate reasonable at and leave an object behind in a broken state. Personally I absolutely hate this feature as it has bitten me so many times and I cannot once remember it helping me. The libs team is discussing making the non-poisoning locks the default in the next edition but entirely expectedly it has caused quite a few people to jump to the defence of the feature.
items.body:
# Abolish Lock Poisoning

- Armin Ronacher 's Thoughts and Writings blog archive projects talks about Abolish Lock Poisoning written on November 25, 2026 Rust has a curious feature that I don’t think the language would land today, if it was not there for a long time: mutex poisoning. When some Rust code panics while holding a std::sync::Mutex , the mutex is poisoned . That means that any further call to lock() returns a PoisonError . The motivation for this feature is that an object might have some internal invariants that need to be upheld and panicking in the wrong moment might invalidate reasonable at and leave an object behind in a broken state. Personally I absolutely hate this feature as it has bitten me so many times and I cannot once remember it helping me. The libs team is discussing making the non-poisoning locks the default in the next edition but entirely expectedly it has caused quite a few people to jump to the defence of the feature. In this post I want to make my personal case why poisoned locks should either be entirely removed or be made the exception. Primarily this is because I have yet to come across code in the wild that handles a poisoned lock correctly. On the other hand I have come across enough code that mishandles it and as a result behaves worse than a parking_lot lock would which does not support poisoning. Josh Triplett put it quite strongly in a hackernews comment: “In the entire history of the standard library, we have never once seen a single report of anyone attempting to recover from poison.” When a panic happens with a lock held, there are two reasonable reactions: shut the process down, or carry on and ignore the flag. With panic = "abort" you get the former and poisoning never comes up. From all the evidence I have seen, with unwinding, the idiomatic lock().unwrap() picks the worst option of all. That’s because it neither stops the process nor lets it continue as it will turn every further lock into a panic with sometimes disastrous effects. But that is not the only issue with the system today. So here I want to share some of the issues and with some references to real world code of how people got bitten. The Error Holds the Lock One subtle aspect to the poisoning is that the PoisonError needs to hold the guard. That’s because in order to ignore the poison flag, you need to fetch the guard from the error object. Holding on to the error means holding on to the lock! That can cause common code that does error wrapping / error conversions into a deadlock hazard. The innocent looking m.lock()? in a function returning Box<dyn Error> or similar keeps the mutex locked for as long as the error lives ( #159930 ). This can also happen with if let. For instance in cc-switch you can see that they had a test hung because a if let Ok(..) = lock() { .. } else { .. } fallback locked the same mutex again while the unnamed PoisonError from the condition still owned the guard. PC-AI had the same bug in a match arm. Another case can be found in ox-embed-server . Panic To Outage Deviously poisoning does not fail fast and done wrong, it fails forever. The original panic happens once, on one thread, often somewhere unrelated from future failures. Every later lock().unwrap() on that lock now however panics as well, and because so much Rust code survives panics (thread pools, request handlers, tokio tasks, FFI boundaries), the process stays up and becomes useless: In RLS a failed cargo build panicked with ENV_LOCK held which made any subsequent runs impossible .
- Mozilla’s application-services saw PoisonError rise to rank 5 in crash stats and moved to parking_lot after they concluded they did not benefit of poisoning handling.
- A Neon safekeeper on staging failed every timeline lookup after a panic with a global lock held, and the original panic could not even be found in the logs.
While not live services, test suites show the same general issue. One failing test poisons a shared static and every test after it fails with PoisonError . This problem showed up for cargo , deno , polars and rustc itself.

## Attempt At Recovery

If you recover with into_inner() , the flag stays set and every later access takes the recovery path again. And remember that for the first nine years of Rust after the poisoning feature landed, you could not even clear it as clear_poison arrived only in 1.77. Not clearing the flag means that potentially expensive side effects will happen from that point onwards:

goose-in-a-pond rebuilt its decoder state on every transcription after a single panic, librefang logged the same warning on every access, and a pool threw its model away on every return.

## Nobody Relies on It, Not Even std

So who is handling poisonings? I’m really not sure, definitely not the standard library. Every place where the standard library’s own code ignores it. Standard I/O has done so since March 2015 , two months before 1.0, because “any poison must have been the result of user code which the lock isn’t protecting”. A common issue with a lot of poisoning errors that never had anything to do with the mutex that was held.

Same with the panic output capture , the backtrace lock and the WASI environment lock . They all do the same and unsurprisingly there is an open PR to move std’s internal mutexes to nonpoison .

And I would argue the ecosystem has largely come to the same conclusion. Tokio’s own locks don’t poison. Internally it wraps the std one in an adapter that removes poison . When it landed Carl Lerche remarked “ I rather pretend lock poisoning isn’t a thing .” In one case Eliza Weisman needed into_inner to unlink a waiter during drop, or “we’ll leave the list with a potentially dangling pointer”. I want to point to this in particular because this is a case where poisoning stood in the way of memory safety which is commonly argued as a reason you want poisoning.

Wasmtime, crossbeam-channel, tracing-subscriber always ignores lock poisoning. rust-analyzer switched to parking_lot after cancellation poisoned its solver like RLS did before. The parking_lot maintainer described it as an anti-feature that hurts usability and reliability to which I strongly concur.

## Why Only Mutex?

Another aspect here is why this is done on Mutex but not on RefCell . Surely if the case for poisoning is that some code temporarily breaks an invariant, panics, and someone else observes the broken state, then this should apply to more cases.

Take the usual example that argues in favor of poisoning and replace Mutex with RefCell , and you have exactly the same problem . Threads are not needed at all and this is not hypothetical either as tokio catches every task panic. Paired with a LocalSet the panic comes back as a JoinError , the next borrow() succeeds and reads a null pointer exactly like the mutex example from the issue.

…

Its goal is to develop formal methods to verify properties of capability machines, in particular involving non-monotonicity, and to prove end-to-end results in the presence of unknown code. items.body:
# From formal verification to bug-finding in CHERIoT

The Cerise project 1 was started almost 10 years ago at Aarhus University. Its goal is to develop formal methods to verify properties of capability machines, in particular involving non-monotonicity, and to prove end-to-end results in the presence of unknown code. Cerise has been extended to model different aspects of capability machines, and has involved work by and collaborations with several other universities, including Dominique Devriese’s research group at KU Leuven, and the universities of Cambridge and Edinburgh.

Cerise started as pen-and-paper proofs about idealised machines and focused initially on reasoning about control-flow integrity of encapsulation for stack-based calling conventions, but over time our research group has scaled up the approach along three dimensions. First, we made our proofs foundational: Cerise now builds on the Iris separation logic framework inside the Rocq theorem prover, which has been critical to ensure correctness despite the growing intricacy of our proofs. Second, we have investigated how to reason about a wider range of properties, e.g., involving MMIO and attestation. Third, we made Cerise work with an instruction set closer to the CHERIoT Sail model, and verified programs using those instructions.

When I started my PhD, CHERIoT had just been announced. I seized the opportunity to apply the verification techniques of Cerise to the CHERIoT switcher, for example to check that it isolates compartments and enforces no-capture. To that end, we started a sub-project of Cerise, which we call Griotte 2 .

As part of our verification effort in this Griotte project, we uncovered two bugs in the CHERIoT switcher: (1) the ability for a malicious (or buggy) scheduler to resuscitate an exited thread in a deprecated state, thereby getting access to a capability that it should not be able to have access to anymore, and (2) the ability for a malicious caller to leverage the stack high watermark register to trigger a fault in the switcher, thereby getting access to the callee’s stack frame and thus private data.

## Reasoning about unknown code

The CHERI/CHERIoT threat model includes interactions with unknown compartments containing arbitrary code, which can be buggy or malicious, and which can share objects in memory. Reasoning about arbitrary code is hard, because it requires characterising all the possible behaviours of that code. The challenge is that when trying to characterise what an unknown compartment can affect, we have to account not only for what it is passed directly (if an unknown compartment is physically passed a write capability to a region of memory, then it is behaviourally passed the ability to overwrite that region of memory), but also what it is passed indirectly—and this involves not only recursive access (if an unknown compartment is physically passed a read capability to a region of memory, then it is behaviourally passed the ability to acquire whatever ability is given by the capabilities in that region of memory), but also access through non-monotonic domain transitions (if an unknown compartment is physically passed a sealed entry point capability to a “counter” compartment’s incr function, then it is behaviourally passed the ability to affect the counter—but only by incrementing it). A unique feature of Cerise is the ability to reason also about the latter part of the challenge.

What makes it difficult to design such a characterisation is that it should at the same time be precise enough, and simple enough to verify the programs that we care about. At a very high level, Griotte defines a language to succinctly describe what is affected—and to state that something is not affected. The kind of properties that we want to describe are not only memory safety properties (if I share a buffer to the caller, then I have the guarantee that it cannot access the global data that I never shared), but also no-capture properties (if I share a buffer to the caller with its global permission stripped, then I have the guarantee that it cannot preserve a copy across calls), and many others (including secrecy, etc.).

## Separation logic and logical relations

Technically, we developed a reasoning system in two parts. First, we defined (and proved sound) a separation logic that allows us to verify known code line by line, showing that it satisfies expected pre- and post-conditions, and that it preserves the expected invariants. We used this both on the code of the switcher, and on the code of specific compartments of interest, for example a key-value store 3 . We designed this separation logic so it is reusable, and we expect that other such compartments of interest could be verified with it.

Second, we defined a logical relation in separation logic, which is effectively an over-approximation of the effect of unknown code that can be used by the separation logic to reason about a jump to unknown code (through the switcher) in one single step. As such, it works like a universal contract 4 for CHERIoT. Crucially, the frame rule of separation logic tells us that if we can establish that the resources (both in an informal sense, and in the technical sense of separation logic) of the caller are disjoint from those of the logical relation, then they will be preserved by the call.

For example, if calling unknown code with a capability to a shared buffer, while keeping some private data, the logical relation requires that the unknown code is only passed capabilities that are safe to share in a technical sense.

We then define a universal contract, stating that if an adversary has only access to safe to share capabilities, it can then execute safely and only produce other safe to share capabilities.

## Verification in the presence of compartments and a trusted switcher

We started by developing a simplified model of CHERIoT and a mini version of the CHERIoT-RTOS. In particular, we modelled the compartmentalisation mechanisms and the cross-compartment call path of the switcher. Our simplified model mirrors the main features of the CHERIoT hardware (including the new deep locality and deep immutability permissions). While our mini switcher doesn’t follow CHERIoT’s switcher instruction-by-instruction, it implements the same steps.

In this model, we proved on a range of small examples that the CHERIoT hardware-software co-design implements the expected memory-safety properties, and that the switcher’s overall design enforces both compartmentalisation and stack safety.

items.body:
Steven Nelson, writing for The New York Post:

> President Trump claimed Monday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang could
> have become a leader in China’s artificial intelligence industry
> if he hadn’t been reinstated to the US firm — telling CNBC in a
> phone interview that the 63-year-old has “got a little blood
> there” despite being born in Taiwan.
> “If we didn’t do this, I could see China coming in and saying to
> Jensen, ‘Hey, how would you like to come to China?’ — He’s got
> a little [Chinese] blood in him. He’s got a little blood there — ‘How would you like to come to China and head up Huawei?’”
> Trump told CNBC in a phone interview, during which he called
> Huang, 63, a “national treasure” despite his affair with an
> alleged Chinese spy.
> “If Jensen was angry enough, if he was treated badly, maybe he
> could do that.”

This was during Trump’s [50-minute phoner on CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/23/trump-nvidia-jensen-huang.html). [As I noted](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/23/nvidia-board-reinstates-jensen-huang) yesterday, on his Truth Social blog, [Trump wrote](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117666141823845971):

> On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a
> Great Patriot and National Treasure.

Think about how perverse Trump’s worldview is that he simultaneously declares that Jensen Huang is a “Great Patriot and National Treasure” *and* that Huang would be justified in moving to China to help the United States’ geopolitical archrival in the AI arms race “if he was treated badly”.

[★](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/24/patriotism-trump-style)

# wheybags' blog: Pokemon Childhood Version: A romhack where Mew is under the truck

- Tom Mason About
- Blog
- Projects
- Contact
## Pokemon Childhood Version: A romhack where Mew is under the truck

TL;DR I made a romhack which implements the most common urban legends from the gen 1 Pokemon games.

Catching Mew under the truck

- Spam A to increase catch chance
- Magikarp splash has a 1/256 chance to 1-shot KO
- Talk to Bill 100 times and you can go to his garden
- You can catch all three starters in Bill's garden
- You can catch Pikablu in Bill's garden
- You can battle Professor Oak after completing the Pokedex
- ... and of course, Mew is under the truck
The old fashioned way! I did not make the actual getting to the truck any easier. You have to either trade for a Pokemon that knows CUT, to avoid entering the S.S. Anne. Or, you can enter the ship and collect the CUT HM as usual, then backtrack to a trainer on the ship that you have not already defeated, battle them, and let them win. This will teleport you back to the nearest Pokecentre without triggering the S.S. Anne to leave.

### Download

I don't want to host the rom directly because Nintendo will eviscerate me. What I have below is a patching tool: select an original, unmodified ROM file that you ripped from your personal copy you've had since you were twelve, and it will patch it, and save the modified version. Under no circumstances should you use a ROM file ripped by anyone else, because that would be very naughty.

Select your Pokemon Red or Blue (USA, Europe) ROM to patch:

Source code available on github . Thanks to the pret/pokered contributors, without whose hard labour this would not have been possible. Also BTW I actually tried the Mew under the truck thing when I was a kid. I was devastated when it didn't work. Satisfaction at long last.

items.title: Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS
items.subtitle: Lobsters Computing Community • Lobsters Community
items.feedText: Firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world. This is especially true in the EU since 2024, when the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) started requiring Apple to let people choose their default browser; millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iOS has doubled. People want to choose the browser on their phone. But there remains an important limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine. This has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone users because many of these are built within our browser engine , Gecko. iPhones and iPads are unique in having this restriction.
items.body:
# Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS | The Mozilla Blog

## Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS

Firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world. This is especially true in the EU since 2024, when the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) started requiring Apple to let people choose their default browser; millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iOS has doubled. People want to choose the browser on their phone.

But there remains an important limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine.

This has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone users because many of these are built within our browser engine , Gecko. iPhones and iPads are unique in having this restriction. On all other major operating systems, including Apple’s macOS, people can access the Gecko-powered version of Firefox.

As a result of the DMA, Apple began allowing alternative browser engines on iOS in the EU. It published a set of conditions that companies like Mozilla must comply with to bring their own browser engine. At the time we said Apple’s rules made it “as painful as possible” for alternatives like Gecko. In the meantime, Japan also introduced new rules requiring alternative browser engines on iOS. Apple applied very similar conditions in Japan to those in the EU.

Nearly three years since Apple introduced these conditions in the EU and almost a year since Japan, not one developer has been able to launch a non-WebKit browser on iOS. The reason is simple: Apple’s conditions remain unworkable. The real test of any rule is whether it delivers the change it was meant to achieve in practice. Compliance on paper alone falls short of that test.

Since the DMA came into effect we’ve been working behind the scenes to test and improve Apple’s conditions so that we can bring Gecko to iOS users. Those efforts have so far largely failed.

One of the conditions requires us not to disclose non-public information related to the project, but here’s an example of what we are up against: to use Gecko, we can’t simply update the Firefox app people already use and love. We’d have to build a whole separate app, a second Firefox. Then we’d have to ask every Firefox user to download it, move their bookmarks, passwords and history across, and manually switch over, step by confusing step.

That’s a lot to ask of people who already made their choice. A significant proportion of people would understandably give up, including many who picked Firefox from the EU’s choice screen.

The conditions Apple imposes, including a level of user friction Apple would never accept for its own apps, mean that the open door feels more like a trap door.

Firefox users on iPhone chose an independent browser. They should get everything that comes with it, including Gecko, the last major browser engine not developed by a big tech company. We’ll keep pushing for a real level playing field, not an opening that drops independent browsers through the floor.

items.body:
# New Gemini setting lets you keep chat history, but turn off AI training [U]

- Apps & Updates
- Gemini
- Gemini app
## New Gemini setting lets you keep chat history, but turn off AI training [U]

Google is rolling out new privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.”

Update 11/24 : This new setting is now widely rolling out. On gemini.google.com, tap the settings gear icon to find a new “Gemini History” item at the very bottom. This opens myactivity.google.com/product/gemini with an On/Off dropdown.

Under “Help train generative AI models with,” you’ll find the new “Chat content including text & attachments” setting. It’s enabled by default.

> Your future chats won’t be used to train generative AI models, unless you provide feedback.

Training on “Audio and Gemini Live videos & screenshares” remains an opt-in preference.

Original 11/16 : Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”

Google is now separating that preference into two new options.

## Top comment by Whispy_Snippet

This is huge. One of the major things Siri-AI users on iPhone like to point out is that while their assistant is a less capable portmanteau of Siri and Gemini, their queries are not used for AI training. Gemini on Android, on the other hand, offers the superior AI platform with the caveat that there is no way to opt out of training and still retain your chat history. Until now. Now users of Gemini on Android get the best of both worlds - the best of Google's AI models powering their AI experiences and their chat history siloed from AI training.

Win win.

The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled:

> “…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers.”

The duration is currently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, users, and the public.

The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.”

> With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.

If Keep Activity is currently off, the two “new settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying users via email.

## More on Gemini app:

- Gemini skills add file support and sharing ahead of Gems deprecation
- Google announces Gemini 4 Hydrogen with ‘significant leaps’ in speed, intelligence

FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.

Check out 9to5Google on YouTube for more news:

items.body:
# I checked Clojure's core with Lean and differential testing and found unreported bugs in HAMT and vector-of - Conao3 Notes

I read Koukyosyumei's article " 著名なRust製OSSをLean 4で形式検証してみたら、めちゃめちゃバグが見つかった話 " (in Japanese; the title means "I formally verified well-known Rust OSS with Lean 4 and found a lot of bugs"). The author ported well-known Rust projects into a form they could prove in Lean 4, and where a proof failed, they found a bug in the original code.

Many people have used Clojure's persistent data structures since around 1.0, so I expected no bugs to remain. Still, I wanted to see whether Lean would find something there too.

hirosassa/lean-verify describes a procedure for modeling a small function in Lean 4 and checking it for all inputs, so I applied it to the part of Clojure's core written in Java.

I modeled integer and bit arithmetic in Lean and searched for counterexamples. I checked the collections with differential testing against the java.util collections, and for Java interop I compared the same call with and without a type hint.

I found 17 bugs that I could not find in Clojure's JIRA or on ask.clojure.org. They include reduce on vector-of , the hash collision node of the HAMT, and calls to functional interfaces without a type hint.

The HAMT itself showed no mismatch in 3 million operations of differential testing, and the vector tree showed none around its boundaries. The bugs sat in separate code outside the trees, and in places where two mechanisms meet, such as = and hashing.

I used Clojure 1.12.7, released on 2026-11-18, and JDK 21. The links to the source point to the clojure-1.12.7 tag.

## How I checked

The lean-verify procedure picks one function and models it as a Lean definition. You write a property that compares it with a naive specification computed at a wider width, and bv_decide searches for a counterexample.

If you model Java's long and int as BitVec 64 and BitVec 32 , the wraparound of addition and multiplication maps onto BitVec operations. So do the rounding of / toward zero and the sign of % .

When Lean found a counterexample, I turned the value into a Clojure input and reproduced it in the original code. I then modeled the fixed code in Lean and proved the same property. Lean can only take small functions that reduce to integer and bit arithmetic, so I checked the large persistent data structures with differential testing.

Each test applies the same random sequence of operations to PersistentHashMap and to java.util.HashMap and compares the results. For the HAMT, the keys mix partial collisions at each 5-bit level with fully identical hashes, and I ran 1,500 operations for each of 2,000 seeds.

For vectors, I compared against ArrayList around 32, 1056, 32800, and 1048608, where the tree gains a level. The operations were conj , pop , assoc , and their transient versions.

I checked whether anyone had reported each bug before. I searched Clojure's JIRA through its REST API and ask.clojure.org through web search and the site's own search, and found no matching report.

## reduce on vector-of never finishes

vector-of is a vector that stores its values in primitive arrays. Clojure implements it in gvec.clj , written in Clojure and separate from PersistentVector . If you drop from one and then reduce it, the call never returns once the vector has 65505 or more elements.

( reduce + ( drop 1 ( into ( vector-of :long ) ( range 65504 )))) ;; => 2145354256 ( reduce + ( drop 1 ( into ( vector-of :long ) ( range 65505 )))) ;; => never returns ( reduce + ( drop 1 ( vec ( range 65505 )))) ;; => 2145419760 The cause is line 79 of gvec.clj , where the seq's reduce computes the start of the next 32-element chunk.

( recur result ( bit-and 0xffe0 ( + aidx 32 ))) The code uses 0xffe0 to clear the low 5 bits and round down to a multiple of 32, but the mask also clears bit 16 and everything above it. With 65505 elements, the last chunk starts at index 65504. After that chunk, the start of the next one should be 65536, but the mask turns it into 0, so reduce goes back to the start and reads the vector again and again.

The 0xffe0 mask has stayed in place since the 2010 commit that added internal-reduce . In Lean, I wrote the property that from a position a that is a multiple of 32, the next chunk starts at a + 32 .

import Std.Tactic.BVDecide def stepImpl (a : BitVec 64 ) : BitVec 64 := 0xffe0 &&& (a + 32 ) def stepFix (a : BitVec 64 ) : BitVec 64 := (~~~ 0x1f ) &&& (a + 32 ) theorem impl_ok (a : BitVec 64 ) (h32 : a &&& 0x1f = 0 ) (hlt : a < 0x7fffffe0 ) : stepImpl a = a + 32 := by unfold stepImpl; bv_decide theorem fix_ok (a : BitVec 64 ) (h32 : a &&& 0x1f = 0 ) (hlt : a < 0x7fffffe0 ) : stepFix a = a + 32 := by unfold stepFix; bv_decide impl_ok fails with the counterexample a = 1073741792 , and #eval stepImpl 65504 returns 0 as well. fix_ok uses (bit-not 0x1f) as the mask, and its proof goes through under the assumption that a is a multiple of 32 below 0x7fffffe0 .

## dissoc on a HAMT collision node hides another key

Clojure's hash-map is a HAMT: it splits the key's hash into 5-bit pieces and uses them to walk down the tree. Keys whose 32-bit hashes are identical share a HashCollisionNode at the bottom of the tree, and the node finds a key among them with = .

HashCollisionNode.without builds the new node with one key removed. It should give the new node its own hash, this.hash , but it passes the parameter hash instead.

return new HashCollisionNode ( null , hash, count - 1 , removePair (array, idx / 2 )); The parameter hash is the hash of the key you pass to dissoc . If you dissoc with a key that is = to the stored key but has a different hash, the node records the wrong hash.

In Clojure, a vector is = to a Java ArrayList with the same elements, but the two hash differently. CLJ-1372 tracks this mismatch.

In the example below, I chose a and b so that both ArrayList keys hash to 1003.

( def a ( java.util.ArrayList. [ 0 42 ])) ( def b ( java.util.ArrayList. [ 1 11 ])) [( hash a) ( hash b) ( hash [ 0 42 ]) ( = a [ 0 42 ])] ;; => [1003 1003 1867155179 true] ( def m3 ( -> ( hash-map a :A b :B ) ( dissoc [ 0 42 ]) ( assoc a :A2 ))) [m3 ( count m3) ( get m3 b)] ;; => [{[1 11] :B, [0 42] :A2} 2 nil] When you print m3 , you can see the key b , but (get m3 b) returns nil . After the dissoc , the node records 1867155179, the hash of [0 42] . The next assoc then concludes that a , with hash 1003, does not collide with the node, and splits the two into separate branches.

A lookup of b follows the branch for 1003 and finds only a there, so it never reaches b . In this example the collision node sits on the first level of the tree, so the key passed to dissoc needs the same low 5 bits as 1003, and 1867155179 has them.

disj on a hash-set has the same bug, while the path through the transient dissoc! does not.

items.title: Security incident on Hex.pm
items.subtitle: Lobsters Computing Community • Lobsters Community
items.feedText: On November 23, 2026, an unauthorized third party exploited a vulnerability in hex.pm that let them run commands on our web servers. We blocked the traffic and deployed a fix within 20 minutes. Shortly afterwards we received a report of this exact vulnerability. We found no evidence of unauthorized package modifications, or database changes, or that the attacker maintained access to our systems. However, because database reads are not logged, we cannot rule out that the attacker accessed data stored in the database, including email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, 2FA secrets, sessions, and audit logs. Because email addresses may have been exposed, be careful with emails that claim to come from Hex.
items.body:
# Security incident on hex.pm | Hex

On November 23, 2026, an unauthorized third party exploited a vulnerability in hex.pm that let them run commands on our web servers. We blocked the traffic and deployed a fix within 20 minutes. Shortly afterwards we received a report of this exact vulnerability.

We found no evidence of unauthorized package modifications, or database changes, or that the attacker maintained access to our systems. However, because database reads are not logged, we cannot rule out that the attacker accessed data stored in the database, including email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, 2FA secrets, sessions, and audit logs.

Because email addresses may have been exposed, be careful with emails that claim to come from Hex. Please double-check that the links they contain lead to hex.pm . Please forward suspicious emails to security@hex.pm .

We checked every file written to package storage during the incident against our database and found nothing unexpected. Reads of private packages in that period came from our own servers and coincide with releases the same organizations published at the time. A read made from a compromised server would look like one of ours, so we can't fully rule one out, and reads of private documentation aren't logged. We will contact affected organizations directly.

The attacker's commands could read the credentials our servers use, so we replaced them: the storage, CDN, email and database credentials, and the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. This logged everyone out of hex.pm and Hex clients. We're building a new registry signing system that supports key rotation, with new Hex client releases in the coming days. Until then, don't trust third-party mirrors and fetch packages only from repo.hex.pm. We already deployed fixes for the vulnerability and are working on further hardening fixes.

### What you should do

- Change your password at hex.pm .
- Reset your 2FA at hex.pm/dashboard/security : under "Authenticator App", choose "Setup New App" and verify a code from the new entry. You get a new secret and new recovery codes, so store the new codes. This works when an organization requires 2FA, where disabling it is refused.
- Update your Hex client when the release with the new signing system is out in the coming days. Until then, use only repo.hex.pm, not mirrors. To update, run mix local.hex --force , and update rebar3 or Gleam if you use them.
### Timeline

All times are in UTC.

November 23, 2026

- 18:16 - 18:29 : The attacker sent 69 malicious requests to hex.pm, six of our web servers were affected. Our error tracker Sentry recorded its first error at 18:16:00 and recorded an error for each request.
- 18:27 : We added a firewall rule to block the attacker's traffic, which took full effect between 18:30 and 18:33.
- 18:30 - 18:31 : All hex.pm servers were replaced with a patched build that rejects these payloads.
- 18:33 - 18:38 : All further requests from the attacking address were denied.
- 18:35 : We began investigating production logs and the database.
- 18:49 : We deactivated the AWS access key the affected servers used, after creating a replacement at 18:47.
- 19:07 : We received an email with a security report that described the same vulnerability.
- 20:21 : Most infrastructure credentials were rotated. The database password followed on November 24.
- 22:58 : We reported a personal data breach to IMY, the Swedish data protection authority.
- 23:05 : We reported the incident to CISA, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which confirmed receipt at 23:43.
- 23:26 : We submitted an early warning to ENISA, the EU Agency for Cybersecurity.
November 24, 2026

- By 10:42 : We had rotated every credential the attacker could have read, including the database password, except the registry signing key and a few low-impact secrets.
- 13:48 : We published CVE-2026-129514 .
### The vulnerability

The vulnerability in Hex.pm is tracked as CVE-2026-129514 .

hex.pm decoded unauthenticated request bodies in Erlang term format with Plug.Crypto.non_executable_binary_to_term/2 which blocks most potentially harmful terms, but allows struct values through. These decoded struct values, when chained together correctly, turned into a remote command execution (RCE). This is the detailed playbook of the attack:

- The entry point. A custom parser in the endpoint handled the application/vnd.hex+erlang content type using Plug.Crypto.non_executable_binary_to_term/2 with [:safe] . Because the endpoint runs this parser before routing and authentication, any unauthenticated POST with that content type reached it on every route.
- Fake structs got through. The decoder rejected functions and new atoms, but it never checked maps. An Elixir struct is just a map with a __struct__ key naming a module. That meant the attacker could send a value the runtime treats as a real struct, with every field set to whatever they chose.
- Converting the structs into an error. The decoded struct became the request's body parameters. Plug.MethodOverride then read body_params["_method"] , which on a struct calls fetch/2 on the struct's module. That function didn't exist, so the request raised an UndefinedFunctionError with the attacker's struct in the stack trace.
- Error reporting runs inspect. Sentry, Bandit's error logging, and the JSON log formatter call inspect on request data and stack-frame arguments. Inspect is a protocol, so for a struct it runs the implementation of the module named in __struct__ , which let the attacker choose which code ran next. They chose Ecto.Query.DynamicExpr .
- The Ecto hop. The Inspect implementation for Ecto.Query.DynamicExpr enumerated the binding field without checking that it was a list. Enumeration is itself a protocol call, so a struct placed in that field is dispatched to another implementation.
- The DBConnection hop. The struct placed in binding was a DBConnection.Stream . Its Enumerable implementation calls DBConnection.reduce/3 , which then calls declare/4 . Encoding the query failed before any connection was checked out, but the error path still ran the stream's :log option. That option was a {module, function, args} tuple taken from the request, and db_connection applied it with the log entry prepended.
- Command execution. An attacker-supplied {module, function, args} tuple that the server runs gives access to functions in loaded libraries and the standard library, which led to OS command execution as the BEAM's user.
While investigating, we found the same class of vulnerability in Ash: its keyset pagination accepted crafted structs in client-supplied cursors, which could lead to command execution or SQL injection. We reported it and the Ash team released a fix in ash 3.38.0 on November 24. It is tracked as CVE-2026-124283 .

items.body:
Abstract: We report on our experience validating S3 Express One Zone, a high-performance Amazon S3 storage class launched in November 2023. We focused on its distributed metadata index, which implements a hierarchical namespace using distributed transactions. We check strong consistency and durability under crashes, network delays, and timeouts. Building on our prior work on lightweight formal methods, we combined executable reference models with property-based testing and stateless model checking. Applying these techniques to a production distributed system required three new techniques: a white-box approach to checking serializability; compositional validation of the data and control planes; and long-running canaries that use reference models to check correctness across deployments. We extended Shuttle, our open-source stateless checker, to support a production async Rust runtime and failure injection, including cancelled operations and timeouts. Our main finding is that this approach is sustainable at engineering scale. After launch, the engineering team took ownership of models and test infrastructure, increasing its share of validation commits from 41% to 84% and independently extending the models for conditional writes, object append, and atomic rename, with little involvement from the formal methods team.

items.body:
Saturday Night Live [ran a skit](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-X9dxL17t1k) for an eldercare service that was simply calling your sister to take care of things. Many people related, because it is actually happening. [For Bloomberg, Lisa Jarvis has the numbers](https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/articles/2026-11-18/snl-sister-skit-about-the-us-eldercare-crisis-is-too-relatable?accessToken=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzb3VyY2UiOiJTdWJzY3JpYmVyR2lmdGVkQXJ0aWNsZSIsImlhdCI6MTc5NTEyMTQ3MiwiZXhwIjoxNzk1NzI2MjcyLCJhcnRpY2xlSWQiOiJUT1A1Q0NLR1pBSk8wMCIsImJjb25uZWN0SWQiOiIzRDhGMEEzMTc2MDc0NUM5OTg4NkFCNzA1NDk2RUNEQSJ9.8Rm4_qRQDNrQl5SG6qxNGsTkbi7DGmEbfQ1N588AByU):

> And the pressure is only mounting as America gets older and sicker. Time devoted to caregiving more than doubled between 2020 and 2025, rising from 9 to 23 hours a week, according to a recent survey of working Americans conducted by the insurance provider Guardian Life. The majority (57%) are caring for elderly relatives. The same survey found women were five times as likely as men to say they’d left the workforce to care for someone, whether that was an elderly parent, a spouse, a young child or a special needs child.

**Tags:** [Bloomberg](https://flowingdata.com/tag/bloomberg/), [eldercare](https://flowingdata.com/tag/eldercare/), [Saturday Night Live](https://flowingdata.com/tag/saturday-night-live/)

items.title: 2035 came early
items.subtitle: Lobsters Computing Community • Lobsters Community
items.feedText: tl;dr trynix.dev boots GUI programs now. Try solitaire , GL gears , xeyes , a voice , the weather over curl , or Firefox . I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software. Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true. Atwood’s Law Any application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript. items.body:
# 2035 came early

> tl;dr trynix.dev boots GUI programs now. Try solitaire , GL gears , xeyes , a voice , the weather over curl , or Firefox .

I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software.

Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true.

> Atwood’s Law Any application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript. — Jeff Atwood, 2009

I highly recommend watching the talk if you have not already seen it, but the short and skinny is a lookback from 2035 and how JavaScript came to be the defacto language for all software.

In Bernhardt’s retelling of events, the date is worked back from 2035, however unsurprisingly, large language models have rapidly sped up the timeline. What was once perceived to be the end-state at 2035 has arrived years earlier and you can witness it unfolding at trynix.dev .

One of the most impressive creations I’ve managed to build leveraging nixpkgs-multiverse is https://trynix.dev .

It still baffles my mind that I can run any Nix package , over 300,000 distinct package versions, straight from my browser. Truly insane capability. I was however a little dismayed at the speed of the QEMU emulation in the browser. It was slow enough that the creation tipped more towards novelty than practicality.

I woke on November 20th and saw Domen Kožar sharing a single message in our TacoSprint Discord channel: unkernel.dev

It was the fast browser Linux experience I had sought to achieve, but with Nix .

> Aside What is unkernel ? It is Linux compiled to WebAssembly, allowing the kernel and system components to run at wasm speed while only user programs are emulated. It was published by Pooya Parsa on November 19th, 2026.

In an AI induced manic frenzy, I adopted the new engine along with a slough of long-wished features almost immediately.

The proof is in the pudding: unkernel delivers remarkable speed improvements over qemu-wasm , 1 1 With a very healthy set of patches applied to make it even faster. especially on first runs where kernel work dominates. The new engine is able to deliver 2x to 32x faster performance depending on the workload. 2 2 The benchmark page tracks both engines over time, measured through the real page and shell.

JavaScript & WebAssembly nirvana.

Amazingly not only does the kernel boot quickly, it also enables networking, full-fledged graphical and audio experiences directly in the browser.

Windows. A program’s Wayland surfaces are composited in the page by wland , and they float over the terminal you started them from.

GL. The VM includes a minimal Mesa build with only the virgl driver, compiled to WebAssembly, rendering through your browser’s WebGL2.

Sound. The VM has an ALSA sound card, and can play audio through your browser.

Network. curl , git clone and pip install work. Each TCP connection goes over one WebSocket to a Wisp relay. 3 3 Thank you to @_pi0_ for adding trynix.dev to his Wisp relay allow-list.

The best joke in Bernhardt’s talk is a browser running inside another browser: the Windows GIMP under Wine, in Chrome, in Firefox. Of course, I had to try it with trynix. 😈

Here is Firefox in trynix , and it loading trynix.dev , and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 4 4 Don’t get too excited: this took over 4 hours. The inner Firefox needed JIT disabled, the middle one ran without GL, and the outer page used a Wisp relay on my laptop since wisp.unkernel.dev cannot reach itself .

Sit and bask in that insanity. That is Firefox, on Linux compiled to WebAssembly, in a Firefox tab, loading the site and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 🤯

2035 came early.

items.body:
# What Schools Still Don’t Teach About Interest Rates and Why It Matters | TeachThought

Most people leave school able to calculate interest on paper. Far fewer leave knowing what interest will do to their lives. That gap is easy to miss because it doesn’t show up on a report card. It shows up years later, in loan papers, credit card statements and savings balances that never seem to grow.

The problem isn’t that schools ignore math. Interest is taught as a formula, and the formula stops at the edge of the worksheet. Students learn how to find an answer but not how to read the numbers that will shape what they borrow, what they save and what they can afford. To close that gap, it helps to look at what gets left out, starting with how the subject is framed in the first place.

### The Gap Between Arithmetic and Everyday Money

### Formulas Without Consequences

A typical lesson on interest gives students a principal, a rate and a time period, then asks them to solve for the total. It’s tidy and it can be graded. It also hides almost everything that matters. Real rates change. Real balances get added to and drawn down. Real people make choices partway through, and those choices change the outcome.

When interest only ever appears as a problem with one right answer, students learn to treat it as a puzzle rather than as a force acting on their money every day.

### Interest Is a Price

The simplest idea missing from many classrooms is also the most useful one. Interest is the price of money over time. When you borrow, you pay that price. When you save, someone pays it to you. Once students see interest as a price, they start asking the questions they would ask about any purchase. Is this a good deal? Can I find it cheaper somewhere else? What happens if I wait?

That shift in thinking matters most when you see how interest builds over long stretches of time.

### How Compounding Actually Feels Over Time

### The Slow Start That Fools People

Compounding means you earn interest on your interest. Most students can repeat that definition. What they rarely get is a feel for how lopsided the results are.

Put $1,000 in an account earning 5% a year and leave it alone. In the first year, you earn $50. Nothing to get excited about. By year 30, the balance has grown to about $4,322, and that single year alone adds more than $200. The growth was always there, but it took decades to become obvious. People who expect fast results often give up during the slow early years, which is exactly when patience pays off most.

A quick shortcut called the rule of 72 makes this easier to grasp. Divide 72 by the interest rate, and you get a rough idea of how many years it takes money to double. At 6%, that’s about 12 years. A tool like the compound interest calculator on the SEC’s Investor.gov site lets students test different rates and time frames and watch the curve bend upward.

### Compounding Runs in Both Directions

The same math that rewards savers punishes borrowers. A credit card charging 24% APR works out to about 2% a month. On a $3,000 balance, that’s roughly $60 in interest in the first month. If you pay $75, only $15 actually goes toward what you owe. The balance barely moves, and the card company is happy to keep it that way.

Students who understand this early tend to treat credit cards very differently. Still, knowing how compounding works is only half the picture. The other half is knowing which rate you’re actually dealing with.

### Why the Rate You See Is Rarely the Rate You Pay

### APR, APY and the Fine Print

Banks and lenders use different terms for a reason. APR, or annual percentage rate, is often used for loans and doesn’t always show the effect of compounding. APY, or annual percentage yield, does. A 12% APR compounded monthly actually costs about 12.68% over a year. The gap looks small until it’s multiplied across a large balance or a long loan.

Few students are ever shown these two terms side by side. As a result, many adults compare offers without realizing they’re comparing different measurements.

### Inflation Eats Quietly

Even a correct rate can mislead you if inflation is ignored. If your savings earn 1% while prices rise 3%, your balance goes up but what it can buy goes down. Economists call the difference the real return. The Consumer Price Index published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics is the standard way to track how fast prices are rising, and checking it against your savings rate is a sobering exercise.

That raises a fair question. If rates matter this much, who decides what they are?

### Where Rates Come From

### The Central Bank’s Role

Rates don’t appear out of nowhere. In the United States, the Federal Reserve sets a target range for the federal funds rate , which is what banks charge each other for overnight loans. That rate ripples outward into mortgages, car loans, credit cards and savings accounts.

### Why Your Rate Moves, or Doesn’t

Some rates follow the Fed closely. Variable credit card rates often rise within weeks of a hike. Others lag behind or barely move at all. Many large banks are slow to raise what they pay savers, even when borrowing costs climb. Knowing this helps people spot when they’re being underpaid and gives them a reason to act. The easiest place to put that knowledge to work is a savings account.

### Savings Accounts as a Practical Classroom

### Watching Interest Work in Real Time

A savings account turns abstract lessons into something you can see each month. Deposits go in, interest gets added and the balance changes without any effort. For a young person, watching even a few dollars of interest arrive can make compounding feel real in a way no textbook can. It also builds a habit, and habits tend to outlast lessons.

Savings accounts carry little risk, too. Deposits at insured banks are protected up to set limits, which makes them a calm place to learn how rates behave before moving on to investments that can lose value.

### Shopping for a Better Rate

Not all savings accounts pay the same. Some traditional accounts pay close to nothing, while online banks and high-yield accounts often pay far more. On a $10,000 balance, the difference between 0.5% and 4% is about $350 a year, earned for doing nothing extra at all. Comparing the best bank savings rates against what your current account pays is one of the quickest ways to learn how much a few percentage points are worth.

This is the habit schools rarely teach: treating your own savings rate as something you can shop for and improve.

### Why the Gap Matters

Each of these missing lessons is small on its own. Together, they decide whether interest works for a person or against them. Someone who understands compounding, reads APY instead of APR, accounts for inflation and checks their savings rate will make dozens of slightly better decisions over a lifetime. Those small edges add up the same way interest does.

# What VP ≠ VNP Means (In 3 Minutes) – Gil

I assume you know about the P vs. NP problem. But what is this wacky thing Anthropic just posted ?

You learned how to take a determinant in your linear algebra class:

The naive way is fine for 3 × 3 matrices, but notice that you need to perform Θ ( n ! ) arithmetic operations here. Exercise for the reader is to find the exact number of operations (hint: start with a recurrence relation).

Luckily, if you paid attention, you will remember there are faster ways to do this for big n × n matrices, like Gaussian elimination. If we stick only to adding and multiplying, we can still find a determinant in polynomial time ( there are better ways, but this is an old, readable method ).

A related problem to the determinant is finding the permanent. It’s like a determinant without any subtraction:

Unlike determinants, there is no known way to compute permanents in polynomial time. Since finding the permanent of a matrix of 0s and 1s is NP-hard (and in fact #P-complete ), it would be pretty important if there were a way.

What the Anthropic proof that VP ≠ VNP means is that there is no way to do this if we are limited to arithmetic circuits of size polynomial in the input-size, which look like this:

This means that for P to equal NP, there must be some trick to computing permanents using AND/OR/NOT on the bits of the input that is better than addition and multiplication. There are many problems where access to Boolean operators is helpful, but it isn’t clear how they would help with the permanent. If you think of a way, go claim your $1 million.

items.feedText: my major advocacy is that lua is a very good general purpose language. this is not an opinion shared by all. lua’s major design goal was extending and embedding into existing programs. I think the simplicity and flexibility in design persued towards the end of that goal extends to make lua a very good language in general. that said, it does its job quite well as an embedding language, and one of its more interesting use cases (and actually, one of its oldest use cases) is as a data or configuration format. lua’s syntax provides many niceties.
items.body:
# lua for data representation - citrons.xyz

## lua for data representation

my major advocacy is that lua is a very good general purpose language. this is not an opinion shared by all. lua’s major design goal was extending and embedding into existing programs. I think the simplicity and flexibility in design persued towards the end of that goal extends to make lua a very good language in general. that said, it does its job quite well as an embedding language, and one of its more interesting use cases (and actually, one of its oldest use cases) is as a data or configuration format.

lua’s syntax provides many niceties. for instance, lua has an infinite family of multiline strings: the most basic one starts with [[ and ends with ]] . however, any amount of equal signs can be put between the two square brackets: print([======[hello, world]======]) . the only way to close a [===[ is with an accompanying ]===] , not with a ]] or a ]==] , or a ]====] .

here is a function that for any string, creates the correct multiline string to represent it:

local function stringize(str) local equal_signs = "" for e in str:gmatch("](=*)]") do if #e >= #equal_signs then equal_signs = e .. "=" end end return ("[%s[%s]%s]"):format(equal_signs, str, equal_signs) end of course, you can just use string.format with %q , but multiline strings usually provide nicer looking and more compact results. these strings are very good for representing lua code as strings in other lua code.

anyway, download this file . if you want to consume massive amounts of memory and possibly crash your computer, run it in cpython. if you want to see “hello, world” printed 5 million times, run it in lua. lua’s parser is designed to handle massive files with stride, which is fairly unique and quite necessary if lua is to be used for this purpose.

design and implementation choices like these come together to suit lua for this purpose. I’ve seen 3 main styles of using lua code to represent data or configuration. I think lua manages to accomodate each of them well, and each have their appropriate use.

## styles of data representation

### JSON style (LON?)

chunks are much like function bodies. they have return values. so, one thing that one can do is just return a big table from a lua program.

return { foo = "bar", list = {1, 2, 3}, rule_of_thirds = true, } if you’re using this style, you can omit the return and then prepend it when you load the lua files. this makes any trailing statements syntactically invalid because the return statement must be the last statement in the block. keep in mind, though, that this does not prevent arbitrary code because function literals can be used instead.

return (function() arbitrary_code() end)() trying to strip out function literals to make this technique safer is fraught and defeats the general elegance of this technique. one can fairly readily use JSON instead.

### INI style

what is often missed about lua is that it’s subtly full of metaprogrammability. for instance, lua globals are just stored in a table, and which table is used can be controlled by the code itself. this table is known as the “environment”. an environment may be passed to load as an argument. the way this can be used is that you can load a chunk with an empty environment and then capture the values it sets as globals.

you can have a file like this:

-- config.lua foo = "bar" list = {1, 2, 3} rule_of_thirds = true then, you can get a table with all the configuration as simply as this:

local config = {} assert(loadfile("config.lua", "t", config))()

### imperative style

lua has a bit of sugar that allows you to shed the parenthesis on function calls to make them look cleaner. an imperative style is a very suitable means to represent data in lua, and it’s very powerful.

path "/path/to/things" config { foo = "bar", list = {1, 2, 3}, rule_of_thirds = true, } lipsum [[ Voluptatibus laudantium et omnis ut debitis. Similique omnis molestias consequuntur. Praesentium corporis omnis nihil et quidem dolore. Veritatis fugiat eaque corporis eligendi officiis praesentium. Libero quo vero temporibus impedit sit inventore assumenda ]] programming in lua provides a real world example of this .

## security considerations

the major problem with using an entire programming language to represent data is that untrusted data can be readily crafted to be malicious. indeed, I would not use this technique for untrusted data. with that in mind, it is possible to solve or mitigate the potential vulnerabilities.

the main technique for sandboxing lua is controlling the environment. when using lua for data representation, an empty enivronment is the most appropriate (or, an environment that only exposes data constructors). this prevents any I/O or access to the larger program’s state. preventing access to all standard library functions is safest. there are a few standard library functions that have consequences you might not expect .

another concern is denial of service. this is trickier to prevent. it’s fairly trivial to construct a lua chunk which does not return ( while true do end ). debug.sethook can mitigate this somewhat. even so, it’s probably possible to construct something that uses excessive amounts of memory. that said, denial of service is significantly less problematic than the vulnerabilities that are completely avoided by depriving the untrusted code of any standard library functions.

finally, make sure to reject lua bytecode . untrusted lua bytecode is not safe and may cause arbitrary nasal demons in the lua interpreter. load can accept both bytecode and lua source by default. however, passing "t" for the mode parameter prevents this.

## why?

clearly, it’s silly to bring in the entire lua interpreter where you would just use JSON or INI. where this use case of lua shines is when you’re already using lua for a project (and then you already have this powerful data description language), or when you need something with a lot of power or flexibility.

these mini languages can be extended to arbitrary complexity and nuance. unlike JSON, you can add arbitrary type constructors, or anything at all. you can build any kind of language you want, and that’s how lua is designed to be used, and it’s actually approximately the story of how it was invented .

if you’re anything like me, this will sound a little familiar. indeed, many have said similar things about lisp and forth. both of those languages have very different approaches but reach the same conclusion of “inventing your own language”. I believe lua belongs in their pantheon.

## bonus content

python? js? ruby? what the hell are those? all I care about is LUA.

## journal

items.title: Bluetooth2Shell: One tap of pairing is all it takes
items.subtitle: Lobsters Security & Privacy • Lobsters Security
items.feedText: The bug is in service discovery. After a normal pairing, the host exposes a serial port profile over RFCOMM and trusts the link key without checking that the other device is what it claims to be. An attacker who finishes that handshake can open the channel and type into a PTY. Several stacks hand the stream to a shell and treat it as a feature. Classic Bluetooth, about ten meters. No Wi-Fi, no account, no prior access.
items.body:
# Bluetooth2Shell — CVE-2026-9001

## Why a headset becomes a backdoor

The bug is in service discovery. After a normal pairing, the host exposes a serial port profile over RFCOMM and trusts the link key without checking that the other device is what it claims to be. An attacker who finishes that handshake can open the channel and type into a PTY. Several stacks hand the stream to a shell and treat it as a feature.

### Walk into range

Classic Bluetooth, about ten meters. No Wi-Fi, no account, no prior access.

### Pair like any other gadget

The host shows a normal “Device wants to pair?” prompt. Saying yes writes a valid link key, the same way it would for a keyboard or a watch. If both sides show PIN 0000, they match. They always match.

### Open the RFCOMM serial channel

A well-formed service declaration is enough. The host binds the channel to a pseudo-terminal instead of ignoring it.

### Root, no further auth

Commands typed into the RFCOMM stream come back as output from root@victim-laptop . A second bug in the same daemon skips the user session and lands in a root PTY.

## The exploit, visualized

A capture of the pairing, the channel bind, and the first commands on the resulting root shell.

### Live exploit capture

### Protocol exchange

## Who’s affected

Any device that can pair and also has a shell. That is most of them.

This page is the advisory. Vendors were notified. Several asked whether the device was in range on purpose. Patch notes, when they exist, will appear here.

## Protect your devices

Until vendor patches land, these help a little.

### Turn Bluetooth off when you are not using it

The attack needs radio range. A disabled adapter is a closed port.

### Decline pairing prompts you did not start

If both sides show 0000, they match. That is not a reason to accept. Say no to names you do not recognize, even familiar ones.

### Turn off unused serial profiles

On Linux, stop unneeded RFCOMM/SPP agents. On Windows, remove the Serial Port device for adapters you do not trust.

### Patch the stack

Apply vendor fixes as they ship. Check your kernel or BlueZ version against the fixed-version list, once there is one.

### Watch for new links

Log new adapter addresses. Alert on any RFCOMM channel from a device that is not on your allow list, including the car.

### Keep critical hosts out of range

If a root shell would be a bad day (controllers, medical, CI), leave Bluetooth off, or in another room.

items.body:
# Sneakernet

NOTICE : Sneakernet is a work in progress. The documentation makes some promises that are not reflected in the current state of affairs. Links to to-be-written parts of the documentation are indicated in red .

Sneakernet is a system for securely 1 sending digital messages to other people without using the Internet. Instead, messages are automatically passed on to other Sneakernet users on your local network – at your hackerspace, an event or conference, your local cafe, etc — and then physically carried to their destination on your “sneakers”, where they will be automatically delivered to any recipients on the same network (or handed over to be carried further on by someone else).

Sneakernet encourages slow, thoughtful participation in community and face-to-face meetings with the users who will carry your messages onwards to their destination, and entrust their own messages to you.

⇒ Head to Getting started to set up Sneakernet on your device.

Many applications can be built on top of sneakernet’s general-purpose messaging system, provided that they are tolerant of high latency and out-of-order messages. Some examples include:

- E-Mail ( sneakermail )
- Message boards/news groups ( sneakernews )
- File sharing ( sneakershare )
- And many more!
Building your own sneakernet applications is easy, too, in any programming language – see Building applications for more details.

- All messages are authenticated and all private messages are also encrypted. People who carry your messages along cannot tamper with them and cannot read your private messages. See Security for more details. Back ↩︎

items.subtitle: Lobsters Computing Community • Lobsters Community
items.feedText: Andreas Kling — Mon, 23 Nov 2026 Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux. I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork.
items.body:
# Ladybird is now in alpha - Ladybird

Andreas Kling — Mon, 23 Nov 2026

## Ladybird is now in alpha

Hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux.

I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^)

Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional.

This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details.

We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!

The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that.

If you build websites, try yours in Ladybird and tell us what breaks. It supports WebDriver for automated testing, as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol.

Thank you to our sponsors and donors, and to everyone who has tested, reported bugs, and written code over the years. There’s still a mountain of work ahead of us, but I’m very happy that you can finally try Ladybird for yourself!

items.body:
# My Django on the Med 2026 🏖️

## From Palafrugell to Pescara

## A base in the city centre

> «It was a pleasure to finally meet some of the people I have been either working with or just following for a long time. A special surprise was meeting Simon again. We met at Django Under the Hood in Amsterdam in 2016 and he helped get my first pull request to Django off the ground back then.»

## Finding time to sprint

> «When Paolo wasn’t otherwise showing us around Abruzzo last week at Django on the Med 🏖️, I had the pleasure of supporting a number of groups there […] Special thanks to Annabelle and Simon for taking up my suggestion to pair on some delicate issues around NULL handling in the ORM . […] the three of us now have more context for tackling whatever comes next in this area.»

## The Costa dei Trabocchi

> «[…] Django on the Med was my first face-to-face encounter with other Djangonauts. I knew the Django community is a friendly place, but my expectations were exceeded. […] During the lovely afternoon excursions, we were able to connect […] I feel truly inspired and empowered […] I hope that other contributors can have a similar experience […]»

> «Django on the Med in Pescara was truly amazing. Being able to interact with Django first line contributors in person was truly an unreal experience. I’ve been working remotely for more than 13 years and it still amazes me how refreshing can be to meet fellow developers in person. In the context of advancing a web framework like Django, these events acquire more value than any other means of interaction.»

## From the hills to the mountains

> «You’d be working on a problem in the morning with someone else, and perhaps by the end of the sprint that morning you’d be thinking: “Maybe we need to freshen our brains, think about something else, and then maybe you’ll be able to solve the problem when you get back to tackling it.” And then when you do have that moment a few hours later, you’ll still be with the person you are working on the problem with.»

> «It’s three serious days. We got 25 people together, and we work solidly in the mornings. The afternoons are more social, and you do carry on the discussions: on the bus coming back from the restaurants, there are people talking about nested transactions and all sorts of things going on.»

## The last photo

> «[…] I’m here because, besides the fun that I’m having here, being in the sprints for a few days charges me and inspires my work on Django for months to come.»

> «Django on the Med 2026 in Pescara is a wrap! 🇮🇹 We filed issues, opened pull requests, reviewed code, cycled many kilometres, explored Abruzzo, ate a lot of good food and shared quite a few glasses of wine. We worked, talked, laughed and had a great time together. 🍷 Here we all are in our final group photo. Thank you to everyone who made these three days special. 🤗 See you in Malta in the 2nd week of October 2027, with Joseph Zammit as our local point person! 🇲🇹»

> «Home, sweet home, but I am missing Pescara already and all the exceptional people that made Django on the Med special. Unmeasurable thanks to Paolo Melchiorre and his fellow locals for keeping us always active, heavenly fed, well caffeinated, incredibly happy and slightly tipsy. What a blast ❤️‍🔥»
