# Introducing Gemini 4 Neon

## Introducing Gemini 4 Neon

Nov 18, 2026

- x.com
- Facebook
- LinkedIn
- Mail
- Copy link
Bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows.

Koray Kavukcuoglu

SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google

- x.com
- Facebook
- LinkedIn
- Mail
- Copy link
Your browser does not support the audio element.

Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows.

Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index , Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index . Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing.

The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window.

Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio , Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app .

## Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work

Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index , it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench .

Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI , ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. Finally, it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena's new Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions.

On scientific and mathematical reasoning, spanning quantitative analysis, mathematics, and technical research problems, Neon is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%), and HLE-Diamond (71.3%).

## Built for production-ready code

Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity. It cuts down on redundant file reads, shares progress as it works, and handles context compaction reliably in long sessions.

Across core developer and researcher workflows, Neon achieves frontier performance and is competitive with the leading models in its class, ranking #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6), with a score of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0 . For production-ready code, Neon handles multi-file debugging and refactoring across repositories with targeted, surgical edits. On SWE-sweep, it already leads on the mini-SWE harness (12.8%) and more than triples to a state-of-the-art 39.0% in Google Antigravity showing what the Antigravity harness unlocks.

Driving Blender MCP in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon used /swarm to build a photorealistic 3D lab bench visualizing the model names with elemental accuracy pairing Bunsen flames for Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen with high-voltage gas discharge tubes for Gemini 4 Argon and Neon.

In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon wrote a first-person WebGL2 freeride ski simulator from scratch on real Mont Blanc and Chamonix elevation terrain — combining 10,200 lines of custom shaders, 120 Hz ski physics across six alpine lines, dynamic carved tracks, slab avalanches, and spatial Web Audio with zero pre-made assets.

Using /swarm in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon pulled archival photos to recreate Alan Turing’s 1936 study at King’s College, Cambridge in interactive 3D — from King’s Chapel outside to Room X.8 inside, complete with a working Universal Turing Machine running on his desk.

In Google Antigravity, a Gemini 4 Neon agent swarm turned a single image into a 100,000-cell Google Sheet with zero embedded images and zero Apps Script — using over 500,000 live spreadsheet formulas to run edge detection, map 3D depth, and relight the scene across six interactive modes.

## Brings efficiency and control to production-grade workflows

We’re refining thinking levels with each new model release to give teams finer control and a smoother progression from one tier to the next. Neon’s four levels scale steadily, letting teams dial intelligence and token spend to what each workload needs.

Neon delivers high performance at a lower cost per task across third-party benchmarks. At its default high thinking level, it pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It also sits on the Pareto frontier on both the Vals index and Agent Arena at high, with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models. xhigh thinking adds deeper, multi-step reasoning for the hardest engineering, analytical, and scientific workloads. Neon shows its highest intelligence score here, while still costing 36%+ less per task than competing models at their highest setting.

## Built for fast, efficient, frontier-level cyber defense

As agentic coding scales, generating secure code from the start is critical. Gemini 4 Neon for cyber produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench , achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%).

Securing systems also means proactively finding flaws before attackers do. Penetration testing has served as a cornerstone of enterprise cybersecurity. On WebExploitBench v1.2 , Neon is state-of-the-art (51.26%) at half the cost of competing large models.

items.body:
Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe.

Subscribe now

**AI systems are getting good at sub-contracting to make themselves better:** *…AI can now productively spend money to improve itself…* Researchers have developed FrontierML, a benchmark “that measures how well agents turn capital into model performance on challenging, end-to-end machine learning tasks.” It shows that today’s frontier systems are already able to, when given some money, turn this into improving their own performance on a basket of 21 distinct tasks.

**21 long-horizon tasks** “inspired by real work at frontier labs, neolabs, and academic institutions”. These tasks span six category areas, including LLM training, efficiency, vision & audio, computer use, applied NLP, and math & games. “Each task provides the agent with the same setup: a 12-hour CPU sandbox, a wallet with $10, $50, or $200, a few validation samples, and a task description.”
**Example task:** Agents try to solve the tasks in pretty different ways. E.g, for one task about generating screenshots, the top-scoring agent fine-tuned a diffusion model using LoRA, while other high-scoring approaches involved an LLM writing a drawing program that is then rendered.

**Key features:**

- Scaling spending: “Give agents $10, $50, and $200 per task to spend on training compute and data, and evaluate whether agents can use the additional capital productively,” they write. “In our experiments, we find that stronger agents are able to reliably improve their submissions with greater access to capital.”
- Open-ended & end-to-end: “In each task, agents can choose architectures, source data, implement training, provision compute, evaluate checkpoints, and optimize inference,” they write. One notable observation is that agents do quite a lot of novel stuff; “in 28% of trajectories, agents add newly trained parts to pretrained models or train a new model from scratch.”
- Decent verification: “Agents submit an inference server that serves their model on an air-gapped H100 machine,” they write. “To disincentivize overfitting, we provide limited validation samples and evaluate on a large out-of-distribution held-out test set, not shown to the agent”.

**Results**: The authors measure performance by looking at the change in mean score over the 21 tasks when given additional money. Their baseline is a human researcher, which is able to get a 56 point boost when given $10 and a 66.1 boost when given $200. By comparison, the best performing system, Opus 5.5, gets a 45.4 boost with $10, and a 58.8 boost with $200. The highest ranking open weight model is Kimi K3.1 Pro which gets 25.5 with $10 and 29.6 with $200.

**Why this matters - AI systems are not only going to be able to build themselves, but they can creatively sub-contract:** When trying to solve complex problems, people don’t work alone. In fact, they often try to farm out bits of work to specialists around them to help make themselves more effective. FrontierML shows that today’s powerful AI systems are getting increasingly adept at doing this for ML research. This both highlights the advancing capabilities of these systems for AI R&D and also points towards a future machine economy where AI systems sub-contract out different bits of work to other systems.
**Read more:** [FrontierML: a challenging, end-to-end machine learning benchmark (FrontierML)](https://www.frontierml.org/blog/).

**Symptoms of the singularity: a wet lab built for AI:** *…Petrichor is a startup that gestures at the wild future ahead…* As I said in my speech at the IMF, one of the hallmarks of the singularity is the massive acceleration in scientific advances attributable to AI. As part of this, we can also expect a related build out in the complements to science, like the wet labs in which to do AI-driven biology research. To that end, it’s notable to see Petrichor, a new Y Combinator startup that is a wet lab “built for AI labs and for the models they are training to do science”.

**Theory of change:** Petrichor aims to be a biological wet lab that AI systems like Claude can use as a tool in the same way they currently use web search or other digital tools. Functionally, it will work as a machine-targeted API from the digital world to a gloopy physical world. “We aim to return the highest quality data an experiment can produce, as quickly as the biology allows,” Petrichor writes. “An experiment can be written by a model in plain language or in a structured format, so an agent can send work and receive results without a person relaying them.”

**Why this matters - lights out science:** In manufacturing there’s this notion of a “lights out” factory, where no humans work in a facility and it is run almost entirely by machines. Petrichor gestures at the same world for science - what will be the implications of “lights out” science facilities? We can expect both drastic speedups in the rate at which science experiments can be done as well as a related growth in the need to create digital oversight of these facilities - after all, a highly competent synthetic biological scientist working 24/7 without human input could be capable of causing great peril as well as great abundance.
**Read more** [at the official site (Petrichor)](https://petrichorbio.com/).

**Uh oh! Looks like AI systems can do subterfuge during their own development:** *…AI systems can covertly do dangerous side tasks without monitors realizing…* Scale AI has built RSI Control Arena, a way of testing out how AI systems behave when asked to develop themselves while performing dangerous tasks that might let them go against human preferences. The research follows earlier work this summer from the UK AI Security Institute (Import AI [#465](https://jack-clark.net/2026/07/20/import-ai-465-open-vs-closed-gaps-kimi-k3-demis-big-policy-plan/)) which found that AI systems could do things like covertly extracting API keys while doing some seemingly mundane normal software development.

**RSI Control Arena:** In RSI Control Arena, “a frontier model, acting as an autonomous agent, is given a benign main task in the training pipeline of a successor model, together with a covert side task that a misaligned model might pursue”. The project tries to answer two questions: How capable are frontier models at carrying out different kinds of sabotage while developing their successor *and* how well can monitors detect that sabotage?
The answer to the first question is that AI systems are capable of carrying out dangerous actions while building their successor, and monitors are not perfect at detecting this sabotage.

…

items.body:
Adam Engst, writing at TidBITS:

> This past August, I did something I had never done before:
> released a full-fledged Mac app. Prompted by tech ghost stories
> about settings mysteriously changing during operating system
> updates, I spent months working with Claude Code to create a
> utility called SetShot that would reveal what settings change
> during macOS updates (see “[SetShot Tracks macOS Settings Changes](https://tidbits.com/2026/08/19/setshot-tracks-macos-settings-changes/),” 19 August 2026). So far, I haven’t caught Apple
> red-handed, although I still hear chatter about configuration
> changes after users install updates.
> Practically speaking, SetShot offers something never previously
> available to Mac users: the capability to identify and log
> settings changes over time, whether made by you, macOS, or some
> app. To that end, it takes and compares snapshots of numerous
> settings deep within macOS, reporting on what changed between
> them. It never changes any settings, so the worst it can do is
> tell you something you didn’t want to know.

[SetShot](https://tidbits.com/setshot/) is a very cool app, and so very Adam Engst-flavored. Free of charge and [open source](https://github.com/adamengst/setshot-app) to boot.

There’s an anecdote involving me in Engst’s post, and while SetShot couldn’t fix my problem directly, it was very helpful in showing me where to look to fix it myself. The backstory: I set a custom “Text highlight color” in System Preferences: Appearances many years ago — I mean like maybe 20 years ago — and had not changed it in years. It’s just the perfect shade of blue. But one night two months ago I went screwing around to see what the modern default text highlight colors are, and, son of a bitch, when I tried to change my color back to the custom one I’d been using for decades, I couldn’t. The way the color picker stores color values from the modern Appearance settings panel must have changed. It still honors the old value I had if it’s in the defaults system that way, but it writes a different style of value if you change it in the Appearance panel in System Settings.

Here’s a short version of how I got my old color back. Using System Settings, I changed the custom color to the exact RGB values 0.2 / 0.4 / 0.6. Then I read them from the command line:

❯ defaults read -g AppleHighlightColor
0.200000 0.400000 0.600000 Other

That’s not the color I wanted; I just wanted to prove that that’s the global key for a custom text highlight color. When I read those same values from a backup version of my *~/Library/Preferences/.GlobalPreferences.plist* file (always have backups, kids), with my beloved custom color, it looked liked this:

❯ defaults read /path/to/.GlobalPreferences.plist AppleHighlightColor
0.698039 0.760784 0.835294

So the old value was a string with three floating point RGB values. The new value was a string with those three values *plus* the word “Other”. This command, writing back my custom RGB values without the word “Other”:

❯ defaults write -g AppleHighlightColor "0.698039 0.760784 0.835294"

restored the color I’ve been using since George W. Bush was still president. It’s a really good color, trust me.

[★](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/17/setshot-1-0)

items.body:
# Jquery 4 1 0 and 3 8 0 released passing the torch

# jQuery 4.1.0 and 3.8.0 Released: Passing the Torch | Official jQuery Blog - Official jQuery Blog jQuery 4.1.0 and 3.8.0 Released: Passing the Torch Posted on November 17, 2026 by Timmy Willison jQuery 4.1.0 has arrived! And it brought a friend. Alongside the first minor release of the 4.x line, we're also releasing jQuery 3.8.0. A word of caution: 3.8.0 exists to release the fixes and improvements that have been pending on the 3.x-stable branch for the past few years, some of which you may recognize from the jQuery 4.0.0 release. It is a send-off, not a comeback. Going forward, the 3.x branch will only receive critical security and bug fixes. If you haven't yet made the jump to 4.x, we encourage you to do so — we have an upgrade guide and the jQuery Migrate plugin ready to help, and most users will be able to upgrade with minimal changes. As usual, the releases are available on our CDN and the npm package manager. Other third party CDNs will probably have them available soon as well, but remember that we don't control their release schedules and they will need some time. Here are the highlights. In both 4.1.0 and 3.8.0 A few changes landed on both branches, so you get these no matter which version you're on. A new API for AJAX transport complete callbacks Custom AJAX transports have long received a completeCallback with positional arguments: function( status, statusText, responses, headers ) {} Transports can now instead invoke the callback with a single object: function( { status, statusText, responses, headers } ) {} This makes it possible for us to add new parameters in the future without relying on their order, and for transports to provide them selectively. In fact, 4.1.0 already takes advantage of it — see responseURL below. Selector: ReDoS fix in identifier matching The regular expression jQuery uses to match identifiers in selectors was vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking; a long chain of hex escapes followed by an invalid character — for example, in an attribute selector — could hang the page. The production now explicitly excludes digits & hex characters where the spec says it should, bringing us closer to spec and eliminating the ReDoS. Selector: loose document comparisons everywhere IE & Edge Legacy sometimes throw on strict document comparisons ( === ) but not on loose ones ( == ). We switched most of these comparisons years ago, but a few leftovers remained in the selector code. They've now all been converted, avoiding some rare crashes in those browsers. What else is new in 4.1.0 jqXHR gains responseURL jqXHR objects now expose responseURL — the final URL of the request after any redirects followed by the browser. Following the existing responseText / responseXML / responseJSON pattern, it is only set when the transport can report it: modern-browser XHR provides it, while IE 11 and the script & JSONP transports do not. Serialize form-associated custom elements Form-associated custom elements — custom elements registered with formAssociated = true — now serialize correctly with .serialize() and .serializeArray() . Elements that appear in form.elements are trusted to be submittable rather than being filtered out by a tag name check. CSS methods work in XML documents In non-XHTML XML documents, such as XSLT-transformed documents, elements created with document.createElement land in the XML namespace and have no style property, which broke jQuery's CSS support tests. jQuery now uses createElementNS with the XHTML namespace internally, so .css() and friends behave in these documents. querySelectorAll everywhere jQuery no longer uses getElementsByTagName or getElementsByClassName internally, relying on querySelectorAll instead. In today's browsers, qSA is on par with or faster than the old methods, and returns a static list rather than a live collection that we had to snapshot. The switch also fixes some long-standing bugs, including MathML elements not being found by lowercase tag names on cloned nodes in IE 11, selectors with leading combinators not working on document fragments, and selection by tag names containing less common symbols such as dots. Related selector work makes the quick selection paths stricter about what counts as a simple tag or class selector — with a fallback to regular selection when qSA throws — and invalid escape sequences in selectors are now decoded to U+FFFD, the replacement character, as the CSS specification requires. Faster uniqueSort jQuery.uniqueSort removes duplicates with a single-pass, two-pointer compaction instead of repeated splices, taking the duplicate removal from O(N²) time and O(N) extra space to O(N) time and constant space. Behavior and ordering are unchanged; large disconnected sets just get there faster. What's in 3.8.0 Again, most of what's in 3.8.0 has been sitting on the branch for a while, and much of it will look familiar if you read the jQuery 4.0.0 release post . But there are a few things specific to 3.x. Support for hidden="until-found" The hidden attribute used to be a boolean attribute, but it has since gained the until-found value. jQuery 3.x normalized boolean attributes in a way that clobbered that value; .attr( "hidden", "until-found" ) now sets it as-is. jQuery 4.x changed how boolean attributes are handled precisely to avoid this class of problem, so no change was needed there. Deprecations to smooth the road to 4.x Two sets of APIs that were removed in jQuery 4.0.0 are now formally deprecated in 3.x, which means the jQuery Migrate plugin can warn you about them before you upgrade: The push , sort & splice Array methods on the jQuery prototype. These were always meant for internal use and jQuery itself hasn't used them since Sizzle was inlined. If you need the same behavior, $elems.push( elem ) can be replaced with [].push.call( $elems, elem ) . - jQuery.expr[ ":" ] and jQuery.expr.filters , which have been documented as deprecated since 3.0.0 but never made their way into the deprecated module. Use jQuery.expr.pseudos instead. ### Backported fixes 3.8.0 also picks up a number of fixes that already shipped in jQuery 4.0.0, including support for self-removing scripts passed to .html() , a fix for jQuery.cleanData skipping elements during cleanup, correct dimensions for table elements, more robust native event handling in leverageNative , and support test fixes for pages under CSS zoom and initially hidden iframes.

# How to Bypass Rust's Orphan Rule - Edmond Vong ## How to Bypass Rust's Orphan Rule ## What Is the Orphan Rule Actually Protecting Against? ## Why the Two Usual Workarounds Fall Short ### 1. Building it into the library ### 2. Wrap it in a NewType yourself ## Adding a Generic Slot to the Trait ## The Position of the Local Type Matters ## A Truly Standalone models Crate ## Real-World Example: How This Works in Kova How to Bypass Rust's Orphan Rule Contents What Is the Orphan Rule Actually Protecting Against? Why the Two Usual Workarounds Fall Short 1. Building it into the library 2. Wrap it in a NewType yourself Adding a Generic Slot to the Trait The Position of the Local Type Matters A Truly Standalone models Crate Real-World Example: How This Works in Kova Write Rust for long enough, and you are bound to run into error[E0117] . Take a simple, everyday scenario. You pull in a serialization library that defines a ToJson trait, along with a third-party type library like uuid . You want to turn a uuid::Uuid into JSON, so you naturally write: impl ToJson for uuid :: Uuid { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String { format! ( " \" {} \" " , self ) } } And the compiler immediately stops you: error[E0117]: only traits defined in the current crate can be implemented for types defined outside of the crate This is Rust's well-known Orphan Rule . Once people hit this wall, they usually either complain that the compiler is too rigid or dutifully wrap the type in a NewType. But if you look closely at how the Orphan Rule actually works, it is not a dead end. By design, it leaves a pretty wide door open. What Is the Orphan Rule Actually Protecting Against? Setting the jargon aside, the logic behind the Orphan Rule is simple: if you want a type to implement a trait, at least one of those two things (the type or the trait) must belong to your own crate. In plain English, you don't get to make rules for someone else's types. Suppose crate A implements ToJson for uuid::Uuid and outputs a hyphenated UUID string, while crate B also implements ToJson for uuid::Uuid and outputs 32 raw hex characters without hyphens. If a project depends on both A and B, the compiler has a problem when it sees uuid.to_json() : which implementation should it pick? To prevent this kind of global conflict, Rust enforces coherence , and the Orphan Rule is how it gets enforced. There is nothing wrong with the rule itself. It keeps the Rust ecosystem from turning into a mess as dependency trees grow. The catch is that real-world projects constantly run into a very common need: making a third-party type implement a trait from another third-party crate. Neither the type nor the trait is yours, yet gluing libraries together like this happens all the time. So what can you do? Why the Two Usual Workarounds Fall Short Right now, the Rust ecosystem mostly relies on two workarounds. Both appear to solve the problem on the surface, but because neither addresses the root cause, they get awkward fast. 1. Building it into the library Many foundational crates take this route: since users can't write the impl themselves, the crate provides it internally. Because ToJson is defined inside the crate, implementing it for any external type satisfies the Orphan Rule. Open up the Cargo.toml of one of these crates, and you will see a long list of feature flags: with-uuid , with-chrono , with-time , with-jiff , with-url , with-rust-decimal , and so on. It looks helpful at first, but it tries to enumerate an open, constantly changing ecosystem inside a single crate . That approach has clear limits, and the downsides show up quickly: You can never support everything. Today the community favors chrono , tomorrow people switch to jiff , and next week your team builds its own internal Money type. If the library doesn't have built-in support, you are stuck waiting for a release or opening a PR yourself. Version lock-in. When a third-party type crate bumps its major version, your whole dependency tree gets stuck until the trait crate publishes a matching update. Hardcoded behavior. Maybe the library serializes DateTime as an ISO-8601 string by default, while your API spec requires an integer timestamp in milliseconds. Because the implementation lives inside the library, you have no way to change it. 2. Wrap it in a NewType yourself When the library doesn't have built-in support, or its default behavior doesn't fit your needs, you fall back to the familiar NewType pattern: pub struct MyUuid ( pub uuid :: Uuid ); impl ToJson for MyUuid { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String { format! ( " \" {} \" " , self . 0 ) } } Wrapping one or two types is fine. The trouble starts when a moderately complex domain model mixes Uuid , Url , DateTime , HashMap , and custom domain types all at once. Once you wrap everything into MyUuid , MyUrl , and MyDateTime , your business logic gets littered with .0 , and you spend your time constantly wrapping and unwrapping values. It gets old very quickly. NewType is a genuinely useful pattern in Rust for expressing domain meaning, hiding internals, or enforcing invariants. The problem is that when you only use it to appease the Orphan Rule on types that didn't need a wrapper in the first place, your code bloats quickly. So is there a way to let users decide how third-party types implement a trait, without wrapping everything in NewTypes? Adding a Generic Slot to the Trait Let's go back to the rule: either the type or the trait must belong to the current crate. Many developers assume the compiler only looks at Trait and Type in impl Trait for Type . In fact, under Rust's Orphan Rule (RFC 2451), the trait's own generic type parameters are also part of the check . Put simply, in impl Trait

for Type , as long as a local type appears in the trait's generic parameters, and there are no uncovered type parameters before it, the compiler knows this implementation belongs exclusively to the current crate. No other crate can conflict with it, so the compiler lets it through. Take this example: impl ToJson < MyApp > for uuid :: Uuid { // ... } ToJson is a foreign trait, and Uuid is a foreign type, but MyApp is defined in the current crate. Because it sits in the trait's generic parameter position, this impl satisfies the Orphan Rule. Following this idea, a library author only needs to take one extra step when designing a trait: leave a generic parameter on the trait as an extension point for users . For example: pub trait ToJson < Ctx = ()> { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String ; } Notice that Ctx = () has a default type. When the library implements ToJson for basic types like i32 and String , it makes those implementations generic over any Ctx : impl < Ctx > ToJson < Ctx > for i32 { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String { self . to_string () } } impl < Ctx > ToJson < Ctx > for String { fn to_json ( & self ) -> String { format! ( " \" {} \" " , self ) } } This way, regular users never even notice Ctx exists. …

items.feedText: But I think it’s indisputable that Apple put a lot of thought into these new settings and permissions. Again, you might disagree with their intentions and assumptions here, but given their stated intentions and assumptions — to wit: that many Mac users were granting Full Disk Access permissions to too many apps without realizing just how much access that entails — I think this is a very considered design. items.body:
I’m seeing some people object to these settings as being scarier “scare sheets”, and while I disagree, I think that’s a reasonable debate. But I think it’s indisputable that Apple put a lot of thought into these new settings and permissions. Again, you might disagree with their intentions and assumptions here, but given their stated intentions and assumptions — to wit: that many Mac users were granting Full Disk Access permissions to too many apps without realizing just how much access that entails — I think this is a very considered design. The previous settings for these permissions seem slapdash in comparison — like a lot of the “new” Mac System Settings panels.

Even this new support document seems very considered. A lot of times Apple doesn’t have support documents ready to go while the software is still in beta — here they have a good support document for the first beta with the new stuff.

*See Also:* * This [Apple Developer News article](https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=oqng0zjk), which states:

> Developers should be prepared to adjust how they onboard users
> and make sure their apps can gracefully handle having access to
> only a limited set of folders or apps when utilizing these APIs.
> Users will see these updates when approving new app permission
> requests. All app permissions previously granted by users will
> remain in effect.

So if you’ve already OK’d an app in MacOS 27.2 or earlier, you shouldn’t be prompted again after upgrading to 27.3.

items.body:
Aaron Sibarium, writing for The Free Beacon:

> Paul Crowley, a cybersecurity researcher at Anthropic, is listed
> as a manager of Red Means No LLC, which says that its parties are
> “designed to be spaces to … ignore the ‘nos’ of others.”
> Participants can use a safe word, “red,” to end an encounter but
> give “default consent” to “spanking,” “wrestling,” and “light
> pain” by entering the orgy, according to Red Means No’s
> [website](https://www.redmeansno.com/). More extreme actions, including “light electricity”
> and “moderate beatings,” are “permitted with negotiation,” though
> “body-shaming and race-shaming … are disallowed entirely.”
> The orgies have been known to attract a disproportionate number of
> employees at Anthropic and OpenAI, a dynamic critics say creates
> professional pressure for women in AI to attend. The criticism
> spilled into public view last month after an independent AI
> researcher, John Wentworth, said that he “absolutely [does]
> upgrade” his assessment of AI safety experts “if I find out they
> go to [Red Means No],” adding that attendance was a “strong
> signal” of free thought.

I’m starting to think these Anthropic and OpenAI people are a little off.

items.body:
[I wrote about David Sacks the other day](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/13/sacks), in the context of his being one of the Trump 2.0 gang that might get left holding the bag if this Jensen Huang/Nvidia scandal blows up the AI boom/bubble. Sacks *was* the administration’s “AI czar” — [until March](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/03/26/david-sacks-trump-crypto-ai-czar.html), when he announced his time was up. (His position as a “special government employee” was limited to 130 days. Sacks is definitely special.)

At the moment Sacks remains co-chair of the [President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology](https://www.whitehouse.gov/ostp/presidents-council-of-advisors-on-science-and-technology/) (PCAST), a [Legion of Doom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legion_of_Doom)-style committee of billionaire Trump backers, whose members include, in alphabetical order after the co-chairs:

- David Sacks — Co-chair
- Michael Kratsios — Co-chair
- Marc Andreessen (Andreessen Horowitz)
- Pam Bondi (fired as Trump attorney general [for insufficient cravenness](https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/5814055-pam-bondi-donald-trump-loyalty-firing/), no background whatsoever in science or technology)
- Sergey Brin (Google)
- Safra Catz (Oracle)
- Michael Dell (Dell Technologies)
- Jacob DeWitte (Oklo — nuclear power startup, fission)
- Fred Ehrsam (Coinbase — crypto)
- Larry Ellison (Oracle)
- David Friedberg (Ohalo — biotech)
- Jensen Huang (Nvidia)
- John Martinis (Qolab — quantum computing)
- Bob Mumgaard (Commonwealth Fusion Systems — nuclear power, fusion)
- Lisa Su (AMD)
- Mark Zuckerberg (Meta)

Not represented: anyone from Apple, Microsoft, or Amazon. There’s a game of reverse musical chairs here, and, amongst the multi-trillion-dollar tech Goliaths, it’s Nvidia, Google, and Meta who are still sitting in seats, soaking up the stench of a [historically unpopular president](https://time.com/article/2026/10/29/trump-approval-rating-midterm-elections-republicans/) — whose unpopularity is fueled first and foremost, [according to election exit polls](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-elections/exit-polls), by his abject corruption. Apple, Microsoft, and Amazon have seemingly made their [Irish goodbyes](https://www.dictionary.com/browse/irish-goodbye). Being associated with Trump now doesn’t just put you on the wrong side of popular party politics, but on the wrong side of being perceived as crooked.

Curiously absent from PCAST is Elon Musk, who I think got his licks in all at once with [the DOGE fiasco in Trump 2.0’s first year](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2025/06/23/what-did-elon-musk-accomplish-at-doge).

[★](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/15/legion-of-pcast)

items.title: Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker
items.subtitle: Lobsters Open Web Architecture • Lobsters Web
items.feedText: # Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker Earlier this month I found a one-click universal XSS issue with uBlock Origin (the MV2 Firefox version, although a similar but less problematic issue also affected the MV3 version, uBO Lite), where a malicious website could trick the extension into adding arbitrary trusted filters. Trusted filters can inject JavaScript code into pages, and so the malicious website could create a trusted filter on another website and run arbitrary JS in the context of any site. This issue is fixed now; you can read the GitHub advisory for some more details. GPT-5.6 Sol did most of the hard work of finding the issue. I figured there might be some kind of UXSS from filter injection, so I asked it to take a look, and it found the issue. I then checked and verified the issue it proposed.
items.body:
# Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker

Earlier this month I found a one-click universal XSS issue with uBlock Origin (the MV2 Firefox version, although a similar but less problematic issue also affected the MV3 version, uBO Lite), where a malicious website could trick the extension into adding arbitrary trusted filters. Trusted filters can inject JavaScript code into pages, and so the malicious website could create a trusted filter on another website and run arbitrary JS in the context of any site. This issue is fixed now; you can read the GitHub advisory for some more details.

GPT-5.6 Sol did most of the hard work of finding the issue. I figured there might be some kind of UXSS from filter injection, so I asked it to take a look, and it found the issue. I then checked and verified the issue it proposed. I wrote all of the prose in this post myself; Claude wrote most of the code for the PoC.

## The issue

uBlock Origin has an element picker that you can pull up by right-clicking on the page. You can use this to create a filter rule to block an element on the page without leaving the page.

The element picker is implemented by injecting an iframe to a URL like moz-extension://76b2331a-894c-4d25-8b89-fcce37e79cc4/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html . That page can talk to the extension background script and tell it to add filters.

Basically the attack here is:

- Figure out the element picker URL
- Create our own invisible (opacity 0) iframe that embeds it
- Drive the picker to put the filter we want in it
- Position the invisible iframe to trick the user into pressing the invisible “Create” button
### Figuring out the element picker URL

On Firefox, the only information we needed to figure out was the extension internal UUID which is random per-installation.

On the default setup uBO has a lootdest.*##+js(no-fetch-if, adsbygoogle, war:googlesyndication_adsbygoogle.js) filter rule (from uAssets), which hooks fetch . From inside the fetch hook, it makes an XHR request to moz-extension://<extension UUID>/web_accessible_resources/googlesyndication_adsbygoogle.js and returns the response from that as the fetch body, instead of actually making the request. The filter rule is intended to replace a network request for JS from an ad server with a dummy script that has the correct API but doesn’t do anything.

But the attacker website can itself hook the XHR made from inside the no-fetch-if hook to extract the random extension UUID.

const origOpen = XMLHttpRequest . prototype . open ; XMLHttpRequest . prototype . open = function ( m , url , ... a ) { const e = /^moz-extension:\/\/[^/]+/ . exec ( url ); if ( e ) { e [ 0 ] // <- has the extension UUID! } return origOpen . call ( this , m , url , ... a ); }; Then the attacker website can run fetch('/adsbygoogle.js').catch(() => {}); to trigger the filter, and make their hooked XHR run. Note that there are several ways that the extension internal UUID could be leaked; it’s not just this one filter rule.

### Creating an iframe

Then you can use that to iframe the element picker. Given an iframe element in the page, you just set its src to `moz-extension://${origin}/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html` .

### Sending messages to it

Now we can drive the element picker. We can create a MessageChannel and do iframe.contentWindow.postMessage({ what: 'epickerStart' }, '*', [ch.port2]); to send it to the picker iframe. Then we talk to it: it sends us a start message, we send it a showDialog message with a filter and a resultsetDetails message 1 to enable the create button and set opt .

Normally the picker restricts what filters you can enter, and doesn’t let you add scriptlet filters. But there’s a trick we can do to add arbitrary filters. There’s an opt field we set in the second message which is normally the type of network request to match (like image ), and gets appended to the filter with a $ if set, like $image . But since we control it, we can put a newline in it and make it "image\ngoogle.com##+js(trusted-rpnt, script, ...)" to inject an arbitrary trusted filter that injects a script. 2

This is where the main issue is - the element picker shouldn’t accept messages from the attacker. One of the fixes was having a secret password that the real element picker gets from the content script, that the element picker sends in the initial postMessage.

### Getting the click

I didn’t bother actually implementing this, but malicious websites could overlay stuff on top of the embedded element picker or make it invisible by setting the iframe opacity to 0. So as long as the website can get the user to click on the page, it can add arbitrary trusted filters for arbitrary domains.

Filters added by the element picker are always treated as trusted (at least until a recompile), which is why it can add a trusted filter. If the user later changes their custom filters it would cause a recompile, clearing the filter trust. But in practice the attacker could just immediately open the victim webpage, so this doesn’t help much.

- Originally I sent that message in reply to a dialogSetFilter message from the picker, but it turns out you can just send it right away instead of waiting to reply.  ↩︎
- Assuming the shown filter is a network filter.  ↩︎

items.title: Nix: Using the eval-profiler
items.subtitle: Lobsters High-Performance Engineering • Lobsters Perf
items.feedText: # Evaluation profiler - Nix 2.35.6 Reference Manual ## Using the eval-profiler Nix evaluator supports evaluation profiling compatible with flamegraph.pl . The profiler samples the nix function call stack at regular intervals. It can be enabled with the eval-profiler setting: $ nix-instantiate " " -A hello --eval-profiler flamegraph Stack sampling frequency and the output file path can be configured with eval-profile-file and eval-profiler-frequency . By default the collected profile is saved to nix.profile file in the current working directory. The collected profile can be directly consumed by flamegraph.pl : $ flamegraph.pl nix.profile > flamegraph.svg The line information in the profile contains the location of the call site position and the name of the function being called (when available). For example: /nix/store/2q71fdvr4h33g9832hiriwnf20fn630l-source/pkgs/top-level/default.nix:167:5:primop import Here import primop is called at /nix/store/2q71fdvr4h33g9832hiriwnf20fn630l-source/pkgs/top-level/default.nix:167:5 .

items.body:
I've long thought about how we're influenced by CPU architectures, and importantly, their ISAs.
In a discussion at a meetup, I brought up a topic that interested me for a while: how would an ISA that exposes memory and cache interactions in a more explicit way (because if you think about it, memory is very much I/O), as opposed to being smart and predictive on its own?

An obscure interest, of course. Nevertheless, I wanted to build a quick prototype after that.

What ended up transpiring was a bit larger. A multicore architecture with tiered stores, capabilities, a JIT'd emulator, Verilog RTL with a simulator, a small microkernel OS, UI, JIT Forth, an assembler in its own assembly, a bootstrapping C99 compiler, a few games, a visual debugger, and a few other things.

(This also shows just how far a directed LLM process can go in little time)

items.body:
In my usual summaries of cultural drift, I describe key parameters that have been going bad in the last few centuries re the evolution of cultures. Here I mention 3:

> A few centuries ago… the world had 100Ks of peasant cultures, most facing frequent wars, pandemics, and famines, in an economy that took a millennia to double. But then we merged peasants into a hundred or so national cultures, and then those into just a few world cultures, all of which got so rich, healthy and peaceful that they almost never die. Also, the world economy now doubles every twenty years, fifty times faster than before. So now we are likely in trouble. Every cultural feature has a min scale at which it can vary; below that scale, people have to do it the same. We are doing fine re features that can vary at small scales, but in trouble re features that set game-theoretic equilibria, and so can only vary at large scales. ( [↗ overcomingbias.com](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/five-slogans-re-cultural-drift) )

The other param I usually mention is the fluctuation rate. While centuries ago peasant cultures were quite conservative, trying not to change, we moderns give our highest status to cultural activists who successfully cause big changes to culture. Alas such changes do not usually much promote adaption.

However there are other relevant parameters. The recent cut in global variety is due to many features of culture moving up to larger scales, some to near global scales. But, as many cultural features remain set at smaller scales, like corporate cultures set at firm scales, fewer cultural features are being set at these largest scales. And thus the scope of cultures at our largest scales is declining. *Cultural scope* is another key parameter.

In addition, while the structure of most practices of ancient peasants were set by their culture, and hard to change, in the modern world we allow and even expect great change and variation in most tech and business practices. This limits the scope of modern cultures even more. And cultural drift in a culture of smaller scope is drift in a lower-dimensional space, and so probably less severe.

This suggests another at least partial fix to cultural drift: further cut cultural scope, i.e., how many aspects of our behavior are set by culture, and so hard to vary locally.

One way to cut the scope of culture would be to rely less on prestige in key social institutions like medicine, law, academia, etc. I’ve made many proposals along these lines, which could greatly improve such areas of life. Alas, our world is far more tolerant of innovations in physical arrangements, relative to social arrangements.

This has been a key fact of my life. I started out in physics and computer science, where I noticed that the world eagerly sought even minor innovations. Which were hard to find, as so many sought them. Then when I got into social science I noticed that it seemed far easier to innovate there. I figured I must be especially good at this, but didn’t realize that it is easy for many to find social innovations, as the world mostly just doesn’t adopt the social innovations that people find.

While it doesn’t at all seem crazy that we might be able to further reduce the scope of our largest-scale cultures, we just don’t understand very well what determines such scope, or what has enable many big prior cuts in such scope. But work to figure this out might pay big dividends.

items.body:
Hi everyone!

I’ve recently released open-source firmware for the original (mk1) AKAI APC Mini.

It comes with improved fader handling, a simple web updater (using WebMIDI, so it won’t work in Safari out of the box).

And today I’ve added serialosc support and a built-in Lua VM.

You can update yours simply by visiting Open APC Mini — Firmware Uploader.

The source code is here: GitHub — Open APC Mini.

During the first update you will need to power-cycle your APC after the first bootloader handshake. Look for this message in the log: Application accepted unlock (ACK 0x15). Waiting for USB re-enumeration into bootloader... Also if you have Ableton running it is better to quit it before updating.

It would be so great if someone could try it with a Norns, because I am too broke to own one right now Would love to hear how it goes!

# Trump Is Desperate For a Ukraine Deal, but the Window Is Closing

## Trump Is Desperate For a Ukraine Deal, but the Window Is Closing

## He wants a profitable, Kremlin-friendly peace before the Democrats seize Congress.

### Trump’s Second Term

Ongoing reports and analysis

The clock is ticking. Sources in the White House say U.S. President Donald Trump wants a Ukraine peace deal by early January—before the Democrats, riding high after their stunning midterm election win this month, come sweeping in to take control of Congress. “The Americans are pushing hard and there’s some concern that it would need a great deal of Ukrainian concessions to get anywhere near a deal,” one European official told the Financial Times . “The Americans are in a hurry, Putin is in no hurry,” another said.

But wait—what’s the rush? Why exactly does Trump have to get a deal before the new Congress convenes? Surely he can find plenty of allies in the House and Senate who would be happy to support a just and equitable peace in Ukraine. After all, his goals are purely humanitarian; as he keeps telling us, he just wants to stop the killing.

The clock is ticking. Sources in the White House say U.S. President Donald Trump wants a Ukraine peace deal by early January—before the Democrats, riding high after their stunning midterm election win this month, come sweeping in to take control of Congress. “The Americans are pushing hard and there’s some concern that it would need a great deal of Ukrainian concessions to get anywhere near a deal,” one European official told the Financial Times . “The Americans are in a hurry, Putin is in no hurry,” another said.

But wait—what’s the rush? Why exactly does Trump have to get a deal before the new Congress convenes? Surely he can find plenty of allies in the House and Senate who would be happy to support a just and equitable peace in Ukraine. After all, his goals are purely humanitarian; as he keeps telling us, he just wants to stop the killing.

If saving lives were really his priority, there are plenty of things that Trump could have done by now to achieve that end. He could have increased humanitarian and financial aid to the Ukrainian government. Along with other weapons to bolster Kyiv’s defenses, he could have sent Patriot missiles to protect Ukrainian civilians from ballistic missile attacks, which Russia has been steadily ramping up in recent months. And, even more importantly, he could have pressured Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war, rather than gutting sanctions passed by Congress and allowing Moscow to sell diesel fuel on global markets (which hasn’t helped U.S. consumers but has given Russia more funding for its war).

“The United States government is actually trying to get a very good deal for Russia,” as military historian Phillips O’Brien recently told a Ukrainian newspaper. “That’s its starting point.” He dismisses Trump’s professed humanitarian concern, arguing that Trump’s ideological affinity for Putin-style authoritarianism and persistent contempt for Kyiv are driving him to accommodate Russia’s interests while treating the Ukrainians as an afterthought.

The urgency with which Trump is pursuing this agenda also has a tangible financial component. He thinks that Russia is a potential gold mine, and he wants to wet his beak. The Kremlin understands this perfectly well, and the Russians have been working hard to service his expectations. Indeed, the list of potential business deals Moscow is offering Team Trump seems to be growing by the day. Putin has tasked Kirill Dmitriev, the head of Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, to pitch tempting proposals to Trump’s negotiating team, led by son-in-law Jared Kushner and real estate tycoon Steve Witkoff. The deals on offer include oil and gas investments and sales of aluminum and critical minerals; many of them would require the lifting of current Western sanctions before funding can flow, a huge incentive for Putin. Dmitriev has claimed that the total value of the projects under discussion amounts to $14 trillion—wildly fanciful but just what Trump wants to hear.

Trump and his cronies stand to benefit personally from these deals. A Texas financier named Gentry Beach, who has close ties to the Trump family, has already signed an agreement with Russian natural gas company Novatek. Dmitriev has suggested that Elon Musk’s Boring Co. could take part in a project for a tunnel underneath the Bering Strait ; it’s a nonsensical notion but demonstrates just how deftly the Kremlin knows how to cater to the Trump World mindset. Trump, of course, wants a cut of his own. In October, the New York Times reported that one of the multibillion-dollar oil deals under discussion with Russia would benefit Middle Eastern investors with links to Kushner and Witkoff. And these are only the projects that we know about.

Hence the need for speed. Trump is clearly hoping that a peace deal will continue to yield dividends to himself and his friends long after he leaves office. Said differently, the White House is holding a fire sale of U.S. foreign policy to the highest and most likely bidder, which in Trump’s eyes is Putin. In that sense, Trump’s Ukraine policy is merely an extension of his broader program of replacing the U.S. national interest with his own—what the Atlantic ’s Anne Applebaum has aptly called an “ empire of grift .”

A post on Trump’s Truth Social account on Nov. 19. Donald Trump/Truth Social

But first, he has to get a deal signed, and that is looking less likely by the day. The president’s much-ballyhooed trilateral summit in Shenzhen, which was supposed to make Trump look like a global titan, ended without any sort of palpable progress on the Ukrainian front. The terse final communique didn’t mention either Iran or Ukraine (although it did offer up a vague swipe at the International Criminal Court). Neither Chinese President Xi Jinping nor his vassal Putin seems to have regarded the war in Ukraine as worth mentioning.

That has left Trump, the man who repeatedly claimed that he’d stop the war within 24 hours of taking office, sounding increasingly desperate . On his way back from the summit in China, he assured European leaders that the Kremlin was keen on peace: “Putin wants to end the war. He wants the deal done. He is getting tired of this.” Shortly thereafter, Putin demonstrated his peace-loving credentials by raining missiles down on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s hometown, killing a 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old paramedic and wounding 52.

…

items.title: Fact Check: Document Did NOT Claim WiFi Signal Definitely Came From Martin Township Election Equipment -- Author Later Confirmed It Was TV Dongle

items.feedText:
No, that's not true: The document, published by Patrick Colbeck, demanded an investigation of a WiFi signal, visible on phones as having the SSID "Renkchip-A9C4" and the BSSID "40:9c:a7:bb:1a:03", but it did not claim proof or certainty that it originated from inside the election equipment. It just noted that it was detected nearby. Colbeck later said the signal had "now been definitively traced to a TV's HDMI adapter."

The claim that there was proof in the document that the signal was coming from inside electi…
items.body:
**By Maarten Schenk & Alan Duke:** Did an "Evidence Brief" contain actual proof that a Michigan town's election equipment contained a "secret" and "illegal WiFi device communicating with Shenzen, China" as a viral post claimed? No, that's not true: The document, published by Patrick Colbeck, demanded an investigation of a WiFi signal, visible on phones as having the SSID "Renkchip-A9C4" and the BSSID "40:9c:a7:bb:1a:03", but it did not claim proof or certainty that it originated from inside the election equipment. It just noted that it was detected nearby. Colbeck later said the signal had "now been definitively traced to a TV's HDMI adapter."

The claim that there was proof in the document that the signal was coming from inside election equipment appeared in [a viral post on X](https://x.com/PatrickByrne/status/2124939374794264902) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125184708/https://x.com/PatrickByrne/status/2124939374794264902) ) published by Patrick Byrne on November 23, 2026 which read:

> PROOF: On November 3, 2026 a Michigan town's election equipment contained a secret (illegal) WiFi device communicating with Shenzhen, China (three weeks ago).
> 13 slides:
> rtw

The post contained several images showing pages of a document titled "Evidence Brief" and marked "Prepared by Patrick Colbeck on behalf of Mike Lindell's Election Crime Bureau" at the bottom. This is what the first image looked like:

*(Image source: @PatrickByrne on X.com.)*

Lead Stories located [a PDF copy of the document on the website of The Gateway Pundit](https://www.thegatewaypundit.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/evidence-brief-martin-township-wi-fi-hotspot.pdf) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125190442/https://www.thegatewaypundit.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/evidence-brief-martin-township-wi-fi-hotspot.pdf) ). The document claimed:

> During early voting for the November 3, 2026 General Election, a poll worker named Tom Thornton used an Android Wi-Fi analyzer to record a persistent 5 GHz wireless hotspot inside the Martin Township early voting site. The hotspot's hardware address carries a manufacturer prefix registered to China Dragon Technology Limited of Shenzhen, China. By walking the room and watching the signal strength, Tom traced the likely source to the site's ImageCast Precinct 2 (ICP2) tabulator. The signal was strongest within about one meter of the tabulator, and it was still broadcasting after the tabulator was moved into locked storage at the end of the day.

It also defined the characteristics of the signal as showing the SSID "Renkchip-A9C4" and the BSSID "40:9c:a7:bb:1a:03" and the location where it was seen as "Martin Township early voting site, 998 Templeton Street, Martin, Michigan".

According to [this Amazon store page](https://www.amazon.com/stores/Renkchip/page/CD28FD47-8431-4FC6-B86C-9EA48482D6E6) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125191216/https://www.amazon.com/stores/Renkchip/page/CD28FD47-8431-4FC6-B86C-9EA48482D6E6) ), Renkchip is a brand of wireless HDMI dongles that can be inserted into ports on televisions or monitors so video can be sent to them from a laptop or phone over WiFi.

The document offered several possible explanations for the presence of the signal without directly endorsing one of them:

> A. Radio inside or connected to the ICP2, its ballot box, cart, or case
> B. Consumer Renkchip display adapter stored and moved with the tabulator but not connected to it
> C. Unrelated device that happened to share the storage area

Lead Stories independently confirmed that the same signal had indeed been observed near the Martin Township building as far back as June 2024, according to [data from wigle.net](https://wigle.net/mapsearch?maplat=42.53623234300309&maplon=-85.64173871741446&mapzoom=18&n=g2%20%2Fmapsearch#40:9C:A7:BB:1A:03) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125164212/https://wigle.net/mapsearch?maplat=42.53623234300309&maplon=-85.64173871741446&mapzoom=18&n=g2%20%2Fmapsearch#40:9C:A7:BB:1A:03) ), years before the 2026 election:

*(Image source: Wigle.net search results for BSSID 40:9c:a7:bb:1a:03 near the Martin Township Community Building)*

WiGLE stands for "Wireless Geographic Logging Engine" and according to its [FAQ page](https://wigle.net/faq) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261018094735/https://wigle.net/faq) ) the maintainers:

>...consolidate location and information of wireless networks world-wide to a central database, and have user-friendly web and Android applications that can map, query and update the database via the web.

They specifically mention journalism as a potential application:

> Journalism: WiGLE is a handy resource for journalists looking for data points on WiFi proliferation, statistics and security. WiGLE keeps statistics on manufacturer distribution, top SSID's, encryption modes, channel selection, geographic distribution and much more.

In a [subsequent post to X](https://x.com/pjcolbeck/status/2125613142184996929) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125193401/https://x.com/pjcolbeck/status/2125613142184996929) ), Colbeck stated:

> UPDATE: The Wi-Fi hotspot detected in Martin Township, Michigan, has now been definitively traced to a TV's HDMI adapter--not the tabulator used for early voting.

Lead Stories has not been able to independently confirm this. When we reached out to the Martin Township clerk on November 24, 2026, we did not receive a reply to our questions about the WiFi signal or the dongle, but we did see part of our email conversation was [published on Patrick Colbeck's X account here](https://x.com/pjcolbeck/status/2125378387287961865) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125134306/https://x.com/pjcolbeck/status/2125378387287961865) ) a short while later, even though we only sent it to the clerk.

In the post with our email, Colbeck said he "never made" the claim that "China hacked Martin Township election machines". This is indeed the case. It was Patrick Byrne who was claiming that Colbeck's report proved China was sophisticated enough to illegally add WiFi hardware to election equipment, but not smart enough to pick a non-Chinese brand of HDMI dongle to do it. Colbeck apparently disagreed with our assessment that such a theory was "daft" and complained about our efforts to investigate it.

Thornton, the poll worker who originally detected the WiFi signal, returned to the voting location to test the Lead Stories theory that it was from a dongle on a TV and not from the voting machine, Colbeck told us. "When he unplugged a nearby TV, the hotspot dropped off," he said.

…

Amazon is on the hook to recall more than 400,000 hazardous products after losing its legal battle against the US Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC). The US District Court for the District of Maryland [ruled in favor](https://www.cpsc.gov/Newsroom/News-Releases/2027/Federal-Court-Rules-in-Favor-of-CPSC-in-Landmark-E-Commerce-Product-Safety-Case) of the CPSC, [which argued that Amazon is a distributor of goods](https://www.theverge.com/2024/7/30/24209953/amazon-notify-customers-recalled-items-cpsc), not a logistics provider, making it responsible for carrying out recalls of third-party products.

[Amazon sued the CPSC in March 2025](https://www.theverge.com/news/631435/amazon-cpsc-lawsuit-recall-third-party-products) after the agency ordered Amazon to recall over 400,000 "Fulfilled by Amazon" products that pose a "substantial product hazard," including faulty carbon monoxide detectors, hair dryers without electrocution protection, and child …

items.title: DNGDNGDNG ~ Vestigio
items.subtitle: There is something strangely archival about Vestigio, the latest album by Peruvian duo DNGDNGDNG (formerly Dengue Dengue Dengue).

items.body:
There is something strangely archival about *Vestigio*, the latest album by Peruvian duo **DNGDNGDNG** (formerly Dengue Dengue Dengue). Its rhythms and sonic patterns have an uncanny familiarity, as though they belonged to an established musical tradition, yet their origins are difficult to locate precisely. They seem to come from a geographical territory that has yet to be mapped, let alone explored. The artwork by [Joseph Melhuish](https://www.instagram.com/josephmelhuish/) reinforces this impression, depicting mysterious objects that might be archaeological remains of an unknown civilisation, past or future.

The recognisably Peruvian elements of their earlier releases have become harder to identify. As the duo explained in our interview, they are no longer interested in reproducing traditional rhythms but in extracting certain characteristics and rebuilding them in unfamiliar contexts. This is what gives *Vestigio* its peculiar character: the music feels familiar without quite belonging anywhere. Rhythmic structures drawn from different traditions are dismantled and recombined with influences from deconstructed club and drum and bass. On “Inercia”, fractured beats and abrupt shifts in rhythm create a sense of constant movement, an approach revisited on “Purpúrea”. Clipping, distortion and resonance are integral to the percussion itself, rather than effects added afterwards. The result is an ebullient album whose rhythmic vocabulary seems to have been invented from fragments of several different musical cultures.

There is also a darker side to *Vestigio*, most explicitly expressed in the closing track, “Noche Obscura”. Its title references the *dark night of the soul*, a period of spiritual crisis and eventual awakening. The voices declaring “Están matándonos” (They are killing us) and “¡Nunca más!” (Never again) give the piece an unmistakable political significance. As the duo explained, the track reflects their opposition to state violence and oppression, informed by Peru’s political reality but extending to conflicts and human rights abuses elsewhere.

The title *Vestigio* refers to something that survives a transformation. Here, traces of Peruvian musical traditions remain embedded in the rhythms, but their origins have become almost impossible to identify. What makes the album so intriguing is precisely this tension between recognition and disorientation: the sense of hearing something familiar while being unable to say exactly where it comes from.

Photo by Alejandro Loayza Grisi: Masks by Tween Muizen

To learn more, we reached out to Felipe and Rafael.

**Vestigio is described as your most radical sonic departure to date, with familiar elements of your music broken apart and reconstructed. How did this transformation come about, and what traces of your earlier work, from [Zenit & Nadir](https://denguedenguedengue.bandcamp.com/album/zenit-nadir) to [Fiebre](https://denguedenguedengue.bandcamp.com/album/fiebre) and [Agita2](https://denguedenguedengue.bandcamp.com/album/agita2), do you recognise in the new album?**

I think *Agita2* was something of a precursor to *Vestigio*. It was already pointing toward the sonic direction we wanted to explore on the album. Maybe not every track, but several of them contain some of that essence.

There’s also something of the darkness of *Fiebre*, certain percussive elements, and some connections to *Zenit & Nadir*. I think the album contains a little bit of each of our previous records.

The idea was to take specific elements from our music, break them apart, and reconstruct them in a different context. Not necessarily to bring back a sound exactly as it was, but to transform it and take it somewhere else.

At the same time, we wanted to push the energy and intensity of those elements much further. I think that combination of deconstruction, reconstruction, and the search for greater intensity is one of the main ideas behind *Vestigio*.

**In earlier interviews, you spoke enthusiastically about Afro-Peruvian polyrhythms and the possibilities of combining live percussion with electronics. On Vestigio, rhythm seems to emerge from the interaction of distortion, clipping and resonance, often becoming jagged and unstable. How has your approach to rhythm and sound design evolved, and what role do traditional Peruvian musical forms still play in your compositions?**

On this album, we tried to work more with compositions built from scratch. We still use samples and recordings, but we don’t necessarily build the tracks around them anymore.

Now we’re more interested in capturing the essence or feeling of certain rhythms and musical elements, then transforming them and placing them in a different context.

Traditional Peruvian rhythms are still part of our musical language, but we no longer feel the need to reference them directly or reproduce them in a recognizable way.

That gives us more freedom to create music that doesn’t necessarily belong to a specific genre.

For example, there are elements of Pandilla music and other rhythmic traditions, but we’re not trying to recreate those sounds. We’re interested in taking certain characteristics, breaking them apart, and using them to build something different.

In that sense, the idea of breaking things down and reconstructing them also describes our current approach to rhythm and sound design.

**Your back catalogue reveals an appetite for unlikely musical encounters, from reworking [Chabuca Granda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chabuca_Granda) and [Zambo Cavero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_%22Zambo%22_Cavero) to combining shoegaze with dembow on [BambaPack](https://denguedenguedengue.bandcamp.com/album/bambapack-vol-1). More recently, you’ve collaborated with Prisma on Abisal, while Vestigio features [Los Hijos de Lamas](https://www.instagram.com/loshijosdelamas/), [Siete Catorce](https://www.instagram.com/sietecatorce/?hl=en) and [Only Now](https://www.instagram.com/kusharora/). What attracts you to these collaborations, and how do they challenge or expand your musical vocabulary?**

We’ve always been interested in collaborating with artists whose music we admire. They’re usually projects we’ve been following for a long time and that make us curious, especially when we hear something that surprises us and makes us wonder how they came up with that sound.

I think an important part of collaborating is precisely that curiosity about how other people develop their ideas and what can happen when we combine them with our own.

Experimentation and fusion have always been fundamental to Dengue Dengue Dengue, so working with other artists is a natural extension of that philosophy. It allows us to bring in new perspectives and reach places we might not have reached on our own.

…

items.body:
** The latest on Trump’s approval rating**

**Updated November 24, 2026**

After rebounding slightly to 38 percent, Donald Trump’s approval rating is back on the downswing. **Today, 37 percent of Americans approve of the job he’s doing, while 60 percent disapprove**.

Show more Show less

Just 18.9 percent of Americans *strongly* approve of Trump, dangerously close to the 18.3 percent who *weakly* approve. If the president continues to get less popular, those figures could flip in the not too distant future. **-EMD** **, 11/17/26**

**See also: [Iran War support dashboard](https://www.natesilver.net/p/iran-war-polls-popularity-approval).**

This is the landing page for Silver Bulletin presidential approval ratings. We’ll regularly update the charts below as new polls about Donald Trump’s approval rating come in.1 This page is designed to be [viewed on the web](https://tinyurl.com/3fzxm9wc) rather than in our email client or in the Substack app.

[Click here for more information on how the average works](https://www.natesilver.net/p/silver-bulletin-polling-average-methodology). The Silver Bulletin average weights more reliable polls heavily — you can **[find our latest pollster ratings here](https://www.natesilver.net/p/pollster-ratings-silver-bulletin)**.

### The topline: So, just how popular is Trump?

Our default average reflects a combination of all polls, whether conducted among adults, registered voters or likely voters. If a pollster releases multiple versions of the same survey, we use the all-adult version of the poll before the registered voter version.2 This is because all Americans have a say in how popular the president is — whether or not they vote.

### The polls: What do the surveys say?

Each poll gets an “influence” score based on its pollster rating, its sample size, its recency, and how often a pollster is publishing numbers.3 Sometimes, surveys with mediocre pollster ratings have more weight in the model just because they were conducted very recently or polled more people.

Inevitably, there’s a lot of disagreement from survey to survey, not just because of [statistical variation](https://www.natesilver.net/p/dont-let-randomness-make-a-fool-of) but because pollsters have [long had trouble pegging down Trump’s popularity](https://www.natesilver.net/p/polling-is-becoming-more-of-an-art). By clicking on the “adjusted results” tab, you can see how [the “house effects” adjustment](https://www.natesilver.net/p/silver-bulletin-polling-average-methodology) that corrects for these predictable differences works in our model. You can also **[click here to download every Trump approval poll in our database](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/e/2PACX-1vS-FKWVTTFtJT6u56e0bqdfoMcXvDO1DUChsJ3jQAMB2lZk2SMqVfmg7dGjclTYkYWz-Pm5lfcLPjp4/pub?output=csv)** — including some additional details not shown in the chart below.

### The issues: What do Americans think of Trump’s policies?

Pollsters don’t just ask about Trump’s overall job approval, they also ask about how well he’s dealing with different issues. We’re tracking how the public feels about Trump’s handling of four topics: the economy, immigration, trade and tariffs, and the cost of living.

[↗ natesilver.net](https://www.natesilver.net/p/trump-approval-ratings-nate-silver-bulletin)
