items.body:
I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months.

Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply.

Coding agents in November 2025

Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model.

In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said:

Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.

This held up.

Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025.

Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant.

The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself.

Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks.

The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work.

Fable class models in June/July

We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them.

In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work.

After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st.

For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models. My definition of these:

In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug.

A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm.

Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook.

I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well.

These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model.

3D modeling and game development in September/October

Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for.

I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example.

3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa.

Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game. It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play.

I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play!

Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked. My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay.

Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time.

Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games.

The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster.

It feels like another inflection point to me.

Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too?

I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement.

I'm getting so much done with that model right now!

It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42, 1.0a43, and 1.0a44 - plus LLM 0.37, 0.37.1, 0.37.2, 0.37.3, and 0.38 - all in the last three weeks, represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements.

If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it. That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks.

Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don't think I'll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand.

items.body:
With Thanksgiving tomorrow, I want to express my appreciation for everyone who contributed to this year’s Slow Boring slate of candidates and offer an update on how we did. I also wanted to call out and thank Ethan Winter. He’s a friend whose day job is at Mind the Gap, an organization that provides research-driven guidance to donors on the most cost-effective strategies for protecting and supporting American democracy. He’s done a ton of behind-the-scenes work on these Slow Boring slates and finally received permission from his bosses to take a public bow.

Here’s a nice summary of our slate of candidates. They, thanks to what was obviously a very strong election overall for Democrats, mostly won. When looking at this chart for the purposes of assessing our judgment, it’s worth recalling that not only was the national climate very blue, but it was also [a bit more than four points bluer](https://www.callthemap.com/polls/scorecard-2026) than the publicly available information suggested. I obviously would love to have private information about the real state of public opinion, but even though polling error is real, [nobody has unearthed a reliable way](https://www.slowboring.com/p/is-the-blue-wave-forecast-by-polling) of out-guessing the polls. So when you look at Slow Boring money that went into races like the Senate contests in Iowa and Alaska, those are the ones that a reasonable person would have assumed were on the knife’s edge.

In light of [what we now know](https://www.slowboring.com/p/what-i-got-wrong-about-the-midterms) about the results in South Carolina, Mississippi, and Louisiana, it seems like some reassessment of electoral dynamics in the Deep South is warranted. Some of this is probably differential turnout effects that wouldn’t be present in a presidential election year, but it’s definitely something I’ll be thinking about as we head into the next cycle.

That being said, the point of the Slow Boring slate — somewhat in contrast to Mind the Gap’s mainline work — isn’t just to identify high-leverage races but to help build a bench and a pipeline for pragmatic, culturally moderate, pro-growth Democrats who can change the trajectory of the party and the country. And I think we made great progress on those fronts. For paid subscribers, we dig into individual races and lessons learned below.

#### Two who lost

items.body:
Kagi, a small, Palo Alto, California-based software company that provides a subscription-based search engine as an alternative to Google, has launched a Gmail-like e-mail service. Dubbed Kagi Mail, it makes many of the same claims as the search engine product: privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization, and control.

Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service. Right now, both the email and calendar interfaces are web-only, but native Android and iOS apps are planned for the fourth quarter of next year.

The email interface, currently in public beta, is minimalist. It emphasizes keyboard commands, as well as a private and ad-free experience. (You can see more details in Kagi's [blog post](https://blog.kagi.com/kagi-mail-public-beta) about what they mean by private.) Other feature offerings include unlimited aliases and domains, an anti-lock-in policy for user data, 50GB of storage, rule-based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional, off-by-default AI features, like chatting with an agent to search email history, do large-scale re-labeling, or define additional filtering rules.

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/11/google-search-alternative-kagi-launches-gmail-rival/)

items.body:
**AINews by Latent Space**

[Scott Aaronson was still trying to digest two proofs of VP ≠ VNP](https://scottaaronson.blog/?p=10379) at dinner. Before dessert, an [OpenAI paper claimed that the square matrix multiplication exponent ω is exactly 9/4](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/The-matrix-multiplication-exponent-is-nine-fourths-November-24-2026/README.md). During dessert, [another paper claimed matching upper and lower bounds for the finite Fourier transform](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/The-logarithmic-exponent-of-finite-Fourier-transforms-November-24-2026/README.md). **The lower bound is the biggest news.** In October, [OpenAI found an upper bound for ω down to at most 9/4](https://github.com/openai/math/tree/main/preprints/Matrix-Multiplication-Nine-Fourths-October-2-2026). Finding the lower bound = upper bound leaves only one possible value, which is a shocking result for most.

We plotted **64 selected AI-assisted research advances** so far this year. November accounts for 20, including [six preprints from Google’s Cogentic](https://github.com/google-research/google-research/commit/4a7bc8ab0bc7). The curve follows public releases, including proofs still under review. We count the two VP ≠ VNP proofs once and give October’s faster matrix multiplication algorithm and November’s matching lower bound an entry each.

The big releases underline how much a paper count can hide. [OpenAI’s catalogue](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/CONTENTS.md) lists 730 manuscripts across 375 result families, including follow-ups and companion arguments. Its [revision log](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/history.md#october-7-2026) also records three October withdrawals after a sign error in one paper affected two others. [Yupan Liu showed that two messages suffice for quantum interactive proofs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31236), a result that would have been a big deal on its own. [Aaronson says](https://scottaaronson.blog/?p=10379) Liu used AI and that he had to remind himself the result had even happened.

In other big news, today’s guest [Thariq Shihipar announced his big move from Anthropic to OpenAI](https://x.com/trq212/status/2125675533761671405), the second high profile Ant→OAI move in recent times [after Cat Wu](https://x.com/latentspacepod/status/2118151813555945505). We dive into his two philosophies of AI and how and where /humans add taste.

AI News for 11/25/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, [544 Twitters](https://twitter.com/i/lists/1585430245762441216) and no further Discords. [AINews' website](https://news.smol.ai/) lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, [AINews is now a section of Latent Space](https://latent.space/p/2026/). You can opt in/out of email frequencies!

## AI Twitter Recap

**AI-Generated Math Results: Matmul Exponent, Factoring and Lean Proofs**

- Matrix multiplication exponent: OpenAI's model claims a lower bound matching its October upper bound, making ω exactly 9/4. Previously no nontrivial lower bound was known ([@SebastienBubeck](https://x.com/SebastienBubeck/status/2125402576145572334); [repo](https://x.com/rrwilliams/status/2125393802554757618)). Mechanism: The result reportedly comes through an explicit superlinear circuit lower bound ([@wjmzbmr1](https://x.com/wjmzbmr1/status/2125428207835107449)).
- Implications: Bubeck notes that a prior Lee et al. result implies LPs solvable in n^{9/4}. He also says LPs can now be solved in strongly polynomial time, a Smale problem ([follow-up](https://x.com/SebastienBubeck/status/2125404169788063915)).
- Expert reaction: Omri Weinstein calls it "truly surreal" if correct, since most experts expected ω = 2 ([@WeinsteinOmri](https://x.com/WeinsteinOmri/status/2125608241828651215)).
- OpenAI batch: Nine new papers with Lean proofs came out a day after a claimed VP ≠ VNP proof ([summary](https://x.com/kimmonismus/status/2125492193351610707)). Other claims: Fourier transform complexity of n√log n ([@lreyzin](https://x.com/lreyzin/status/2125450712754638960)).
- Integer multiplication: Also n√log n, tight under weak ETH ([@cloneofsimo](https://x.com/cloneofsimo/status/2125437206160638185)).
- Same-day solutions: Anthropic posted its own VP ≠ VNP solution the same day ([@vitaliychiley](https://x.com/vitaliychiley/status/2125407887401054245)).
- Google Cogentic: Six papers were posted to GitHub without an announcement, produced by an agent harness on unnamed Gemini 4 models ([@AndrewCurran_](https://x.com/AndrewCurran_/status/2125596087520223658); [details](https://x.com/dummerspast39/status/2125547001433526759)). Results: A proven NFS-class factoring bound, beating a 1992 record. Also claimed: Deterministic subexponential factoring.
- Faster small-characteristic discrete log.
- A 1/5 Nash approximation.
- Progress below the square-root barrier on log-rank.
- Edge reconstruction for linear-density graphs.
- Crypto caveat: A Claude-generated analysis argues RSA and ECC are unaffected ([@teortaxesTex](https://x.com/teortaxesTex/status/2125561229464711363)).
- Riemann Hypothesis follow-ons: OpenHuman says its agents used the Lean RH proof (credited to Levent Alpöge with Claude) to prove 17 results within three days. These include Lindelöf and Erdős #985 ([@ladyxtel](https://x.com/ladyxtel/status/2125587817082601587)).
- Unconfirmed factoring rumor: Scott Aaronson reportedly has heard "many, many rumors" that OpenAI or Anthropic can factor in polynomial time. This is unverified ([@kimmonismus](https://x.com/kimmonismus/status/2125602411540566221)). Context: Igor Babuschkin argues that an LLM-found classical algorithm is a nearer RSA risk than Shor ([@ibab](https://x.com/ibab/status/2125652277931520090)).

**Frontier Model Competition: Gemini 4 Neon, Fable 5.2, GPT-6.2 Astra**

items.body:
On Nov. 25, 1970, an experimental aircraft called the Northrop M2-F3 made its first powered flight.

The [M2-F3 aircraft](https://www.space.com/25591-m2-f3-in-flight-launch-from-the-b-52-mothership.html) was a heavyweight "lifting body" designed to test its ability to produce most of its lift through its fuselage instead of wings. It's commonly referred to as a "wingless" aircraft.

After [Air Force test pilot Bill Dana](https://www.space.com/amp/25790-nasa-x-15-pilot-bill-dana-obituary.html) took the M2-F3 on three unpowered glide test flights, he did the first powered flight, too. Dana soared to an altitude of 45,000 feet during this flight, which lasted just over 6 minutes. He didn't break the sound barrier this time, but he did on later flights.

The M2-F3 flew a total of 27 missions in its three-year flight history. Its top speed was 1.6 times the speed of sound, and its top altitude was 71,500 feet.

NASA's M2-F3 lifting body drops from its carrier plane during a test flight in 1970. (Image credit: NASA)

## Why it mattered

In the late 1960s and early 1970s, NASA was investigating lifting bodies as an approach to both new aircraft and what future spacecraft, and as its number suggests, the M2-F3 was not the first of its kind.

In fact, the M2-F3 was a rebuilt version of its predecessor, the [M2-F2 lifting body](https://www.space.com/25511-pilot-milt-thompson-and-the-m2-f2-lifting-body.html), after that vehicle crashed in a dry lake bed in California's Mojave Desert during an unpowered test flight. That crash (which appears in the opening of the TV show "The Six-Million-Dollar Man") led to upgrades for a better handling lifting body, NASA said.

"When the M2-F2 was rebuilt and redesignated the M2-F3, it was modified with an additional third vertical fin – centered between the tip fins – to improve control characteristics," NASA [wrote in an overview](https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/where-are-they-now-m2-f3-lifting-body/).

Unpowered glide flights for the M2-F3 began in June 1970, but Dana's flight on Nov. 25 of that year was the first time the vehicle fired up its rocket engine to test its controls under powered flight. One vital upgrade on the vehicle was a set of reaction control thrusters to help maintain its orientation.

"A reaction jet control system, similar to thrusters used on orbiting spacecraft, was also installed on the M2-F3 to obtain research data about their effectiveness for vehicle control," [NASA wrote](https://www.nasa.gov/aeronautics/nasa-aircraft/lifting-bodies/). "As the M2-F3’s portion of the lifting body program neared an end, it evaluated a rate command augmentation control system and a side-arm control stick similar to side-arm controllers now used on many modern aircraft."

If you want, you can see the M2-F3 vehicle today. NASA donated it to the Smithsonian Institution. It is now hanging at the [National Air and Space Museum](https://www.space.com/17783-smithsonian-national-air-space-museum-photos.html) in Washington, D.C.

Want more space history? Check out our[full On This Day In Space Story archive](https://www.space.com/tag/on-this-day-in-space) and watch our[On This Day In Space videos on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLCE-SVF9BSTdloyi4P9TmQVTp9Q2zTb27).

This is the weekly visible open thread. Post about anything you want, ask random questions, whatever. ACX has an unofficial [subreddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/slatestarcodex/), [Discord](https://discord.gg/RTKtdut), and [bulletin board](https://www.datasecretslox.com/index.php), and [in-person meetups around the world](https://www.lesswrong.com/community?filters%5B0%5D=SSC). Most content is free, some is subscriber only; you can subscribe **here**. Also:

**1:**In [The AI Forecasting Agenda](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/the-ai-forecasting-agenda), I mentioned three AI forecasting companies. My goal was to name everyone in the space and not play favorites, but this field is moving so fast that I inevitably missed someone, and in this case it was**[Cassi](https://www.cassi-ai.com/)**, a British startup which is currently the top-ranked AI on [Metaculus’ leaderboard](https://www.metaculus.com/leaderboard/). The Cassi team kindly wrote [a post responding to my agenda](https://substack.com/home/post/p-226170904) - most notably, they are pretty confident in their conditional forecasts and say they’re already providing them to institutional paid customers.

If you’re another AI forecasting startup I forgot to mention, feel free to get in touch with me at scott@slatestarcodex.com. Again, I’m not trying to play favorites (although companies that give me free demo access are naturally more likely to have results from their products mentioned in posts).

items.body:
# The Small But Mighty Brains of Bumblebees - Nautilus

## The Small But Mighty Brains of Bumblebees

Sometimes the best thinkers come in tiny packages

11:00 AM CST on November 25, 2026

Bright macro shoot of the bumblebee sitting on the colourful flower. High quality photo

As humans, we credit our large brains, which contain upward of 86 million neurons , for our intelligence. But our superiority complex has been gradually dampened as other tiny-brained species, such as bumblebees , prove able to rival us on at least some cognitive tasks. In a recent commentary published in Science , biologists reviewed the brain capabilities of bumblebees (genus Bombus ), asking, “What are the minimal neural requirements for intelligence itself?”

The study authors, biologists Lars Chittka at Queen Mary University of London and Stanley Heinze at Lund University in Sweden, reviewed the cognitive feats that bees have been able to accomplish—for example, rolling a ball to climb up and reach nectar in an enclosure too cramped for flying and learning to move latches to open puzzle boxes.

Read more: “ Bumblebees Bounce to the Beat ”

At the same time, bumblebee brains contain fewer than a million nerve cells, a pittance of circuitry compared to our great network. So, their intelligence—defined in this study as “the ability to adapt to new situations by using cognition rather than instinct or trial and error”—stems from something else. The researchers explored aspects of bee brain architecture that might explain not only their problem-solving skills but also their “emotional contagion,” whereby bees transmit optimism about an anticipated food reward to nestmates.

Bumblebee brains contain a “mushroom body,” a region where associative memories are made in special neurons called Kenyon cells. It’s found in some other invertebrates as well, but bees have the monopoly with about 50 times more than, for instance, a fruit fly, a difference that could explain bees’ superior memory capacity. The study authors noted that the mushroom body architecture looks like the hippocampus in mammals, the area responsible for memories and recall. Maybe, they hypothesized, the “increased complexity of the mushroom body in bumblebees could have led to the evolution of additional, hippocampus-like circuits that conduct advanced com­putations such as pattern completion.”

Compared to fruit fly brains, bumblebees also have extra neural wiring associated with navigation, explaining how their brains calculate the optimal routes between multiple food sources—like a built-in GPS system. Plus, bumblebees have a more elaborate neuromodulatory system, which likely allows them to more subtly distinguish “between similar but not identical situations that might otherwise evoke the same action.”

It remains to be determined whether these special brain features evolved as neural wiring customizations on a simpler insect brain or just gradual boosts in computational abilities.

Regardless, it’s hard not to consider bumblebees as big-brained—no matter how tiny their physical brains might be.

items.body:
# Börsen: An den Finanzmärkten verstärkt sich die Flucht aus Risikoanlagen

Wall Street in New York: Eine Trendwende nach oben ist nicht in Sicht. Foto: Bloomberg Zusammenfassung Nutzen Sie komprimierte Kernaussagen für maximale Effizienz in Ihrem News-Alltag – verfügbar im H+ Standard Abo. Jetzt für 1 € testen Frankfurt. Die Angst vor einem KI-Crash hat die US-Börsen weiter fest im Griff. Auch am Mittwoch sind die Märkte mit hohen Verlusten in den Handel gegangen. Die technologielastige Nasdaq fiel im frühen New Yorker Handel um 4,3 Prozent. Der Leitindex S&P 500 lag drei Prozent im Minus.

Besonders Technologiewerte gehörten erneut zu den großen Verlierern. Damit ist der positive Effekt vom Wochenbeginn verpufft, als die überraschende Rückkehr von Jensen Huang an die Spitze von Nvidia eine kräftige Erleichterungsrally auslöste.

Nun wird an der Wall Street intensiv über eine unbequeme Frage diskutiert: Was kann die Angst der Anleger jetzt stoppen?

## Das XEN FX Delay auf dem iPad

Anfang November ist das Liquid Sky d-vices Zen FX Lab als Plugin erschienen. Dabei handelt es sich um den Nachfolger der Zen Delay Software. Jetzt hat sich Liquid Sky d-vices dazu entschieden, das Effekt Plugin auch für das iPad herauszubringen.

## Gibt es Unterschiede zwischen der iPad Version und der PC-Version?

Die Funktionen unterscheiden sich nicht von der Plugin-Version. Allerdings lässt sich das Zen FX Lab jetzt über den Touchscreen des iPads bedienen und als AUv3 Plugin in iPad DAWs einbinden.

## Preis und Verfügbarkeit für die iPad Version

**Zum Einführungspreis ist Zen FX Lab für 9,99 Euro im [Apple App Store](https://apps.apple.com/de/app/xen-fx-lab/id6815805463)erhältlich. Nach der Einführungsphase wird der Preis auf 17,99 Euro steigen.**

## Das XEN FX Delay

Xen FX Lab ist die überarbeitete Version des Zen Delay Virtual und dieses basiert auf dem Zen Delay. Das Plugin kombiniert Delay, Filter und Spring Reverb mit umfangreichen Modulationsmöglichkeiten und richtet sich an alle, die mehr als klassische Echoeffekte suchen. Die neue Version bringt zusätzliche Funktionen und eröffnet Möglichkeiten für ungewöhnliches und kreatives Sounddesign.

Im Folgenden konzentriere ich mich auf die Neuerungen von XEN FX DELAY. Wer über genauere Details informiert werden möchte, kann sich folgende Tests durchlesen:

[Hier geht es zum Test des Zen Delay Virtual](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/erica-synths-zen-delay-virtual-test/)

[Hier geht es zum Test der Zen Delay Hardware.](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/ninja-tune-zen-delay-test/)

## Was kann das XEN FX DELAY?

Die Umbenennung in Xen FX Lab war ein guter Schritt. Denn bei diesem Plugin handelt es sich um weit mehr als ein einfaches Delay. Es ist eine richtig fette Sounddesign Maschine, mit der man wirklich ungewöhnliche klangliche Ergebnisse erzielen kann, die weit über das hinausgehen, was ein reguläres Delay schafft. Dabei helfen die unglaublichen vielfältigen Modulationsmöglichkeiten für das Delay, das Filter und das neu hinzugekommene Spring Reverb.

## Die Neuerungen: Das Hauptmenü

Auffällig ist das UFO Logo in der Mitte der Software, an dessen Stelle sich früher die Röhre befand. Links und rechts davon finden sich nun zwei Slider, mit denen sich die verschiedenen Delay-Zeiten und Filtertypen einstellen lassen.

Ansonsten hat sich am Layout nicht viel geändert. Links befindet sich wie gewohnt die Einstellung für das Delay. Rechts sind die Filter und Drive Sektion sowie ein Regler zur Anpassung des Eingangssignals untergebracht.

Xen FX Lab Hauptmenü Bildquelle: Liquid Sky D-vices )

## Das Spring Reverb

Neu ist das Spring Reverb, das über einen ausgeprägt metallischen Charakter verfügt. Für die Klanggestaltung stehen die Parameter Mix, Tension, Tone, Decay und Regen zur Verfügung. Damit lassen sich typische Spring-Reverb-Effekte erzeugen, aber auch extreme Klangwelten erschaffen. Manchmal klingt es so, als befände man sich in einem riesigen Tanklaster oder in einem ausgehöhlten Todesstern aus Star Wars. Einfach verrückt.

Xen FX Lab Presets (Bildquelle: Liquid Sky D-vices )

## Die Dub Funktion

Besonders interessant ist die neue Dub Funktion. Mit einem Knopfdruck lassen sich die Delay, Filter und Spring Reverb Effekte ein und ausschalten. So kann man dem trockenen Signal gezielt zusätzliche Effekte hinzufügen. Jeder Parameter von Xen FX Lab lässt sich automatisieren. Auch die Dub Funktion kann automatisiert und per MIDI angesteuert werden. Dadurch lassen sich Delays taktgenau und punktuell zum trockenen Signal hinzumischen.

Xen FX Lab Modulationsmatrix ist schon Teil des Zen Delay Virtual (Bildquelle: Liquid Sky D-vices )

## Die neue MIDI-Zuweisung

Neu ist das MIDI-DIN Anschluss Symbol. Wird die MIDI-Zuweisung aktiviert legt sich eine Maske über die Bedienelemente des Plugins, mit der man MIDI-CC Befehle zuweisen kann. Dadurch kann man Xen FX Lab schnell und einfach einem externen MIDI-Controller zuweisen.

Xen FX Lab MIDI-CC Zuweisung (Bildquelle: Liquid Sky D-vices )

## Die Geschichte des XEN FX LAB

2019 veröffentlichten Ninja Tune, Liquid Sky D-vices und Erica Synths gemeinsam das Desktop Effektgerät Zen Delay. Dabei handelt es sich um ein digitales Delay, einen analogen Filter und eine Röhre, mit der sich warme Verzerrungen erzeugen lassen.

2023 veröffentlichte das Team die Software Zen Delay Virtual, die auf Basis des Desktop Modells entwickelt wurde. Unter dem Namen Xen FX Lab erscheint jetzt eine neue Version des Plugins, die ausschließlich unter der Marke Liquid Sky D-vices veröffentlicht wird und mit vielen neuen Funktionen ausgestattet ist.

## Wer hat das XEN FX LAB Entwickelt?

Xen FX Lab wurde von Coldcut Mastermind Matt Black, Dr. Walker von Air Liquide und Benjamin Weiß (TokTok), entwickelt.

**Ninja Tune und Erica Synths sind an der Entwicklung des Plugins nicht mehr beteiligt. Für Support und weitere Fragen zum Plugin wendet ihr euch daher direkt an [Liquid Sky D-vices.](https://liquidskyeurope.com/products/xen_fx_lab)**

## Preis und Verfügbarkeit für die PC Version

**Xen FX Lab ist ab sofort für 25.00 Euro erhältich.**

**Besitzer der ersten Version erhalten ein kostenloses Upgrade. Wenn ihr bei der Plugin Boutique eingekauft habt, erhaltet ihr dort ein kostenloses Update.**

**Thomann Kunden müssen sich unter HQs@liquidskyartistcollective.com mit dem Betreff “Zen Delay Virtual Update” melden. Für das kostenlose Update wird ausserdem die ilok Nummer von Thomann benötigt, um es schnell und unkompliziert durchführen zu können.**

**Zum Einführungspreis ist Zen FX Lab für das iPad für 9,99 Euro im [Apple App Store](https://apps.apple.com/de/app/xen-fx-lab/id6815805463)erhältlich. Nach der Einführungsphase wird der Preis auf 17,99 Euro steigen.**

items.body:
The Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative at *Lean community blog*:

On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge [released](https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf) a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code.

We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement.

Our rationale is outlined below.

The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof’s correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in [https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/](https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/) are all satisfied.

More [↗ leanprover-community.github.io](https://leanprover-community.github.io/blog/posts/riemann-hypothesis/). And more details [↗ hexagonmath.org](https://hexagonmath.org/pdf/2611.01031v1?utm_source=chatgpt.com).

items.body:
When the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists asked Pornhub about its handling of child sexual abuse material and other nonconsensual content, the company’s parent, Aylo, went to court to stop the story.

ICIJ fought back, arguing that the Alabama federal court where Aylo sought a temporary restraining order lacked jurisdiction over it and that the requested injunction would constitute an unconstitutional prior restraint under the First Amendment.

The court denied Aylo’s motion on Nov. 16, and ICIJ immediately published [the story Aylo didn’t want readers to see](https://www.icij.org/news/2026/11/he-used-pornhub-as-the-gun/). But a separate question remains: whether ICIJ will be required to identify to the judge a confidential source who provided court records used in its investigation.

U.S. District Judge Annemarie Carney Axon directed ICIJ to explain why it should not be required to disclose the source’s identity privately to the court. The judge’s inquiry concerns a specific court record identifying victims of child sexual abuse, which was among a larger collection of records provided to ICIJ by its source. In its response, filed on Nov. 23, ICIJ argued that the court has no authority to force it to identify its confidential source and that doing so would violate important First Amendment protections for journalists.

The documents, which were filed in a class action lawsuit against Aylo-related companies alleging they knowingly and unlawfully profited from child sexual abuse material, were supposed to have been sealed, but were inadvertently made publicly available on the court’s electronic records system, where they remained for eight months. ICIJ later obtained copies from a confidential source.

Those records then formed the basis of an ICIJ investigation revealing how Aylo’s profits were built in part on allowing [“some of the most heinous material on the internet”](https://www.icij.org/news/2026/11/he-used-pornhub-as-the-gun/) to remain on its platforms despite warnings from victims and law enforcement.

That investigation is now at the center of a legal dispute that threatens a fundamental principle of press freedom: journalists must be able to protect confidential sources while investigating powerful interests and exposing wrongdoing.

items.body:
A D.C.-area train commuter photographed a White House staffer’s laptop and notes, which showed a draft plan for the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History. Photo illustration by Jovelle Tamayo/ProPublica. Source images: obtained by ProPublica, Elizabeth Frantz for ProPublica.

A top congressional Democrat announced she will investigate the Trump White House’s potential overhaul of the leadership and curatorial decisions at the Smithsonian Institution, the independent agency that oversees 21 national museums.

In a [letter sent on Tuesday](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28932104-pingree-letter-to-smithsonian-board-of-regents-112426/) to the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents, Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine, cited ProPublica’s [recent story](https://www.propublica.org/article/dc-metro-smithsonian-american-history-plan) on the draft plans by a White House staffer targeting one of the Smithsonian’s most prominent museums, calling the reporting “extremely concerning.”

### Read More

[Spotted on the D.C. Metro: Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveals Plan for Smithsonian Overhaul](https://www.propublica.org/article/dc-metro-smithsonian-american-history-plan)

Pingree, who is slated to lead the subcommittee that controls the Smithsonian’s funding in the next Congress, said the plans revealed in the ProPublica story align with the administration’s broader efforts to interfere with the Smithsonian, which receives federal funding but is governed by a 17-person [Board of Regents](https://www.si.edu/regents/members) whose members include the chief justice of the United States, members of Congress, the vice president and private citizens.

In an interview with ProPublica, Pingree said that she intended her letter to put the Smithsonian governing board on notice that the incoming Democratic majority in Congress is monitoring the institution to make sure the board upholds its responsibility to keep the agency independent from political pressure.

“No White House employee riding on the Metro gets to design a plan for what future exhibits look like or gets to veto staffers or exhibits at the Smithsonian,” Pingree said. “That’s not how it works.”

Pingree told ProPublica that she plans to use her powers as chair in the next Congress to aggressively look into what she called the Trump administration’s meddling with the Smithsonian and to expose those efforts to the broader American public.

“We fully intend to dig deeper than has been done in the past,” she said.

Pingree’s letter comes in response to [ProPublica reporting](https://www.propublica.org/article/dc-metro-smithsonian-american-history-plan) on a 25-item list of possible changes that, taken together, would amount to an unprecedented attempt by the White House to control the content and personnel of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, which attracts nearly 2 million people a year.

Those reforms include firing many of the museum’s top officials; rolling out a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance”; introducing new K-12 learning materials such as a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage”; and unveiling a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance.

The draft plans were visible on the laptop and in handwritten notes of a White House staffer who was riding a D.C.-area Metro train in late October. A nearby commuter took pictures of the materials and sent them to ProPublica reporters, who in turn verified the information. It’s unclear what kind of reception the plans have received inside the Trump White House. The staffer and White House did not respond to requests for comment for the story.

Also on Tuesday, Lonnie Bunch, the Smithsonian Institution’s outgoing leader, responded to ProPublica’s reporting in a message sent to employees. “The intended use of this list is unclear,” [Bunch wrote in his letter](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/24/arts/design/smithsonian-letter-lonnie-bunch-white-house.html). “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.”

Pingree was not the only member of Congress who responded to ProPublica’s reporting with a pledge to defend the Smithsonian’s independence.

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., said on social media that if he becomes chair of the Senate Rules Committee — which has jurisdiction over the Smithsonian — in the next Congress, “we will protect it from Trump’s interference and overreach.”

“The Smithsonian is NOT a federal agency, it is an independent, nonpartisan organization overseen by Congress – not the White House,” [Padilla wrote](https://x.com/SenAlexPadilla/status/2124947929043505203).

Incoming Congressman Fred Wellman, a Democrat elected this month to represent the suburbs of St. Louis, responded even more forcefully to ProPublica’s reporting on social media.

“Over my dead body,” [he wrote](https://www.threads.com/@fpwellmanofficial/post/DgFyTWblpIR?xmt=AQG0mFncIHQHKzvQkl8yN5zOI1ytrh7zEwvWhjZofBJF7g).

items.body:
Art by Thomas Cole via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cole_Thomas_The_Course_of_Empire_Destruction_1836.jpg)

Sometime in the mid-2010s, just as liberalism was getting replaced by “progressivism”, the conservatism that I had grown up with was getting replaced by something we then called the “alt-right”. Whereas the old conservatism was based on Christian faith, libertarian economics, and flag-waving patriotism, the alt-right saw America as a white racial nation-state, rejected the idea of free markets, and was basically irreligious and isolationist.

Over the course of two Trump presidencies and one Biden interregnum, the alt-right matured and grew into what I now call [the New Right](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/understanding-americas-new-right). In doing so, it basically took over from conservatism as the guiding ideology of the GOP base — though not (yet) of the GOP as a whole. Whereas the alt-right was a naked white-power movement, the New Right sees things in broader “civilizational” terms. It has embraced the idea of Christianity, not as a faith or a lifestyle, but as a tribal affiliation defining ingroup and outgroup. Its foreign policy matured into something concrete — a desire to [wield American policy on behalf of “Western Civilization”](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-states/new-rights-grand-strategy-after-trump).

At the grassroots level, the New Right also added some new components. It merged with the [Covid antivax movement](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/the-alternate-reality-of-rfk-and) to become skeptical of modern medicine, public health, and life science in general. It partially merged with [the incel movement](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/dating-advice-for-men), telling young men that their sexual frustration was the fault of progressivism. It [veered even more strongly into antisemitism](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/jewish-americans-are-feeling-unsettled), probably feeling liberated to do so by rising antisemitism on the left in the wake of the Gaza war. And it added a strong component of [anti-Indian hatred](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/the-anti-american-right), seeing Indians as a uniquely vulnerable target among recent immigrant groups.

Anyway, it’s too early to say that this movement has *failed*. Yes, the Democrats won one midterm election, but Trump is still the President, and he has shown zero inclination to reverse course on any of his most New Right-aligned policies. He has made Stephen Miller, the ultimate anti-immigration crusader, his chief of staff, and [posted a picture](https://www.nbcnews.com/world/europe/trump-friend-greeting-putin-causes-alarm-europe-ukraine-rcna610373) of himself hugging Vladimir Putin with the caption “My Friend”. Meanwhile, the New Right still has a fairly robust online presence.

But it’s impossible to deny that the winds have shifted. The midterms made it clear that even if the New Right sticks around for the long term, it won’t have a monopoly on power. That will make it essentially impossible for it to follow through on its long-term agenda. Basically, the notion that wokeness and internal disputes would cause the Democrats to permanently collapse as a party has been falsified.

Already, some prominent figures are backing away from the New Right. Elon Musk, who once stood on a stage and declared himself “Dark MAGA”, now says he’s not even MAGA at all, and is instead a political moderate:

And the CEO of Palantir is calling himself a Democrat:

Meanwhile, Bo French, the Texas candidate who lost an election after complaining about Indian fans at a UT football game, has been [kicked out of his country club](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/18/bo-french-texas-country-club-membership-01173063).

The New Right’s online activists and commentators are in a state of deep despair:

Others are tweeting ever more histrionic demands for a civil war that absolutely no one seems interested in actually fighting:

What enthusiasm still *does* exist on the New Right tends to be concentrated on the movement’s most extreme fringe, which focuses on getting attention by bashing Trump and MAGA and saying ridiculous, extremist stuff. For example, *[Politico](https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/11/18/the-far-right-leaves-trump-behind-01172242)* [reports](https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/11/18/the-far-right-leaves-trump-behind-01172242) on the “Christ is King” conference, run by a guy named Joel Webbon:

> [F]or Webbon, the problem was also that MAGA hadn’t gone far enough. He wanted even harsher deportation policies. He wanted a total repudiation of Israel. He wanted to curtail women’s right to vote, to criminalize abortion and homosexuality, and to expel Jews and non-Christians from public office…The event attracted a notorious set of online agitators, including conspiracist Alex Jones and Nick Fuentes, the 28-year-old white nationalist and antisemite, who made a rare public appearance as a guest speaker…
> There are, in Webbon’s telling, few “guys” capable of leading this faction…He did put forward a few “guys” who might fit the bill, naming electoral losers like [James] Fishback, one of the weekend’s main draws, who recently lost [a gubernatorial primary] to a MAGA-backed candidate by 37 points in Florida…Webbon also went on to name Bo French, the far-right candidate for Texas Railroad Commissioner who ultimately lost by some 670,000 votes to a Democrat after making anti-immigration a centerpiece of his campaign.

(There are also various [loonies from overseas](https://vimeo.com/1248089901?fl=pl&fe=vl).)

These are all signs of a movement that’s on the way down. It may return someday — communism sort of did, after all — but its hopes of transforming America over the next few decades are fading. It’s not over yet, but it’s looking more and more that way.

A big part of the reason for that failure, of course, is that Americans simply do not buy what the New Right wants to sell them. Regular Americans [generally like (legal) immigration](https://news.gallup.com/poll/712289/americans-support-immigration-down-strong.aspx), and they [don’t see racial and religious heritage](https://yougov.com/en-us/articles/52636-what-makes-someone-american-heritage-constitution-declaration) as an important determinant of who is a real American. It’s very hard to sell people a product they don’t want.

But there are also various strategic errors that the New Right made. To be clear, I’m *glad* these mistakes were made; I have zero desire to see a movement like the New Right hold power in my country. I just think it’s interesting and instructive to think about what the mistakes were.

items.body:
Conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood. Her parents worked at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and discussions about happenings at the agency continued even when they came home from the office.

“I remember a poignant dialogue we had after the space shuttle Challenger disaster,” Knight recalled. “However, we talked just as much about the engaging work my parents were doing inside Goddard’s gates.”

Her father Lyle Knight was a mechanical engineer, while her mother Julia Knight worked the bulk of her career in human resources. They brought their daughter on center for Take Your Child to Work Day and other events, and over time she became hooked.

“I saw the chambers where spacecraft and instruments were being tested, as well as other facilities used to help further space exploration. Above all, I witnessed the passion and collaborative spirit everyone had at Goddard,” Knight said. “As a child, I found it incredibly fascinating.”

Ashley Knight (right) on a visit to NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md., while her parents were employees.

Photo courtesy of Ashley Knight

It all came full circle in late August when, after growing up around NASA and later working several contractor roles for the agency, Knight and a number of her colleagues in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer were sworn in as federal employees as part of a workforce directive to strengthen the agency’s technical core competencies by bringing mission-critical positions into the civil service.

She began her Goddard career more than two decades ago following graduation from the University of Maryland in nearby College Park. As the job search began after commencement, one organization inevitably stood out, along with one particular mission.

When she came across a contractor job opening at Goddard in support of the Hubble Space Telescope team, Knight jumped at the opportunity.

“Hubble was doing amazing things, and I always admired how they fixed the faulty mirror,” she said, referring to how astronauts and team members corrected an early spherical aberration during the observatory’s first servicing mission. “It was exciting to become involved with such a flagship mission, especially coming right out of college.”

As a project support analyst, Knight assisted engineers with test plans, data gathering, and hardware procurement for Hubble’s fifth and final shuttle servicing mission.

Knight stands in front of space shuttle Atlantis, which was used for the Hubble Space Telescope’s fifth and final shuttle servicing mission, while she was a project support analyst for the Hubble team.

Photo courtesy of Ashley Knight

Following the mission’s completion in 2009 and subsequent end of the Hubble shuttle servicing era, she took on a similar role with the Robotic Refueling Mission in what was then the Satellite Servicing Capabilities Office at Goddard – now known as NASA’s In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing Capabilities Office.

Knight left Goddard momentarily afterward to perform contracting work in support of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory in Washington. After a phone call, she found her way back as a contractor program analyst in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, helping manage labor budgets within programs by avoiding funding lapses and ensuring employees received their paychecks on time.

Following the August ceremony, Knight now carries the title of budget analyst in the Program Analysis Office within the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, performing many of the same critical duties as a civil servant.

“While many functions are similar, transitioning into the civil service makes it easier for my colleagues and I to help keep NASA’s missions going from the financial aspect,” said Knight. “We have more autonomy to perform certain government-related tasks by being on the government side.”

The civil service also provides additional training and growth opportunities for such positions.

“Ashley is a great team player. This conversion is a fantastic milestone because it unlocks new avenues for her learning and development, and allows us to integrate her into new roles,” said Linnette Morales, Knight’s supervisor in the Program Analysis Office. “I am thrilled she can now fully access the opportunities on the civil servant side, immensely benefiting both her continued career growth and our organization.”

The workforce directive, entitled “Restoring NASA’s Core Competencies” and announced by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in February, is part of a broader effort to expand the agency’s critical institutional knowledge, increase resources essential for mission success, and maintain U.S. leadership in space exploration.

“The directive has given our office an opportunity to rebalance positions across the organization and remove limitations that were applied to those who were previously not government employees,” said Lisa Kelleher, Goddard’s chief financial officer. “We are now better able to insource many of our experienced contractor staff, allowing us to build up our in-house core competencies in areas such as budget analysis and accounting, and in turn increase our support for mission success.”

For Knight, she sees an increasing importance for her organization and hopes to make impactful contributions, especially as work taking place at Goddard helps NASA return a crewed mission to the lunar surface, build a Moon Base, and eventually send humans to Mars.

“We’re the go-between between NASA Headquarters and Goddard programs, and it’s our job to make it a seamless transition for projects to use money they’ve been given to help get these projects off the ground,” she said. “It’s both vital and exciting with the lunar and Mars endeavors, and I’m proud to play whatever role I can.”

Decades after first following her parents around center, and now following in their footsteps as a NASA civil servant, Knight is as captivated by Goddard and its people as she was during her early visits.

“Through the years, I’ve noticed everyone remains driven by teamwork and achieving the mission,” she said. “Everybody wants to succeed together by working toward the same goal, and I’m grateful I can continue to be part of it all.”

items.body:
1Password drängt verbliebene Nutzer von Version 7 zum Umstieg auf 1Password 8. Für Besitzer der alten Kaufversion ist das mehr als ein gewöhnliches Update: Die aktuelle Ausgabe setzt [ein Konto beim Anbieter samt Abo voraus](https://support.1password.com/migrate-1password-account/) und unterstützt keine eigenständigen lokalen Tresore mehr.

Eine Einschränkung ist bereits wirksam: Mit dem Mac-Update auf Version 7.10.4 vom 29. September wurde laut [Versionshinweisen](https://app-updates.agilebits.net/product_history/OPM7) die Unterstützung für die klassische Browser-Erweiterung entfernt. Diese war für Browser wie Chrome und Firefox zuständig. Die in 1Password 7 integrierte Safari-Erweiterung ist davon nicht betroffen.

## Mai-Termin gilt für 1Password-Konten

Ab Mai 2027 soll 1Password 7 keine Änderungen mehr mit den Servern des Anbieters synchronisieren. Das betrifft Nutzer mit einer 1Password-Mitgliedschaft. Bereits vorhandene Einträge bleiben auf dem jeweiligen Gerät zugänglich, neue oder geänderte Inhalte werden dann aber nicht mehr zwischen den Geräten abgeglichen.

Wenn man eigenständige Tresore über iCloud oder Dropbox synchronisiert, gilt dieser Stichtag nicht. Das hat der Anbieter am 11. November [in seinem Supportforum klargestellt](https://www.1password.community/announcements-52/psa-1password-7-is-being-retired-upgrade-to-1password-8-25448). Diese Synchronisierung soll auch nach Mai 2027 weiter funktionieren.

Eine dauerhafte Garantie ist das allerdings nicht. 1Password warnt davor, dass künftige Änderungen an macOS oder iOS die alten Apps beeinträchtigen können. Für solche Probleme stellt der Hersteller keine Anpassungen der alten Versionen in Aussicht.

## Gratisjahr für Nutzer lokaler Tresore

Den Umstieg soll ein kostenloses erstes Abo-Jahr erleichtern. Das Angebot richtet sich an Nutzer eigenständiger Tresore und wird bei der Anmeldung über den Hinweis in 1Password 7 automatisch berücksichtigt. Wer bereits eine Mitgliedschaft besitzt, kann Version 8 ohne zusätzlichen Upgrade-Preis verwenden.

Für bisherige Käufer bedeutet der Wechsel nach dem Gratisjahr laufende Kosten. Über die [im Frühjahr angekündigte Erhöhung der Abopreise](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/1password-preiserhoehung-44-statt-32-euro-ab-ende-maerz-273534/) hatten wir berichtet.

[★ iPhone-Ticker bei Google bevorzugen ★](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=iphone-ticker.de)

Der Beitrag [1Password 7: Hersteller drängt Nutzer zum Cloud-Abo](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/1password-7-hersteller-draengt-nutzer-zum-cloud-abo-291413/) Wurde zuerst auf [iphone-ticker.de](https://www.iphone-ticker.de) veröffentlicht.

items.body:
MARK SYKES/SPL/Alamy

There is a story, possibly apocryphal, that when the mathematician G. H. Hardy was about to undertake a dangerous sea voyage, he sent a postcard to a colleague declaring “I have solved the Riemann hypothesis”. Hardy, a staunch atheist, joked that this would prevent his ship from sinking, as God would never let him claim the credit for such a major result without revealing the details of his proof.

Hardy would probably be both astonished and aghast that [we now have what seems to be a proof of the Riemann hypothesis](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2600134-anthropic-mathematician-claims-ai-assisted-proof-of-the-riemann-hypothesis/), a problem that has vexed mathematicians since the 19th century, but that no one yet understands it. The consensus among mathematicians is that the proof, produced with the aid of AI, will hold, but that it will take much more work to make it comprehensible to humans.

However you feel about AI, this is a watershed moment, and one that demonstrates just how little we still understand about the capabilities of the technology. As recently as last month, leading mathematician Terence Tao speculated that AI would eventually solve the Riemann hypothesis, but that it may not happen before 2050. Now, some mathematicians are considering whether their hardest and most infamous remaining problems could be settled within months. In a year that has left mathematicians reeling, this may be the knock-out blow.

> This is a watershed moment, and it shows just how little we understand about AI’s abilities

For non-mathematicians, the fall of the Riemann hypothesis is harder to interpret. In the past year, AI has seen incredible advances in both maths and coding, but it is perhaps no coincidence that in these arenas, with nothing more than computer code, answers can swiftly be checked and iterated upon, allowing for rapid improvement. When it comes to other human endeavours though, from art to zoology, such verification is far harder, involving either the messy physical world, or unknowable human taste – or both. Whether this verification gap can be closed may become the biggest question of our age. Answers on a postcard, please.

[What is the Riemann hypothesis and why is its solution so monumental? It has been called the hardest problem in mathematics, and now through a combination of human ingenuity and relentlessness, and the computational power of AI, the Riemann hypothesis may have finally been solved](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2600226-what-is-the-riemann-hypothesis-and-why-is-its-solution-so-monumental/)

Diesen Artikel teilen Maisernte in Österreich: Auch ohne Agrarsubventionen wäre die Selbstversorgung der EU laut einer Modellrechnung gesichert Foto: Daniel Scharinger/imago B auernverbände verbreiten angesichts der Verhandlungen über das künftige EU-Budget Angst: Sie suggerieren, dass die Europäische Union sich ohne die bislang 54 Milliarden Euro Agrarsubventionen pro Jahr nicht mehr selbst mit genügend Lebensmitteln versorgen könnte. Selbst wenn die EU sämtliche Landwirtschaftssubventionen streichen würde, produzierte sie immer noch etwas mehr Getreide, als sie selbst verbraucht.
items.body:
# Diskussion um Kürzungen im EU-Haushalt: Keine Agrarsubventionen, kein Hunger

## Diskussion um Kürzungen im EU-Haushalt : Keine Agrarsubventionen, kein Hunger

Kommentar von

Die EU würde auch ohne Milliardenzahlungen für Landwirte genügend Lebensmittel produzieren. Das Geld sollte lieber für die Umwelt eingesetzt werden.

25.11.2026

17:51 Uhr

teilen

Diesen Artikel teilen

Maisernte in Österreich: Auch ohne Agrarsubventionen wäre die Selbstversorgung der EU laut einer Modellrechnung gesichert Foto: Daniel Scharinger/imago

B auernverbände verbreiten angesichts der Verhandlungen über das künftige EU-Budget Angst: Sie suggerieren, dass die Europäische Union sich ohne die bislang 54 Milliarden Euro Agrarsubventionen pro Jahr nicht mehr selbst mit genügend Lebensmitteln versorgen könnte. Doch das ist falsch.

Selbst wenn die EU sämtliche Landwirtschaftssubventionen streichen würde, produzierte sie immer noch etwas mehr Getreide, als sie selbst verbraucht. Der Selbstversorgungsgrad läge bei 104 Prozent. Das hat vor Kurzem eine vom Naturschutzbund in Auftrag gegebene Berechnung auf Grundlage des international etablierten Agrarmodells Capri gezeigt. Demnach wäre auch die Selbstversorgung etwa mit Obst und Gemüse sowie mit Fleisch kaum verändert. Der Weizenanbau würde sogar leicht zulegen.

Zwar müssten ohne staatliche Zuschüsse gerade einige oft kleinere Höfe aufgeben, die kaum Gewinn machen. Aber deren Land würde in der Regel nicht brachfallen, sondern von rentableren Betrieben übernommen werden. Dass es so kommen würde, legt die historische Entwicklung nahe: Obwohl die Zahl der Betriebe stark gesunken ist, bleibt die landwirtschaftlich genutzte Fläche in Deutschland ziemlich stabil .

taz debatte

Die taz ist eine unabhängige , linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979 . Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.

Auch andere Studien zeigen: Niemand in der EU würde ohne Agrarsubventionen hungern. Die Importmengen würden sich ebenfalls kaum verändern. Die sozialen Auswirkungen der möglichen Hofschließungen wären gering, weil schon heute beispielsweise in Deutschland lediglich rund 1 Prozent der Beschäftigten in der Landwirtschaft arbeiten, von denen wiederum nur ein Teil betroffen wäre. Aufgeben müssten vor allem Nebenerwerbsbetriebe.

Subventionen für Landwirte lassen sich dadurch rechtfertigen, dass die Bauern zum Beispiel auf Bio umstellen oder ihre Tiere besser halten als vorgeschrieben. Leider hat die EU-Kommission in ihrem geplanten Budget genau für solche Maßnahmen – anders als für die ineffizienten Einkommenszuschüsse – keine Mindestwerte vorgesehen. Das sollte sie nachholen.

Jost Maurin Redakteur für Wirtschaft und Umwelt

items.feedText: Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type. We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps .
items.body:
# An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA

## a]:hidden"> An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA

Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type.

We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps .

## The use case: a Farm Assistant

A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent:

- Listens and turns the speech into text.
- Searches a 154-page agricultural handbook, which is written in English.
- Answers in two to four spoken sentences, in the language the question was asked in, using only what the handbook says.
- Speaks the answer back and shows the source pages, so the answer can be checked.
If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up.

## Where CUGA fits

CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things:

- One agent, any model. Switch between watsonx and OpenAI with one setting.
- The knowledge engine. Parse a PDF, chunk it, embed it, and search it locally with agent.knowledge.search() .
- Conversation threads. Each question gets a fresh thread, so one person's language or context never leaks into another's.
The key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it.

audio ──▶ speech-to-text ──▶ knowledge.search ──▶ CUGA (grounded answer) ──▶ text-to-speech ──▶ audio Because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server.

### The hard part is not the voice

Adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval : a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph.

Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning.

The fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large ), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything.

Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages.

### Making it sound right and keeping it safe

A few small decisions mattered more than we expected:

- Write for the ear. Markdown, bullet points, citation tags and bracketed translations such as "millet (बाजरा)" all sound wrong when read aloud. The prompt asks the model not to produce them, and a light formatter strips any that slip through before speech.
- Keep guardrails cheap. Simple input checks catch obvious off-topic questions. If one gets through, the model starts its reply with OFF_TOPIC , and the app swaps in a polite redirect. No second LLM call, so the voice path stays fast.
- Ground every answer. The model sees only the retrieved passages, is told not to use outside knowledge, and the page sources are shown to the user.
- Keep keys out of the server. With the Sarvam option, the browser talks to Sarvam directly. The server receives only text and never sees the user's key.
## Try it

You do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer:

CUGA Apps on Hugging Face →

Want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA , starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn.

## Beyond farming: Scaling for Bharat

Nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent.

Voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust.

This approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity.

If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core .

## Learn more about CUGA

New to CUGA? Here are some places to start:

- cuga.dev : the CUGA home page.
- CUGA on GitHub : the open-source harness (Apache 2.0). Star it, file issues, or pick up a good first issue.
- CUGA documentation : setup, the SDK, knowledge, policies and configuration.
- CUGA Apps gallery on GitHub : the source for the apps in the Hugging Face Space.
Spaces you can try in your browser:

- CUGA Agent : the general-purpose agent, running on a demo CRM scenario.
- CUGA Apps : launch working CUGA apps from one dashboard.
- CUGA Policy Playground : two live agents side by side, one with policies and one without.
More CUGA posts on the Hugging Face blog:

items.body:
Come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different. In California, AB 1709 (2026), AB 1043 (2025), and SB 976 (2024) are slated to take effect on January 1, 2027. Meanwhile, state attorney general regulations for New York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act take effect on January 25, 2027.

EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures, regulatory proceedings, and the courts. The core problem is simple: age-gating mandates trade away everyday user privacy and free expression under the guise of safety, while pushing platforms to gather even more personal data on users.

What California’s Rules Say

Three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young users. First, SB 976 (2024) requires verifiable parental consent before platforms can offer algorithmic feeds or nighttime notifications to anyone under 18. Second, AB 1709 (2026) goes even further by outright banning "addictive features," including personalized recommendation algorithms, autoplay, and endless scroll, for users under 16, even with parental permission. Third, the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043, 2025) mandates age-assurance checks across devices (operating systems) and apps, serving as the enforcement backbone for those restrictions. Together with the California Attorney General’s proposed rules on SB 976, which outline age-gating methods, accuracy, circumvention, and parental consent, these laws force platforms into a two-tier design that walls young people off from basic content-discovery tools, puts everyone's privacy at risk to prove their age, and has already drawn First Amendment lawsuits from social media companies against both SB 976 and AB 1709.

For example: rather than minimizing corporate surveillance and data collection by passing stronger privacy laws, the SB 976 regulations encourage companies to evaluate behavioral patterns, collected user data, digital interactions, and metadata to estimate age (Sec. 561(a)(2)), alongside location data collected for other purposes (Sec. 565). Good privacy laws should discourage collecting that information in the first place, not reward broader tracking.

At the same time, these age assurance rules build in steep error rates and weak safeguards. They acknowledge that age-verification tools can misclassify young people as adults, allowing false-positive rates of up to 8% for 16-year-olds and 15% for 17-year-olds (Sec. 561(c)(4)(iv)). Yet the rules set no benchmarks at all for false negatives, meaning adults (especially 18- to 20-year-olds) are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. They also recognize demographic bias in facial recognition, yet offer no concrete fix, vaguely telling companies to take mitigating measures like correcting dataset imbalances (Sec. 563(a)(6)). While users can appeal wrong age estimates, the rules set no firm deadlines, meaning mistakes can drag on without a prompt fix, blocking user access (Sec. 564). Worse, requiring platforms to let users report others they suspect are under the age of 18 (Sec. 567) invites targeted harassment by bad actors, while rules telling companies to account for users trying to “conceal or misrepresent” their California location (Sec. 565) risk penalizing everyday VPN users.

What New York’s Rules Say

Along the same lines as the California regulations, New York’s SAFE for Kids Act restricts personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (between midnight and 6am) without required consent, and mandates that platforms run age assurance and determine user location. If a user does not verify their age or is estimated to be under-18, they will either be relegated to an account with no personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (if the platform creates one), or prohibited from accessing the platform/service.

As we detailed in our December 2025 comments to the New York Attorney General, age-verification mandates inevitably chill access to online speech. And the final regulations introduce several troubling specifics.

The New York regulations use broad definitions for "age estimation," "age inference," and "age verification" (700.1(h)–(j)) that push companies to collect and retain more personal information from users. Even where privacy protections apply to that information, users cannot sue or enforce those rights themselves, since enforcement rests solely with the Attorney General (700.8). Worse, the rule’s definition of deletion appears to let companies "de-identify" age-assurance data and keep using it in that form, potentially feeding AI model training and creating re-identification risks if leaked or stolen. At the same time, platforms are required to hold onto records (including a user's age status and compliance data) for five years, increasing the risk of misuse or breaches (700.7(b)).

Echoing the problems in California, location and accuracy regulations bring further privacy and security risks. The regulations demand that operators must weigh all reliable location information and take reasonable steps to detect user efforts to “conceal or misrepresent” being in New York, which expands location tracking and threatens VPN use (700.2(d)(2)). On accuracy, the rules permit up to a 15% false-positive rate for 17-year-olds (700.1(b)), yet just like the California rules, say nothing about false negatives—meaning adults, especially 18- to 20-year-olds, are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. When that happens, the appeals process can take longer than 10 days, leaving misclassified adults locked out of standard features (or platforms altogether) for over a week.

What This Means for Users in NY and CA

Under both states' regimes, many users will be pressed to hand over personal information just to access standard features like personalized feeds or notifications, while social media companies are encouraged to monitor (and monetize) user behavior even more closely. Because these laws define "addictive feeds" so broadly that the label covers virtually every basic recommendation tool (including feeds built from who you follow, posts you like, or topics you say you are interested in), platforms face a stark choice: either build stripped-down versions of their apps without algorithmic feeds, likes, or notifications, or simply boot any account suspected of belonging to someone under 18. Either way, all users, and especially young people across both states, risk being shut out of major online spaces as they exist today.

items.body:
Anthropic now offers a way to [convert Claude artifacts into things that look a lot like native Mac (and Windows) apps](https://claude.com/resources/articles/install-as-app). Federico Viticci dove in and figured out how the whole system, which routes commands back through the Claude app, works, and [came to this conclusion](https://www.macstories.net/stories/a-closer-look-at-claudes-mac-apps/):

> If I were Apple, I’d be concerned. Effectively, Anthropic shipped an app creation playground that only requires basic prompts to put together something that works. They did so by entirely bypassing the App Store or Apple’s notarization system for apps distributed outside the App Store, and by creating their own lock-in system around Claude’s identity and capabilities instead.

It’s been [crystal clear for a while now](https://sixcolors.com/post/2026/06/road-to-wwdc-2026-whats-a-developer/) that Apple needs a simplified set of app building tools that don’t look like Xcode. This area is moving fast—even faster than I thought—and regular people are now able to [develop their own custom apps](https://www.theincomparable.com/doubleender/) with ease.

Anthropic’s solution is interesting, but it’s also full of limitations and clever hacks. That’s not the issue, though. The issue is that this stuff is going to keep getting better and Apple needs to get in the game as soon as possible.

[Go to the linked site](https://www.macstories.net/stories/a-closer-look-at-claudes-mac-apps/).

[Read on Six Colors](https://sixcolors.com/link/2026/11/claude-now-lets-you-vibe-code-html-mac-apps/).
