items.body:
Mit dem [Referentenentwurf vom 2. November 2026](https://www.bmjv.de/SharedDocs/Downloads/DE/Gesetzgebung/RefE/RefE_Aenderung_Sexualstrafrecht.pdf?__blob=publicationFile&v=3) will das BMJV erhebliche verbale und nonverbale sexuelle Belästigungen ohne körperliche Berührung unter Strafe stellen. Das Phänomen, weithin bekannt als sog. Catcalling, ist vielgestaltig: Es umfasst Äußerungen zu sexualbezogenen Handlungen („Bei deinem Aussehen verliere ich garantiert die Kontrolle über mein Glied“ 1), „Komm, schwing deinen Arsch für uns“, „Ich werde deine Fotze ficken, bis sie blutet“, „Du siehst so aus, als ob du auf Analsex stehst“), Kommentare zum äußeren Erscheinungsbild („Saftige Schenkel, mein Mädchen.“, „Du siehst toll aus! Richtig fickbar!“) oder nonverbales Verhalten wie das Verfolgen, sexuell assoziierte Geräusche oder Gesten.

Der Entwurf will damit den strafrechtlichen Schutz der sexuellen Selbstbestimmung in ihrer nichtkörperlichen Dimension ausbauen. Ein näherer Blick auf die konkrete Tatbestandsfassung und die Entwurfsbegründung zeigt jedoch, dass sich der Entwurf vom Leiblichen nicht recht lösen will. Wohl keine der exemplarisch genannten Äußerungen wäre vom neuen Tatbestand erfasst, wenn sie am helllichten Tag im öffentlichen Raum zwischen einander Unbekannten fiele. Damit kriminalisiert der Entwurf nur einen kleinen Ausschnitt des Phänomens, und zwar auf systematisch widersprüchliche Weise.

## Eine lange Diskussion

Das BMJV schlägt folgenden § 184i Abs. 2 StGB-E vor:

> „Wer eine andere Person durch eine sexuell bestimmte Äußerung oder Geste belästigt, die geeignet ist, sie einzuschüchtern oder zu bedrängen, wird mit Freiheitsstrafe bis zu einem Jahr oder mit Geldstrafe bestraft.“

Seit [geraumer Zeit](https://kripoz.de/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/gemmel-immig-catcalling-umfrage-zur-strafwuerdigkeit.pdf) wird darüber gestritten, ob es eine solche Vorschrift überhaupt braucht. Manche meinen, es gebe gar keine Strafbarkeitslücke, weil der Beleidigungstatbestand diese Fälle auffangen könne, entweder weil die Äußerungen ohnehin eine Formalbeleidigung enthielten (z. B. die [Anrede als „Schlampe“](https://openjur.de/u/2506665.html)) oder zumindest weil die Äußerungen die Betroffenen stets zum [Sexualobjekt reduzierten](https://kripoz.de/2022/05/31/catcalling-eine-phaenomenologische-und-strafrechtliche-betrachtung/). Diese Auslegung hat sich in der [Rechtsprechung](https://openjur.de/u/2119618.html) aber nicht durchgesetzt. Praktisch bleibt daher ein weiter Bereich von Verhaltensweisen [straffrei](https://kripoz.de/2023/05/30/strafbarkeit-sexualbezogener-aeusserungen/). Den geflügelten Begriff der „Strafbarkeitslücke“ vermeiden wir allerdings, weil er voraussetzt, was erst zu begründen wäre: dass das bislang nicht erfasste Verhalten strafwürdig und strafbedürftig ist. Ob eine weitere Kriminalisierung aber überhaupt etwas (Wünschenswertes) bewirkt, haben [Kritiker*innen wiederholt bezweifelt](https://www.humanistische-union.de/publikationen/vorgaenge/vorg-250/publikation/die-geplante-einfuehrung-der-strafbarkeit-nichtkoerperlicher-sexueller-belaestigungen-zugleich-ein-beitrag-zur-opferorientierung-und-zu-den-grenzen-des-strafrechts/). Sie verweisen auf [Kapazitätsgrenzen der Justiz](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/de/document/doi/10.1515/zstw-2026-2005/html?srsltid=AYCX9vL7KIJRm5xy6UZA7MpDPzAOtj6slzMRlBKzJuEtSqyGzsnbcV9L) und enttäuschte Betroffene, die man auf den Privatklageweg verweist und die einen unbekannten Täter nicht selbst ermitteln können. Aus kritischer Perspektive liegt zudem ein Vorwurf nahe, den man dem *Carceral Feminism* generell macht: Er [individualisiere ein gesellschaftliches Problem](https://verfassungsblog.de/der-ruf-nach-strafe/) und greife dafür zum kostengünstigen Mittel des Strafrechts. Unsere Kritik fokussiert sich auf die konkret vorgeschlagene Formulierung des Tatbestandes: Diese würde eine restriktive Anwendung des Beleidigungstatbestandes weiter verfestigen.

Zum Hintergrund des Entwurfs gehört der – auf den ersten Blick ähnliche – Vorschlag des Landes Niedersachsen aus dem Herbst 2024 ([BR-Drs. 519/24](https://dserver.bundestag.de/brd/2024/0519-24.pdf)). Dieser Vorschlag war an entscheidender Stelle knapper gefasst als der Referentenentwurf. Er forderte als Taterfolg bloß eine erhebliche Belästigung und setzte nicht voraus, dass die Tat geeignet sein muss, zu bedrängen oder einzuschüchtern. Der Referentenentwurf kritisiert den niedersächsischen Vorschlag als zu unbestimmt, weil offenbleibe, welche Verhaltensweisen letztlich „erheblich“ seien (RefE, S. 12). Diesen Mangel zu beheben, gleicht der Quadratur des Kreises. Der Referentenentwurf musste die vielgestaltigen Erscheinungsformen hinreichend bestimmt abbilden und zugleich eine objektive [Bagatellschwelle](https://verfassungsblog.de/der-ruf-nach-strafe/) einziehen. Diese Schwelle ist schon deshalb nötig, weil der Tatbestand die Meinungsfreiheit (Art. 5 Abs. 1 GG) beschränkt und daher verhältnismäßig sein muss.

## Zwischen Sexual- und Bedrohungsdelikt

Der Referentenentwurf konkretisiert die Erheblichkeitsgrenze nun so: Die Äußerung oder Geste muss geeignet sein, die belästigte Person einzuschüchtern oder zu bedrängen. Damit verwendet der Entwurf zwei Merkmale, die dem StGB bislang weitgehend unbekannt sind. Definitionen liefert er in seiner Begründung aber gleich mit:

> „Eine Einschüchterung liegt insbesondere vor, wenn die Äußerung oder das Verhalten aufgrund seines Inhalts, seiner Intensität, seiner Begleitumstände oder des Auftretens des Täters geeignet ist, bei einer verständigen Person den Eindruck hervorzurufen, dass ein Widerspruch oder eine Zurückweisung nicht ohne weiteres möglich oder folgenlos bleiben wird. Eine erhebliche Bedrängung liegt insbesondere vor, wenn der Täter der betroffenen Person Sexualität in einer Weise aufdrängt, die ihre Möglichkeit, sich der Situation ohne Weiteres zu entziehen, wesentlich beeinträchtigt.“

Trotz ihrer Kritik am niedersächsischen Entwurf wollten sich die Entwurfsverfasser*innen also nicht ganz von der Erheblichkeit trennen. Sie haben ihr vielmehr einen Platz in der zweiten Reihe zugewiesen – in der Begründung, an der Seite der Bedrängung. Warum dann nicht im Gesetzestext selbst? Zudem fragt sich, warum es zweier Begriffe bedurfte, um die Erheblichkeit zu konkretisieren, wenn die Gesetzesbegründung beide anschließend selbst als „Bedrohungssituation“ zusammenfasst.

Folgenreicher ist aber: Bei beiden Eignungsmerkmalen soll es nicht auf die Äußerung oder Geste selbst ankommen, sondern auf den situativen Kontext. Das hätte der Wortlaut durchaus aufnehmen können (z. B. „den Umständen nach geeignet, (…)“). Denn derzeit knüpft der Entwurf die Eignung – grammatisch missverständlich – an die Äußerung oder Geste. 2)

items.body:
When Siddhartha Gautama gave his first teaching after enlightenment, it was to five friends in the deer park at Sarnath, not far from Varanasi in the Ganges Valley. Wanting to transmit to them the essence of his breakthrough, he crystallized his insights into what would become known as the four noble truths. These include the truth of the way out of suffering, known as the noble eightfold path: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

The eightfold path offers a way to touch awakening as Gautama did. These insights were not the result of thinking or study, nor were they a creed or philosophical doctrine. They were the fruit of Gautama’s own direct experience and meditative realization, and they conveyed a path that traced a “middle way” between the two extremes of asceticism and indulgence. It was a way, he believed, that could lead anyone to realize understanding, liberation, and peace.

#### “You don’t hurry to get the dishes done quickly so you can get on with something else. You encounter the miracle of life that includes dishes.”

As a species we’re still struggling to find a middle way, to steer a wise course through the extremes of fanaticism, greed, nihilism, rage, and despair. The ancient wisdom of the eightfold path offers eight matrixes that are powerfully relevant today as a guide to help us navigate these extremes and bring a meaningful direction to our daily lives, actions, and relationships.

All elements of the eightfold path inter-are. You cannot extract any of them from the context of the path. So, for example, if you take mindfulness out of the ethical context of the path, it is no longer right mindfulness. All eight elements are interrelated and interdependent. They enhance each other. When practiced deeply, each element of the path contains the other seven within it, and they complement each other to create a complete path to liberation.

My teacher, Thich Nhat Hanh, taught that right mindfulness is at the heart of the eightfold path. So, with the energy of right mindfulness as the foundation, we’re able to develop right concentration. This gives rise to insight or “right view,” which Thich Nhat Hanh described as the “insight of interbeing.” It is this deep view of the world that guides us to an ethical and beneficial life through right thinking, right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right effort. So, when you generate the energy of mindfulness, you are naturally concentrated on the object of your mindfulness, whether it’s your breathing, your body, the sunset, or the presence of the person in front of you.

Photo © Noumae | Dreamstime.com

The energies of mindfulness and concentration naturally give rise to insight, right view. You touch the insight of interbeing between your breath and the earth, or between your body and your ancestors and descendants, or between your heart and the sun in the sky. You realize that you inter-are with the person in front of you.
Already, this insight of interbeing helps us touch peace, joy, and freedom.

Now, with the energy of mindfulness, concentration, and insight, your thinking will naturally be right thinking.

It will be free from discrimination and separation, and on the basis of that thinking, your speech will be right speech and your action right action.

Cultivating right diligence (or effort) in that moment, you’ll be able to see and calm any unwholesome seeds that may get triggered in your consciousness, such as anger or despair, and identify and activate positive seeds, such as gratitude and compassion. With all those energies alive in you, the way you spend your time, energy, and labor—your livelihood—will be “right.” It will be beneficial for you and everyone around you.

Of course, if there’s “right,” there must also be “wrong.” The Buddha’s teaching does assert that there’s a right and wrong way to go about things. There’s a distinction, for example, between “right mindfulness” and “wrong mindfulness,” between “right concentration” and “wrong concentration,” between “right speech” and “wrong speech.” There’s a way of practicing mindfulness, concentration, and the others that goes in the direction of healing and well-being, and there’s a way that goes in the direction of harm and ill-being.

This is where ethics comes into every aspect of the eightfold path. The wrong path *does* exist—it’s the “ignoble” path of wrong view, wrong thinking, wrong speech, and wrong action that leads to suffering for ourselves, for others, and for the planet. It’s the reason why we’re in the state we’re in. And it’s why we need to find another way of being.

You may wonder, how can there be a wrong way to practice mindfulness? Surely *all* mindfulness is beneficial? In 2014, Thich Nhat Hanh’s last year of teaching, he spoke about the importance of not diluting or appropriating mindfulness as it spreads in the West and reaches new audiences and settings. He explained that the first way to distinguish “right” from “wrong” mindfulness is to realize that right mindfulness is not an instrument or tool but *a way*, a path. It cannot be used as a means to an end.

Yet many of us do speak of mindfulness as a tool. We say that with mindfulness we can heal, with mindfulness we can reconcile, with mindfulness we can make more money, and, in applying mindfulness in the military, with mindfulness we can kill the enemy more effectively. To appropriate mindfulness in this way is to instrumentalize it. Used as a means to an end, whether for profit, success, or even for apparently “beneficial” ends, mindfulness loses its true, authentic spirit. In fact, if you extract any of the eight elements out of the wider ethical context of the path, it is no longer “right.”

The image of “path” or “way” is essential to Buddhist spirituality, and yet it may be challenging for those of us educated in Western capitalist countries. We prefer there to be a goal, a destination, a clear program. We may be seeking a powerful, final moment of “grace” or “attainment.” But as Thich Nhat Hanh used to ask us teasingly,
“Why haven’t you ever asked if the Buddha kept practicing after enlightenment?”

The eightfold path is not so much linear as circular, which is why it’s often seen more as an eight-spoked wheel than a list. The Western-educated mind may struggle with this. We want to know where to start and where we end up. We want to know which element is more important.

The eight-spoke dharma wheel symbolizes the eightfold path. Photo: godongphoto / shutterstock.com

But in his later years of teaching, Thich Nhat Hanh revised his translation of the eightfold path to be not merely “the path leading to happiness,” but “the path of happiness.” He taught that in the true spirit of the insight of interbeing, every step along the path leading to happiness *must be happiness itself*. If we suffer along the way, we’ve lost the game already.

…

items.title: Deviation from the neutral mutational spectrum in driver genes reveals the distribution of effects of missense oncogenic mutations
items.subtitle:
Bazykin

Although many cancer driver genes have been identified, the full set of variants within these genes that can promote tumorigenesis remains…
items.feedText: Stolyarova, Georgii A. Bazykin Although many cancer driver genes have been identified, the full set of variants within these genes that can promote tumorigenesis remains unknown. The contribution of a variant to cancer depends on both its probability of occurrence and the selective advantage it confers. Here, we introduce a metric that quantifies how selection biases the spectrum of observed missense variants in driver genes compared to neutral expectation, and use it to develop a method for estimating the total number of potential driver variants and the distribution of their fitness effects within individual genes. Applying this framework to large cancer cohorts, we estimate that in most oncogenes, nearly all possible missense driver variants have already been observed, whereas in most tumor-suppressor genes, the majority remain undiscovered. These results reveal fundamental differences in how mutation and selection shape nucleotide variation across gene classes and provide a framework for interpreting newly detected variants.

## Free lunches (permalink)

[↗ Primärquelle: pluralistic.net](https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/24/move-fast-break-kings/#come-and-take-it)

An old joke: "Two economists are walking down the sidewalk and one of them points and says, 'Look, there's a $20 bill, right there on the ground!' The other one is dismissive: 'No, if that was a real $20, someone would have picked it up by now.'"

If that joke leaves you scratching your head, then you've been lucky enough to avoid the neoclassical economist's view of the world as a market whose participants, in aggregate, know everything about what people are buying and selling. In that world if there's a "free lunch" – like a $20 bill on the sidewalk – someone will have already taken it.

Likewise, if there's a seller who's priced their goods at $10 and a buyer who's willing to pay $30, there will be an "arbitrageur" who will be shuttling those $10 goods to those $30 customers and pocketing the difference. Give it enough time and either the seller will raise their price to $30, or the buyer will realize they should only be offering $10.

The market will "clear," with everyone getting everything they need in the most efficient way possible, meaning there's no way to improve anyone's position without making someone else worse off:

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_efficiency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_efficiency)

When markets *don't* behave like this, neoclassicals hunt for "distortions" that prevent the market from performing this continuous balancing trick. "Distortion" is best understood here as a euphemism for "democratic intervention." If you've ever gotten excited about a commonsense policy solution to a serious economic problem (like public grocery stores as a means of addressing food deserts and greedflation), only to see it shot down by economists who use a lot of jargon to "prove" that it can't possibly work, you've experienced how well "distortion" doomerism keeps us from having nice things.

The economist's allergy to distortions is curiously selective. When a company uses its monopoly power to capture its regulators, or bind its workers to silence, or to erect barriers to entry that keep competitors at bay, somehow that doesn't qualify as a "distortion." Same goes for the situation in which a dominant retailer (Walmart) and a dominant manufacturer (Pepsi) come to a secret agreement to force everyone else to raise prices a *ton* so that Walmart can raise its prices by a (smaller) ton and still be "the cheapest":

[https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/14/the-price-is-wright/#enforcement-priorities](https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/14/the-price-is-wright/#enforcement-priorities)

Economists are in love with the idea of the economy as a self-licking ice-cream cone, a beautiful machine that operates all by itself, processing all the information we inject into it by buying and selling and finding the optimal way to produce more of the things we want best at the lowest prices.

But like any love-drunk suitor, economists habitually overlook the market's glaring imperfections. In the self-correcting market, a company with high margins sends up a flare that alerts other, hungrier companies to swarm it, competing to offer the cheapest price. Likewise any company with lots of customers: those crowds of customers should conjure up armies of clever planners and inventors who find more efficient ways to produce the same goods and services and lure those customers away.

This is the crux of market orthodoxy, the idea that competition lowers margins, goading sellers to offer better goods at better prices. Don't take my word for it, here's Adam Smith:

> It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest. We address ourselves, not to their humanity, but to their self-love, and never talk to them of our own necessities, but of their advantages.

If this is true, then the surest sign of a "market distortion" is persistent high margins and persistent high market-share. Any company that dominates its market and charges far more than its costs is a crisp, $20 bill lying right there on the sidewalk for all to see. If no one picks up that $20, then it's a sure bet that there's a "distorter" who is preventing the market from acting on the "information" that there is an opportunity here.

America's business lobby *loves* distortions, so long as they're the kinds of distortions that let the companies safely entrust their $20 bills to the sidewalk without worrying about having them scooped up by a competitor.

Take Big Tech: this is an industry with such persistently high margins and so many customers that there are *multiple* firms in the sector that were able to piss away *hundreds of billions of dollars* by manipulating their stock prices with buybacks and building AI data-centers that can never turn a profit:

[https://pluralistic.net/2025/09/06/computer-says-huh/#invisible-handcuffs](https://pluralistic.net/2025/09/06/computer-says-huh/#invisible-handcuffs)

If the market was "undistorted" then anyone this rich and this stupid would be in serious trouble. Ask a neoclassical to explain Big Tech's prolonged, morbid wealth and they'll insist that this means that *we're* the stupid ones, because we can't play 11-dimensional chess like Zuckerberg, which is why we can't understand why it was *good* to piss away $80b on the metaverse.

But we don't have to look very hard to find another, simpler explanation. Big Tech owes its profits to its monopoly power, which allows it to form cartels that collude to rig prices:

…

items.body:
[Javier Hidalgo](https://jepson.richmond.edu/faculty/bios/jhidalgo/), a philosopher at the University of Richmond, has developed a classroom simulation game to teach about different ancient philosophies called “Ancient Philosophy as a Way of Life.”

Generously, Professor Hidalgo has created a [website](https://hidalgoj-ai.github.io/Ancient-Philosophy-Game/) to share the game with anyone who may wish to try it out in their own courses.

He writes:

> [Ancient Philosophy as a Way of Life](https://hidalgoj-ai.github.io/Ancient-Philosophy-Game/) is a free classroom role-playing game that introduces students to Hellenistic philosophy, plus a bit of Buddhist philosophy.
> The game is set around 150 BCE at the court of Menander, a king who ruled a Hellenistic kingdom that included part of the Indian subcontinent. Four delegations of philosophers (Stoics, Epicureans, Buddhists, and Skeptics) arrive at court, each claiming to offer the best way of life. Some students play the philosophers, while others play members of the court, each of whom faces a personal dilemma and must decide which philosophical school to join. The philosophers present their views, lead the court through a brief philosophical exercise, and offer advice on the court members’ dilemmas. At the end, the court members announce their allegiances and the king awards royal patronage.
> There is no predetermined winner: when I ran the game in two sections of my ethics course, different philosophical factions won. Students engaged in sustained debate about the merits of the different schools and also seemed to have fun with the game.
> The game takes two class sessions, one for preparation and one for play, although a third session might be useful for larger or more talkative classes. It works for classes of 7 to 30 students and assumes no background in philosophy. The goal of the game is for students to encounter these philosophies as live options rather than merely as historical doctrines. Students have to understand a view well enough to defend it against objections, apply it to concrete problems, and experiment with its practices.
> The game is inspired by [Reacting to the Past](https://reactingconsortium.org/) games (which I love!) but is shorter than a standard Reacting game and is designed to emphasize philosophical debate in particular. The [website](https://hidalgoj-ai.github.io/Ancient-Philosophy-Game/#materials) has everything an instructor needs to run the game: a student gamebook, an instructor’s manual, faction handouts, role sheets, dilemma cards, and ballots. All materials are free to download.

Check it out. Professor Hidalgo adds, “The game is still in development and I would welcome feedback from anyone who tries it.”

# Realitätsferner Dualismus

Maja Apelt | Rezension | 25.11.2026

## Realitätsferner Dualismus

## Rezension zu „Vergessene Soldatinnen. Frauen im Militär und in den Kriegen Europas seit 1600“ von Karen Hagemann

Karen Hagemann: Vergessene Soldatinnen. Frauen im Militär und in den Kriegen Europas seit 1600 Deutschland Berlin 2026: Suhrkamp 1056 S., 48 EUR ISBN 978-3-518-58840-6

Ihr neues Buch beginnt die deutsch-amerikanische Historikerin Karen Hagemann, Professorin an der University of North Carolina at Chapell Hill, mit einer Beschreibung der aktuellen Situation von Frauen in der Ukraine. Zwar stellen Frauen den Großteil der seit 2022 aus dem Land geflüchteten Menschen, zugleich dienen sie in wachsender Zahl in den ukrainischen Streitkräften. Dort sind sie vor allem in Verwaltung, Kommunikation, Logistik und Sanitätsdienst, aber auch in den freiwilligen Territorialverteidigungsverbänden tätig. Obwohl die Wehrpflicht nur für Männer gilt, lag der Anteil an Frauen in den Streitkräften 2016 bei 20 Prozent. Seit 2021 wurden „wehrdiensttaugliche Frauen aus über 100 Berufen, die für die Verteidigung des Landes von besonderer Bedeutung sind, verpflichtet, sich bei den Militärbehörden zu registrieren“ (S. 12). Sie haben demnach einen bedeutenden Anteil an der Verteidigung des Landes, in der internationalen Berichterstattung aber sind sie kaum sichtbar. Im Zentrum des medialen Interesses stehen „ukrainische Männer als heldenhafte Verteidiger des Vaterlandes und ukrainische Frauen und Kinder als verzweifelte Opfer des Krieges“ (S.13). Diese Darstellung, so hebt Hagemann hervor, erfüllt eine wichtige Funktion, wenn es darum geht, militärische Unterstützung und humanitäre Hilfe zu bekommen.

In diesem Auftakt werden die zentralen Leitlinien des Buches von Karen Hagemann bereits deutlich: Frauen haben in allen Kriegen wichtige Funktionen übernommen, sie wurden immer gebraucht, auch wenn man sie gerade im Europa des 19. Jahrhunderts aus den Streitkräften vollständig auszuschließen versuchte. Zugleich wurden sie aber in der Berichterstattung, im kollektiven Gedächtnis und lange Zeit auch in den Geschichtswissenschaften verdrängt. Allein als seltene Ausnahmen, als Amazonen oder der ihnen zugeschriebenen Geschlechterrolle zuwiderhandelnde Frauen, trafen Berichte oder Selbstzeugnisse von Frauen in den Armeen auf das wohl eher lüsterne Interesse einer breiteren Leserschaft. Das duale Geschlechterbild vom kämpfenden Mann und dem zu schützenden, weiblichen Kriegsopfer wurde durch diese selektive Inszenierung und Wahrnehmung produziert und reproduziert. Indem Hagemann eine umfassende Studie zur Lage und Rolle von Frauen in den europäischen Streitkräften und Kriegen seit 1600 vorlegt, zeigt sie, wie dieser Dualismus zwischen den Geschlechtern hergestellt wird, welche Funktionen er erfüllt – und sie belegt, wie realitätsfern dieser Dualismus ist.

Dazu hat sich die Autorin mit drei Fragen auseinandergesetzt: 1. Wie war der Einsatz von Frauen im Militär organisiert? 2. Welche Faktoren beeinflussen den Wandel des militärischen Einsatzes von Frauen und so auch deren individuelle und kollektive Erfahrungen? 3. Warum stellte es über Zeit-, Länder- und Systemgrenzen hinweg für Militär, Politik und Gesellschaft eine solche Herausforderung dar, den Einsatz von Frauen in Militär und Krieg anzuerkennen und sich daran zu erinnern (S. 21)?

Der Einleitung folgen vier Großkapitel: Das erste (S. 29 ff.) bezieht sich auf die frühneuzeitlichen Heere des 17. und 18. Jahrhunderts. Es geht vor allem um die Söldnerheere des Dreißigjährigen Krieges und den Siebenjährigen Krieg, an dem zahlreiche europäische Streitkräfte beteiligt und in dem unter anderem Kolonien und Handelswege von Interesse waren. Die Familien der Söldner und so auch die Frauen waren in diesen Fällen noch selbstverständlicher Teil des Trosses und übernahmen die unterschiedlichsten Funktionen in den Bereichen Versorgung, Ausrüstung, Schanzenbau und Plünderung oder Requirierung von Lebensmitteln und anderen Vorräten.

Im zweiten Großkapitel (S. 145 ff.) stehen Frauen in den Armeen des langen 19. Jahrhunderts im Fokus, vor allem in den Revolutions- und Napoleonischen Kriegen, den europäischen Kolonial- und Imperialkriegen, dem Krimkrieg und den deutschen Einigungskriegen. Die Autorin zeigt, dass der Versuch, Frauen und Familien gänzlich aus den Streitkräften auszuschließen, teilweise dazu führte, dass die Frauen, wenn sie in der Heimat zurückgelassen wurden, sich selbst und ihre Familien nicht ernähren konnten. Vor allem aber wurde offensichtlich, dass Frauen im Sanitätswesen und der Kriegskrankenpflege dringend benötigt wurden. Beginnend mit dem Krimkrieg (1853–1856) und verbunden mit dem Namen Florence Nightingale [1] etablierte sich über einige Jahrzehnte hinweg eine weibliche professionelle Krankenpflege.

Im Ersten Weltkrieg, dem das dritte Großkapitel (S. 347 ff.) gewidmet ist, wurden Frauen in immer mehr Bereichen benötigt, zunächst in der Kriegswirtschaft, da die Männer dort fehlten. Zunehmend kamen Frauen auch als militärische Hilfskräfte, Büroangestellte, Telefonistinnen, Etappen- und Nachrichtenhelferinnen zum Einsatz. Das galt gleichermaßen für die deutschen, britischen, französischen und US-amerikanischen Armeen. Die russische Armee hatte darüber hinaus sogar eigene Frauenbataillone.

Auch im Zweiten Weltkrieg, den das vierte Kapitel (S. 545 ff.) behandelt, konnten weder das NS-Regime und seine Verbündeten noch die Alliierten darauf verzichten, Frauen in den unterschiedlichsten Funktionen und in noch größerem Umfang als im Ersten Weltkrieg einzusetzen. Insbesondere in der Sowjetarmee und in den Partisanenverbänden kämpften viele Frauen, um ihre Heimat zu verteidigen und Deutschland zu besiegen.

In jedem Kapitel gibt die Autorin einen Überblick über die Geschichte der jeweiligen Kriege, die Streitkräfte sowie die Gesellschaften und erläutert die damit verbundenen Geschlechterverhältnisse. Vieles zeigt sie anhand von zeitgenössischer Malerei, Werbekampagnen oder Fotografien, die sie jeweils kritisch einordnet. Hagemann führt auch Dokumente an, in denen Frauen ihre Erinnerungen daran festhielten, wie sie den Krieg erlebt und mit welchen Motivationen sie sich beteiligt haben und erzählen, welche Schicksale sie erlitten. Gerade diese sehr konkreten Darstellungen machen die geschichtlichen Prozesse nachvollziehbar.

Aus mehreren Gründen halte ich das Buch auch über ein engeres Publikum von Historiker:innen hinaus für überaus lesenswert und gewinnbringend:

…

items.title: My Whale Poem
items.subtitle: Illustration from i went fishing with my family when i was five.
items.feedText:
Courtesy of Tao Lin. I wrote this in February 2005, when I was twenty-one:

i went fishing with my family when i was five

when i was five

i went fishing with my family

my dad caught a turtle

my mom caught a snapper

my brother caught a crab

i caught a whale

that night we ate crab

the next night we ate turtle

the next night we ate snapper

the next night we ate whale

the next night we ate whale

the next night we ate whale

…

The first draft repeated the last line 143 times. I sent it to an editor at M…
items.body:
**Illustration from i went fishing with my family when i was five. Courtesy of Tao Lin.**

I wrote this in February 2005, when I was [twenty-one](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2025/08/05/my-college-diary/):

> i went fishing with my family when i was five
> when i was five
> i went fishing with my family
> my dad caught a turtle
> my mom caught a snapper
> my brother caught a crab
> i caught a whale
> that night we ate crab
> the next night we ate turtle
> the next night we ate snapper
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> …

The first draft repeated the last line 143 times. I sent it to an editor at *Monkeybicycle* —an online literary magazine—and he accepted it for publication. He wrote:

> The average weight of a small sea turtle is 60 lbs. The largest whale (the Blue Whale) averages 120 tons. So, that’s 4000 times larger. I was thinking we could repeat the final line 4000 times.

I emailed the poem to my mom, who replied, “Children would enjoy it very much, what do you think? Maybe sometimes you can write something for children someday. Just have a question, there are several hundred lines of ‘the next night we ate whale,’ is it supposed to be like that or it is a mistake? I tried to delete it, but couldn’t.”

The *Monkeybicycle* editor sent me his 24,059-word file of the poem and suggested I find an illustrator and publish it as “a huge chapbook.” Another *Monkeybicycle* editor said he’d illustrate and lay it out, but I wasn’t interested.

I read the poem at readings maybe five or six times. I remember staying focused and serious while reading it by dwelling on how depressed and alienated I felt. The longest I ever read it was seven minutes, I think.

In 2008, my friend recorded a video of the audience as I read the poem. This video is on YouTube. I began the reading by saying, “I’m going to read from my memoir.” Afterward, I sold stapled booklets of a short version of the poem for three dollars.

In 2009, I was paid a hundred dollars to read the poem for four minutes at the New Museum of Contemporary Art. In 2010, the *London Review of Books* published an [overview](https://www.theparisreview.org/letters-essays/8475/gemstone-tao-lin) of my [writing](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2024/09/12/my-childhood-toy-poodles/) [career](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2023/09/11/jets-and-trash/) that referenced the poem, and someone read the poem at a cultural center in Amsterdam. Also in 2010, at an event at Drawn & Quarterly’s bookstore for my second novel, I pitched the poem as a book to D&Q’s owner. I described this in my novel *Taipei* (2013):

> … the owner of Drawn & Quarterly approached and thanked Paul for coming to Montreal. Paul pitched a children’s book, to be illustrated by a known graphic novelist who’d confirmed interest, based on one of his poems—
> when i was five i went fishing with my family
> when i was five
> i went fishing with my family
> my dad caught a turtle
> my mom caught a snapper
> my brother caught a crab
> i caught a whale
> that night we ate crab
> the next night we ate turtle
> the next night we ate snapper
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> —with each line on its own page and the last line repeated as many times as needed. Maybe a different artist could illustrate each page to create a sort of anthology. As a children’s book, due to the content, it would …

The owner didn’t seem interested.

**Illustration from i went fishing with my family when i was five. Courtesy of Tao Lin.**

In 2012, the Asian American Writer’s Workshop asked me to participate in an event. The organization suggested four things I could do. The first was to read the whale poem. I chose another option. I was tired of reading the poem.

In 2013, I got an email that said, “The Head of English at the University of Exeter just randomly sent everyone on the Poetry module a video of you reading ‘i went fishing with my family when i was five’ as an example of how poetry isn’t dull.”

In 2014, Jeffrey Brown, the author of *Clumsy* (2002), one of my favorite graphic novels, agreed to illustrate my whale poem. An editor at McSweeney’s was interested in it for their children’s-book imprint. But this didn’t result in anything.

BBC Singers ’ composition by Jonathan Packham.

I mostly stopped caring about making the poem into a book. Sometimes people messaged me saying they’d performed it at a reading. A band used it as lyrics for a song. A doctoral student at Oxford used it as the text for a composition that the BBC Singers—a professional chamber choir—performed in a workshop setting.

In 2026, I noticed people discussing my poem on X. Pangram had identified it as 100 percent AI-generated. It was the only false positive discovered in a public challenge offering $4,100 to find one from before 2020 that was longer than 749 words.

This gave my poem more attention than it had ever gotten, encouraging me to make and publish the book myself. I handwrote, illustrated, and designed it over a week. I loved the process.

*From* [i went fishing with my family](https://muumuuhouse.com/whalepoem.html)[when i was five](https://muumuuhouse.com/whalepoem.html) *, published today by Muumuu House.*

*Tao Lin is the author of the novels* Leave Society *and* Taipei *, among other books. His poetry collection* Hawaii Years *is forthcoming from Louria Books. His most recent piece for the Daily was “[Taiwan English](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2026/06/24/taiwan-english/).”*

items.title: The Misguided Democratic Opposition to Permitting Reform
items.subtitle: In a break with Congress’s Orwellian naming conventions, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is genuinely bipartisan, pro-affordabil…

items.body:
In a break with Congress’s Orwellian naming conventions, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is genuinely bipartisan, pro-affordability, and would create some jobs. Although affordability is a popular concept—the entire Democratic Party campaigned on it in the midterm elections—it isn’t easy to execute. Bringing down inflation by reducing the budget deficit would require painful choices to raise taxes or cut spending. Ending the Iran war or President Trump’s tariffs would be somewhat easier policy choices, but even those moves, while the right thing to do, have trade-offs: Submitting to Iranian control of the Strait of Hormuz would enrich Iran and impose tolls on energy; eliminating the tariffs would upset some labor unions.

There is probably just one simple method to make life more affordable for Americans without sacrifice: support permitting reform. Incredibly, Democrats in Congress cannot decide whether to help pass it.

The permitting bill, which recently passed the Senate, is designed to streamline the process for building large-scale infrastructure, especially energy projects. The Democrats supplied 31 of the 33 “no” votes the bill received in the Senate. The split caucus is one reason House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has not yet indicated what posture he plans to take on the bill, and it is possible that, without his active support, it will die.

Two of its co-sponsors, Senators Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, are among the Democratic Party’s most devoted environmentalists. Their desire to pare back regulation may sound startling. But, like many green-energy champions, they have come to recognize that decarbonizing the economy requires rapidly building a new electrified infrastructure with solar power, wind power, charging stations, and transmission lines to connect it all. Current regulations make that basically impossible.

*[[Read: The simple message that produced a Democratic landslide](https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/2026/11/trump-jeffries-democrats-midterms/689266/?utm_source=feed)]*

A series of laws dating back to the 1970s erected elaborate legal hurdles to building new housing and infrastructure. The real cost of highways tripled within a generation after the ’60s, and the United States has built one new airport during this time. The worst culprit is the National Environmental Policy Act of 1970, which originally required short environmental-impact statements for any project on public land, but has since swelled into a lawsuit machine that demands thousands of pages of statements and years or decades of hassle. California has spent billions of dollars over two decades on a goal of building high-speed rail with virtually nothing to show for the time and money and little prospect of eventual completion. Heinrich’s interest in reform grew out of a 17-year ordeal to build a wind farm and transmission lines.

Despite having the word *environmental* in its title, the NEPA is not really an environmental law. It is a law that imposes forbidding regulatory processes on any project involving federal land. “Environmental” review held up congestion pricing—a climate-friendly traffic-reduction policy—in New York City for years. Paradoxically, environmental review can be used to block even purely conservationist [projects](https://www.theargumentmag.com/p/what-exactly-are-environmentalists?utm_campaign=email-post&r=230pu&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email) such as restoring wetlands or protecting the Great Lakes from an oil pipeline. Anything that changes federal land use can be targeted with expensive litigation by anybody who wants to block it.

The Biden administration authorized several hundred billion dollars in green-energy investments, only to recognize that little of the spending would materialize unless permitting could be drastically sped up. That realization inspired several efforts to pass permitting reform, of which the BAAJA is the latest and most promising. According to [credible](https://www.rff.org/publications/issue-briefs/projected-effects-of-the-bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-on-the-power-sector/) [estimates](https://rhg.com/research/baaja-us-energy-system-impacts/), the permitting reforms in BAAJA would reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and bring down the cost of energy without spending any taxpayer dollars.

This makes permitting reform an incredibly rare opportunity to press the “lower costs” button. The bill has the support of clean-energy manufacturers, the AFL-CIO—whose members would benefit from the construction boom it would allow—and some environmental groups.

The primary source of opposition is the movement that built the 1970s legal architecture—groups such as the Sierra Club and the Natural Resources Defense Council, which continue to exert influence over the Democratic Party. These organizations have decided that the permitting process, with its opportunities for interminable litigation, represent democracy in its purest form.

Most of the groups themselves were founded in an era when preserving the built environment as it existed at the time, rather than climate change (which was a marginal concern before the 21st century), was the environmental movement’s preeminent objective. The NRDC was founded out of a movement to block a New York hydroelectric power station—that is, a source of low-carbon energy. These organizations use laws such as the NEPA to file lawsuits to block development, especially (but not exclusively) fossil-fuel infrastructure.

Because the BAAJA would apply to all energy technologies, it would allow more fossil-fuel energy as well as more green energy. The net effect would likely be to reduce emissions by favoring wind and solar, which desperately need new transmission lines to move power from states that have lots of wind and sun to states that don’t. Solar energy, in particular, is getting dramatically cheaper, which means it is likely to replace fossil-fuel sources as long as new infrastructure is possible to build.

Because fighting climate change, promoting affordability, and allowing the government to build things again are all popular causes, the movement against the bill has treaded carefully in its public messaging. Opponents have frequently insisted that their goal is not to block permitting reform, but to stop this version so that Congress can write a better and more progressive bill.

This is a familiar ploy. In the past, conservative opponents of health-care reform have used the same message to run out the clock. When a hard-fought compromise measure emerges from Congress, its opponents will piously insist that Congress should simply start over. In reality, Trump is not going to sign a left-wing permitting bill that singles out fossil fuels for punishment.

…

items.title: Trump’s Imperialist Fantasy for Latin America Is Already Failing

items.body:
Last week, self-styled Secretary of War Pete Hegseth headed to Latin America looking for love. It capped off weeks of tumult in which a desperate Hegseth and his Pentagon underlings fought a pitched battle to save his job. Despite their efforts, more than 200 members of Congress gave him a [vote of no confidence](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/hegseth-no-impeachment-house-vote/), and the embattled secretary remains on the hot seat, with potential impeachment looming in 2027.

Things were different in Venezuela, which Hegseth’s military invaded earlier this year, [deposing](https://theintercept.com/2026/01/05/trump-venezuela-war/) and [kidnapping](https://theintercept.com/2026/01/04/trump-maduro-venezuela-war-media/) President Nicolás Maduro. Hegseth was feted at Miraflores Palace by Maduro’s former vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, a once outspoken anti-imperialist leftist who quickly pivoted to become America’s [top quisling](https://theintercept.com/2026/06/25/trump-venezuela-earthquakes-aid-sanctions/). “I’m very thankful for your presence here,” Rodríguez gushed, calling Hegseth “very tall and very young, with a great responsibility on his shoulders.” Acting like a satrap in what is now an American protectorate, Hegseth said that he appreciated Rodríguez’s “leadership” of a country he praised as a “compliant” partner.

Hopped up on neocolonialist fantasies, Hegseth claimed that America’s invasion on “January 3 is the day that will go down in history as a day of liberation for Venezuela.” He praised it as “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America.” After soaking in the adulation of a leader beholden to the Trump administration, Hegseth headed off to Colombia, Ecuador, and Honduras, where he continued talking tough.

“President Trump has prioritized our hemisphere and made it clear … that we will not cede our own backyard to foreign adversaries or to transnational cartels,” he said in Ecuador, where U.S. forces are taking part in “[Operation Total Extermination](https://theintercept.com/2026/03/23/trump-operation-total-extermination-ecuador-colombia-cuba/).” He continued, “Together, we will never back down; we will finish this fight for our citizens and for yours.”

Today, in his inaugural post for TomDispatch, Sam Carliner examines how the U.S. is attempting to impose its will on the Western Hemisphere under the so-called Donroe Doctrine. So far, the Trump administration has wreaked endless amounts of havoc and scored what it thinks are victories in Latin America. But Carliner points out that countervailing forces are rising across the region. One day, we may look back on Hegseth’s viceroy victory lap as the high point of the Trump administration’s gunboat diplomacy — and on Carliner’s analysis as one of the first to lay out what led to its downfall.

*—Nick Turse, editor of TomDispatch*

If you haven’t yet, [sign up to receive TomDispatch in your inbox here.](https://theintercept.com/dispatch/)

## The U.S. “Backyard”

It would have been unimaginable for the United States and longtime U.S. adversary, Venezuela, to enter into a military alliance just one year ago. But that’s exactly what U.S. “Secretary of War” Pete Hegseth announced from its capital, Caracas, on November 18, as part of a surprise meeting with Venezuela’s acting president, Delcy Rodríguez.

The new military agreement — which will include joint training, intelligence sharing, and defense equipment capabilities — and an oil deal signed in August, which even [Bloomberg has called](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-30/trump-s-venezuela-oil-grab-reprises-industry-s-neocolonial-past) a reprise of the industry’s “neocolonial past,” is the most significant achievement of President Donald Trump’s aggressive “Donroe Doctrine” to strengthen U.S. control over Latin America. “In the last year, the country that previously sent its oil wealth to Cuba or to China, from rigs built by Venezuelans and Americans, has now signed a historic oil deal with the United States, through the Department of War,” Hegseth [boasted](https://x.com/CBSNews/status/2123153785530855870?a=J7s4Z_trwMyT7b8PA_M&s=20) at a press conference last week.

[Related Trump Frees Ex-President of Honduras, Right-Wing “Narco-Dictator” Convicted of Drug Trafficking](https://theintercept.com/2025/12/01/honduras-hernandez-pardon-trump-venezuela-drugs/)

That same day, however, the [New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/world/americas/colombia-us-joint-military.html?unlocked_article_code=1.RVE.Y0lb.pfbaHojliNMs&smid=nytcore-ios-share) reported that Colombia rejected a plan to conduct joint military operations with the United States. This led Hegseth to cut a visit to Colombia short; he had originally planned to discuss military cooperation with the country’s new right-wing president, Abelardo de la Espriella. Both [he](https://x.com/ABDELAESPRIELLA/status/2123227348770168857?a=G9-MzL-fseKdDd0p4k0&s=20) and [Hegseth](https://x.com/PeteHegseth/status/2123238686510776325?a=aheKMio8hgNTMkMGJ3c&s=20) took to X deny the Times’s claims. But de la Espriella, who campaigned by aligning himself with the Trump administration and calling for military action against drug cartels and gangs, did not have sufficient support in Colombia’s Congress to ink a military agreement with the United States that would have allowed U.S. troops to conduct counter-cartel operations inside Colombia.

The military agreement with Venezuela and the lack of one in Colombia showcase the contradictions of the Trump administration’s aggressive Latin America policy. On the one hand, the administration has greatly expanded operations in the Western Hemisphere over the past year. But a recent series of setbacks, of which Colombia’s snub is only the latest, show the limits of U.S. power projection even in a region it has treated as its backyard for hundreds of years.

## The Donroe Doctrine in Action

One year ago this month, the Trump administration published its [National Security Strategy](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/2025-National-Security-Strategy.pdf?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email), which candidly advocated for a “Trump Corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine, invoking the policy that the United States historically used to treat Latin America and the Caribbean as the country’s exclusive sphere of influence. Just two months after releasing the NSS, on January 3, the administration carried out a [coup in Venezuela](https://theintercept.com/2026/01/08/venezuela-maduro-trump-oil-american-empire/), which removed its president, Nicolás Maduro, from power. A U.S. strike in southern Venezuela in June reportedly killed a leader of the Tren de Aragua gang. And last month, U.S. aircraft attacked a camp of supposed Colombian guerrillas operating inside Venezuela, killing more than two dozen people.

…

items.title: 25 Films Inspired by Edgar Allan Poe Online: The Fall of the House of Usher, The Tell-Tale Heart, and More
items.subtitle: Rank the films inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, and several adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” will almost certainly come near the top.
items.feedText: At first glance, that story of a man paying a visit to an old friend who lives with his twin sister in their family’s grand house — each of the latter three well advanced into a different process of deterioration — might seem too short, as well as too light on conflict to translate into a conventional screenplay. items.body:
Rank the films inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, and several adaptations of [“The Fall of the House of Usher”](https://www.eapoe.org/works/tales/usherf.htm) will almost certainly come near the top. At first glance, that story of a man paying a visit to an old friend who lives with his twin sister in their family’s grand house — each of the latter three well advanced into a different process of deterioration — might seem too short, as well as too light on conflict to translate into a conventional screenplay. Yet it’s also full of cinematically irresistible images, from the somehow ruinous yet wholly intact titular mansion to the bloodily wretched sister throwing herself upon the terrified brother who entombed her alive while their ancestral home collapses around them.

Of the twenty or thirty versions of “The Fall of the House of Usher” so far made for the screen, the most celebrated remains the one Jean Epstein directed in 1928. [Officially designating it as one of the “great movies,”](https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/great-movie-the-fall-of-the-house-of-usher-1928) Roger Ebert calls that picture’s vision of the great hall “one of the most haunting spaces in the movies. Its floor is a vast marble expanse, interrupted here and there by an item of furniture that seems dwarfed by the surrounding emptiness. An odd staircase rises from one distant corner. It is not impossible that this vision, in one of the best-known French surrealist films, inspired the designers of the great hall of Xanadu in *Citizen Kane*.”

The avant-garde filmmaking duo James Sibley Watson Jr. and Melville Webber (in collaboration with e. e. cummings, who contributed to the script) could hardly manage the same scale of production design for [their own short adaptation of Poe’s story](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eh1Fnxctjsw), which happened to come out the same year.

But the resulting Expressionist take on the material has also been highly acclaimed, and through [this YouTube playlist of Poe films](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLGECP2JNbcRg), you can experience not just both of them, but also other adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” by [idiosyncratic Czech animator Jan Švankmajer](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4f3ZxoLTHkk) and [B‑movie powerhouse Roger Corman](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EgktFwcVXCY). Sensitive to Poe’s sensationalist appeal and air of transgressive decadence, Corman ended up directing an eight-film “Poe cycle,” nearly all of which star Vincent Price.

It’s fair to say that no film actor is more closely associated with Poe than Price, a link Tim Burton [celebrated in animation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hD8uQzu0IL0) at the beginning of his career. Price even played the writer himself in [An Evening with Edgar Allan Poe](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZzyYzK94UU4&list=PLGECP2JNbcRg&index=7), a special from 1970 in which he recites “The Sphinx,” “The Cask of Amontillado,” “The Pit and the Pendulum,” and “The Tell-Tale Heart.” That last, the most screen-adapted Poe story of them all, also appears on [the playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLGECP2JNbcRg) in various forms: an [early D. W. Griffith feature](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=avB4bs4Q6DU), the [directorial debut of Jules Dassin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RW6fdqnN0E0), an [animated short narrated by James Mason](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WAXB2H3SsFg), a [British psychological thriller](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pXMZeSZS_-A), and a [transposition into modern-day New Orleans](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yWworPqU668). And if you haven’t had enough Poe after watching through all 25 of these films, consider watching the recent, well-received *Fall of the House of Usher * miniseries on Netflix — an entertainment platform that satisfies much the same appetites Poe’s stories have been feeding for nearly two centuries.

items.body:
Gladestry primary school is predicted to have only 19 pupils within two years, while its county council is forced to make cuts year after year. But residents still believe it’s worth fighting for

The kitchen in the Alman family farmhouse is large, airy and decorated with hundreds of rosettes awarded over the decades for prize-winning dogs, sheep and cows. I grew up just up the hill, so I know this kitchen well. Apart from the video feed in the corner, showing what the cattle are up to in the barn, it hasn’t changed much since the 1980s when we’d pile in here after helping our fathers with the baling.

From the kitchen, Gladestry’s small, slate-roofed primary school, set against the steep green slope of Hergest Ridge, is clearly visible, and – it being playtime when I visited – clearly audible too. That hasn’t changed much either since the days when Joseph Alman and I were pupils at that tiny school, and our own parents looked out of that same window and heard us calling to each other as we played football.

items.body:
arXiv:2611.31301v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/

sourceReferences.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
sourceReferences.author: Shaina Raza, Mohamed Hafez, Ahmed Y. Radwan, Khalid Elgazzar, Kathryn Hume

items.body: Background: Mental health conditions are a leading cause of disability and economic burden worldwide. Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) may widen access, but economic evidence from community mental health settings, including low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), has not been synthesized by perspective, time horizon, and comparator type. Objective: This study aimed to assess the cost-effectiveness of DMHIs delivered in community mental health settings. Methods: This systematic review followed the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines and was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO CRD420251141326). PubMed, Scopus, the Directory of Open Access Journals, and the Cochrane Library were searched for economic evaluations published from January 2010 to June 2025 involving adolescents (aged 10 years and older) through older adults with mental disorders. Two reviewers independently screened studies, and the quality was appraised using the Consensus on Health Economic Criteria (CHEC) list. Costs were standardized to 2025 US $, and findings were synthesized narratively. Results: Of 2478 records identified, 20 economic evaluations were included: 16 randomized controlled trials, 3 decision-analytic models, and 1 uncontrolled single-arm study, conducted in high-income countries and LMICs (Kenya, Lebanon, China, and Southeast Europe). Depression (n=11, 55%) and anxiety (n=7, 35%) were the most frequent targets. Of 20 studies, 10 (50%) used a health care payer perspective only, 1 (5%) study used a societal perspective only, and 9 (45%) used both perspectives; time horizons ranged from 2 weeks to 10 years. Thirteen (65%) studies were cost-effective at the willingness-to-pay thresholds applied, and 4 (20%) were not; 3 (15%) did not state a threshold. Among the 16 studies reporting quality-adjusted life years, 4 (25%) were dominant (less costly and more effective), 11 (69%) were more costly and more effective, and 1 (6%) was less costly and less effective. The BlueIce smartphone app for self-harm and the NIDUS-Family (New Interventions for Independence in Dementia Studies) dementia intervention were dominant, whereas a societal perspective made some interventions cost-saving, such as Step-by-Step in Lebanon. Interventions that were not cost-effective included those evaluated in Germany, the United States, and Southeast Europe, and 1 psychosis trial with a high incremental cost-effectiveness ratio. Methodological quality was high in 15 (75%) studies, moderate in 4 (20%), and low in 1 (5%). Conclusions: DMHIs in community settings can offer good value for money, particularly guided internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy for depression and anxiety, and may be cost-saving from a societal perspective. The evidence is limited by short time horizons (often 12 months or less), waitlist and usual care comparators, and heterogeneous outcome measures. Future evaluations should use longer follow-ups, active comparators, and a common utility measure, ideally the EQ-5D questionnaire. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD420251141326; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251141326

items.body: BackgroundDelirium occurs in up to 52% of cardiac and vascular surgeries and is associated with long-term cognitive impairment and death. Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a delirium risk factor. In rodents, AKI induces systemic endothelial activation and, when combined with surgery, results in greater neuroinflammation than surgery alone. We hypothesized that systemic endothelial activation and blood-brain barrier BBB disruption are more strongly associated with delirium that occurs concurrently with AKI.MethodsWe performed a prospective study of 150 adults undergoing cardiac and major vascular surgery. We quantified intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) and E-selectin, biomarkers of endothelial activation, and ubiquitin carboxy-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCHL1), a biomarker of neuronal injury and BBB permeability, in plasma collected after surgery. Delirium was assessed using the CAM-ICU tool. KDIGO serum creatinine criteria were used to assess AKI.ResultsPatients with AKI-associated delirium and those with non-AKI-associated delirium had similar clinical characteristics, delirium risk factors, and postoperative sedation scores. In multivariable models, ICAM-1 was not associated with delirium overall (p = 0.29). However, AKI modified the association between ICAM-1 and postoperative delirium (p = 0.01 for interaction between AKI and ICAM-1) such that when the interaction term was introduced, the estimated ICAM-1 OR was 0.57 [95% CI 0.37–0.87], p = 0.01. In post-hoc analyses, higher ICAM-1 concentrations were associated with decreased odds of non-AKI-associated delirium (OR = 0.48 [95% CI 0.28–0.81], p = 0.01) and increased odds of AKI-associated delirium (OR = 1.69 [95% CI 1.05–2.74], p = 0.03). E-selectin was not associated with delirium. Higher UCHL1 concentrations were associated with an increased odds of AKI-associated delirium (OR = 3.68 [95% CI 2.05–6.62], p < 0.001), but not non-AKI-associated delirium (p = 0.33). This association between higher UCHL1 and a greater odds of AKI-associated delirium was potentiated by increased ICAM-1 endothelial activation (p = 0.046).ConclusionDelirium occurring concurrently with AKI may represent a biologically distinct phenotype. Recognition of biologic heterogeneity within delirium populations may help explain inconsistent associations reported for delirium risk factors and biomarkers. Accounting for this biological heterogeneity may improve the identification of delirium biomarkers and therapeutic targets and should be considered in future delirium research. Future multi-center studies with larger and more diverse cohorts and extended cognitive assessment protocols are needed to validate these observations.

items.body: Chemokines and their receptors mediate cell migration and coordinate immune responses, while dysregulation can lead to inflammation. Therapeutic modulation of the chemokine signaling axis has proven difficult. Most drug discovery efforts target the receptors, whereas natural regulatory mechanisms modulate immune responses by directly binding to or modifying the chemokine ligands. Despite this insight, development of effective chemokine-directed modulators has remained elusive. Recent advances in de novo protein design offer an unprecedented opportunity to produce high-affinity binders that efficiently block protein-protein interactions. We implemented a computational workflow leveraging the BindCraft platform to generate miniprotein binders against CCL25, the chemokine ligand for the receptors CCR9 and ACKR4, and implicated in inflammatory bowel diseases. The unbiased development results in several miniproteins designed to block the receptor N-terminus from wrapping the chemokine and preventing productive engagement. Thus, these proteins suppress CCL25-mediated effector coupling and halt MOLT-4 lymphoblast migration. Another class of miniprotein, represented by VUP25111, is predicted to bind CCL25 along the chemokine β1 strand and retained receptor binding. This complex inhibited arrestin recruitment to CCR9, but not to ACKR4, indicating receptor specificity. Additionally, G protein recruitment to CCR9 was unimpeded by VUP25111, suggesting that the miniprotein biased the native agonist towards G proteins. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of differentially targeting CCL25 to suppress CCR9 signaling and new tools to resolve the structural basis of chemokine receptor activation and bias.

items.body: Across species, self-directed action is linked to theta rhythms and better memory, but such action combines choosing, moving, and controlling the outcome. Whether choosing and control over the outcome shape recollection, and the encoding dynamics that support it, remains unclear. Three preregistered experiments in human participants separated these components while holding movement constant. Participants encoded scene pairs by dragging either a freely chosen scene or one indicated by the program, with fluent or disrupted feedback. Recognition was tested after 24 hours (and immediately in Experiment 2), using Remember/Know judgments. Experiment 3 recorded scalp electroencephalography during encoding. Choosing improved recognition, more for recollection than familiarity. A smaller benefit extended to the unselected scene, although less consistently after latency adjustment. Disrupted feedback lowered rated agency but did not reduce memory at 24 hours. In Experiment 2, however, recollection declined less over 24 hours after self-generated than externally generated action, but only under fluent feedback. Choosing increased action-onset-locked theta and alpha phase alignment (inter-trial phase coherence), whereas disrupted feedback reduced alignment later. The selection effects survived matching for response-initiation-latency. Trial by trial, later posterior theta alignment (353-570 ms) predicted Remember over Know responses, whereas early frontal alpha alignment (127-245 ms) predicted Remember over Forgotten responses. These findings link self-generated action to the timing of encoding-related oscillations and to subsequent recollection. The association between later posterior theta alignment and Remember-Know discrimination is consistent with a role for theta phase coordination in associative binding.

items.title: How to Touch the Nothingness Behind Everything: Kahlil Gibran on the Seven Selves
items.subtitle: A self is an illusion, and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.
items.feedText: A self is a forest. A self is a ship. Above all, a self is a sum of selves, contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of l…
items.body:
A self [is a forest](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/11/09/pando/). A self [is a ship](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/03/08/plutarch-the-ship-of-theseus-ted-ed/). A self [is an illusion](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/10/21/iris-murdoch-unselfing/), and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.

Above all, a self is [a sum of selves](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/04/10/parts/), contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of life.

[Kahlil Gibran](https://themarginalian.org/tag/kahlil-gibran) (January 6, 1883–April 10, 1931), who thought deeply about [the art of becoming yourself over the sweep of life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/04/04/youth-and-age-kahlil-gibran/), takes up this question in one of his signature parable-poems found in his 1918 classic [The Madman](http://www.amazon.com/Madman-His-Parables-Poems/dp/0486419118/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](http://www.worldcat.org/title/madman-his-parables-and-poems/oclc/242642&referer=brief_results) | [free ebook](http://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5616)).

The poem unfolds as a taxonomy of the core animating passions we live with and suffer by — sorrow, ecstasy, infatuation, hate, longing, creative possession — each a trap, a cage, a dooming fate the sufferer yearns to rebel against. Then comes the seventh self, seemingly the most pitiable, for it is the self that appears to live in pointlessness, perpetually facing the void, but in the end the freest: Only the empty self that lusts for nothing can touch the essence of everything. (Gibran would have appreciated [the Japanese concept of ma](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/09/07/ma/).)

Kahlil Gibran

> THE SEVEN SELVES
> by Kahlil Gibran
> In the stillest hour of the night, as I lay half asleep, my seven
> selves sat together and thus conversed in whisper:
> First Self: Here, in this madman, I have dwelt all these years,
> with naught to do but renew his pain by day and recreate his sorrow
> by night. I can bear my fate no longer, and now I rebel.
> Second Self: Yours is a better lot than mine, brother, for it is
> given to me to be this madman’s joyous self. I laugh his laughter
> and sing his happy hours, and with thrice winged feet I dance
> his brighter thoughts. It is I that would rebel against my weary
> existence.
> Third Self: And what of me, the love-ridden self, the flaming brand
> of wild passion and fantastic desires? It is I the love-sick self
> who would rebel against this madman.
> Fourth Self: I, amongst you all, am the most miserable, for naught
> was given me but odious hatred and destructive loathing. It is
> I, the tempest-like self, the one born in the black caves of Hell,
> who would protest against serving this madman.
> Fifth Self: Nay, it is I, the thinking self, the fanciful self,
> the self of hunger and thirst, the one doomed to wander without
> rest in search of unknown things and things not yet created; it is
> I, not you, who would rebel.
> Sixth Self: And I, the working self, the pitiful labourer, who,
> with patient hands, and longing eyes, fashion the days into images
> and give the formless elements new and eternal forms — it is I, the
> solitary one, who would rebel against this restless madman.
> Seventh Self: How strange that you all would rebel against this
> man, because each and every one of you has a preordained fate to
> fulfill. Ah! could I but be like one of you, a self with a determined
> lot! But I have none, I am the do-nothing self, the one who sits
> in the dumb, empty nowhere and nowhen, while you are busy re-creating
> life. Is it you or I, neighbours, who should rebel?
> When the seventh self thus spake the other six selves looked with
> pity upon him but said nothing more; and as the night grew deeper
> one after the other went to sleep enfolded with a new and happy
> submission.
> But the seventh self remained watching and gazing at nothingness,
> which is behind all things.

Couple with Gibran on [silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/11/21/kahlil-gibran-prophet-talking/), then revisit Hermann Hesse on [discovering the soul beneath the self](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/02/18/hesse-soul/).

### donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing *The Marginalian* (which [bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/22/brain-pickings-becoming-the-marginalian/) for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a [donation](https://www.themarginalian.org/donate/). Your support makes all the difference.

### newsletter

*The Marginalian* has a free weekly newsletter. It comes out on Sundays and offers the week’s most inspiring reading. Here’s [what to expect](https://mailchi.mp/brainpickings/janna-levin-rebecca-elson-anne-lamott-james-gleick). Like? [Sign up.](https://www.themarginalian.org/newsletter/)
