items.body:
Food historian [Ken Albala](https://kenalbala.blogspot.com/) answered a question from the internet for [WIRED](https://www.wired.com/) about why [turkey is at the center](https://laughingsquid.com/turkey-thanksgiving-bird/) of a traditional [Thanksgiving](https://laughingsquid.com/thanksgiving-united-states-national-holiday/) meal, noting that its origin story is actually a myth. Instead, he explained, the meal was simply what people in the 19th century thought people in the 17th century would have eaten.

> When it became a national holiday, people had in mind what 17th-century food would’ve been like, and they kind of get it right in some very interesting respects.

Albala also noted that writer [Sarah Josepha Hale](https://www.womenshistory.org/education-resources/biographies/sarah-hale), best known for [“Mary Had a Little Lamb”](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/46954/mary-had-a-little-lamb), [petitioned President Abraham Lincoln](https://www.nps.gov/liho/learn/historyculture/lincoln-and-thanksgiving.htm) to make Thanksgiving a national holiday to help heal a nation divided by the [Civil War](https://www.gilderlehrman.org/history-resources/essays/american-civil-war).

items.body:
In contemplating the theory of general relativity, Albert Einstein imagined [a falling lift in which people are performing experiments](https://archive.org/details/evolutionofphysi033254mbp/page/n245/mode/2up):

> One of the observers takes a handkerchief and a watch from his pocket and drops them. What happens to these two bodies? … [F]or the outside observer they are both falling with the same acceleration. But so is the lift, with its walls, ceiling, and floor. Therefore: the distance between the two bodies and the floor will not change.

This notion of the equivalence between gravity and acceleration, which he called “the happiest thought of my life,” came to Einstein in 1907. Interestingly, Lewis Carroll had explored a similar scenario in 1889:

> ‘One can easily imagine a situation,’ said Arthur, ‘where things would necessarily have no weight, relatively to each other, though each would have its usual weight, looked at by itself.’
> ‘Some desperate paradox!’ said the Earl. ‘Tell us how it could be. We shall never guess it.’
> ‘Well, suppose this house, just as it is, placed a few billion miles above a planet, and with nothing else near enough to disturb it: of course it falls to the planet?’
> The Earl nodded. ‘Of course — though it might take some centuries to do it.’
> ‘And is five-o’clock-tea to be going on all the while?’ said Lady Muriel.
> ‘That, and other things,’ said Arthur. ‘The inhabitants would live their lives, grow up and die, and still the house would be falling, falling, falling! But now as to the relative weight of things. Nothing can be heavy, you know, except by trying to fall, and being prevented from doing so. You all grant that?’
> We all granted that.
> ‘Well, now, if I take this book, and hold it out at arm’s length, of course I feel its weight. It is trying to fall, and I prevent it. And, if I let go, it falls to the floor. But, if we were all falling together, it couldn’t be trying to fall any quicker, you know: for, if I let go, what more could it do than fall? And, as my hand would be falling too — at the same rate — it would never leave it, for that would be to get ahead of it in the race. And it could never overtake the falling floor!’

(From [Sylvie and Bruno](https://www.google.com/books/edition/Sylvie_and_Bruno/OTcTEQAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&pg=PT67&printsec=frontcover).)

items.body:
Imagine you’re in a seat in the theatre. The stage has a back and sides, but is open to the audience. And yet, the actors behave as though they can’t see the rows of people watching. It’s as if there’s a fourth wall.

The fourth wall is the imaginary barrier between the fictional world and the audience in TV, film, or theatre.

As the audience, you are in a privileged position of watching these private scenes play out in front of you.

Origin of the Fourth Wall

An early description of this invisible barrier as a wall comes from our pal Denis Diderot (also of The Diderot Effect) in his 1758 writing Discours de la poésie dramatique (translated):

"Whether you are writing or acting, give no more thought to the spectator than if he did not exist. Imagine a great wall at the edge of the stage separating you from the audience; act as though the curtain had never risen."

I love Denis’ comment about acting as though the curtain had never risen. I’m not an actor, but I would guess that being able to ignore that there’s an audience, or a camera, might help create a more realistic performance.

Breaking the Fourth Wall

Now, you might take issue with Diderot’s notion, especially if you’ve ever been to a pantomime. Many shows don’t treat the fourth wall as a wall. A pantomime is expected to engage the audience by acknowledging that there will be things the audience can see on stage that a character perhaps can’t—“It’s behind you!” Other times the audience are explicitly part of the show.

Some shows have characters turn and share private thoughts directly into the camera, or simply give a knowing glance. This is known as breaking the 4th wall. Phoebe Waller-Bridge did this all the time in Fleabag, making the viewers her confidants in the scene.

We recently enjoyed a family viewing of Monty Python and the Holy Grail, which does it rather spectacularly, merging the medieval and the modern.

Related Ideas to The Fourth Wall

Front Stage, Back Stage

Diagonal Billing

The Third Teacher

Information Radiator

The Diderot Effect

Mean-World Syndrome

Here’s Diderot’s passage in the original French:

"Soit donc que vous composiez, soit que vous jouiez, ne pensez non plus au spectateur que s’il n’existait pas. Imaginez sur le bord du théâtre un grand mur qui vous sépare du parterre ; jouez comme si la toile ne se levait pas."

items.title: Beautiful News is back for another year
items.subtitle: We’re a few weeks into a reboot of our Beautiful News project from a few years ago.
items.feedText: Refreshed. Revitalised. Re-visualised. Once more, every day for a year, we are surfacing and visualising some of the amazing, progressive and positive things happening around the world. Trends and events and innovations we can’t always see when fixated on the negativity of the news. We’ve spruced and updated some of data-visualisations from the original collection, as well as adding 160 more stories to be released over the next weeks, months, year and beyond! Every graphic is of course underpinned by open datase…
items.body:
**We’re a few weeks into a reboot of our [Beautiful News](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/) project from a few years ago. Refreshed. Revitalised. Re-visualised.**

Once more, every day for a year, we are surfacing and visualising some of the **amazing, progressive and positive things happening around the world**. Trends and events and innovations we can’t always see when fixated on the negativity of the news.

We’ve spruced and updated some of data-visualisations from the original collection, as well as adding 160 more stories to be released over the next weeks, months, year and beyond!

Every graphic is of course underpinned by [open datasets](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/data/) to support full **evidence-based optimism.**

Swing by and join [our weekly newsletter](https://beautifulnews.myflodesk.com/newsletter) or daily on [the website](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/), or social channels of your choosing: [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/beautifulnews.daily), [Twitter/X](https://x.com/beautiful__news), [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/beautifulnewsdaily/), [Threads](https://www.threads.com/@beautifulnews.daily).

## Some of my favourite graphics and stories so far

» [34 Countries Now Generate 80% or More of Their Electricity from Renewables](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/3021-countries-electricity-renewables/)

» [Tons of new vaccines are in the pipeline](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/524-new-vaccines/)

» [Polio is very nearly wiped out](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/3037-polio-wiped-out/)

» [The Cost of Renewable Energy is Plunging](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/586-cost-renewables-falling/)

» [The EU Gender Pay Gap is (slowly) Decreasing](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/3030-eu-gender-pay-gap/)

» [Everyone, Everywhere, is Living Longer](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/41-everyone-everywhere-is-living-longer/)

**Towards a more nutritious information diet…**

David

# The Global Antiauthoritarian Wave Is an Illusion

## The Global Antiauthoritarian Wave Is an Illusion

## Democracy Can’t Be Saved at the Ballot Box

### Larry M. Bartels

LARRY M. BARTELS is University Distinguished Professor of Political Science and Law and May Werthan Shayne Chair of Public Policy and Social Science at Vanderbilt University.

- More by Larry M. Bartels
### The Global Antiauthoritarian Wave Is an Illusion

Democracy Can’t Be Saved at the Ballot Box

Larry M. Bartels

- Share in email
- Share on Facebook
- Share on X
- Share on LinkedIn
- Copy Link Copied Article link: https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-states/democracy-global-anti-authoritarian-wave-illusion https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-states/democracy-global-anti-authoritarian-wave-illusion Copy

In 2022, many observers celebrated the results of the United States’ midterm elections as a victory for democracy. The Republican Party underperformed at the ballot box, and some of the candidates most outspoken in support of former President Donald Trump’s historic effort to overturn the 2020 election outcome were among the casualties. President Joe Biden concluded that the American people “have proven once again that democracy is who we are.” New York Times reporters Nick Corasaniti, Reid Epstein, and Jonathan Weisman concurred, writing that the midterm outcome demonstrated “the resilience of the country’s democracy” as the electorate rejected “openly extremist Republican candidates.”

But that rosy interpretation was more the result of wishful thinking than careful analysis. Most of the Republicans who lost were simply bad, inexperienced candidates. In fact, Republican members of Congress who had flouted the democratic process by voting to decertify electoral votes on January 6, 2021, suffered no discernible penalty at the polls, while the minority who had stood up for the rule of law faced stiff backlash from their party’s establishment and from primary voters. And, of course, two years later, Trump stormed back into the White House.

In this year’s midterms, Trump’s party took another, even bigger beating. And again, there has been a rush to celebrate the result as a triumph for democratic values. NPR reported that “one of the big, clear winners of the midterms is American democracy itself.” Amanda Taub, an international affairs columnist at The New York Times , upped the ante, writing that “An anti-authoritarian wave appears to be crashing over elections around the world.” Just as in 2022, however, there is reason to fear that this optimistic account seriously misconstrues what happened at the polls on November 3 and what the result means for the future. History shows that voters in the United States, as in other democracies, are much more focused on the competence of their political leaders and their own well-being than on adherence to democratic procedures. To imagine that they have suddenly become guardians of democratic norms is to misunderstand the electorate’s role in the democratic process—and to underestimate the chronic susceptibility of the American political system to democratic backsliding.

### BELIEFS VS. BUTTER

It is natural to “feel pride,” as the New York Times editorial board put it, in the notion that ordinary citizens “stood up” for democratic principles at the ballot box. Democracy is the United States’ civil religion, and the voice of the people is the closest thing Americans have to the voice of God. But as the British jurist and historian Henry Sumner Maine observed in 1885, the oracle of democracy is often “not as intelligible as might be desired.” Electoral behavior is complex, and interpretations of election outcomes constructed in the hours and days after a vote often turn out to be far off the mark. Voters in democracies are less ideological than analysts generally assume. They are also less committed to abstract democratic norms than high-minded observers might hope. In a 2020 study, the Yale political scientists Matthew Graham and Milan Svolik used survey experiments to test the impact of democratic norm violations on Americans’ support for hypothetical candidates. They concluded that “only a small fraction of Americans prioritize democratic principles in their electoral choices when doing so goes against their partisan identification or favorite policies.” In 2022, real voters demonstrated the same point with their willingness to support Republican members of Congress who had participated in Trump’s bogus “stop the steal” effort.

This year, the exit polls run by a consortium of American news organizations provided superficial support for the notion that the midterm “blue wave” was an explicit rejection of Trump’s continuing assault on democratic norms. These surveys asked voters which of six issues was the most important facing the country. A third of respondents chose “the state of democracy,” and an overwhelming proportion of those who did, 79 percent, voted for Democratic congressional candidates. Taken at face value, these data suggest that more than a quarter of the electorate voted Democratic because they opposed Trump’s efforts to subvert American democracy.

Alas, people’s explanations for their own behavior are often misleading. Responses to list choices of this sort are particularly sensitive to the specific options presented and their favorable or unfavorable connotations. Given the choice, most people would probably prefer to attribute their votes to principled support for democracy than to pique at the price of gas. But when a separate YouGov poll conducted just after the vote asked an open-ended version of the same question, only five percent of voters spontaneously cited government corruption or the undermining of democracy as the most important factor motivating their choice.

A closer look at the exit poll data offers additional grounds for skepticism regarding the importance of democratic principles for the 2026 midterm outcome. The largest swing away from the Republican Party, more than 30 points, was among young voters—who are generally much less supportive of democracy than other age cohorts. (A 2025 Kettering Foundation survey, for instance, found that although 89 percent of Silent Generation respondents agreed with the proposition that “democracy is the best form of government,” only 54 percent of Gen Z respondents did.) To suppose that young people are now the vanguard of a sudden urge to defend democracy is implausible.

items.title: Eine Hürde weniger für Rot-Grün-Rot in Berlin
items.subtitle: Vanessa Emde ist raus aus der Berliner Linksfraktion - und auf dem Weg zu Rot-Grün-Rot haben Linke, Grüne und SPD ein Problem weniger.

items.body:
# Linke schliesst Emde aus: Eine Hürde weniger für Rot-Grün-Rot

## Linkenfraktion schliesst Vanessa Emde aus : Eine Hürde weniger für Rot-Grün-Rot

von Markus Gross

Vanessa Emde ist raus aus der Berliner Linksfraktion - und auf dem Weg zu Rot-Grün-Rot haben Linke, Grüne und SPD ein Problem weniger. Das letzte wird es wohl nicht bleiben.

Vanessa Emde wurde aus ihrer Fraktion ausgeschlossen. Sie war wegen ihrer Haltung zu Israel unter Druck geraten. Für die Regierungsbildung in Berlin ist es ein wichtiger Schritt.

Vor Raum 311 im Berliner Abgeordnetenhaus herrscht ein gewaltiger Medienrummel. Drinnen im großen Sitzungssaal diskutiert die Linksfraktion lebhaft über den Ausschluss von Vanessa Emde. Es scheint, als würde die halbe Republik auf ein Zeichen warten. Schafft es die Fraktionsführung, die aus ihrer Sicht widerspenstige Abgeordnete rauszuschmeißen?

Nach zweieinhalb Stunden steht fest: Vanessa Emde ist nicht mehr Mitglied der Fraktion Die Linke . 33 Abgeordnete stimmen für ihren Ausschluss, sechs stimmen mit Nein, es gibt vier Enthaltungen. Die nötige Mehrheit von 30 Stimmen wird erreicht.

- Umstrittene Abgeordnete: Vanessa Emde aus Berliner Linken-Fraktion ausgeschlossen
Sichtlich angespannt verkündet der Fraktionschef der Linken, Tobias Schulz: "Wir haben keine Möglichkeit mehr gesehen, mit Frau Emde weiter zusammenzuarbeiten." Sie habe sich nicht an Partei- und Fraktionsbeschlüsse zum Thema Antisemitismus gehalten. "Ihr Ausschluss ist folgerichtig", so Schulz weiter.

ZDF-Korrespondent Stephan Merseburger ordnet aus Berlin den Fraktionsausschluss Vanessa Emdes ein.

## Unterstützer empfangen Emde mit Jubel

Als Vanessa Emde den Fraktionssaal verlässt, wartet schon ein zwölfköpfiges Unterstützerkomitee auf sie. Es gibt Jubelrufe, als sie erscheint, Umarmungen und Zeichen der Solidarität. Emde bezeichnete ihren Ausschluss in einem Statement als Ergebnis einer "medialen Hetzkampagne".

Ihre Fraktion habe offenbar dem Druck von SPD und Grünen nachgegeben. Sie wolle ihr Mandat behalten. Ihre Unterstützer ruft sie dazu auf, sich zu "organisieren". Kämpferisch ihr Schlusswort:

> Wir sehen uns im Kiez und wir sehen uns am Streikposten! In diesem Sinne: Yalla, yalla, Klassenkampf, Freiheit für Palästina! „

Vanessa Emde

## Grüne und SPD sehen positives Signal

Die möglichen Koalitionspartner SPD und Grüne begrüßten den Ausschluss von Vanessa Emde. Werner Graf, Co-Chef der Grünenfraktion, gab sich zufrieden: "Die Entscheidung zeigt, dass für israelbezogenen Antisemitismus in einer rot-grün-roten Regierung kein Platz ist" . Steffen Krach, Co-Chef der SPD-Fraktion, der zuvor vehement einen Ausschluss Emdes gefordert hatte, ergänzte:

> Die Entscheidung der Linksfraktion ist eine gute Nachricht für die weiteren Koalitionsverhandlungen. „

Steffen Krach, Co-Chef der Berliner SPD-Fraktion

Die Berliner Linke hat die Abgeordnete Vanessa Emde aus ihrer Fraktion ausgeschlossen. Den Schritt hat man sich laut dem Fraktionsvorsitzenden Schulze nicht leicht gemacht.

## Antisemitismus-Vorwürfe gegen Emde

Vanessa Emde, mit über 46 Prozent direkt gewählte Abgeordnete in Neukölln, hatte zuvor mit ihren israelkritischen Aussagen immer wieder für Diskussionen gesorgt. Zuletzt hatte Emde in einem Instagram-Post das Existenzrecht Israels als jüdischer Staat angezweifelt. Ihre Kritiker werteten das als antisemitisch.

Der Zentralrat der Juden zeigte sich tief besorgt und forderte die Linke zum Handeln auf. Auch SPD und Grüne, die möglichen Koalitionspartner, waren verstimmt und machten den Ausschluss Emdes zur Bedingung.

- Schuster: Ausschluss von Emde "nur ein erster Schritt"
Bei den Grünen schaltete sich zuletzt sogar die Bundespitze ein. "Wenn das scheitert, kann ich allen nur abraten, in eine Regierung mit einer politischen Führung zu gehen, die in der eigenen Fraktion keine Macht hat" , hatte die Grünen-Co-Vorsitzende Franziska Brantner noch der "Frankfurter Allgemeinen Zeitung" vom Dienstag gesagt.

Die Berliner Linke hat die Abgeordnete Vanessa Emde aus der Fraktion ausgeschlossen. Was bedeutet die Entscheidung für die Partei und die Regierungsbildung in Berlin? ZDFheute live analysiert.

## Misstrauen bei SPD und Grünen bleibt

Mit dem Ausschluss Vanessa Emdes ist eine der größten Hürden auf dem Weg zu Rot-Grün-Rot in Berlin aus dem Weg geräumt. Doch Entwarnung bedeutet das nicht. SPD und Grüne bleiben misstrauisch. Der Vorwurf, in Teilen der Linken gebe es ein strukturelles Problem mit antisemitischen Tendenzen, ist längst nicht ausgeräumt.

Auch innerparteilich ist der Konflikt keineswegs beendet. Sechs Gegenstimmen und vier Enthaltungen zeigen, dass Emde weiterhin Rückhalt in der Fraktion hat. Wie sich ihr Unterstützerlager künftig positioniert, dürfte für die Koalitionsgespräche entscheidend werden. Der Politikwissenschaftler Thorsten Faas findet: "Der Ausschluss ist nicht so überzeugend, dass jegliche Diskussion innerhalb der Linken beendet ist." Das Bündnis bleibe in einem Schwebezustand.

Vorerst aber können alle Beteiligten aufatmen: Die Gespräche gehen weiter. Bis zum Jahreswechsel soll ein Koalitionsvertrag stehen. Anschließend müssen Linke und SPD noch ihre Mitglieder überzeugen. Doch bis dahin ist es ein weiter Weg - und das nächste Personalproblem womöglich nur eine Frage der Zeit.

Markus Gross ist Redakteur im ZDF-Landesstudio Berlin.

items.body:
# Krebsmedikament erfolgreich in Tabakpflanze hergestellt

Zahlreiche Arzneimittel stammen ursprünglich aus der Natur und werden bis heute vollständig oder teilweise aus pflanzlichen Bestandteilen gewonnen. Dazu zählt auch das Chemotherapeutikum Paclitaxel, das gegen verschiedene Krebsarten zum Einsatz kommt, darunter gegen Brust-, Eierstock- und Gebärmutterhalskrebs sowie bestimmte Arten von Lungenkrebs. Isoliert wurde es ursprünglich aus der Rinde der Pazifischen Eibe (Taxus brevifolia). Allerdings werden große Mengen Eibenrinde für wenig Wirkstoff benötigt und die Pflanzen sterben nach der Ernte ab – eine nicht nachhaltige Strategie.

Heute wird das Medikament stattdessen halbsynthetisch hergestellt, wobei Vorprodukte aus den Nadeln der europäischen Eibe isoliert und anschließend weiterverarbeitet werden. Zudem ist es bereits möglich, den Wirkstoff in Eibenzellkulturen zu produzieren. Der vollständige Syntheseweg des komplexen Moleküls war allerdings bislang noch unklar. „Durch seine strukturelle Komplexität und seine geringe natürliche Häufigkeit ist die Herstellung von Paclitaxel nach wie vor kostspielig und ineffizient“, berichtet ein Team um Feiyan Liang von der Universität Kopenhagen in Dänemark.

## Eingeschleuste Gene

Nun haben Liang und ihre Kollegen erstmals sämtliche Schritte des Biosynthesewegs von Paclitaxel rekonstruiert und in eine artfremde Pflanze übertragen. Für ihre Studie schleusten sie die Baupläne für Enzyme, die in der Eibe an der Herstellung von Paclitaxel beteiligt sind, in die Blätter der Tabakpflanze Nicotiana benthamiana ein. Dazu nutzten sie Bakterien als sogenannte Genfähren. Die eingeschleuste DNA wird dabei nicht fest ins Erbgut des Wirts eingebaut, sondern bleibt nur einige Tage aktiv und wird während dieser Zeit in Genprodukte umgesetzt – in diesem Fall in Paclitaxel und seine Vorstufen.

Anhand der Modellpflanze konnte das Team die einzelnen Syntheseschritte detailliert nachvollziehen. „Dadurch haben wir offene mechanistische Unklarheiten systematisch beseitigt“, berichten die Forschenden. Wie sie feststellten, finden die verschiedenen Herstellungsschritte in unterschiedlichen Bereichen innerhalb der Pflanzenzellen statt. „Das erfordert einen gerichteten Transport der Zwischenprodukte zwischen den verschiedenen Zellorganellen“, erklären Liang und ihre Kollegen.

Auf Basis dieser Erkenntnisse gelang es ihnen, die ursprünglich sehr geringe Paclitaxel-Produktion in der Tabakpflanze um mehr als das 500-fache zu steigern, bis zu einem Wert von 61,05 Mikrogramm pro Gramm Trockengewicht. „Dieser Gehalt ist mit der Konzentration in der Eibenrinde vergleichbar“, berichten die Forschenden. Aus ihrer Sicht liefert die Studie den Nachweis, dass eine biotechnologische Produktion des Chemotherapeutikums in genetisch modifizierten Tabakpflanzen grundsätzlich machbar ist.

## Noch keine Konkurrenz zu bisherigen Methoden

Der praktische Nutzen dieser Methode ist zumindest für Paclitaxel jedoch begrenzt: Das neue Verfahren bietet in seiner bisherigen Form keinen Vorteil gegenüber den gängigen Methoden zur Herstellung des Chemotherapeutikums, wie der nicht an der Studie beteiligte Botaniker Heribert Warzecha von der Technischen Universität Darmstadt erklärt.

„Die Produktion in Eiben-Zellkulturen oder die Isolierung einer Vorstufe aus Nadeln und die anschließende chemische Modifikation zu Paclitaxel sind etabliert und kostenoptimiert“, erklärt Warzecha. „Damit sich der Aufwand der Umstellung auf eine neue Technik inklusive der notwendigen Anlagen lohnt, müsste der Ertrag zehn- bis hundertmal höher sein, oder die Kosten entsprechend niedriger, was hier nicht der Fall ist.“ Hinzu kommt, dass das neue Verfahren auf gentechnischen Methoden beruht, was die Zulassung komplizierter macht.

Doch auch wenn ein unmittelbarer praktischer Nutzen noch aussteht, trägt die Studie Warzecha zufolge entscheidend zum Verständnis der biochemischen Prozesse in den Zellen der Eibe bei, inklusiver aller notwendigen Gene und Enzyme. „Dass die Autoren durch ihre Methode in Tabakpflanzen vergleichbare Mengen an Paclitaxel erzeugen konnten, wie sie auch in der Rinde der Eibe vorkommen, ist ein großartiger Erfolg. Es zeigt, dass einige Verständnisfragen nun geklärt werden konnten“, sagt er. „Ob sich die Menge noch weiter steigern lässt, bleibt abzuwarten. Erst dann wäre die hier vorgestellte Produktionsmethode ‚konkurrenzfähig‘ zu etablierten Methoden.“

Denkbar wäre zudem, ähnliche Methoden für andere Arzneimittel anzuwenden, für die es bislang noch keine Zellkultursysteme gibt.

Quelle: Feiyan Liang (University of Copenhagen, Denmark) et al., Nature Chemical Biology, doi: 10.1038/s41589-026-02376-x

# YouTube's iconic iOS app icon may soon return with new customizable icons [Gallery]

- YouTube
## YouTube’s iconic iOS app icon may soon return with new customizable icons [Gallery]

The iconic YouTube app icon that looked like a retro TV found on iOS might be making a comeback, with new customizable icons showing up behind the scenes of a new YouTube update.

In the early days of the iPhone, Apple built a custom app for YouTube on iOS before Google built its own. That included an app icon that looked like a retro TV and it was later replaced when YouTube’s official app launched on the platform.

Now, that icon might be coming back.

Android Authority spotted several new app icons YouTube for Android is testing in its latest beta update (v21.47.483-BETA). These icons seem to be tied to a new feature that would allow users to customize the homescreen icon for YouTube, and includes seven designs in total including two throwback designs. One is the aforementioned retro TV icon used on iOS, which was never on YouTube for Android, and another is an old stacked YouTube logo design.

Users would be able to change the app icon via a new setting in the app near the “Appearance” section, but nothing is live just yet. We also don’t know if this is Android-only, if this is limited to Premium subscribers, or when this might debut.

That said, it’s very fun to get these throwbacks, and we’ll be excited to see this functionality go live.

items.title: 5 Euro spenden, 2.000 Euro abgebucht: Polizei warnt vor Spendensammlern
items.subtitle: Zwei Menschen wollten in Bardowick jeweils 5 Euro per Karte spenden.

items.body:
# Falsche Spendensammler: Polizei warnt nach zwei Fällen

- KURZMELDUNG · DEUTSCHLAND Vor einem Aldi in Bardowick bittet eine Person eine Frau um eine Spende für Menschen mit Behinderungen. Auf dem mobilen Kartenterminal sieht sie 5 Euro, später fehlen laut Polizei 2.000 Euro auf ihrem Konto. Die Warnung vom 20. November 2026 betrifft diesen Fall vom 30. Oktober und einen zweiten vom 4. November. Die Frau wollte zunächst Bargeld geben, wurde laut Polizei aber zur Kartenzahlung gedrängt. Im zweiten Fall sprach ein vermeintlicher Spendensammler einen Mann nahe einer Sparkasse an. Auch er sah 5 Euro auf dem Terminal und bemerkte später eine Abbuchung über 2.000 Euro. Die Polizeiinspektion Lüneburg/Lüchow-Dannenberg/Uelzen spricht von einer manipulierten Anzeige. Wie die Abweichung zwischen dem sichtbaren und dem abgebuchten Betrag technisch zustande kam, geht aus der Mitteilung nicht hervor. Die beiden Fälle belegen daher keine allgemeine Unsicherheit von Kartenzahlungen. Wer eine verdächtige Abbuchung entdeckt, soll laut Polizei sofort die Bank wegen einer Kartensperre verständigen und Anzeige erstatten. Bei einer spontanen Spendenbitte empfiehlt es sich, die Entscheidung aufzuschieben und die genannte Organisation selbst zu überprüfen. Mimikama berichtete bereits im März 2026 über eine ähnliche Spendenmasche. Ein mobiles Kartenlesegerät bestätigt weder die Identität der sammelnden Person noch den Spendenzweck. Das wiederkehrende Muster ist der Zeitdruck: Wer später über einen selbst geprüften Weg spendet, entzieht der Masche ihre wichtigste Grundlage. Quellen Polizeiinspektion Lüneburg/Lüchow-Dannenberg/Uelzen via Presseportal: POL-LG: ++ Polizei sensibilisiert: Betrug durch vermeintliche Spendensammler mit Karten-Lesegerät ++ nach verbaler Auseinandersetzung mit Messer gedroht und Mann angegriffen – Jugendlicher vorl. festgenommen , 2026-11-20
- Mimikama: EC-Kartenbetrug vor Supermarkt: Wie funktioniert die Spendenmasche? , 2026-03-24

items.body:
# Worshipping at the altar of Brendan Gregg

Okay, I am the first to admit that I’m a bit manic with AI. When you are working on a problem that has endless possibilities, it is difficult to constrain yourself to a limited set of features.

Can I just add one more?

I have been amazed at all the fun and useful things that a deterministic VM like Rewind enables. I have been using it to help find heisenbugs , to make profile-guided optimization reproducible , and to make Nix builds bit-reproducible . But the most fun has been using it to understand performance.

Turns out that performance is yet another area where Rewind shines. I have been using it to analyze the critical path of builds.

What is the critical path?

The critical path is the longest chain of dependent work in a program. It is the minimum time that the program can take to complete, regardless of how many resources you throw at it. The only way to make a program faster is to shorten the critical path.

If you worship at the altar of Brendan Gregg, you know he spent years turning performance analysis from a dark art into a science. This is a small offering to him. 🤲

I added a new rewind time command to Rewind that analyzes a recording and tells you where the time went and what would make the run finish sooner. You can drill into any part of that answer and see the source lines responsible for it. It’s like Brendan Gregg’s flame graphs but on steroids for the critical path and with a debugger attached. 1 1 All the ideas for the command are either inspired by or directly influenced by Brendan Gregg’s work . Kneel before Zod!

> Aside: New to Rewind? Start with a flaky build you only catch once and dafuq is a deterministic VM?

Let’s see how it works by analyzing the critical path of a libuv build and test run. The build and test suite takes 78 seconds inside Rewind, and even with 64 cores it still takes 47 seconds. Why?

The usual answer is to look at a CPU profile, and in this case a CPU profile would be almost useless. For two thirds of those 47 seconds, the work the build is waiting on is not computing at all: it is asleep . 💤💤💤

## § Where the time goes

Every rewind time starts with two numbers:

$ rewind time 7a29e716 libuv-1.51.0 78.0 s elapsed on the VM's one CPU 47.4 s critical path: the least it can take on any number of CPUs 67% asleep (epoll_pwait 23.1 s, clock_nanosleep 8.53 s, futex 100 ms), 33% computing The first is how long the run took on the VM’s one virtual CPU. The second is the critical path : the longest chain of work where each step had to wait for the one before.

No number of CPUs makes a run shorter than its critical path, so the gap between the two numbers is all that parallelism can buy you.

The line under the two numbers applies Gregg’s thread state analysis . Here the biggest state is asleep: 23 seconds in epoll_pwait and 8.5 in clock_nanosleep .

A sleeping thread is invisible to a CPU profiler. Gregg’s answer is off-CPU analysis : look at where threads block, not only where they compute.

On a live machine, off-CPU analysis is hard. Linux can trace which thread woke which, and Gregg built wakeup and off-wake profiling on top of that, but you have to be tracing before the slow run happens, the tracing has a cost, and most of the sleeps you capture are noise. Rewind already logs every context switch because it needs them to replay, and now it records every wakeup and who caused it too. All that juicy information is in every recording. 🤤

Here is the whole output for libuv:

$ rewind time 7a29e716 libuv-1.51.0 78.0 s elapsed on the VM's one CPU 47.4 s critical path: the least it can take on any number of CPUs 67% asleep (epoll_pwait 23.1 s, clock_nanosleep 8.53 s, futex 100 ms), 33% computing The critical path by phase 3.54 s configurePhase ██ 1.67 s buildPhase █ 42.0 s checkPhase █████████████████████ 99 ms 5 other phases The critical path by process on path pid process, with what it started 47.4 s 34 init › bash -e source-stdenv.sh default-builder.sh 41.9 s 4076 ├─ make -j8 SHELL=bash-5.3p3/bin/bash VERBOSE=y check 36.4 s 4910 │ ├─ make › bash › lt-run-tests 3.38 s 5412 │ │ ├─ lt-run-tests hrtime hrtime asleep in clock_nanosleep 3.38 s 2.00 s 5013 │ │ ├─ lt-run-tests delayed_accept delayed_accept asleep in epoll_pwait 2.00 s 1.62 s 5126 │ │ ├─ lt-run-tests fs_event_watch_dir fs_event_watch_dir asleep in epoll_pwait 1.62 s 1.60 s 5103 │ │ ├─ lt-run-tests fs_event_close_in_callback fs_event_close_in… asleep in epoll_pwait 1.60 s 1.60 s 5508 │ │ ├─ lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time metrics_idle_time asleep in epoll_pwait 1.00 s, computing 600 ms 1.24 s 6095 │ │ ├─ lt-run-tests tcp_write_ready tcp_write_ready 1.14 s 5510 │ │ ├─ lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time_thread metrics_idle_time_t… asleep in epoll_pwait 1.00 s 1.10 s 5132 │ │ ├─ lt-run-tests fs_event_watch_file_current_dir fs_event_wat… asleep in epoll_pwait 1.10 s 22.6 s │ │ └─ 279 more 5.59 s 4077 │ └─ make test/run-tests 2.22 s 4183 │ ├─ gcc -fPIC -fstack-clash-protection -O2 -U_FORTIFY_SOURCE … 2.10 s 4189 │ │ └─ cc1 /build/source/test/test-fs.c 3.35 s │ └─ 20 more 1.99 s 68 ├─ sh ./autogen.sh 1.99 s │ └─ 9 more 1.67 s 2642 ├─ make -j8 SHELL=bash-5.3p3/bin/bash 1.67 s │ └─ 5 more 1.53 s 403 └─ bash ./configure --disable-static --disable-dependency-tracking… 1.47 s └─ 581 more What would shorten it sooner pid if this took no time 36.1 s every lt-run-tests, 600 processes 6.66 s every cc1, 283 processes 3.38 s 5412 75 sleeps in clock_nanosleep: lt-run-tests hrtime hrtime 2.00 s 5013 2 sleeps in epoll_pwait: lt-run-tests delayed_accept delayed_accept 1.76 s 4189 cc1 /build/source/test/test-fs.c 1.62 s 5126 30 sleeps in epoll_pwait: lt-run-tests fs_event_watch_dir fs_event_watc… 1.60 s 5103 16 sleeps in epoll_pwait: lt-run-tests fs_event_close_in_callback fs_ev… 1.60 s 5508 lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time metrics_idle_time 1.22 s every perl, 9 processes 1.14 s 5510 lt-run-tests metrics_idle_time_thread metrics_idle_time_thread Look closer rewind time 7a29e716 --in PID one process: its threads, sleeps and waits rewind time 7a29e716 --folded the path for flamegraph.pl or speedscope.app rewind time 7a29e716 --perfetto F every process on a timeline, for ui.perfetto.dev The second table is the path as a tree of processes based on Gregg’s colony graph idea. Each line is a process with everything it started, and its time on the critical path. 2 2 A ps snapshot might miss short-lived process invocations; the recording has every fork, regardless of how brief.

In this build, make check needs 41.9 of the total 47.4 seconds, and 36.4 of that is lt-run-tests , libuv’s test runner. The test runner invokes 287 tests each spending 1-3 seconds.

All of those tests are on the path, and the path is a single chain, so the runner ran them one after another. Worse, most of each test is spent asleep, waiting on timers.

Drag can be less than time on the path.

items.title: Paint in the memory of other programs

items.feedText: core is a program that I wrote which spills the viscera of other programs onto the screen and allows you to prod them. it could be called an “esoteric debugger” or a “paint program.” the visual content of the program is constructed as follows: as well as the display of program memory, core allows for its manipulation. if core shows you a picture of a program’s insides, then it is only natural that it allows you to scribble on it. the overcommitted empty space below the stack stack provides an inviting empty space to scribble in.
items.body:
# paint in the memory of other programs - citrons.xyz

## paint in the memory of other programs

core is a program that I wrote which spills the viscera of other programs onto the screen and allows you to prod them. it could be called an “esoteric debugger” or a “paint program.”

the visual content of the program is constructed as follows:

- pages of memory (hardcoded for now as 4096 bytes) are arranged on a Z-order curve.
- each page of memory is displayed as a 256x128 rectangle.
- each pixel represents a bit. a white pixel represents one, and a black pixel represents zero.
- the bits are arranged in rows, and the bytes are arranged in columns
as well as the display of program memory, core allows for its manipulation. if core shows you a picture of a program’s insides, then it is only natural that it allows you to scribble on it. the overcommitted empty space below the stack stack provides an inviting empty space to scribble in. it’s a perfect place to hide your terrible secrets in some poor, innocent process.

core is the logical conclusion of blinkenlights, “Allblinkenlights,” if you will. the intended experience is evocative aimlessness. the human visual system is highly parallel and very good at recognizing patterns. you are encouraged to allow these patterns to wash over you.

many textures arise from different kinds of data in memory. ASCII text is incredibly recognizable, by virtue of being a 7-bit encoding, as well as having a biased distribution of values. 64-bit pointers are similarly easy to recognize because their last two bytes will either be zero or one.

in the mesmerizing undulations of complex programs, these textures may blink or move around or stay boringly still. if you are keen, you may catch some large data structure being allocated or filled in. or you may see the first generation of a garbage collector fly by as short-lived objects are created at a rapid rate. in games, the stack can be seen flickering rapidly and changing every frame.

core can make stark the immensity of memory and the way that programs use it. data structures and programming patterns appear in the physical reality of which bits are toggled where.

I was very keen to see what a program would look like that uses continuation passing style implemented as in the famous paper, CONS should not CONS its arguments, part II: Cheney on the M.T.A . I compiled a game programmed in CHICKEN scheme and was delighted to see a stack that moved like a waterfall.

graphical programs can be the most interesting. visual patterns in graphics in memory can emerge vividly.

when attached to virtual machines or emulators, core gains omniscience over an entire operating system.

it is astounding to see an immense creature flicker to life. pages fill empty space in speckled patterns. panning over a chasm, the page tables can be seen vibrating and filling in with new allocations. it is reminiscent, perhaps, of insects, like a beehive.

one could not hope to wholly understand the way that physical memory is arranged, but they may peer voyeuristically into random pages of process memory, abound with text strings and recognizable graphics.

programs often exist in the mind as something ineffable, intangible, and abstract. even their physical existence is locked inside black plastic squares, harboring impossibly tiny transistors. in my opinion, to lay visceral the individual bits in a computer program is an idea that despite being simple, is immensely potent.

peer into the core.

items.body:
# The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning

The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning October 27, 2026

Ali Behrouz and Vahab Mirrokni, Google Research

We introduce a sleep phase in continual learning, enabling large language models to continuously integrate new facts and enhance reasoning while mitigating catastrophic forgetting or static knowledge cutoffs.

Modern LLMs achieve impressive performance via pre-training and in-context learning (ICL). However, once deployed, they remain largely static, operating with a fixed knowledge cutoff date that leaves them unable to acquire long-term capabilities or adapt to new information.

While updating models with new data seems like the obvious solution, continual parameter updates often trigger catastrophic forgetting , a fundamental issue where learning new tasks severely degrades performance on previously learned ones. Alternatively, relying strictly on ICL limits knowledge retention to the immediate context window: once the context session ends, the acquired short-term information is forgotten.

Inspired by how the human brain processes and stabilizes memory during rest, we introduce a sleep framework in continual learning: a learning paradigm that equips large language models (LLMs) with a continuous periodic lifecycle, enabling them to continually learn, consolidate fragile short-term context into stable long-term parameters. With this framework, we demonstrate that alternating between active interaction and offline memory consolidation allows LLMs to continuously acquire new facts, retain long-context knowledge up to 10M tokens, and improve complex reasoning.

## Rethinking machine learning: Active (wake) vs. sleep phases

Traditional machine learning relies on a strict separation between training and inference. In a continual learning framework, this distinction becomes artificial; an intelligent agent must constantly learn, adapt, and process information.

Under the sleep paradigm, an LLM operates across two primary states:

- Active (wake) phase : The model actively receives, processes, and interacts with inputs, storing temporary information in fast, short-term memory components.
- Sleep phase : The model pauses processing new inputs and redirects its internal computations toward memory consolidation and self-improvement.
While terms like "sleep," "dreaming," and "self-improvement" borrow from neuroscience, our framework operates entirely within a fixed model architecture and human-defined training rules. During the offline sleep phase, the model unlocks pre-allocated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) memory blocks and updates its numerical weights using self-generated practice examples. This automated post-training cycle helps a deployed model absorb new facts and sharpen its reasoning accuracy while keeping its core codebase and design unchanged.

## Key components of the sleep process

The sleep paradigm addresses catastrophic forgetting and continuous adaptation through two stages: memory consolidation and dreaming.

### 1. Memory consolidation

In the human brain, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) slow-wave sleep consolidates fragile memories into long-term structures via abstraction and distillation. Our proposed sleep framework mirrors this natural phenomenon through two key technical mechanisms:

- Parameter expansion & continuum memory hierarchy: To prevent catastrophic forgetting, the model dynamically scales its capacity during sleep. Using a Mixture of Experts (MoE) and Hope architecture , newly unlocked, low-rank experts are integrated into stable, lower-frequency memory blocks to store incoming knowledge without disrupting older parameters.
- Knowledge seeding (upward distillation): Fragile short-term memories stored in high-frequency layers (e.g., in-context memory) are transferred into the newly expanded long-term parameters. This is achieved through Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD) combined with reinforcement learning (RL)-based imitation learning : On-policy distillation: The expanded student model learns token-specific feedback from teacher distributions generated on self-sampled sequences.
- Learning to imitate (LTI): The student model is rewarded based on semantic and absolute similarity ( Levenshtein distance ) when completing prefixes of teacher-generated text.
- Synaptic pruning: Once the memory consolidation into lower-frequency modules is complete, the high-frequency temporary parameters are reset, freeing up capacity for future active sessions.
Overview of our sleep framework: Input streams from the active phase are stored in short-term memory before entering the sleep cycle, which bifurcates into Consolidation (transferring fragile short-term tokens into expanded long-term parametric memory using low-rank structures and MoE) and Dreaming (autonomous self-improvement via synthetic routing with random experts and RL refinement).

### 2. Dreaming for self-improvement

During REM sleep , the human brain actively simulates scenarios, consolidates emotional/semantic connections, and explores novel neural pathways. Mirroring this, during the “dreaming stage”, the sleep framework implements an autonomous self-improvement loop:

- Random expert selection: During synthetic data generation, the MoE router randomly activates non-standard experts. This forces the model to mix disparate domains of knowledge and uncover latent patterns.
- Curated rehearsal: The model generates synthetic training samples ("dreams") and filters them using gradient-based data selection to prioritize samples with the highest potential to boost overall model capability.
- RL refinement: The model performs supervised fine-tuning on top-rated dream samples and evaluates whether the generation improves performance on downstream tasks.
## Theoretical foundations

Beyond the empirical results, our sleep paradigm is grounded in a theory that clarifies why its two stages (memory consolidation and dreaming) can support continual learning without simply trading new knowledge for old capabilities.

For memory consolidation, the analysis shows that knowledge seeding can be understood as a structured, low-rank compression problem. The model is not asked to copy every detail of its short-term traces into its parameters. Instead, it identifies a compact set of directions that best preserve both the model’s own on-policy behavior and the semantic qualities rewarded by the learning objective.

items.body:
Groups often define themselves in part via shared beliefs, and this induces group members to show loyalty via strongly affirming group beliefs. And your group-binding beliefs seem less strong if you arrive at them via particular data or assumptions, as you might later be convinced to reject such things, thereby undermining such beliefs.

This induces group members to base their beliefs on foundations that seem less likely to be overturned. In our society, that most stable foundation tends to be moral views, supported by strong internal feelings from the heart/conscience. While it is possible to derive such moral views from other sources, few in our world actually do that.

For example, I’ve long been adjacent to many libertarians, who as groups strongly reward loyalty to their cause. Individuals compete to show themselves to be more extremely and completely devoted to this cause. Believing in this cause due to simple moral axioms, supported by strong raw feelings, is the most popular route among those considered the most loyal. Many of us lean libertarian due to instrumental reasons, but we are less common among core libertarian organizations, and are seen as less reliable or loyal by core folks.

To solve cultural drift, I want many people to consider revising key behaviors in light of this problem. I want them to see our morals as instruments of Darwinian cultural evolution, and thus to consider revising such views in light of how cultural processes are going bad. But, alas, this tendency to justify our behaviors in terms of simple moral views, supported only by strong feelings, seems a big obstacle to my hopes.

items.body:
# WhatsApp launches highly requested new feature for sending messages later - 9to5Mac

## WhatsApp launches highly requested new feature for sending messages later

WhatsApp just announced that it is rolling out scheduled messages, which it says is one of users’ most requested features. Here are the details.

## Here’s how to send a scheduled message in WhatsApp

From WhatsApp’s blog post announcing support for scheduled messages:

> You can write a message when you think of it and send it anywhere from 10 minutes to 14 days later, in both your 1:1 and group chats. To schedule a message, press and hold the send button and pick the date and time you want it to arrive. It will look like any other message to the person receiving it. You can see all future messages you have lined up, and delete them beforehand if you change your mind. Even if your phone is off or out of battery, your scheduled message will still show up at the time you chose, and it remains end-to-end encrypted like all your personal messages, so no one else can read it, not even us.

WhatsApp says this feature is “rolling out globally over the coming weeks.” So you might not see it right away, but even if you don’t, it should show up on your account soon.

Scheduled messages work not only for text, but also when sending media like photos and videos.

To get access to scheduled messages, make sure you’ve updated to the latest WhatsApp app update, which was just released today.

# Raumsonde „Hera“ erreicht Asteroiden Dimorphos - Wissen - SZ.de

Die Raumsonde „Hera“ ist aktuell etwa 30 Kilometer von den Asteroiden Didymos und Dimorphos entfernt. Esa 2022 ließ die Nasa eine Sonde auf den Asteroiden Dimorphos prallen, um ihn aus seiner Bahn zu lenken. Nun ist eine Sonde der Esa eingetroffen. Was die Bilder zeigen.

sun stands still is a celebration of the coming Winter Solstice, supported by three poles of expansive, exploratory music performance. join us for a float somewhere between ambient and electronica, experimental noise and infectious synthpop, all guided by hand-built software & circuits.

details

happening in the beautiful upstairs lounge of Wayside Cider in Andes, NY

on Saturday, December 19th 2026

from 7-9pm

for $20 (no one turned away for lack of funds!)

if you're in NYC, the Trailways bus to Andes will drop you off a three minute walk away... (click for more details)

about the artists

softbits is kelli cain (@kelli_cain) and brian crabtree (@tehn). they make music for and about weather, volcanos, barns, dead scientists, eccentric architects, geology, birds, the invisible, the apocalypse, snacks. they also make electronic music instruments used by musicians all over the world, run an art store in delhi, tend a farm and orchard, make art in various mediums, and sometimes travel to play music in faraway places.

Kiki Garland’s (@synthetivv) work is a product of their obsession with psychoacoustics and near- or non-patterns, and is marred by a relentless pursuit of imperfection. Most recent performances involve the use of a custom software instrument built for abstract & tangible sound. They have performed and recorded as 1/2 of Garlands, 1/2 of M(K)G, 1/3rd of S.P.A.L.L., and roughly 1/5th of Music for Furniture.

Gray Schiller (they/them) is an drone artist, songwriter, and instrument maker living in the Hudson Valley. They are the founder of the nonprofit organization Atmospheric Music Alliance and record label StretchMetal Records.

dani derks is part of the day-to-day operations at Whimsical Raps, assisting with the development of new musical instruments, testing and iterating interface designs, and producing accessible technical documentation for artists. Their personal projects are centered on coding through improvisation, creating their own environments for playful and exploratory music performance gestures.

items.title: Did Abdul El-Sayed suggest making Second Amendment the 'right to have healthcare'?
items.subtitle: Posts also claimed the Michigan Democratic senator-elect wanted to ban fireworks from Independence Day celebrations.
items.feedText: Rumors that Democratic Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed once said that he believed in replacing the U.S. Constitution's Second Amendment — the right to bear arms — with a right to healthcare, as well suggesting that fireworks be banned from Independence Day, circulated in November following his midterm election victory. People on Facebook shared posts making the claims against El-Sayed, who defeated his Republican opponent by about 7 percentage points. Abdul El-Sayed, a Michigan Democrat, is facing questions after old videos surfaced showing him suggesting that America replace the Second Amendment with a constitutional right to health care. In one video, he asked what would happen if the Constitution were changed so Americans had a right to health care instead of the right to bear arms. In another video, he criticized Fourth of July fireworks and encouraged Americans to find other ways to celebrate Independence Day.
items.body:
# Did Abdul El-Sayed suggest making Second Amendment the 'right to have healthcare'?

- The claim that Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed once said he wanted to replace the U.S. Constitution's Second Amendment, the right to bear arms, with a right to receive healthcare, circulated in November. The claim included other alleged statements such as El-Sayed wanting to ban fireworks on Independence Day.
- The rumor stems from a CNN report in August about El-Sayed making the alleged statements in videos posted to his official YouTube channel that were removed prior to the launch of his campaign for office.
- The statements appear to be correctly attributed to El-Sayed based on CNN's reporting and El-Sayed's response to the outlet. However, we've been unable to verify the videos firsthand, so we've left this claim unrated.
- Snopes will update this report if we are able to acquire the original videos or receive a response from El-Sayed.
Rumors that Democratic Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed once said that he believed in replacing the U.S. Constitution's Second Amendment — the right to bear arms — with a right to healthcare, as well suggesting that fireworks be banned from Independence Day, circulated in November following his midterm election victory.

People on Facebook shared posts making the claims against El-Sayed, who defeated his Republican opponent by about 7 percentage points.

One user wrote:

> Abdul El-Sayed, a Michigan Democrat, is facing questions after old videos surfaced showing him suggesting that America replace the Second Amendment with a constitutional right to health care. In one video, he asked what would happen if the Constitution were changed so Americans had a right to health care instead of the right to bear arms. In another video, he criticized Fourth of July fireworks and encouraged Americans to find other ways to celebrate Independence Day.

The quotes appeared to be accurately attributed to El-Sayed based on the available evidence and previous reporting about the videos being removed prior to El-Sayed's campaign.

However, Snopes bases its ratings on primary evidence. We were unable to obtain the original videos in which the quotes were allegedly made, as they have been made private by El-Sayed and he has not yet responded a request for comment and verification of the old clips. Therefore, we've left this claim unrated. We will update this article if we're able to obtain the original videos or receive a reply from El-Sayed.

The rumor stemmed from an Aug. 11 report by CNN that mentioned the specific claims that recirculated after the midterm elections: that El-Sayed said "fireworks suck" regarding Independence Day celebrations and that he suggested replacing the Second Amendment with a Constitutional right to healthcare.

Each rumor stemmed from a separate video posted to El-Sayed's official YouTube channel but since made private. According to CNN's report, El-Sayed's office confirmed the authenticity of the videos but said they do not reflect his current views and had been removed.

"Abdul is the former captain of his high school football team, loves Michigan football on Saturdays, and celebrates the Fourth of July with fireworks like the next Michigander," CNN quoted a campaign spokesperson as saying. They added, "Cherry-picked comments from old podcasts don't reflect his beliefs today."

A wide range of major media outlets, including HuffPost , The Hill , Fox News and Forbes , picked up CNN's report, as did gun advocacy organizations such as the National Association for Gun Rights and The Firearm Industry Trade Association and independent journalism outlet The Reload , which described its aim to be the "best place to find fair and discerning reporting on firearms and how they intersect with politics."

The archived link for El-Sayed's now-private video dated April 6, 2023, showed it was titled " The Right to Bear Arms The Right to Have Healthcare!"

The archived link did not play the video, and a thorough search for the original clip yielded no results. Based on the video's date, it appeared that it was made in response to an April 5, 2023, school shooting in Nashville .

According to a transcript of the video uploaded by The Reload, El-Sayed referenced the events of the shooting and said, "What if we tweaked the Constitution? Amended the amendment, and instead of the right to bear arms, we change it to the right to have healthcare."

The transcript further alleged that he said:

> Imagine what that would mean. That would mean fewer people dying by guns and more people living because they have healthcare. Maybe two words of a change, but it would address two of America's most pernicious social ills. Literally deadly problems that we could fix with two words. So, you should think about it, huh?

The second part of the claim addressing El-Sayed's alleged comments on fireworks came from a July 10, 2024, video ( archived ) titled "Can we PLEASE find another way to celebrate July 4th? Four reasons why fireworks suck." That video also had been made private as of this writing.

The description for the video read:

> After July 4th, the city of Detroit experienced the worst air quality in the entire world. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed explains what fireworks are made of, why exploding them over large bodies of water might not be the best idea, and the several safety risks they bring.

In addition, one chapter of the video's contents was titled "Fireworks just aren't worth it: hear us out."

While the archived link could not play the video in question, it is reasonably clear from the text on the video page that El-Sayed was not in favor of fireworks, though whether he called for a ban on them was unclear.

items.body:
# What Does the ICJ Ruling Mean for Myanmar?

## What Does the ICJ Ruling Mean for Myanmar?

## The junta thinks it might find a sympathetic ear from Trump.

- Southeast Asia
Welcome to Foreign Policy ’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: What the ICJ’s genocide ruling means for Myanmar , a flurry of trade deals in the region, and new U.S. chip controls threatening Malaysian and Thai business .

Welcome to Foreign Policy ’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: What the ICJ’s genocide ruling means for Myanmar , a flurry of trade deals in the region, and new U.S. chip controls threatening Malaysian and Thai business .

ICJ: Myanmar Committed Genocide

The state of Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in 2017, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the main judicial arm of the United Nations, ruled last Thursday.

The ruling documents how, following attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA), Myanmar carried out a campaign of genocidal violence against the Rohingya. It estimates that 10,000 Rohingya, about 1.2 percent of the total population, were killed.

The court ruled 9-6 that the “only reasonable inference” was that this violence showed genocidal intent to destroy the Rohingya as a group—not just drive them out of Myanmar or exact collective punishment.

The ruling orders Myanmar to cease violence against the group and prosecute those responsible, allow the safe return of Rohingya to their homes, and pay compensation.

Sadly, none of this is likely. The junta has rejected the judgment as “unfair.”

Meanwhile, another armed group called the Arakan Army, which controls most of Rakhine province and mainly represents ethnic Rakhine Buddhists, has also committed large-scale violence against the Rohingya. Fighting between the Arakan Army and Rohingya militant groups—which has seen the Rohingya militants, including the ARSA, occasionally cooperate with the junta—has added to the hostility.

The Arakan Army has made some overtures to Muslim communities in the province.

For now, though, the Arakan Army is taking a wait-and-see attitude to the ICJ judgment. A spokesperson told local media, “We are constantly monitoring the current developments. We will stand firmly on truth and justice and take appropriate action for the benefit of the Arakan region.”

The country’s National Unity Government (NUG)—representing the civilian government overthrown by the junta in 2021 and associated with some of the main rebel forces— endorsed the judgment.

This was not a given. When Aung San Suu Kyi, an icon of the NUG, was acting as the country’s de facto leader, Myanmar consistently denied that the military’s actions against the Rohingya constituted a genocide.

In opposition, the NUG may now find its position easier. Its statement focused heavily on the junta’s culpability.

But it may find the whole judgment hard to accept. The ruling finds the state of Myanmar—not just the military—guilty of genocide. And at that time when the most severe offense took place, in 2016 and 2017, the paramount power in the state apparatus was Aung San Suu Kyi.

In Southeast Asia, could this be a stumbling block for junta leader Min Aung Hlang’s push for diplomatic normalization with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)?

Thailand—the most vocal advocate for Myanmar’s full readmission to ASEAN—looks unmoved. “Thailand must take the position that best serves the country,” Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters.

Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow argued that Thailand’s engagement did not contradict the ruling, as Thailand’s aim was to curb the current violence.

Meanwhile, two other countries—Malaysia and the Philippines—have issued official statements on the matter.

Malaysia’s brief statement said that it “respects the judgment.” The Philippines’ statement seemed a shade weaker, saying it “acknowledges the judgment” and, unlike Malaysia, does not mention the Rohingya by name.

Other ASEAN countries have yet to make official statements .

Still, for countries opposed to Myanmar’s full readmission to the bloc—most notably Singapore, which serves as the ASEAN chair next year—the judgment will reinforce this skepticism.

On the global stage, China has objected. “China has concerns over issues such as overreach of jurisdiction and expansive interpretation, and believes such practices are not conducive to dispute resolution,” a spokesperson said.

Regarding the United States, this judgment—plus the results of the country’s midterms—will likely impede the U.S. push toward normalization.

Parts of the American right reject the judgment. While the U.S. government declared in 2022that the anti-Rohingya violence constituted a genocide, some on the right are concerned that the ICJ judgments lay the groundwork for a finding of genocide against Israel, linked to its war in Gaza.

And the Myanmar junta clearly still thinks that it might find a sympathetic ear from the Trump administration.

When objecting to the ICJ ruling, a spokesperson for the Myanmar military cited a recent joint statement by U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin that the International Criminal Court “must not abuse” its jurisdiction.

While the International Criminal Court is distinct from the ICJ, the spokesperson for Ming Aung Hlaing drew a parallel.

What We’re Watching

Trump deals details. On Thursday evening, the White House disclosed the details of some of the various deals struck at last week’s ASEAN summit.

The ASEAN deals, worth a total of $17 billion, include a $12 billion sale of Boeing aircraft to Philippine Airlines.

The United States is also looking at providing $2 billion in loans for Philippine defense purchases and $400 million in military financing (though much of the funding was already committed).

Thailand will also purchase $123 million of High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems (HIMARS) from the United States.

The terms of the Thai deal, which are not yet final, are already provoking opposition there. Many in the agricultural powerhouse are unhappy with the prospect of more agricultural imports from the United States—in particular, pork. The government is on the defense, saying that it’s the best deal it could get.

Amid controversy over the price tag, Thailand has also insisted that the HIMARS purchase is unrelated to the trade deal and was driven by national security considerations.

The Malaysian government also announced that a U.S. consortium will help develop a sovereign artificial intelligence cloud for the Malaysian government, with the United States offering $50 million in support.

EU-Indonesia trade deal. On Saturday, the European Union and Indonesia signed a trade deal that was 10 years in the making.

items.feedText:

items.body:
Did Pinal, Yavapai and Gila counties in Arizona fail to show ballots cast in the 2026 governor's race? No, that's not true: The State of Arizona's official canvass shows ballots cast in the governor's race in all three counties. The Nov. 3, 2026, General Election Canvass was signed on Nov. 23, 2026. Lead Stories found no matching reports supporting the claim from established news outlets.

The claim appeared in [a post](https://x.com/_Patriot1776Q_/status/2125118974048571469) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125200244/https://x.com/_Patriot1776Q_/status/2125118974048571469) ) by the @_Patriot1776Q_ account on X on Nov. 24, 2026. It read:

> 🚨 NEW: Arizona's official results don't add up.
> Three counties show ZERO ballots cast for Governor.
> But the same official file counts 304,487 votes in those counties.
> Pinal. Yavapai. Gila.
> Zero ballots. 304,487 votes. How?

This is what the post looked like on X at the time of publication:

*(Image source: post by @_Patriot1776Q_ on X.)*

#### State of Arizona Official Canvass

The [State of Arizona Official Canvass](https://azsos.gov/elections/election-information/2026-election-info) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125200831/https://azsos.gov/elections/election-information/2026-election-info) ) tells a different story. Signed on Nov. 23, 2026, [the document](https://apps.azsos.gov/election/2026/canvass/2026-GE-Canvass-Signed.pdf) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125200659/https://apps.azsos.gov/election/2026/canvass/2026-GE-Canvass-Signed.pdf) ) is the official tally of the Nov. 3, 2026, general election. A canvass is an official review of election results to check vote totals and confirm the final count. The secretary of state certifies the canvass, which is conducted in the presence of the governor, attorney general and chief justice of the Arizona Supreme Court. In part, it reads:

> I, Adrian Fontes, Secretary of State, do hereby certify that the foregoing canvass is a true, correct and complete tabulation of the votes cast at the 2026 General Election held in the State of Arizona on the 3rd day of November, 2026. This canvass displays the name of each person who appeared on the ballot for a federal and state office in the election and the number of votes received for each person, as shown by the tabulations received from the Boards of Supervisors of each county in the State of Arizona. IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand and affixed the Great Seal of the State of Arizona, this 23rd day of November, 2026, at the State's capital in Phoenix.

This is what a screenshot of the document looked like at the time of publication:

*(Image source: Arizona Secretary of State website.)*

[A video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=09gfFa1c4SY&t=318s) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125203416/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=09gfFa1c4SY&t=318s) ) of the certification on YouTube on Nov. 23, 2026 is embedded below:

#### Total ballots cast

The official canvass shows the "total ballots cast" in Arizona's Nov. 3, 2026, general election: 21,130 in Gila County, 161,571 in Pinal County and 121,818 in Yavapai County. Not everyone votes in every race, so the number of votes in a particular race may be lower than the total number of ballots cast in a county. None of the counties listed zero ballots as suggested in the social media post.

The post's 304,487 figure is close to the 304,519 total ballots cast in the three counties, but Lead Stories could not determine how the poster arrived at it.

This is what a screenshot of the document looked like at the time of publication:

*(Image source: Arizona Secretary of State website.)*

#### Governor's race

The votes cast in the governor's race totaled 20,877 in Gila County, 160,204 in Pinal County and 120,610 in Yavapai County, according to the official canvass and Lead Stories' tally of the figures cited in the claim.

This is what a screenshot of the document looked like at the time of publication:

*(Image source: Arizona Secretary of State website.)*

#### News searches

Lead Stories searched [Google News](https://news.google.com/search?q=%22Pinal%2C%22%20%22Yavapai%2C%22%20%22Gila%2C%22%20%22governor%2C%22%20and%20%22ballots.%22&hl=en-US&gl=US&ceid=US%3Aen) (archived here) and [Yahoo News](https://news.search.yahoo.com/search;_ylt=A2RRt2ZhPgdrmwIAc5TQtDMD;_?fr=uh3_news_web&.tsrc=uh3_news_web&fr2=sb-top&p=%22Pinal%2C%22+%22Yavapai%2C%22+%22Gila%2C%22+%22governor%2C%22+and+%22ballots.%22) (archived here) and found no matching reports about the claim from established news outlets using the search terms: "Pinal," "Yavapai," "Gila," "governor," and "ballots."

Lead Stories contacted the Arizona Secretary of State's Office and the election offices in each county but did not receive an immediate response.

In an interview with Giulio Pecci, Senhaji (aka Cheb Runner) recalls playing as a child in the streets of Ihchach in Agadir, making music from instruments, household objects and car parts, and later learning software in order to translate the rhythms he already had in his head into…
items.body:
The rhythmic skeletons of Ahwach, Gnawa and related musical traditions meet 808s, sampling and electronic production on **Cheb Runner** ‘s *80K*, retaining their physical force even as their shapes change. The result feels rooted in a specific place while constantly pushing beyond it. This is sound that has no borders, in keeping with the ethos of Beat Machine Records.

That approach has deep roots in Reda Senhaji’s own musical history. In an [interview with Giulio Pecci](https://sshhhpeaceful.substack.com/p/cheb-runner-immigration-has-given), Senhaji (aka Cheb Runner) recalls playing as a child in the streets of Ihchach in Agadir, making music from instruments, household objects and car parts, and later learning software in order to translate the rhythms he already had in his head into electronic form. He describes his tracks as emerging from street recordings, archived sounds and processed percussion before arriving at a “collision” with electronic music. *80K* makes that collision tactile. This is music that nourishes the hair follicles of the skin.

On “Iznagn Engines”, rhythm seems almost motorised, its cyclical momentum generating heat ripples as acoustic and synthetic percussion rub against one another. “Azn Oudrar” opens the music outward without dissipating its tension, while “Gn-Awa” is all glistening friction, metallic percussion locking into an intoxicating, heliotropic pulsing that seems perpetually drawn towards greater intensity. Yet the density never becomes oppressive: the album’s sleek electronic production acts as a sonic nictitating membrane, softening the relentless polyrhythmic Gnawa beats without blunting their impact.

The 808 becomes crucial to this balancing act. As the liner notes stress, it operates as a “structural force rather than an accent”, something especially apparent on “Afouss Adar 808”, where the electronic low end doesn’t sit beneath the traditional rhythmic language so much as enter into it. This is precisely the question the album raises: whether the distinction between traditional percussion and the drum machine remains particularly useful when both are being made to participate in the same rhythmic system. “Tarwan Ganga” deepens the rhythm into an auburn haze, locking the listener into a meditative trance, before Guedra Guedra’s closing reworking of “Gn-Awa” opens up and lifts the source material into a dreamy, solar finale.

This is the second release in the Terra Tempo series, which Beat Machine Records describes as “redefining the boundaries of global sound by blending rich cultural heritage with the dynamic energy of modern club beats.” Although the album cover depicts a number of instruments that AI has kindly idenfied for me as the qraqeb, the guembri / sintir, the tallunt / allun, and possibly the naqus, *80K* is far from an exercise in heritage preservation.

Speaking to Pecci, Cheb Runner describes Morocco as the endpoint of historical caravan routes and its rhythms as the product of a “multitude of tribes” and the interplay of cultures brought by migration. The album extends that process rather than merely representing it. The qraqeb, guembri, hand percussion, samples, machines and 808 belong to a continuum in which inherited forms remain alive precisely because they can be transformed. Intoxicating and intensely physical, *80K* treats tradition as a living source of energy. ( **Gianmarco Del Re** )

** The latest on the Iran War’s popularity**

**Updated November 24, 2026**

**After a couple of bad recent polls, opposition to the Iran War has hit an all-time high in our average of 60.4 percent.** Just 30.8 percent of Americans support the conflict.

Show more Show less

Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said “there’s really no need for major combat operations any longer,” [according to The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/us/politics/rubio-iran-war.html). The administration’s posture could always change, but for now, further escalation seems unlikely. **-EMD** **, 11/17/26**

**See also: [Donald Trump approval rating dashboard](https://www.natesilver.net/p/trump-approval-ratings-nate-silver-bulletin).**

Subscribe now

This is our landing page for polls about the Iran War1, tracking support for U.S. military action in Iran since March 1, the day after the war began.2 We’ll regularly update this average as new polls come in.3 This page is designed to be [viewed on the web](https://tinyurl.com/yfh38r8x) rather than in our email client or the Substack app.

[Click here for more information on how the average works](https://www.natesilver.net/p/silver-bulletin-polling-average-methodology). The Silver Bulletin average weights more reliable polls more heavily — you can **[find our latest pollster ratings here](https://www.natesilver.net/p/pollster-ratings-silver-bulletin)**. Our process for calculating support for the Iran War is similar to that for calculating [President Trump’s approval ratings](https://www.natesilver.net/p/trump-approval-ratings-nate-silver-bulletin).4

### The topline: So, just how popular is the Iran War?

This average includes polls that ask about support for the Iran War, strikes in Iran, or U.S. military involvement in Iran. Compared with tracking approval ratings, questions about war can be less straightforward. Our goal is to limit the analysis to polls that ask neutral questions rather than introduce assumptions about how the war is going or its objectives. (See below for more details on how we make this assessment.) Our default version of the ratings reflects a combination of all polls, whether conducted among adults, registered voters, or likely voters.5
