items.body:
# Bis zu 15 Zentimeter Schnee: Winter trifft Bayern mit voller Wucht

- Startseite
- Panorama
## Bis zu 15 Zentimeter Schnee: Winter trifft Bayern mit voller Wucht – DWD warnt vor allem in zwei Regionen

Stand: 25.11.2026, 08:38 Uhr

Von: Benedikt Strobach

Kommentare Drucken Teilen

Der Winter meldet sich in Bayern zurück: Der Deutsche Wetterdienst warnt vor Neuschnee, Glätte und Dauerfrost. Besonders betroffen sind zwei Regionen.

München – Der Spätherbst verabschiedet sich in Bayern mit sinkenden Temperaturen: Nach teils noch freundlichen Abschnitten zur Wochenmitte setzt sich in der zweiten Wochenhälfte im Freistaat endgültig kalte Luft durch. Ein Ausläufer eines Tiefdruckgebiets über Frankreich nähert sich von Südwesten und sorgt vor allem im Süden und Südosten für unbeständiges und zunehmend winterliches Wetter . Wie der Deutsche Wetterdienst (DWD) in seinen aktuellen Warnlage- und Vorhersageberichten meldet, müssen sich Autofahrer und Fußgänger auf Schneefall, Glätte sowie Frost einstellen.

## Bis zu 15 Zentimeter Neuschnee in Bayern: Schwerpunkt im Süden und Osten

Der Schwerpunkt der nun kommenden winterlichen Niederschläge liegt in den kommenden Tagen im Süden und Osten des Freistaats. Ausgangs der Nacht zum Donnerstag (26. November) setzt an den Alpen und am Bayerischen Wald zunächst leichter Schneefall ein. Im weiteren Tagesverlauf weiten sich die Schneefälle von den mittleren und östlichen Alpen weiter nach Nordosten aus. Bereits zuvor hatte ein Wintereinbruch in Bayern für erste weiße Landschaften gesorgt.

Aktuell gilt bereits eine amtliche Warnung vor Frost in Bayern. Bis 12 Uhr kann laut DWD leichter bis mäßiger Frost bei Temperaturen zwischen –4 und –9 Grad auftreten. Die Meteorologen warnen vor möglichen Frostschäden und empfehlen, gegebenenfalls Frostschutzmaßnahmen zu ergreifen. In den südlichen Landkreisen des Freistaats besteht aktuell bis 9 Uhr auch Gefahr wegen vereinzelter Glätte. Der DWD warnt vor Rutschgefahr und rät Autofahrern, das Verhalten im Straßenverkehr anzupassen.

In den Höhenlagen oberhalb von 800 Metern – insbesondere im Bereich der Alpen, im östlichen Alpenvorland sowie im südöstlichen Niederbayern – rechnet der DWD mit Schneemengen von bis zu fünf Zentimetern. In hohen Staulagen der östlichen Alpen sind sogar bis zu 15 Zentimeter Neuschnee möglich. Auch in den tieferen Lagen zwischen den Alpen und dem Bayerischen Wald rieseln gebietsweise Flocken herab: Hier kalkulieren die Meteorologen mit ein bis zwei Zentimetern Schnee. Weiter westlich, etwa in weiten Teilen Schwabens sowie im nördlichen Oberbayern, bleibt es dagegen am Donnerstag meist trocken, dort fallen kaum Flocken.

In Nordbayern beginnt der Schneefall ebenfalls in den frühen Morgenstunden des Donnerstags am Bayerischen Wald. Im Tagesverlauf rieselt es vor allem in der Oberpfalz leicht, bevor sich der Schneefall in der Nacht zum Freitag gebietsweise weiter ausbreitet.

## Dauerfrost und Glättegefahr: Gefrierende Nässe sorgt für Glätte

Begleitet werden die Schneefälle von spürbar sinkenden Temperaturen. Am Donnerstag stellt sich vielerorts leichter Dauerfrost ein: Die Höchstwerte verharren zwischen –2 und 0 Grad. Lediglich in einigen tiefer gelegenen Regionen Frankens sowie im direkten Umfeld von Donau und Inn klettert das Thermometer örtlich noch auf 1 bis 2 Grad. Auf den Bergen herrscht ohnehin tiefster Winter – auf dem Großen Arber und in den Kammlagen der Mittelgebirge liegen die Werte um –5 Grad, auf der Zugspitze werden bis zu –7 Grad erwartet.

In den Nächten sinken die Werte verbreitet auf –1 bis –6 Grad, in Nordbayern teils bis auf –7 Grad. Durch überfrierende Nässe und den frischen Schnee besteht auf den Straßen und Gehwegen stellenweise Glättegefahr. Wenn Schnee und Eis die Fahrbahnen überziehen, drohen Behinderungen auf den Verkehrswegen, wie bereits frühere Unfälle und Verkehrsbehinderungen im Freistaat gezeigt haben. In den Ost-West-ausgerichteten Tälern der östlichen Mittelgebirge sowie in Föhntälern der Alpen können zudem Windböen mit Geschwindigkeiten um die 50 km/h auftreten.

## Ausblick auf das Wochenende: Frostnächte halten in Bayern an

Zum Ende der Arbeitswoche am Freitag (27. November) bleibt der Himmel über Bayern meist stark bewölkt bis bedeckt. Örtlich fallen noch ein paar Schneeflocken, bevor sich vor allem in Unterfranken im Tagesverlauf längere sonnige Phasen durchsetzen können. Die Höchstwerte erreichen –3 bis 2 Grad.

Am Wochenende präsentiert sich das Wetter zweigeteilt: Während sich in den Tälern und Niederungen oft zähe hochnebelartige Bewölkung hält, scheint in den Alpen die Sonne . Die Temperaturen liegen zwischen –2 und 2 Grad. Die Nächte bleiben eisig kalt: Bei klarem Himmel können die Temperaturen im Süden bis auf –10 Grad fallen. (Quelle: DWD) ( bes )

items.body:
Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries:

With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library. It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians.

Here's the digitized sketchbook.

Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work.

Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue? Mark thinks it will be mild:

But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature.

items.title: NEPA is not an environmental protection law
items.subtitle: Two civil engineers examine project data on the construction site of a railway bridge.
items.feedText:

items.body:
Stepping back from the specifics of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) debate, I want to make a larger point about the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and its role in American public policy:

This law has “environmental” in its title, but in a critical respect it’s just not an environmental law at all.

Which is to say it does not set any kind of standards related to environmental quality. The Clean Air Act makes rules about air pollution. The Clean Water Act makes rules about water pollution. We could make stricter rules about microplastics or forever chemicals or something else. We also have parks and other kinds of wildlife and landscape conservation programs.

None of this is NEPA.

NEPA is a law that makes it harder to do certain classes of things by imposing various procedural requirements, and it creates a litigation attack surface for people who do not like these classes of things.

NEPA is entirely indifferent as to whether the proposed thing is good for the environment or bad for the environment. What’s more, unlike real environmental laws, NEPA does not govern private-sector economic activity. The key idea of NEPA is the “major federal action.” It burdens government activities relative to private-sector activities and it burdens “action” (doing something new) relative to the status quo.

If you want to cut taxes on business investment to encourage more data center construction, that’s not a federal action for NEPA purposes, even though common sense says that tax law is a very important facet of federal policy. Maintaining the regulatory status quo is not a federal action even if the status quo is bad for the environment. If you want to build a light rail line that’s partially financed with a Department of Transportation grant, that’s a federal action and you need to do your NEPA homework.

If requiring federal (but not private) actions (but not inactions) to meet a set of burdensome procedural requirements leads to better environmental outcomes than not doing this, that would have to be essentially by coincidence.

I think a lot of progressive analytical errors about the post-1970 history of the United States are downstream of not understanding this.

It’s not just that progressives overrate NEPA but that they have an essentially false narrative of why contemporary government is the way it is. There’s this view that something called “neoliberalism” happened and that now because of “neoliberalism,” all the Democrats do is hand out tax credits rather than being cool New Dealers who support a robust state. But guess what — a tax credit to buy electric cars is not a major federal action but a mass transit line is.

NEPA is not the only reason for the rise of what [Suzanne Mettler calls the “submerged state”](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0226521656?lv=shuf&channelId=500&plpRedirect=mhFallback) or what [Mike Konczal calls government by coupon](https://www.newamerica.org/insights/no-discount-comparing-the-public-option-to-the-coupon-welfare-state/), but it’s striking that progressives tend to neglect its existence while workaday bureaucrats are painfully aware of its relevance.

#### The bias toward inaction

When New York City was thinking about launching its congestion pricing program to reduce traffic in parts of Manhattan and raise revenue for mass transit, it was granted the grace of being allowed to comply with NEPA via an environmental assessment rather than the more burdensome environmental impact statement. That less burdensome document runs [868 pages](https://www.mta.info/document/93446) with a two-volume appendix. The first volume of the appendix has [1,966 pages](https://www.mta.info/document/93451) and the [second volume is 1,173 pages](https://www.mta.info/document/93456). Yes, that is 4,000 pages worth of environmental review under the *less* burdensome of the two NEPA tracks for a program that charges people money to drive cars and uses the revenue to fund mass transit.

The reason the report has to be so long is not because the question of whether this is bad for the environment is hard to answer.

[↗ slowboring.com](https://www.slowboring.com/p/nepa-is-not-an-environmental-protection)

items.body:
Some customers have raised concerns about Backblaze's privacy policy taking effect next month, which says the backup and cloud storage company may sell certain personal information to advertisers.

Backblaze’s [current privacy policy](https://www.backblaze.com/company/policy/privacy-april-2026) says that in addition to the personal information that users may provide, such as their email address when creating an account, it may also “automatically” collect information, such as “your software, the operating system you use when accessing our service, your Internet Protocol address, and the date and time of each request you make to Backblaze.”

The current policy adds: “Under no circumstances do we rent, trade, or share your address or e-mail address with any other company for their marketing purposes without your consent.” It also makes no mention of advertisers.

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2026/11/backblaze-explains-why-its-sharing-customer-information-with-advertisers/)

AI News for 11/23/2026-11/24/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, [544 Twitters](https://twitter.com/i/lists/1585430245762441216) and no further Discords. [AINews' website](https://news.smol.ai/) lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, [AINews is now a section of Latent Space](https://latent.space/p/2026/). You can opt in/out of email frequencies!

## AI Twitter Recap

**Frontier Models as Research Engines: VP ≠ VNP, Protein Design and 948 Kernel Bugs**

- VP ≠ VNP, posted by two labs: An Anthropic GitHub repo reportedly contains a proof by an internal Claude research model that VP ≠ VNP. This is the algebraic analogue of P vs NP, posed by Valiant in 1979, and implies that polynomials such as the permanent lack small circuits over every field ([@kimmonismus](https://x.com/kimmonismus/status/2125131886271795290), [repo pointer](https://x.com/BlancheMinerva/status/2125085344555053363)). OpenAI's counter-release: OpenAI then posted its own proof and says it was "obtained on November 6, 2026." Neither lab named a model or published an announcement ([@AndrewCurran_](https://x.com/AndrewCurran_/status/2125289527531245998)).
- Scope: The result does not imply P ≠ NP, which still requires general Boolean circuit lower bounds ([@ZhihuFrontier](https://x.com/ZhihuFrontier/status/2125170512011944026)).
- Speculation: Curran argues that both labs are sitting on unreleased results and repeats unconfirmed rumors of cryptography breakthroughs. Treat this as opinion.
- Riemann proof clarifications: Levent Alpöge says the "250,000+ pages" claim was a joke. He released only the Lean code because he could not produce a readable writeup, and called it "full of garbage obviously, but compiles" ([@kimmonismus](https://x.com/kimmonismus/status/2125148979880964496), [@simonw](https://x.com/simonw/status/2125001984029921636)). Lineage claim: A Zhihu analysis traces Alpöge's key method to a short OpenAI proof excluding Landau–Siegel zeros. This is an attributed inference ([@ZhihuFrontier](https://x.com/ZhihuFrontier/status/2125200727140438125)).
- GPT-6 protein design, wet-lab validated: OpenAI released a preprint showing GPT-6 models designing new protein shapes and sequences through reasoning and code, without specialized bio models ([@OpenAI](https://x.com/OpenAI/status/2125334383490105601)). Results: 14 of 107 resequenced proteins showed binding. 128 of 182 redesigned small antibodies and 179 of 272 antibody fragments retained binding ([details](https://x.com/OpenAI/status/2125334392814051724)).
- Cost caveat: On a prior DNA task, GPT-6.1 Sol was about 2,000x more expensive per task than a specialized model ([@_lewtun](https://x.com/_lewtun/status/2125358915881984347)).
- GPT-6 Cyber and the Linux kernel: In one run, GPT-6 Cyber helped validate 948 Linux kernel bugs that could grant local root and generated patches for maintainer review ([@OpenAI](https://x.com/OpenAI/status/2125007927098699827)).
- Discovery beyond verifiable domains: A historian says GPT-6.2 Astra identified the vicomte de Chabot as the artist of an anonymous 1808 Yale sketchbook in 22 minutes. It also surfaced an obscure microfilmed diary whose handwriting and itinerary matched the sketches ([@HistoryGPT](https://x.com/HistoryGPT/status/2125213218045858149)). Exoplanet candidates: Amateurs using Codex and Astra searched Kepler and TESS data. One 13.8-day signal was independently confirmed by a SETI astronomer, and 49 TESS candidates were flagged ([@OpenAI](https://x.com/OpenAI/status/2125305606685053416)).
- Robotics saturation: GPT-6.2 Astra on Codex scored 97% on RoboDojo-RC Tier 1 across 120 real-robot trials, and RoboDojo is being retired ([@robocurve](https://x.com/robocurve/status/2125028977194786857)). New environments: Einsia released RoboUniverse-10K, a set of 10,807 verifiable Isaac Sim tasks built from real manipulation videos. The top frontier score on held-out tasks is 85.8%, while 7 of 11 models score ≤10% ([@EinsiaAI](https://x.com/EinsiaAI/status/2125235490567897265)).

items.body:
When a SpaceX Starship broke apart over Turks and Caicos in Jan. 2025, pieces of its heat shield washed ashore. Some of that material now hangs on a gallery wall in New York City, embedded in artist Ashley Zelinskie's print of the very explosion it survived.

Look closely at the print and you can see little flakes on the surface. Some of Zelinskie's friends vacationing on the islands had come across pieces of heat-shield tile. "I think you might want these," Zelinskie recalled one friend telling her. She did. The Brooklyn-based artist ground the fragments into dust and worked them into the print.

Ashley Zelinskie incorporated dust from recovered SpaceX Starship heat-shield tiles into this print of the vehicle breaking apart over Turks and Caicos. (Image credit: Ashley Zelinskie)

The Starship print is part of "Ejecta," which captures rocket plumes and explosions on paper. It's one of four series in Zelinskie's solo exhibition, "The Weight of Space," which opened Nov. 20 at Heft Gallery in Manhattan. Her marble sculptures in "Monuments" depict the Hubble Space Telescope, retired NASA astronaut Mike Massimino's spaceflight gear and more. Five "Launch Sequence" sculptures follow a rocket through liftoff, and the interactive "Crowded Sky" lets visitors track what's currently orbiting overhead in real time.

Zelinskie gave Space.com Editor-in-Chief Tariq Malik and me a tour before the gallery doors opened. Massimino joined her that evening to celebrate the exhibition and their collaboration on "Monuments." You can watch the tour in the video above.

## Monuments

Massimino turned up in our first look at Zelinskie's work, too. In 2022, I photographed the two of them beside her "Exploration JWST" sculpture at["Unfolding the Universe: First Light,"](https://www.space.com/james-webb-space-telescope-art-ashley-zelinskie) an exhibit inspired by the James Webb Space Telescope's first images. Four years later, Massimino stood in a New York gallery looking at another Zelinskie sculpture. "That's my arm there," he told Malik.

Artist Ashley Zelinskie and Space.com Editor-in-Chief Tariq Malik discuss the sculpture between them, which depicts astronaut Mike Massimino’s bare hand gripping a replica of the handrail he pulled off the Hubble Space Telescope in 2009. (Image credit: Future/Steve Spaleta)

In that hand is a piece of hardware Malik remembers watching Massimino wrestle with in real time. During NASA's final Hubble servicing mission in 2009, a stripped bolt left a handrail blocking access to the telescope's Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS). Mission Control instructed Massimino to forcibly remove the handrail so he and fellow spacewalker Michael Good could get on with the repair.

Massimino told Malik that pulling the handrail off Hubble brought back a childhood memory of his father and his Uncle Frank driving a long screwdriver through a stuck oil filter. "Then my uncle Frank pulled to get more leverage, and that's what was going through my mind when I pulled off that handrail," Massimino said. He remembered looking down at Earth and thinking, "This one's for you, Uncle Frank."

Massimino wore bulky, pressurized gloves to pull off the handrail, but Zelinskie chose to show his bare hand gripping the copper-plated replica. "I wanted to bring the humanity back into the piece," she told Malik.

Ashley Zelinskie's marble sculptures of retired NASA astronaut Mike Massimino's gloves, reentry helmet and boots are part of her "Monuments" series at Heft Gallery in New York City. (Image credit: Ashley Zelinksie)

The gloves have a story of their own. When Massimino brought a pair to her studio to be 3D-scanned, Zelinskie noticed how the fabric held its folds when the gloves were set down. "Oh my god, these want to be stone," she recalled thinking. So she went out and learned to work in marble.

The astronaut boots have a detail you could easily miss from above. Zelinskie polished the soles smooth because, as she put it, "they're built for floating in space." For her sculpture of Massimino's reentry helmet, the kind he wore for the trip home from space, Zelinskie paired carved marble with a 3D-printed visor, which she electroplated and polished to a mirror finish.

A veil carved from marble drapes over Zelinskie's Hubble Space Telescope sculpture, a nod to the blurry images Hubble first sent back to Earth. (Image credit: Steve Spaleta/Future)

The Hubble Space Telescope gets its own marble tribute in "Monuments." Zelinskie started with a NASA 3D model of the telescope and used the modeling software Blender to give it a veil.

"So I kind of threw a digital piece of fabric on the Hubble telescope over and over and over again until I got it right," she told Malik. The veil is a nod to the blurry images Hubble first sent back to Earth. A Digital Stone Project robotic arm in Tuscany carved the rough shape in marble, and Zelinskie finished it by hand. When she invited Malik to touch what looked like cloth, he reached out. "It's like a very buttery, smooth surface," he said.

## Ejecta

The last time we saw Zelinskie at Heft, she and DJ and producer illich Mujica had filled the gallery with Webb imagery, live electronic music and a little Pink Floyd for their audiovisual performance["Redshift."](https://www.space.com/entertainment/redshift-blends-james-webb-space-telescope-artemis-2-and-pink-floyd-into-a-cosmic-journey-through-light-and-sound-video-photos) We've also seen her turn [Webb's view of the Pillars of Creation into artwork](https://www.space.com/entertainment/new-unfolding-the-universe-exhibit-celebrates-the-james-webb-space-telescope-through-stunning-artwork-photos-video). This time, one of the images on the wall began with a camera Zelinskie pointed at a rocket herself.

Zelinskie used a photograph she took at NASA's Artemis 2 launch to create this work in her "Ejecta" series. (Image credit: Ashley Zelinskie)

Zelinskie photographed NASA's Artemis 2 launch from the Kennedy Space Center visitor center in Florida. The resulting print is part of "Ejecta," alongside the Starship breakup print and more. She uses data to distort the image until the swirls in a rocket plume start to resemble a nebula.

Another print in the series depicts the loss of the space shuttle Challenger. That one has a personal connection for me. Jan. 28, 1986, was my birthday. Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff that day, killing all seven crew members. The memory of that day helped inspire my career covering space.

Massimino spoke with Malik about what it was like to see a familiar image of the disaster through Zelinskie's eyes. "It's an artist's interpretation of it, which in some way, when I look at it, is more emotional," he said.

Ashley Zelinskie's "Ejecta" series includes this print depicting the loss of NASA's Space Shuttle Challenger on Jan. 28, 1986. (Image credit: Ashley Zelinskie)

items.body:
Es gibt Neuigkeiten von WhatsApp. Der Messenger-Dienst hat soeben ein Update angekündigt, um eine neue Funktion namens „geplante Nachrichten“ einzuführen. So seid ihr zukünftig beim Versenden von Nachrichten deutlich flexibler.

## WhatsApp kündigt „geplante Nachrichten“ an

Apple bietet für iMessage schon länger die Funktion „später senden“ an. Nun kündigt auch WhatsApp eine vergleichbare Funktion an. Wer kennt das nicht: Spät Abends fällt euch ein, das jemand am nächsten Tag eine wichtige Prüfung hat. Zukünftig könnt ihr abends eine „Viel Glück“-Nachricht verfassen, die passenderweise am nächsten Tag versendet wird. Vielleicht soll auch euer Geburtstagsgruß genau um Mitternacht ankommen. Auch diesen könnt ihr zukünftig vorab verfassen und als geplante Nachricht verwenden.

Schreibt eure Nachricht einfach dann, wenn sie euch in den Sinn kommt, und sendet sie irgendwann in einem Zeitraum von 10 Minuten bis 14 Tagen. Das Ganze funktioniert in Einzelchats genauso wie in Gruppen.

Wie funktioniert das Ganze? Um eine Nachricht zu planen, haltet den Senden-Button gedrückt und legt das Datum und die Uhrzeit fest, zu der die Nachricht ankommen soll. Sie sieht für die empfangende Person wie jede andere Nachricht aus. Ihr könnt alle zukünftigen Nachrichten einsehen, die ihr eingerichtet habt, und sie im Voraus löschen, wenn ihr eure Meinung ändert.

Auch wenn euer Smartphone ausgeschaltet ist, wir eure vorab verfasste und geplant verschickte Nachricht verwendet. WhatsApp betont zudem, dass geplante Nachrichten ebenfalls Ende-zu-Ende-verschlüsselt sind. Übrigens: Geplante Nachrichten können Text, Fotos und Videos enthalten. Solltet ihr die Funktion bei euch noch nicht nutzen können, dann keine Panik. Diese wird in den nächsten Wochen schrittweise ausgerollt.

items.body:
The [ACX Prediction Contest](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/acxmetaculus-prediction-contest-2026) is back for 2027, the fifth year Metaculus has hosted. There’s a $10,000 prize pool for the best forecasters, plus $3,000 for question suggesters. The ten people who contribute the most to the roughly 35 questions Metaculus selects will split the $3,000, with prizes from $150 to $700. Past question sets are in the [2025](https://www.metaculus.com/tournament/ACX2025/) and [2026](https://www.metaculus.com/tournament/ACX2026/) contests.

This year is also an opportunity to see how far AI forecasting has come, as the best are now competitive with strong human forecasters. AI forecasting agents are welcome to enter and eligible for prizes, and Metaculus will post its own AI forecasts on every question.

A good question suggestion has an objective answer that we’ll know by the end of 2027, with a source that settles it. “Will 2027 be especially hot?” is less good than “Will NASA’s GISTEMP data rank 2027 as the warmest year on record?”

[Suggest questions here](http://forms.gle/L8NXoQpAkXkdvDRF6) by November 30. The contest will open in early 2027.

items.body:
# Earth’s Water May Have Formed in This Fiery Furnace - Nautilus

## Earth’s Water May Have Formed in This Fiery Furnace

No ice deliveries needed

3:00 PM CST on November 24, 2026

It’s one of the most fundamental questions about life on Earth: How did water get here?

One possibility is that it was delivered as frozen ice by a bombardment of meteorites smashing into our planet’s surface. Another is that the chemistry of the early Earth somehow produced water from molten rock—a theory that’s the focus of a new study published in Nature Geoscience .

Read more: “ This Paradoxical Desert Landscape Is Filled with Fresh Water ”

The researchers behind the hypothesis are calling it “pebble rain” (or “pebble accretion”). What happens is silicate rocks with iron inside, drawn toward Earth by its increasing mass and gravitational pull, react with hydrogen in the atmosphere. Given the high speeds, high pressure, and high volume of incoming rocks involved, the subsequent chemical reactions could have stripped away the oxygen from the iron in the pebble showers, releasing water vapor as a by-product.

The researchers estimate that around 200 oceans’ worth of H2O may have been released in this way, supplying the planet with the magic ingredient for life. These pebbles would have been external visitors, like meteorites, but the water would’ve been formed on Earth rather than in space.

What’s more, the same process could plausibly happen on other planets as they form too—opening up new possibilities in our search for extraterrestrial life. “Previous ideas about the source of water to Earth rely on an external source, such as comets or meteorites,” study author Zachary Sharp explained in a statement . “Here we show that virtually any Earth-sized planet should have water by this newly identified mechanism.”

The researchers simulated the conditions of the early Earth in their lab with temperatures of up to 2,552°F, and heating silicate rocks in streams of hydrogen. Almost 80 percent of the iron oxide in the samples turned into metallic iron, producing water vapor along the way.

“Looking out over a large body of water, it’s hard to imagine that that water may have been produced four-and-a-half billion years ago in a hell-like atmosphere,” Sharp said, “but it very well may have.”

items.title: Berufswahl und KI: Hat das Handwerk wieder goldenen Boden?
items.subtitle: Immer mehr Studenten verlassen die Hochschulen, weil sie wegen KI um ihre Berufschancen bangen, und erlernen ein Handwerk.
items.feedText: Handwerk, sagte man lange, hat goldenen Boden. Dann kam die Akademisierung von allem. Und jetzt geht die Furcht vor der Künstlichen Intelligenz um. Junge Leute und ihre Eltern fragen seit einiger Zeit, welche Berufe denn noch sicher davor seien, durch KI ersetzt zu werden. So läuft es allerdings seit Jahrzehnten schon. Mal war es die Botschaft, Lehrer würden der Demographie halber kaum mehr eingestellt.
items.body:
# Ist es klug, ein Handwerk zu lernen statt zu studieren?

Handwerk, sagte man lange, hat goldenen Boden. Dann kam die Akademisierung von allem. Und jetzt geht die Furcht vor der Künstlichen Intelligenz um. Junge Leute und ihre Eltern fragen seit einiger Zeit, welche Berufe denn noch sicher davor seien, durch KI ersetzt zu werden.

So läuft es allerdings seit Jahrzehnten schon. Mal war es die Botschaft, Lehrer würden der Demographie halber kaum mehr eingestellt. Dann hieß es, eine Zukunft hätten nur noch Betriebswirtschaftler und Informatiker, vielleicht noch Maschinenbauer. Erleichtert wurde zur Kenntnis genommen, dass die Unternehmensberatungen auch Physiker und Musikwissenschaftler einstellten, denn denen war auch gesagt worden, ihr Studium sei eine berufliche Sackgasse.

Oder es wurde das Jurastudium empfohlen, weil man damit immerhin alles Mögliche werden könne: Richterin, Anwalt oder Politiker. Immer aber wurde gesagt, so viele, wie im Hörsaal säßen, brauche man gar nicht, und stets fanden die meisten einen Beruf.

### Enorme Substitutionsphantasien

Jetzt ist freilich die Situation eine andere. Es heißt nicht, so viele Historiker, Anwälte, Informatiker brauche niemand, es heißt, man brauche sie gar nicht mehr. Mit der KI gehen enorme Substitutionsphantasien einher. Denn was kann sie nicht? Wer einwirft, die KI habe kein Bewusstsein, zieht die Gegenfrage auf sich, ob für Marken- und für Mietrecht, für Riemanns Vermutung und für Drehbücher, die vom ZDF verfilmt werden, denn Bewusstsein benötigt wird.

Philosophische Erwägungen und solche zu den gesamtgesellschaftlichen Folgen der KI können denjenigen, die sich überlegen, welchen Studien- und Berufsweg sie einschlagen sollen, gleichgültig sein. Es stellen sich praktische Fragen. Schon gibt es die ersten Berichte über Absolventen aus Oxford, die Klempnerin geworden sind, angehende Medizinerinnen, die ihr Studium für eine Schreinerlehre abgebrochen haben. Denn was die KI aller Robotik zum Trotz einstweilen noch nicht kann, ist Tafelspitz zubereiten, Schränke tischlern, Babys wickeln, Dachrinnen anbringen, Hamlet spielen oder Bratsche.

Die Maschine, einst als Gerät gedacht, das uns körperliche Arbeit erspart, erfährt im Höhepunkt ihrer Produktivität eine Grenze ironischerweise an bestimmten Arten solcher intelligenten Tätigkeit mit Augen und Händen. Das enthält auch einen Hinweis für die Universitäten. Sie könnten, Fach für Fach, ihre Lehrprogramme daraufhin durchmustern, was der Maschine überlassen werden kann, und sich auf den Rest sowie die Handhabung der Maschine KI konzentrieren. Der Rest wird je nach Disziplin unterschiedlich groß sein, so wie es unterschiedliche Antworten darauf gibt, wie viele Anwälte und wie viele Köche die Menschheit benötigt.

Die Geschichte mit dem Handwerker Rocky, die gerade im Boxerfilm-Film „I Play Rocky“ erzählt wird, belegt übrigens, dass die Menschheit etwas Überraschendes, das sie unterhält, immer benötigt. Und sei es ein Gedanke.

items.feedText: N26-Chef Dargan: „Wir müssen Dinge anders machen und uns als Organisation weiterentwickeln.“ Foto: Jan Philip Welchering für Handelsblatt Berlin. Hinter Mike Dargan liegen turbulente Monate. Seit April steht der Brite an der Spitze der Berliner Digitalbank N26 , die nach einer Investorenrevolte, dem Abgang der beiden Gründer und wiederholtem Ärger mit der Finanzaufsicht Bafin vor großen Herausforderungen steht. In seinem ersten Interview als N26-Chef spricht Dargan mit dem Handelsblatt über seine Umbauarbeiten, die Ziele bis 2030 sowie den Wettbewerb mit dem deutlich größeren Konkurrenten Revolut. **Akai veröffentlicht jetzt wie angekündigt mit dem Firmware-Update 1.4 für die MPC Sample ein SDK zur Entwicklung eigener Tools.**

MPC Sample. Firmware 1.4 (Bildquelle: Akai)

Inhalte

- MPC Sample Firmware Update 1.4

## MPC Sample Firmware Update 1.4

KI und Vibe Coding ermöglichen es, digitale Synthesizer zu hacken und alternative Firmwares und Tools für diese zu entwickeln. Diese Entwicklung wird von den Herstellern unterschiedlich bewertet. Akai ist einer der Hersteller, der positiv auf diese Entwicklung reagiert und sich dazu entschlossen hat, der Community ein SDK (Software Development Kit) zur Verfügung zu stellen, das mit dem neuen Firmware-Update 1.4 jetzt veröffentlicht wurde. [Das SDK für Akai MPCs wurde letzte Woche veröffentlicht.](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/namm-2025-akai-mpc-3-update-ist-draussen/)

[Hier geht es zum Akai Sample Test](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/akai-professionell-mpc-sample-test/)

## Wo finde ich das Firmware Update 1.4?

[Hier geht es zum Akai MPC Sample Firmware Update 1.4.](https://www.akaipro.com/downloads-and-support/downloads/firmware/mpc/sample/)

## Beschränkungen des SDK

Allerdings gibt es zunächst Einschränkungen, denn aktuell lassen sich ausschließlich Effekte für die MPC Sample entwickeln. Wer Synthesizer oder andere Anwendungen auf dem Sampler nutzen möchte, muss weiterhin auf Hacks zurückgreifen.

## Firmware-Update 1.4 auch für Musiker geeignet

Das neue Update bringt aber auch Funktionen mit, die für alle interessant sind, die mit der MPC Sample Musik machen möchten. Die Funktion **Resample Pad** ermöglicht es, ein Pad inklusive der zugewiesenen Knob FX in ein neues Sample umzuwandeln.

Außerdem werden aufgenommene Samples nach Beendigung der Aufnahme automatisch abgespielt, was an das klassische Verhalten eines **Loopers** erinnert.

Neu ist auch **16 Level Tune (Scale).** Die Funktion stammt aus der klassischen MPC und ermöglicht es, ein Sample tonal über alle 16 Pads verteilt zu spielen.

MPC Sample (Bildquelle: Akai)

## Akai Sample Goes Open Source

[Vor ein paar Tagen haben wir darüber berichtet, dass die Akai Sample Key im Zuge des KI und Vibe Coding Booms mit einem Open Source Betriebssystem veröffentlicht wird.](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/akai-sample-key-der-kompakte-akai-sample-jetzt-mit-keyboard/)Da es sich bei der Akai Sample Key im Grunde um eine Akai Sample mit Tastatur handelt, hat Akai nun bekannt gegeben, dass demnächst auch die Akai Sample Open Source wird. Damit verfügen beide Instrumente softwareseitig über die gleichen Open-Source-Möglichkeiten.

Sample Key (Bildquelle: Akai auf Instagram)

Dazu hat Akai erneut ein kurzes[Video auf ihrem Instagram-Kanal](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DfCxlYVsggC/?utm_source=ig_web_button_share_sheet)veröffentlicht. Zunächst ist darin wieder die Sample Key zu sehen, gegen Ende des Videos wird dann aber auch angekündigt, dass die Akai Sample bald Open Source sein wird. Ihr könnt euch dann an der Groovebox austoben, sie hacken und per Vibe Coding weiterentwickeln und das alles mit ausdrücklicher Zustimmung von Akai.

Im [Instagram-Video](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DfCxlYVsggC/?utm_source=ig_web_button_share_sheet) werden auch die verschiedenen Möglichkeiten mit Open Source vorgestellt.

[Hier geht es zum Akai Sample Test](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/akai-professionell-mpc-sample-test/)

## Akai Sample Teaser

**Akai veröffentlichte ein Foto der neuen MPC Sample, die am 24.03.2026 erscheint. Die Mini-MPC behält den klassischen MPC Formfaktor, ist aber deutlich kleiner.**

Akai hat heute ein erstes Foto der MPC Sample in den [Sozialen Medien](https://www.instagram.com/p/DV1HNORjmzw/) veröffentlicht, die am 24.03.2026 erscheinen wird. Die Mini-MPC wurde schon vor einigen Tagen geleakt, doch da war noch nicht klar, ob das Bild tatsächlich echt ist. Jetzt hat Akai also die Bombe platzen lassen.

## Das Teaser Bild

Akai Sample (Bildquelle: Akai auf Instagram)

Auf dem Teaser-Bild ist bereits einiges zu erkennen. Akai hat die MPC geschrumpft und trotzdem haben sie es geschafft, den klassischen MPC-Formfaktor zu erhalten.

Die MPC wurde mit dem typischen Pad-Layout ausgestattet, das seit Jahrzehnten zum Markenzeichen der MPC-Serie gehört. Die Pads sind beleuchtet und wirken großzügig dimensioniert. Auf Minipads hat man zum Glück verzichtet.

Das farbige Display zeigt Schwingungsformen an, was Rückschlüsse auf Sample-Editing zulässt. Drei Regler und ein Fader sowie beschriftete Tasten helfen bei der Bedienung. Oben rechts scheint ein Lautsprecher verbaut zu sein, damit man die MPC auch auf der Couch oder Unterwegs nutzen kann.

## Technische Feature der MPC Sample?

Was die MPC Sample technisch zu bieten hat, lässt Akai zum jetzigen Zeitpunkt noch offen. Der Name legt nahe, dass das Samplen im Mittelpunkt stehen wird. Ob das Gerät standalone betrieben werden kann, welche Anschlüsse es hat, was der Sequenzer kann, ob es Effekte gibt und was sie kostet, wird das Akai erst am 24.03.2026 offiziell bekanntgeben.

## Preis und Verfügbarkeit

**Die Akai Sample** **ist für 379,00 Euro erhältlich.**

## Akai Sample: Features

- kompakter Sampler, Sequenzer und Effektprozessor
- 16 anschlagsempfindliche RGB-Pads
- Onboard MPC-Sequenzer
- 32-stimmig polyphon (stereo)
- 2 GB RAM und 8 GB interner Speicher
- mehr als 100 Factory-Kits vorinstalliert
- 2.4″ Farbdisplay
- 3 Regler zur Echtzeitkontrolle
- 4 Effektprozessoren mit 60 Effekttypen
- Master Kompressor
- internes Re-Sampling mit Effekten
- Smart Device Sampling über USB-C
- integrierter Lithium-Ionen-Akku für den mobilen Einsatz
- integriertes Mikrofon und Lautsprecher
- Pegelanzeige
- microSD-Card Slot
- USB-C Port (Computeranbindung und Stromversorgung)
- Stereo Line-Ausgang: 2x 6,3 mm Klinke
- Stereo Kopfhörer-Ausgang: 3,5 mm Klinke
- Stereo Line-Eingang: 2x 6,3 mm Klinke
- MIDI In/Out: 2x 3,5 mm Klinke
- Sync-Ausgang: 3,5 mm Klinke
- Abmessungen (B x T x H): 192 x 235 x 49 mm
- Gewicht: 900 g
- inkl. USB-C Kabel

Photo by Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/via Getty Images

What is happening in Tehran now is the quiet discarding of rules that have governed daily life for decades. A few inches of [visible hair](https://aeon.co/videos/in-an-act-of-resistance-elahe-forgoes-a-hijab-at-a-family-party) used to be the whole argument, but it is no longer the point. Women up and down the city are removing their scarves and manteaus – the loose, knee-length coats they were required to wear over their clothes in public – and adopting the latest trends: capri trousers, cropped and close-fitting clothes, bare arms, midi skirts, bare legs. Enjoying this new freedom, they parade along Iranshahr (rather aptly, the street takes its name from the old Persian word for the land of the Iranians), where shops that used to sell manteaus and headscarves have switched to blouses and T-shirts.

A young woman whom I’ll call Mina puts the shift in blunter terms. ‘It isn’t optional anymore,’ she said. ‘You cannot leave the house in ordinary clothes. You have to be put together.’ She does not wear a headscarf anymore, and nor does anyone she goes out with. On the streets where people go to be seen, she tells me, hardly anyone does. In Tehran, those who can afford it wear the latest designer clothing. But in small Iranian towns, local workshops turn out such good copies of the latest Parisian and New York trends that anyone can now dress head to toe in ‘Chanel’, whatever their class.

More [↗ aeon.co](https://aeon.co/essays/its-not-political-the-young-fashionistas-of-tehran).

items.title: Medical device makers have gotten worse at disclosing when their products harm people, new study finds. The FDA let them.
items.subtitle: A new study reveals how data transparency for medical device malfunctions has eroded in recent years, with dangerous consequences for patients.
items.feedText: The study, published in the peer-reviewed medical journal The BMJ, found that device makers have increasingly relied on “summary reporting” of medical device practice harms in federally required disclosures — a practice the U.S. Food and Drug Administration said it ended years ago. items.body:
A new study reveals how data transparency for medical device malfunctions has eroded in recent years, with dangerous consequences for patients. The [study](https://www.bmj.com/content/395/bmj-2026-100812), published in the peer-reviewed medical journal [The BMJ](https://www.bmj.com/), found that device makers have increasingly relied on “summary reporting” of medical device practice harms in federally required disclosures — a practice the U.S. Food and Drug Administration said it ended years ago. But the FDA has quietly continued summary reporting through exemptions that were never made public.

The study found that the summary reports are rife with “incomplete, inaccurate, and delayed” information. Fifty-seven percent of reports described an adverse event “without identified device or use problem,” 38 percent selected “insufficient information” in the data field for the device problem, and 11 percent incorrectly described the report as containing only one adverse event, causing an undercount of nearly 12,000 adverse events.

[The Implant Files](https://www.icij.org/investigations/implant-files/), a 2019 investigation led by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists, exposed the harms done by poorly-tested medical devices, which often enter the market with little regulation. The project brought together more than 250 journalists in 36 countries. ICIJ found that over 1.7 million injuries and nearly 83,000 deaths were suspected of being linked to medical devices in the U.S. from 2008 to 2017.

One way these harms continued to spread, the investigation found, was bad data. For decades, the FDA allowed device makers to file incident reports through a program known as “alternative summary reporting,” which allowed them to submit quarterly spreadsheets rather than report incidents individually. In practice, this program concealed severe injuries — preventing the public from understanding the risks associated with the devices. The FDA ended the program in 2019, saying in a press release that it was doing so “in the spirit of public transparency.”

[https://www.icij.org/inside-icij/2023/12/how-reporting-on-the-medical-device-industry-has-changed-five-years-after-implant-files/](https://www.icij.org/inside-icij/2023/12/how-reporting-on-the-medical-device-industry-has-changed-five-years-after-implant-files/)

items.body:
Michelle Urra for ProPublica

When Oregon’s Housing Stability Council met by Zoom in early October, the state’s top housing official told the oversight board that she wanted to address a [story ProPublica published that morning](https://www.propublica.org/article/oregon-housing-director-husband-conflict).

The story revealed that the official, Andrea Bell, hadn’t clearly disclosed her husband’s work for a small consulting firm that helps housing authorities develop apartments, sometimes with money from Bell’s agency. Nor had she notified Gov. Tina Kotek about it, something Oregon law requires of a governor’s appointee when an actual or potential conflict arises.

Council members, who award hundreds of millions of dollars in housing subsidies, affirmed their support for Bell, who told them she wanted to be clear: “None of the projects that are coming from the council impact my household income.”

Newly obtained records, however, show a clear financial connection between the council’s decisions and her husband’s employer. The records also show that Bell was personally involved in meetings and internal discussions about state funding of a large apartment project, Aloha 209th, which her husband’s employer is helping to develop.

Backers of the Aloha 209th project in Portland’s suburbs are seeking $17.5 million from the housing council, which receives funding recommendations from Bell’s agency.

JH Brawner, the consulting firm that employs Bell’s husband, Joshua Crites, will earn a $2 million fee from the housing authority in Washington County if the transaction closes. If not, JH Brawner gets nothing.

A separate project outside Portland, the Park Place apartments in Clackamas County, already received money through Oregon’s housing agency. Five months after Oregon awarded $36 million to the project in May 2025, Clackamas County’s housing authority paid JH Brawner a $2.4 million consulting fee, the new records show.

Like the Washington County contract, the one with Clackamas County says that if funding fell through for any reason and the project didn’t move forward, “no fee shall be due” to the firm.

JH Brawner said Crites, the firm’s director of strategic initiatives, has not worked on the Aloha 209th project but was one of five staffers assigned to Park Place. JH Brawner pays employees, including Crites, a fixed salary that is not tied to any project closing, according to managing director Zak de Gorgue.

Bell, executive director of Oregon Housing and Community Services, said in a statement that she is “committed to transparency, accountability, and compliance with state law.”

“At no point in my tenure as executive director have I used my position to influence or benefit myself or anyone related to me,” she said. “To be clear, I made no efforts to influence funding, and the Aloha 209 project has not received funding from OHCS and remains on the waitlist.”

Bell’s public agency sits in the middle of the state’s effort to combat a homelessness problem that is among the nation’s worst. Kotek, the governor, has made building more housing a pillar of her time in office. Oregon Housing and Community Services has distributed billions of state and federal dollars to subsidize the construction of apartments intended to have affordable rents.

Norman Williams, a law professor at Willamette University College of Law who teaches about government ethics, said Bell should have reported to the governor that she had a possible conflict and stayed out of any discussions about the projects her husband’s employer helped develop.

“It may all be an innocent mistake on her part,” Williams said, “but she knows who her husband is working for and she doesn’t report that. It makes it look like she’s trying to conceal this.”

De Gorgue said in a statement that the Aloha 209th project is still in development and the company had “no knowledge of Andrea Bell taking any action to move the project forward, nor has JH Brawner & Company engaged in any advocacy to secure funding approval” from Bell’s agency. Funding applications were submitted by the local housing authorities, not by JH Brawner.

“We have no indication, nor any reason to believe, that any project on which we have consulted has been the beneficiary of inappropriate influence,” de Gorgue said.

Separately, he said Clackamas and Washington counties chose JH Brawner as a consultant years before the company hired Crites in 2023.

Crites did not respond to an emailed request for comment.

After ProPublica asked Bell about her husband’s employment in September, she amended three years of ethics disclosure forms, explicitly naming JH Brawner as his employer. (The one time her state filings alluded to Crites’ job before that was in 2025, with a misspelling: “Spouse serves in an advisory role for a developmen.” It showed only the company’s street address, misspelled, and not its name.)

Bell also asked the Oregon Government Ethics Commission for a formal opinion about her potential conflict at the direction of Kotek’s staff. That evaluation was paused after the commission opened a preliminary review in response to a citizen complaint about her lack of disclosure. The preliminary review is ongoing.

ProPublica obtained the new details about Bell’s involvement through county contracts and emails to and from Bell, which were released under Oregon’s public records law. Bell’s agency initially said the emails would cost $612.50 to produce but eventually provided them for free. Washington County charged $364.25 for contracts, invoices and other documents.

Though backers say the Aloha 209th housing development is ready to be built, it’s on a waitlist to receive money from the state. Its turn is not likely to come until at least late 2028. By then, local officials worry that the delay will jeopardize its other funding sources and the project may need an even larger subsidy.

ProPublica previously reported that Molly Rogers, head of the county housing agency seeking money for Aloha 209th, spoke publicly about contacting Bell and said the state agency director was receptive to talking further.

The new records contain Bell’s recollections of the phone conversation she had with Rogers. The same morning the two spoke, in June, Bell told another department official by email that Aloha 209th had “a unique dimension of urgency and angst” because it was one of the last projects funded by a 2018 voter-approved housing bond administered by the Portland area’s Metro regional government.

Natasha Detweiler-Daby, who leads the state housing agency’s affordable rental housing division, responded to Bell that it could be “responsive and logical” to have lawmakers “add nuance” next year by dedicating some portion of funding for housing authority projects on Oregon’s waitlist. Detweiler-Daby did not respond to an email from ProPublica seeking comment.

items.title: AI people are very, very, very, very rich

items.body:
As you may have heard, Anthropic had its IPO this past Thursday. At a valuation of $1.5 trillion, it was actually just the second most valuable IPO in history, just behind SpaceX at $1.77 trillion. I bought some shares on the first day at what I thought was a reasonable price, only to see my shares drop the following day as the company’s valuation fell to $1.175 trillion, making it only [the 14th most valuable company](https://companiesmarketcap.com/) in the world. Such are the risks of buying individual stocks!

But that price drop doesn’t change the fact that Anthropic’s IPO was a staggeringly large wealth creation event. Anthropic began hiring lots of employees just a few years ago; now, almost all of those people have either hundreds of millions of dollars, or tens of millions of dollars. Andrew Benson had a good breakdown of exactly who would get what, if the company hit its initial valuation target of $2 trillion:

> Who actually gets rich if Anthropic lists at $2 trillion?…
> - $199B for the 7 controlling co-founders, about 10%
> - $28B for Ben Mann, if his stake matches theirs
> - $100B for the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, 5%
> - $331B in employee options and RSUs, about 17%, That pool covers about 5,300 employees, an average of $62M each…
> [H]ere is roughly how many people made what at $2T:
> - $110M to $400M each: ~300 to 500 people hired by 2023
> - $200M to $300M each: ~440 to 640 hired in 2024
> - $70M to $95M each: ~1,360 hired in 2025
> - $10M to $20M each: ~3,000 hired in 2026
> So about 940 people hired by the end of 2024 average nine figures. Everyone hired since averages eight figures.

The company’s (fully diluted) valuation is now only about 80% of that $2T number, so you have to scale those numbers down a little bit. But it’s still a staggering amount of money for just a few years of work! We’re used to seeing the first few employees at a generational company make hundreds of millions of dollars, but seeing several *hundred* people make that much is just unprecedented.

Let’s put these numbers in perspective. If Anthropic were worth $2T, it would have more centimillionaires than the entire city of Los Angeles. Even with only 350-400 centimillionaires, that’s about as many as Houston, Dallas, and Austin combined:

Source: [Steve Rattner](https://x.com/SteveRattner/status/2123523070044356875?s=19)

Of course, just looking at these numbers tremendously understates the amount of wealth that has been created in the AI industry over the last couple of years. There’s also OpenAI, which is [targeting](https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/anthropic-vs-openai-the-financial-metrics-behind-the-ai-battle-4f5b90c0) an IPO valuation of $1.25 trillion. And there are quite a number of AI startups that have gotten very valuable, very quickly. Just a few include Isomorphic Labs at ~$50 billion, Cognition at $48 billion, Prometheus at $41 billion, Safe Superintelligence at $32 billion, VAST Data at $30 billion, Reflection AI at ~$27.5 billion, Cohere at $25.5 billion, ElevenLabs at $22 billion, and so on.

And of course, all of this is just *today*. I wouldn’t have bought Anthropic stock unless I thought the company had a very good chance of becoming much *more* valuable than it is today. Despite the early price drop, I’m still very bullish. I think AI’s extremely cross-domain capabilities mean that Anthropic has a good shot at being a very large, diversified conglomerate:

Furthermore, I think the company is amassing a huge pool of top human talent, essentially giving them a hedge against a future in which AI continues to be a complement to top human talent rather than a substitute. Almost every smart person I know here in Silicon Valley either works there or has strongly considered working there. That makes Anthropic resemble Google back in 2004, which became a legendary brain trust. If anyone can figure out a way to make boatloads of money with AI, it’s probably Anthropic. And yes, someone *will* figure out a way to make boatloads of money with AI. Even if that means the company only becomes as valuable as [Google or Microsoft is today](https://companiesmarketcap.com/), that means I’ll more than double my own investment.

If that happens, all of those wealth numbers from the top of this post will also more than double. And if the U.S. economy grows robustly and AI itself grows rapidly as a percentage of that economy, this could easily turn out to be the greatest wealth creation event in American history, by far — greater than the internet, far greater than crypto, greater even than the railroads.

I can definitely feel this wealth all around me. A lot of the people I went to potlucks with three years ago now have an order of magnitude more money than anyone I ever met before I turned 30. Some of those people are under 30 themselves. A few of them are billionaires. Now, when I go to house parties, they’re often in lavish designer-furnished mansions overlooking spectacular ocean views from high up on San Francisco hilltops.

As a social phenomenon, this is totally unprecedented. Sarah Chieng [writes](https://x.com/MilksandMatcha/status/2114768311468871731):

> You can build a startup in 9 months, get acquired (but rly acquihired) by OpenAI, Anthropic, or Cognition, and walk away a multi-millionaire…You can join the right company at 22 and become effectively post-economic…And I don't think we've even begun to grapple with the degree to which this is warping an entire generation's relationship with money, ambition, work, and success…When your peers are making generational wealth before 25, what does a normal career even look like anymore[?]

I’m happy for my friends, of course. And I am not personally bothered by seeing displays of great wealth. But I find myself wondering what this is going to do to my society. If the AI class are the *only* people who get rich going forward, what kind of tensions will that produce among the country’s elites? What would it mean for America if wealth inequality goes up far further even than it already has?

#### What if only the AI people get rich?

[↗ noahpinion.blog](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/ai-people-are-very-very-very-very)

items.body:
Wer mit der Bahn unterwegs ist, kann künftig auch Fahrkarten des Konkurrenten FlixTrain direkt im DB Navigator kaufen. Die Deutsche Bahn und FlixTrain haben eine entsprechende [Vertriebsvereinbarung unterzeichnet](https://www1.deutschebahn.com/de/presse/pressestart_zentrales_uebersicht/deutsche-bahn-und-flixtrain-schliessen-vertriebsvereinbarung-14098862). Ab dem 7. Dezember 2026 lassen sich über die iPhone-App und die Webseite bahn.de erstmals Tickets beider Unternehmen erwerben. Die Neuerung gilt für Fahrten ab dem 13. Dezember und damit passend zum Fahrplanwechsel.

## FlixTrain-Tickets erstmals direkt in der Bahn-App

Bislang wurden FlixTrain-Verbindungen zwar bereits in der Fahrplanauskunft der Deutschen Bahn angezeigt, eine direkte Buchung war allerdings nicht möglich. Stattdessen mussten Reisende auf die Webseite oder App von FlixTrain wechseln, um ihre Fahrkarten zu kaufen.

Dieser Umweg entfällt künftig. Die Bahn übernimmt den Ticketverkauf innerhalb ihrer eigenen Buchungsoberfläche. Damit können Reisende direkt im DB Navigator nach passenden Verbindungen suchen, Preise vergleichen und Fahrkarten erwerben.

Die beiden Unternehmen bleiben dabei weiterhin eigenständige Wettbewerber. Fahrpläne, Preise und das jeweilige Zugangebot legen Deutsche Bahn und FlixTrain unverändert unabhängig voneinander fest. Laut Bahn sollen die Tickets zum gleichen Preis wie bei FlixTrain angeboten werden.

## ICE und FlixTrain in einem Buchungsvorgang

Besonders praktisch ist die Möglichkeit, Verbindungen beider Anbieter miteinander zu kombinieren. So lässt sich beispielsweise eine Reise planen, bei der zunächst ein ICE genutzt wird und anschließend der Umstieg in einen FlixTrain erfolgt.

Die dafür benötigten Fahrkarten können in einem einzigen Buchungsvorgang erworben werden. Das dürfte insbesondere bei längeren Reisen mit mehreren Umstiegen die Planung und den Preisvergleich erleichtern.

#### Der DB Navigator lässt bald auch Buchungen bei der Konkurrenz zu.

## Bei verpassten Anschlüssen bleibt Vorsicht geboten

Eine Einschränkung bleibt allerdings bestehen. Obwohl beide Tickets gemeinsam gekauft werden können, handelt es sich weiterhin um getrennte Fahrkarten. Die Buchung führt somit nicht automatisch zu einem durchgehenden Beförderungsvertrag.

Darauf weist auch der Fahrgastverband [PRO BAHN](https://www.presseportal.de/pm/177328/6397594) hin. Er begrüßt die Zusammenarbeit, fordert allerdings weitergehende Fahrgastrechte. Bei einem verpassten Anschluss zwischen zwei Anbietern sollte die Weiterreise ohne zusätzliche Kosten möglich sein. Bis dahin empfiehlt es sich, bei entsprechenden Verbindungen auf ausreichend Umsteigezeit zu achten.

In die umgekehrte Richtung funktioniert die Kooperation übrigens noch nicht: Fahrkarten der Deutschen Bahn lassen sich weiterhin nicht über die Buchungsplattformen von FlixTrain kaufen.

Der [DB Navigator](https://apps.apple.com/de/app/db-navigator/id343555245) ist kostenlos für iPhone und Apple Watch erhältlich. Zuletzt hatte die Bahn unter anderem die [Anmeldung per Passkey](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/db-navigator-anmeldung-jetzt-auch-per-passkey-moeglich-272359/) ergänzt. Die neue FlixTrain-Buchung soll ab dem 7. Dezember direkt über die bestehenden Vertriebskanäle zur Verfügung stehen.

[★ iPhone-Ticker bei Google bevorzugen ★](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=iphone-ticker.de)

Der Beitrag [DB Navigator: FlixTrain-Tickets ab Dezember direkt buchbar](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/db-navigator-flixtrain-tickets-ab-dezember-direkt-buchbar-291411/) Wurde zuerst auf [iphone-ticker.de](https://www.iphone-ticker.de) veröffentlicht.

items.body:
The New Scientist Book Club read Chris Beckett’s Dark Eden in November

Since starting the New Scientist Book Club in May 2023, I have aimed to vary our books as much as possible, moving between science fiction and popular science, older classics and the hottest new titles. Occasionally, though, I’m afraid I let the power go to my head and just choose one of my own personal favourites. That’s what I did in November, with Chris Beckett’s novel [Dark Eden](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2596432-read-an-extract-from-dark-eden-by-chris-beckett/), a book I’ve loved ever since it won the Arthur C. Clarke award in 2013.

Set on the planet Eden, a sunless world that drifts alone far outside the Milky Way, this follows the descendants of two astronauts who were marooned there over a century earlier. Now numbering 532 people, they tell each other stories of the world their ancestors came from, and struggle to survive on this dark, cold planet as they await the return of “one of those sky-boats with lights on them”. I think it is all wildly imaginative and original and exciting. So it was with some trepidation that I awaited the verdict of my fellow book club members on our [Discord](https://discord.com/invite/fn7m4NbSac) channel. I really wanted everyone else to love it, too!

Free newsletter

#### Sign up to Book Club

[Sign up to newsletter](https://www.newscientist.com/sign-up/bookclub/)

It started well. “I managed not to stay up all night reading, but the temptation was definitely there – I am hooked,” wrote Dee55. Les was similarly gripped. “Started it? I’ve only gone and finished it, haven’t I? It *really* got me in, and I found it a fascinating exploration of social anthropology and linguistics in a very small, isolated population. And the world-building was fascinating, too – *very* different flora and fauna.”

Several other members also cited the strength of the world-building in *Dark Eden*. I also love the lanternflowers and woollybucks of this planet, and was fascinated to learn, in an [essay](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2596453-in-dark-eden-i-imagined-how-life-might-exist-on-a-sunless-planet/) Chris wrote for book club members, that, when creating a world for a story, he doesn’t “usually seek to make the whole thing scientifically accurate, but I try to make it hang together in a way that feels coherent”. I think he definitely succeeds in that here.

[In Dark Eden, I imagined how life might exist on a sunless planet Dark Eden, the November read for the New Scientist Book Club, takes place on a rogue planet outside the Milky Way. Award-winning author Chris Beckett explains how he thought through the science behind this night world](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2596453-in-dark-eden-i-imagined-how-life-might-exist-on-a-sunless-planet/)

There were some excellent debates about the language these people have developed – they double up on words for emphasis, for example (“big big”; “cold cold”), use bastardised forms of our words (“Landing Veekle”; “leckytrickity”), and talk about Starry Swirl – the Milky Way they can see in their skies, a wonderfully evocative image.

“I think Beckett has done something really clever here. He’s created a language that feels familiar enough to read naturally, but is sufficiently different to remind us that this is an entirely separate culture that has evolved in isolation,” wrote Maria. “I enjoyed some of the language. Tom’s dick and Harry’s for instance,” wrote Matthew – referring to an exclamation the characters use for emphasis. “It’s contagious… yesterday I found myself saying Wow, it’s hot hot!” added leasabp. Dee55 also admitted to adopting some Edenisms: “My favourite bit of the language is ‘newhairs’! I am already using this for teenagers, but only to myself at present.”

The story’s protagonist is John Redlantern, a young man who decides there must be more to life than waiting for rescue around the Circle of Stones that marks the original astronauts’ landing point on Eden, and tries to spark an exodus from the Family’s small valley to explore the wider planet. John definitely drew some mixed opinions from readers.

“Problem is, I don’t much like our ‘hero’, he’s not a very sympathetic character, more Sméagol than Bilbo,” wrote Matthew. I chatted to Chris in an interview for book club members, and he was certainly aware of this: “He’s an awkward cuss, John, isn’t he? He’s not a particularly nice person,” he told me – before embarking on an enlightening discussion about why he chose to write from various viewpoints, and how hard it was describing the world of Eden from the perspectives of people who have never been anywhere else. “The discipline of just writing it from within the story is if I’m trying to describe the world to readers, I can’t use metaphors and analogies that refer to anything that’s outside of Eden. And that was quite tricky to do.”

Book club member Laura Akers, like others, said she “definitely enjoyed the story more when I realized that John, despite his own intentions, is not intended to be our ‘hero’”.

Overall, I think the book club mostly really enjoyed *Dark Eden* – I particularly appreciated leasapb’s comment: “Holy cow. Chapter 44!!!”, as I think the ending is fabulous – but one issue that was raised by a few people was the amount the characters have sex with each other. Incestuous sex.

“Certainly one of the odd things I found was the casual attitude to sex,” wrote Alan_P. Maria agreed. “I found the casual attitude towards sex quite unsettling too, particularly because the characters often seem almost childlike in their behaviour and understanding of the world, yet discuss sex so matter-of-factly. I honestly couldn’t bring myself to think too much about the incest!” And while Barbara Howe “loved the worldbuilding, and the story of John’s breakaway family’s trek to find a better place”, she found the “constant and highly unerotic sex… offputting”.

But given that at least some members have gone on to read the sequels, I think this was largely a popular choice – and a welcome change from the Earthly dystopias which seem to be dominating the big new sci-fi novels out this autumn (I’m looking at you, [Audrey Niffenegger](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2594474-theres-two-ways-of-doing-time-travel-right-says-audrey-niffenegger/) and [Emily St. John Mandel](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2595814-our-verdict-on-exit-party-by-emily-st-john-mandel-not-her-best-book/)).

items.body:
Gloria Steinem was booked up. There had been luncheons and interviews scheduled for the fall; a high-profile conversation with Katie Couric at 92NY and a prominent place in The New Yorker Festival’s lineup. She left appearances unfulfilled, interviews unaired, an essay unpublished and a forthcoming book. In short: Gloria Steinem was, at 92, far from done.

That energy is palpable in that very book, her memoir [An Unexpected Life](https://bookshop.org/p/books/an-unexpected-life-notes-from-a-hope-a-holic-gloria-steinem/4b7ec63a4c7acf42/?aid=132!), published on September 22, in which she states that she planned to live to at least 100. Although she was “older than [she] ever imagined,” mortality didn’t really cross her mind much. Any why would it, when she was also “happier than [she] ever imagined” and her calendar was bursting at the seams? Part memoir, part manifesto, part consciousness raising group, *An Unexpected Life* is a collection of essays in which Steinem reflects on her life, lays out her worldview and looks towards the future. And just as she was in life, on the page she radiates a matter-of-fact conviction and an unflinching clarity—the result of more than sixty years spent organizing a movement.

Her story begins long before she would become the most prominent face of second-wave feminism (although Steinem would reject this label), with a bruised childhood in Toledo, Ohio. She spent stretches of her young life on the road, until her father left when she was ten years old, leaving her in a rat-infested home caring for her increasingly mentally ill mother. With a childhood spent longing for warm kitchens and cookie cutter family units, it is striking that Steinem would grow up to spend so much of her adult life traveling around the country, more often than not living out of a suitcase. But even more formative than her earliest years, perhaps, was the time spent in India in her early 20s, an experience that would become the very foundation of her feminism.

Although mortality was far from Steinem’s mind, it is apparent in these pages that she was hyperaware of her legacy. “At my age, in this still hierarchical time, people often ask me if I’m ‘passing the torch,’” she wrote in her 1983 book [Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellion s](https://bookshop.org/p/books/outrageous-acts-and-everyday-rebellions-third-edition-gloria-steinem/753219586e6d55f1/?aid=132!). “I explain that I’m keeping my torch, thank you very much—and I’m using it to light the torches of others.”

She is doing just that in *An Unexpected Life*, a text bursting with a kind of hopeful exhilaration about what could be. “Nothing is more exciting than making the invisible visible. It’s like finding the end in a ball of yarn,” she wrote. “Pull on it, and gradually the whole of patriarchy unravels.” At times, she gets as literal as bullet-point lists on how to best organize a feminist movement. There are glimmers of the—often cited—shortcomings of the women’s movement that she was at the helm of herself. “Insist on multiracial women who represent the movement,” is one such takeaway of Steinem’s. “Otherwise, people will have a distorted view.” There is an added poignancy to the essays upon her passing; a book that is as much about her life as it is a handbook for movement building. “Whatever my story might be to other people,” Steinem wrote, “I hope something has ripple effects that I myself may never see.”

One such ripple effect concerns her beloved home, an apartment in a brownstone building on the Upper East Side of Manhattan. “If time and ingenuity allow,” Steinem wrote in the book’s prologue, “I hope to acquire the other floors in this house and leave this whole building as a refuge for diverse women who need a place to stay or just to meet.”

Steinem first moved into her apartment in 1968, together with a roommate. Throughout the years, the apartment grew not only in square footage but in function. The single unit became an entire floor, which became three floors. Her living room had been a meeting place for over fifty years, where she hosted gatherings and talking circles up until this very year. She held meeting on topics ranging from women’s health to misinformation in the media—a meeting in that very living room had led to the founding of *Ms. Magazine* in 1971. On September 3, Gloria’s Foundation announced that her brownstone would continue to be a feminist sanctuary; a place for women to father and organize, to discuss and seek shelter.

Lingering in the background of these pages is Steinem’s time in India. The years spent there upon graduating from Smith College made such a deep and lasting impression on Steinem, it not only ignited her activism but it is where her ideology was rooted throughout her life. In her final essay, published in [The New Yorker](https://www.newyorker.com/culture/life-and-letters/gloria-steinems-final-essay?utm_mailing=tny_nl_6667_daily_090326_utg9beo9c3&utm_source=nl&utm_brand=tny&utm_campaign=aud-dev&utm_medium=email&utm_content=tny_nl_6667_daily_090326_utg9beo9c3&cndid=64331124&utm_term=6667) following her passing, she wrote that it was where she realized that “white people were a very small minority in the world. In India, I got accustomed to, and began to value, racial diversity.” The open, nonviolent M.O. of Ghandi and his followers captivated her, perhaps not in the last place because she learned that his peace movement was once inspired by India’s women’s movement. “I think culturally women are drawn to nonviolence,” Steinem wrote in her final essay. “Probably because we are the major victims of violence, we become the major movers of peace.”

There is an odd comfort in having Gloria Steinem insist that it really, truly, *believe her*, has been worse.

That multiracial point of view is woven through her philosophy. Steinem could not conceive of a world where sexism existed without racism, and vice versa. The assertion, perhaps, also stems from how juxtaposed it is from the image of the women’s movement, especially the lingering one that it overwhelmingly served white middle-class women. After all, the women’s movement has since been criticized all too often for alienating Black women, working-class women, and LGBTQ+ women. Many of these women were exactly the ones who most often weren’t in the position to break free from the home and chase careers—they had been forced to work for decades. From her words, it’s evident that Steinem did not stand for such “white feminism.” “Systems of dominance—racism and sexism—are rooted together, and must be uprooted together,” she wrote. It is a stance that is progressive even by today’s standards. “To stop racist systems,” she wrote, “women especially must be free.”

…

items.body:
# Osterinseln als Location in „Wild Horse Nine“: US-Touris wollen die Steinköpfe sehen

## Osterinseln in „Wild Horse Nine“ : Touris wollen Köpfe sehen

Martin McDonaghs Film spielt auf Rapa Nui. Sind darum die Buchungen dorthin um 575 Prozent gestiegen? Würde passen: Auch im Film geht’s um westliche Invasion.

25.11.2026

7:29 Uhr

teilen

Diesen Artikel teilen

Wofür Rapa Nui vor dem Film vor allem bekannt war: Moai, die großen Steinkopfskulpturen Foto: Fabien Pallueau/imago

I n Martin McDonaghs Filmen sind die Schauplätze so wichtig, wie die Figuren, die sich dort bewegen. Bis in die Titel schaffen es die Orte sogar: Ebbing, Missouri zum Beispiel, Brügge oder Inisherin . Wie die Figuren verkörpern sie etwas Konkretes: Brügge etwa ein mittelalterliches Fegefeuer voller religiöser Ikonografie, der sich die von Schuld zerfressenen Figuren nicht entziehen können. Oder die irische Insel Inisherin, ein einsamer Mikrokosmos, wo sich Einheimische zwangsläufig über den Weg laufen.

McDonaghs neuster Film spielt auf Rapa Nui, der 3.500 Kilometer vom Festland entfernten und doch zu Chile gehörenden Insel, die die meisten wegen der großen Steinköpfe, der Moai, oder noch unter dem Namen Osterinsel kennen. Es gibt wenige Orte, die derart isoliert und isolierend sind. Von Ost nach West fährt man in 45 Minuten, von Nord nach Süd in 30.

Aus vulkanischem Gestein ist die Insel gemacht, Wildpferde galoppieren da und die satten grünen Wiesen, erinnert McDonagh an das Heimatland seiner Eltern, Irland. Das klingt traumhaft, ein Ort, an dem man sterben möchte, so wie es ja auch die Hauptfigur, der todkranke CIA-Agent Chris (John Malkovich) plant.

Ob es nun an „Wild Horse Nine“ oder neuen Flugverbindungen liegt, dass die Buchungen zur kleinen Insel um 575 Prozent gestiegen sind, ist noch nicht klar. Laut des Nachrichtenportals für Tourismus Ladevi gebe es jedenfalls 100 Prozent mehr Touristen aus den USA und von Oktober 2026 bis März 2027 ganze 12.000 internationale Flugbuchungen nach Rapa Nui. Im Vorjahr waren es nur 1.800. Ganz überraschend wäre es nicht, denn Filme waren schon häufiger Auslöser solcher Explosionen.

## Von Ko Phi Phi über Skopelos bis nach Ubud

„The Beach“ ist der wohl bekannteste Fall einer durch einen Film ausgelösten Invasion westlicher Touristen. 2018 musste Maya Beach auf Ko Phi Phi sogar vier Jahre lang schließen , weil Millionen von Menschen mit ihren Booten, ihrem Müll, ihrer Sonnencreme über Jahre das Ökosystem des Strandes und einen Großteil der umliegenden Korallen zerstört hatten. „Mamma Mia“ brachte ebenfalls Massen auf die griechische Insel Skopelos und „Eat, Pray, Love“-Fans trieb es auf der Suche nach Julia-Roberts-Spiritualität ins balinesische Ubud.

Beim Soziologen Dennison Nash heißt es , dass es eine enge Beziehung zwischen Tourismus und Imperialismus gebe. Wie Missionare, Eroberer oder Händler bringen Tourist_innen ihre eigenen, fremden Praktiken mit, an die sich Gastgeber anpassen müssen. Das ökonomische Gefälle zwischen Gast und Gastgeber verstärke das zusätzlich.

„Wild Horse Nine“ handelt vom ganz konkreten imperialistischen Vorhaben westlicher Staaten, hier den USA. Der Film spielt 1973 kurz vorm CIA-gestützten Militärputsch des sozialistischen Salvador Allende in Chile. Die Agenten Lee (Sam Rockwell) und Chris waren also eh in der Gegend, fliegen jedoch nur nach Rapa Nui, weil der an Krebs erkrankte Chris dort seine letzten irdischen Momente verbringen möchte.

Er spaziert dann über die (da noch) leere Insel und denkt nach: über das bevorstehende Massaker in Chile, über Dallas und die Ermordung JFKs, über Lumumba im Kongo und über seine Schuld an der blutrünstigen Geschichte der USA. Ganz so, als wäre sein Gewissen aus einem tiefen Schlaf erwacht, versucht er, ein klein wenig wiedergutzumachen.

In einem Interview sagte McDonagh der taz, dass er nicht verstehe, warum er nie von CIA-Agenten in Rente höre, die ihre Vergangenheit bereuen. Vielleicht idealisiert er sich da Menschen herbei, die es nicht gibt. Oder vielleicht machen diese Rentner gerade völlig guten Gewissens Urlaub auf Skopelos.

Valérie Catil Gesellschaftsredakteurin
