items.body:
# Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton

## a]:hidden"> Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton

## TL;DR

Add local obstacle avoidance to Microduck while keeping its walking policy fixed. Build varied courses with reusable SimReady assets, model ToF sensing with Newton’s raycaster, and train a controller in Isaac Lab to adjust gamepad velocity commands around obstacles. This tutorial covers simulation training, evaluation, export, and real-robot deployment.

## Introduction

A walking policy can keep Microduck balanced, but it does not tell the robot how to steer around an obstacle in its path. In this workflow, we reuse the walking policy from our first Microduck tutorial and keep its weights fixed. This follow-up trains a separate avoidance controller using time-of-flight (ToF) sensing. You choose a direction with a gamepad; the controller adjusts the velocity command before passing it to the walking policy.

NVIDIA Isaac Lab is an open-source framework for training policies across thousands of GPU-parallel simulations and it provides the robot-learning environment. Newton simulates physics and the sensor’s depth measurements. We will cover the control architecture, train on varied obstacle layouts, evaluate the resulting policies, and prepare the interface for hardware testing.

## 1. Set Microduck obstacle avoidance in Isaac Lab

For simulation and training, prepare:

- A Linux system with a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver. See the Isaac Lab installation guide for platform requirements.
- Git with Git LFS, and the uv package manager.
For physical-robot testing, prepare:

- A configured Microduck. Load the same backlash walking-policy export used by the navigation task.
- A supported ToF sensor with its configuration recorded.
- A paired gamepad and a level test area with obstacles.
### Quick install

Install uv if it is not already installed. Then clone the exp/microduck branch of the Isaac Lab repository and install its dependencies:

git lfs install git clone --branch exp/microduck https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab.git cd IsaacLab uv sync --frozen Once setup is complete, list the available Microduck environments and presets:

uv run isaaclab list_envs --keyword MicroDuck --show_presets Download the walking policy Download and export the upstream backlash walking checkpoint once before training. The obstacle avoidance task loads the exported walking policy automatically.

uv run isaaclab play \ --task IsaacContrib-Velocity-Rough-MicroDuck \ --rl_library rsl_rl --checkpoint pretrained \ --num_envs 1 --visualizer none \ --video newton_gl --video_length 1 \ presets=backlash 2. Build the obstacle course The environment combines simple primitives with OpenUSD assets available through SimReady Central on Hugging Face. We use a cardboard box , office bin , bedside cabinet alongside cones. From the IsaacLab repository root, download the pinned box, bin and cabinet packages into assets/simready.

uvx --from huggingface-hub hf download nvidia/simready-assets \ --repo-type dataset \ --revision 9d4556bfe80868c1d27a7a7ba1c2774e63e8cedd \ --include "box_cardboard_a01/*" \ --include "trashCan_office_black_a03/*" \ --include "table_bedside_b01/*" \ --local-dir ./assets/simready At each episode reset, the environment code automatically samples a layout, shuffles the props, and varies their placement and rotation. Most courses scatter obstacles ahead of the duck, with a smaller mix of clear paths, barriers and passages. The code also mirrors layouts and mixes aligned and staggered rows.

Goals start ahead of the duck. Movement commands guide it toward the goal while the policy adjusts them around obstacles.

Figure 1. Varied obstacle-course layouts with SimReady assets and primitive geometry.

## 3. Understand how ToF sensing guides the walking policy

The IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck task separates obstacle avoidance from balance. A navigation policy uses ToF sensing to adjust forward, lateral, and yaw commands at 50 Hz. The frozen walking policy then converts those commands into joint actions, allowing the robot to learn obstacle avoidance without retraining its walking behavior.

During training, the navigation policy’s actor receives ToF history and body and controller state available on the real robot. Its critic has access to additional simulation state to guide learning, but is not needed for deployment.

Rewards encourage progress toward the goal, safe arrivals, and movement around obstacles. Following a movement command earns credit only when the robot makes progress with sufficient clearance; risky approaches reduce that credit. Penalties discourage fast approaches, abrupt command changes, collisions, and falls.

The obstacle-avoidance task lives in isaaclab_tasks.contrib.microduck_obstacle . Its configuration is in obstacle_avoidance_env_cfg.py , ToF sensing is in sensors.py , and actions, commands, observations and rewards are organized under mdp/ .

### Model the ToF sensor

MicroDuckToFCamera extends Newton’s LegacyMultiMeshRayCasterCamera to model the VL53L5CX—a compact time-of-flight (ToF) sensor on the microduck that measures distance across an 8×8 grid at 15Hz. The simulated sensor has a 45° field of view and a 0.12–4 m range. It follows the duck’s head, with placement similar to the sensor on the real duck.

Real recordings informed the sensor placement and floor readings in simulation. Training adds noise, delays and missing measurements—including near the grid’s edges—to expose the policy to imperfect data. The excerpt below shows selected sensor settings already included in the task configuration. You do not need to edit or run this code separately.

# Selected settings; mount and raycast targets omitted. head_tof = MicroDuckToFCameraCfg( prim_path=MICRODUCK_HEAD_BODY_PATH, update_period= 1.0 / 15.0 , pattern_cfg=patterns.PinholeCameraPatternCfg( focal_length= 1.0 , width= 8 , height= 8 , horizontal_aperture=_TOF_APERTURE, vertical_aperture=_TOF_APERTURE, ), randomization=ToFRandomizationCfg( mount_pitch_degrees=(- 10.0 , 10.0 ), mount_height_m=(- 0.02 , 0.02 ), floor_validity_midpoint_offset_m=( 0.0 , 0.13 ), near_floor_edge_impairment_probability= 0.5 , ), data_types=[ "distance_to_image_plane" , "distance_to_camera" ], max_distance=TOF_MAX_RANGE, depth_clipping_behavior= "zero" , ) 4. Train the Microduck policy across parallel environments Train the navigation policy with PPO across 16,384 parallel environments for 1,500 training iterations. Its actor, critic, normalizers, and optimizer start fresh. The task configuration loads the fixed walking checkpoint, robot model, and obstacle assets.

items.body:
> Between 1970 and 1990 the U.S. legal services industry underwent a dramatic demand shift. Its employment share more than doubled and the relative wages of lawyers rose by 60%, in contrast to stability before and after. We attribute this shift to three related changes in the legal environment: a wave of new legislation and regulation broadened the scope of the law, left its application uncertain, and enlisted private lawyers to enforce it through fee-shifting. Using over a century of data, we show that lawyers’ employment and compensation track all three changes. Event studies link specific statutes to increased litigation and demand for the affected fields of law. Other explanations, including lawyer quality, industrial composition, and technology, do not account for the demand shift. We estimate that legislative uncertainty accounts for roughly 13% of the demand shift—a cost of about $23 billion in 2024 alone.

That is from [a new paper](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5acd55db36099bfff90bf5d6/t/6ab43b507bff7c595f110ab3/1790196560274/ReshefSlattery_Lawyers_Sept2026.pdf) by Ariell Resheff and Cailin Slattery. Via [Krzysztof Tyszka-Drozdowski](https://tyszka-drozdowski.com/).

items.body:
Signal announced an update to its mobile apps on iOS and Android that seeks to curb issues with AI agents accessing private chats. This is a useful new barrier against a problem we’ve been highlighting this year in our Encrypt It Already campaign. And good news, it’s enabled by default so you don’t need to do anything except update the app.

Over the last year, both Google and Apple* have released AI features in their operating systems that can read the contents of apps. One of the ways it can do this is through screen analysis. Google calls this feature “Intelligent Screen Context,” while Apple refers to it as either “Onscreen Awareness” or “Visual Intelligence.”

Apple now provides a way to block Siri AI’s access to apps, but by default every app is available to Siri AI, so it’s up to the user to go in and put these guardrails up. Signal requests that protection on your behalf. Google doesn’t currently offer any sort of similar option. So Signal on Android does the best it can, by turning off screenshots when it detects an AI assistant attempting to access the screen. Signal’s solution helps ensure that, unless you go in and change the setting yourself, it defaults to the most private option.

While this is a clever solution to the current issues facing Signal (and potentially useful for any other app that does its best to promise privacy), we need all operating systems to provide stronger methods and clear documentation to developers so they can safeguard their users without needing to jump through hoops. Both developers and users should have the tools they need to safeguard their own data from AI agents and other AI tools.

*Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

items.body:
For many years, I have been frustrated by a simple question, one I ask myself all the time: what the hell did I do in my eight hours at work today? I’m a freelancer and micro-publisher, and my time may consist of moments spent each day across a thousand different tasks. This leaves me unable to recall comprehensively what I’ve done.

I finally have an answer in the form of [the Timing app](https://timingapp.com/): it offers app-driven, document- and dialog-level tracking. It’s not the first or the only such app, but it’s the first I’ve tried, found worthwhile, and stuck with. I now have many months of data about what I do, and it is truly revealing, particularly for the writing portion of my life.

Timing [1](https://sixcolors.com/post/2026/11/timing-review-let-an-app-track-what-you-do/#fn-42510-sponsor) tracks every context switch when you move from foreground app to foreground app, which includes the titles of windows and other identifying details. At the end of the day, I can see how much time I spent and most of what I did within each app.

Timing captures what you do by app using window titles, pathways, and more.

The reason Timing works for me? Powerful rules-based task filtering that, as I’ve set up over time, handles most of the work in letting me see what I’m doing without tediously categorizing pieces of time or individual documents and windows. I can mark time chunks manually or reassign them, but I rarely need to spend many of my precious minutes doing that.

This review isn’t exhaustive—the app has many features I never use, but the subset I describe below has a high value to me.

## Identifying what you’re doing

Timing records data about what’s happening in the foreground. While this has limitations, it has generally worked for me across many programs and types of work. Timing pulls titles from documents, tab titles from browser tabs, Terminal job information (often shown in a Terminal window’s title), people from Messages, channel names and DM names from Slack, and paths to files that are open. If you have Timing installed on multiple Macs, it syncs this data. You can manually start timers and edit information that’s been captured.

The Devices filter lets you include or exclude your linked devices for clarity.

While there’s no way for an iPhone or iPad app to extract document-specific usage, Timing Software extracts information from synced Screen Time data. The company notes that [this is a workaround](https://timingapp.com/help/screen-time), and Apple could break this method in the future. The company avoided iOS/iPadOS app development by [offering a web app](https://timingapp.com/help/web) for manual time recording that works on any platform.

Timing records data by app, with the details broken out. As data accrues, Timing sorts it in the Activities view. There are two other main views—Stats and Reports—which I have barely touched in nearly a year of using it. Most of what I need I find in Activities.

This report view may be useful to some people. It shows I have tracked 1856 hours of my time so far in 2026, starting in mid-January!

The three features that helped me use Timing effectively were:

The single-day view lets you get a densely layered graphical view of your work across all your devices.

- Time slicing: At the top of every view, there’s a time period button you can click to choose among presets, like the Past 30 Days, and custom ranges. If you choose Today or single day in Activities, you get a bonus graphical chronological view of the entire day’s behavior divided by platform, with some algorithm-generated text that defines the primary activity in that period.
- Projects: Create projects and sub-projects to organize what you’re doing. Because I have so many different things going on, I have my tiny publishing business, Six Colors, Take Control (books I write for royalties and books/consulting I do under contract), sites I’ve developed, and clients. I also set up projects for non-billable overhead stuff, which includes household work. (For clients, I don’t rely on Timing, but rather a separate timer-based accounting app that handles invoices and other tasks, too.)
- Rules: The most powerful feature, mentioned in the introduction, is Timing’s rules. The rules use pattern matching to assign an item identified in Activities to a project. You can create these rules automatically or by hand. For instance, I set up rules for specific paths for documents to always be part of a specific project, but I use automatic rule creation to add entries that don’t correspond to a path, like Safari windows that have a title that always starts with the same words.

The powerful rules editor includes all automatically created filters. Tweaking rules automates time tracking.

Those are the pieces; now I’ll tell you how I join them.

## Using dragging and rules to build the picture

To bring this all together, I start in the Activities view. All Activities shows everything that’s been tracked in the currently selected time period. Anything assigned to a project appears under My Projects. The Unassigned section has all the uncut gems you can work with to bring order to your tracking chaos. (I should note that Activities defaults to Unified, which shows tasks by apps. You can also use By Category—website, path, etc.—or Chronological.)

Depending on the app, you can drill down by clicking expansion triangles. So for Safari, I might click next to Safari, then Kickstarter, then find there are many different entries all related to a project I was working on. I can also hover over or click grouped or individual entries in the Today or single-day view at the right side of Timing, as shown above.

The Activities view set to a single day lets you reveal a lot of information about ranges of time, and assign them to projects.

In all these cases, I can assign tasks to a project, or drag windows, selections, or entire apps onto a project in the My Projects list.

If I’m sure I want to have that assignment stick—the document entry I’m dragging is always part of a given project—I can Option-drag, and Timing adds a rule. Over weeks and months, I have accumulated many rules and tweaked the entries by hand to make sure I was sweeping in the right documents.

For instance, I can review recent work on an update to *Take Control of Apple Wallet* by selecting the last 90 days as a time period, selecting the project name TCo Wallet in the sidebar, and then clicking Chronological. I can expand the time entries to make sure tasks were properly assigned, and look over the time I spent.

I can see exactly how much time I’ve spent on this book update.

My two greatest tips from using Timing are:

- I should be using tab groups in Safari more so that I have more discrete information when a Safari tab’s title tag lacks enough information for me to review later.
- Examine rules regularly to ensure you’ve got the right level of granularity to match what you want included in a project.

Der Sterling StingRay 50th Anniversary LTD besitzt einen Korpus aus Okumé. Der Hals ist aus wunderschön geröstetem Ahorn gefertigt und hat ein Griffbrett aus Palisander obendrauf. Dieses ist mit großen, weißen Pearloid-Block-Griffbretteinlagen geschmückt. Die Hardware ist komplett in Gold gehalten und besteht aus einem klassischen, von Sterling entworfenen Steg und offenen Mechaniken. Das macht auf dem Papier zunächst einmal einen sehr soliden Eindruck.

Sterling StingRay 50th Anniversary LTD · Quelle: Sterling

## Aktiver Tonabnehmer

Besonders hervorzuheben ist der **aktive Alnico-Humbucker**, der über ein**3-Band-Preamp** geregelt wird. Damit lässt sich, wie vom StingRay bekannt, klanglich enorm viel abdecken. Stilistisch seid ihr mit dem Bass niemals in einem Korsett gefangen. Das Batteriefach für den Preamp ist dezent über die Rückseite des Korpus zugänglich.

Sterling Alnico-Humbucker · Quelle: Sterling

APOD

Astronomy Picture of the Day

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that

[supports HTML5 video](https://videojs.com/html5-video-support/)

## SPHEREx Seeing Through Dust

**Explanation:** What is blocking the center of the Milky Way? During its [13 billion years](https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/galaxies-age/en/), our Milky Way has collected a lot of dust. In contrast to the skin cells, dirt, pollen, and other debris that make up the dust behind your couch, [cosmic dust](https://science.nasa.gov/universe/stories/quick-reads/be-glad-you-dont-have-to-dust-in-space/) is hundreds of times smaller and made of tiny compounds of oxygen, carbon, and other elements [released into space](https://www.thesciencewriter.org/small-things-stories/cosmic-cycle-of-dust) when a [star dies](https://science.nasa.gov/universe/stories/quick-reads/the-lives-times-and-deaths-of-stars/). Today’s video shows [infrared](https://science.nasa.gov/ems/07_infraredwaves/) light from the Milky Way’s center gathered by NASA’s [SPHEREx](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/spherex/) satellite. Each [false color](https://science.nasa.gov/ems/04_energytoimage/) in the video corresponds to the infrared color associated with the [wavelength](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble/science/science-behind-the-discoveries/wavelengths/) shown in the top left. In the near-infrared, like 1.2 [microns](https://pa.msu.edu/machine-shop/mils-vs-microns.aspx), light gets absorbed and scatters off of dust particles. SPHEREx then sees the Galactic Center almost entirely blocked by [clouds of dust](https://science.nasa.gov/image-article/apod-2026-may-20-the-dark-wolf-nebula/). In the mid-infrared, though, light is able to pierce through the dust and reach SPHEREx. This is similar to, but not exactly, [why sunsets are red](https://gml.noaa.gov/grad/about/redsky/)!

**Tomorrow’s picture:** a sandy view of the Milky Way

Date:

November 25, 2026

Authors & editors:

Keighley Rockcliffe, Robert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti

[ASD](https://science.gsfc.nasa.gov/astrophysics/) at [NASA](https://www.nasa.gov/) / [GSFC](https://www.nasa.gov/centers/goddard/),

items.title: Ninajirachi’s studio gear, from Ableton stock plugins to iPhone voice memos

items.body:
[Ninajirachi](https://musictech.com/artists/ninajirachi/) is still riding her meteoric ascension into superstardom. The Australian-born producer just won another ARIA Award for Best Dance/Electronic Release for *WannaCry*, her collaboration with [Porter Robinson](https://musictech.com/artists/porter-robinson/) (who just so happens to be one of her personal heroes). She won three last year for her debut album, *I Love My Computer*, followed by a performance at [Coachella](https://musictech.com/brands/coachella/), which was brimming with her self-described “girl EDM” sound. She’s also slated for a massive closing set at [Primavera Sound](https://musictech.com/brands/primavera-sound/) 2027, playing back-to-back with [Skrillex](https://musictech.com/artists/skrillex/), and just released the remix album of her debut, titled *I Love My Computer, All My Friends Are Inside It.*

*MusicTech* has hosted Ninajirachi many times along this epic journey. She was [a cover star in 2024](https://musictech.com/features/interviews/ninajirachi-interview-girl-edm-disc-1/), and she was [on our My Forever Studio podcast in 2025](https://musictech.com/shows/podcasts/my-forever-studio/my-forever-studio-ninajirachis-endearing-soft-synth-selection/). In these chats, she went deep into her philosophy and process behind her bombastic, computerised beats that harken back to the global EDM movement.

Below are some of her favourite pieces of gear that she’s used along her upward journey.

## Ableton Live

Nina made the shift from [FL Studio](https://musictech.com/tag/image-line-fl-studio/) to [Ableton Live](https://musictech.com/tag/ableton-live/) in 2018, with the [DAW](https://musictech.com/tag/daws/) and its tools becoming a key driver of her definitive girl EDM sound.

Having started with only her laptop, she developed a natural workflow in Live, leaning on some of its stock plugins such as Wavetable, Operator, and Simpler. She’s specifically cited Wavetable as her go-to for making Reese basses.

“I feel like it’s everything I need and nothing I don’t for a simple sound design moment,” Nina told *MusicTech* in her cover feature. “I think because of the way I learned to use Ableton really methodically when I was 18 or so, it just stuck with me. I can navigate and edit so fast. The most streamlined process from brain to page is always what I’m looking for, and Ableton has done that for me.”

[deals ids=”411f0e62-a32f-4217-b258-3ceb2f6338cf”]

## Genelec 8330A Studio Monitors

Despite only needing a DAW and a laptop to design award-winning sounds, Nina invested in a pair of [Genelec](https://musictech.com/brands/genelec/) 8330A [monitors](https://musictech.com/tag/monitors/). She previously produced music using her [Apple](https://musictech.com/brands/apple/) wired EarPods, but as she began to progress in her career, she realised how much difference a reliable pair of speakers can make.

“I think they really have improved my work a lot. I can just hear everything really well on them,” Nina says, speaking of the Genelec 8330A’s. When it came to picking from the vast array of [studio](https://musictech.com/tag/studios/) monitors available, she cites a friend/professional [mixing](https://musictech.com/tag/mixing/) and [mastering](https://musictech.com/tag/mastering/) engineer in her *My Forever Studio* interview who was dedicated to the Genelec brand.

“He was all about Genelec and his room sounded so amazing. I started to get better at mixing my own music just by virtue of working in his room.”

## Bluebird SL Mic

An essential element of Nina’s girl EDM sound is her own [vocals](https://musictech.com/tag/vocals/) that she’s delivered on tracks such as *Sing Good*, *Cut the Rope*, and *Fuck My Computer*. She has several mics she uses for [recording](https://musictech.com/tag/recording/) vocals, but her favourite is the lesser-known [Blue](https://musictech.com/brands/blue-microphones/) Bluebird SL XLR Cardioid Condenser [Microphone](https://musictech.com/tag/microphones/).

The mic is surprisingly affordable, packs a vintage-inspired chassis, and is primed for vocals, acoustic instruments, and podcasts recordings. It also has a high-pass filter and -20dB pad to customise it to your recording source.

“I’ve got a few different little mics at home, but the one I probably like the most is the blue Bluebird mic. It’s nice and crisp, and I like how it makes me sound…My favourite colour is blue, so it’s nice to look at,” Nina told us on *My Forever Studio.*

## FabFilter Pro-L 2

[FabFilter](https://musictech.com/brands/fabfilter/)’s celebrated limiter plugin has helped turn many a laptop into a professional mastering house, and that includes Ninajirachi. When she started touring a lot, the tracks she made in transit were not up to snuff to play out at the next gig.

“I can’t just go to studios while I’m touring all the time to fix this stuff,” Nina says. She put out a tweet explaining the issue, and her friend and fellow producer Gaszia replied recommending [FabFilter Pro-L 2](https://musictech.com/products/fabfilter-pro-l-2-limiter-plugin/). “I know the [FabFilter] bundle is super popular. I’d seen heaps of people using it, but I mostly just use native software, so I hadn’t really thought about it up until that point. But I’ve been a fan of his music for more than 10 years. Everything he releases just sounds so good all the time. I always play his music in DJ sets. So, I took his advice and bought it, and I love it.”

[deals ids=”32cc6020-1402-427a-801b-6f821ef07770″]

## Sonic Charge’s Synplant 2

Nina gave this AI-powered plugin a place in her forever studio. It was between this and [Serum 2](https://musictech.com/reviews/software-instruments/xfer-records-serum-2-review/), but she chose [Synplant 2](https://musictech.com/reviews/plug-ins/sonic-charges-synplant-2-review/) because of its penchant for creating happy accidents.

Centred around a plant graphic, the plugin lets you morph and wrangle synth sounds using 12 Branches, and planting new Seeds to manipulate. The headline feature of Synplant 2 is the Genopatch, which lets you import an audio sample, and watch the synth try to generate optimal synth settings to match the sample.

“That thing is so cool. It’s got that section where you can drop in any bit of audio, and it’ll try to recreate it,” Nina says. “It’s kind of like a sample digging machine, but then it’s a patch. So you can also do all of the standard synth stuff with it as well…The part that’s cool is when it gets it wrong. So it’s trying to recreate a kick drum, and it sounds like a fart or something, but in an interesting way.”

## An Apple iPhone

Ninajirachi. Image: Billy Zammit for MusicTech

items.body:
In a Grade 2 classroom in Rautahat, in Nepal’s southern plains, teacher Renuka Dahal holds up a picture card of a mango. She gives the Nepali word, then asks her students what they call it at home. They respond in Tharu and Maithili, the languages many of them speak with their families.

“I ask my students to teach me words in their language,” [she told UNICEF in 2025](https://www.unicef.org/nepal/stories/speaking-their-language). “It makes them feel that I care about who they are.” And that small exchange marks a real change.

For Canadians interested in Indigenous language revitalization, and for teachers welcoming newcomer students, Nepal’s experience shows what it takes to move language rights off paper and into the classroom.

For generations, many children in Nepal started school in a language they didn’t understand. Yet [research shows that beginning school in a familiar language can strengthen learning and make it easier to acquire additional languages](https://www.unesco.org/en/languages-education/need-know?hub=67098), including Nepali and English.

Nepal has written that lesson into its [2015 Constitution, which guarantees communities the right to education in their mother tongue](https://shisiradhikari.com.np/library/567/1321).

## A country of 124 mother tongues

Nepal is one of the most [linguistically diverse countries in the world](https://languageonthemove.com/counting-the-uncountable-linguistic-diversity-in-nepal/), though the state has [not always acknowledged it](https://shs.hal.science/halshs-03083343/document). The 2021 census [recorded 124 mother tongues](https://doi.org/10.3126/jns.v16i1.71780).

Fifty years earlier, in 1971, when the [Panchayat regime](https://doi.org/10.1177/002088176400600202) was promoting Nepali above all other languages, [the census counted just 17 languages](https://irjmmc.edu.np/index.php/irjmmc/article/view/265). Today, Nepali is the first language of [just under 45 per cent of the population](https://nepalitimes.com/decoding-diversity).

I have worked in Nepal since 1991, first as a volunteer schoolteacher and later as a linguist and anthropologist. I have spent decades researching [the country’s linguistic diversity](https://soscbaha.org/book-release-a-grammar-of-the-thangmi-language/). The census numbers reflect a shift I have witnessed on the ground, in communities.

In 2021, for the first time, [the census asked people about their ancestral language](https://myrepublica.nagariknetwork.com/news/use-of-nepali-language-rises-sharply-over-two-decades-69-76.html) as well as their mother tongue. [Nearly three million more people name Nepali as their mother tongue than they name it as their ancestral language](https://censusresults.nsonepal.gov.np/files/result-folder/Language%20in%20Nepal.pdf), a sign that many families have shifted to Nepali.

For other languages, the gap goes the other way. [Some 300,000 more people name Nepal Bhasa, the language of the Newar community, as their ancestral language than name it as their mother tongue](https://censusresults.nsonepal.gov.np/files/result-folder/Language%20in%20Nepal.pdf).

Nepali is also spreading as a second language: [46 per cent of the population now speaks it that way, up from 33 per cent in 2011](https://censusresults.nsonepal.gov.np/files/result-folder/Language%20in%20Nepal.pdf). Whatever pressures Nepal’s other languages face, Nepali is certainly not a language at risk.

## Rights on paper

On paper, Nepal’s laws side with children. The government’s [School Education Sector Plan 2022-32](https://www.globalpartnership.org/content/school-education-sector-plan-2022-2032-nepal) commits to scaling up early-grade teaching in children’s mother tongues.

In practice, implementation has been sluggish and uneven. [As comparative education scholar Uma Pradhan has shown](https://doi.org/10.1093/9780190685065.003.0027), policy has long treated mother tongues as a bridge to Nepali, a stepping stone to be left behind, with the state offering little support.

[In a 2026 study from Tanahun](https://doi.org/10.1080/01434632.2026.2656490), one grandparent spoke about a granddaughter in Grade 2 who was being taught only in Nepali and English: “She [does not have the] opportunity to study in [her ancestral] language; so, there is a gap.”

Grade 1 students at Shree Sahara Bal Primary School in Pokhara, Nepal, in June 2013.
[(Photo by Jim Holmes for AusAID)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Grade1,_Shree_Sahara_Bal_Primary_School,_Pokhara,_Pokhara,_Nepal._(10699534855).jpg), [CC BY](http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)

## The evidence for local languages

[A 2024 study commissioned by UNICEF Nepal](https://www.unicef.org/nepal/reports/understanding-impact-languages-and-language-policies-childrens-learning-outcomes-nepal) examined language use in 30 schools across all seven provinces. Its conclusion was unequivocal. When children learn in their mother tongue or a familiar language, they take a more active part in lessons and do better in assessments and exams.

Many schools have rushed to switch to English-language teaching, often for financial reasons and with little teacher training. Yet [students taught in Nepali outscored their English-taught peers in Nepali, in science and even in English](https://www.unicef.org/nepal/reports/understanding-impact-languages-and-language-policies-childrens-learning-outcomes-nepal), according to the study’s analysis of school assessment results, which was limited in scale.

In Dailekh, in western Nepal, principal Sher Bahadur Rana [told UNICEF that teachers once corrected children who used their own “language or dialect.”](https://www.unicef.org/nepal/stories/speaking-their-language) After training in multilingual teaching, he said, “we learned that children learn faster and feel more confident when we teach them in the language they speak and understand best.”

## Obstacles to implementation

A recent review by education researchers Pariksha Onta and Amado Padilla, [covering 111 studies and policy documents](https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1931390), points to a “persistent disconnect between constitutional commitments, classroom practice and targeted funding.”

Where mother tongues are taught at all, they are usually a subject rather than the language children learn in. Textbooks in children’s mother tongues remain scarce, and most of those that do exist are translations of Nepali materials with little locally relevant content. Far too few teachers who speak local languages are recruited or trained.

…

items.body:
In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.

Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”

Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.

At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.

### Transparency, monetized

The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.

This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “[FOIA, Inc](https://scholarship.law.duke.edu/dlj/vol65/iss7/2/).”

Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for [79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies](https://scholarship.law.duke.edu/dlj/vol65/iss7/2/) like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says.

SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies.

The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors.

Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.”

While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites.

But the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment.

The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices.

In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job. Chautauqua County, New York, [hired a paralegal](https://www.observertoday.com/news/top-stories/2026/06/county-says-ai-creating-overload-of-foil-requests/) this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell.

In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she says. A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used. FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s [often half her day](https://michiganadvance.com/2026/02/21/process-of-foia-the-unseen-work-of-providing-government-transparency/), she told the *Michigan Advance* earlier this year.

### The AI detection problem

items.body:
### 🔄 Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO

[↗ Primärquelle: wccftech.com](https://wccftech.com/nvidia-reinstates-jensen-huang-ceo-board-of-director/)

- Nvidia has brought Jensen Huang back as president and CEO and a board member, effective immediately, weeks after he resigned over an admitted affair with a Singaporean data center executive tied to banned US AI chips in China.
- The board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang after talks with him and senior US government officials, saying it was confident his return posed no national security risk and that interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress had served well during the gap.
- A committee of independent directors will finish investigating a reported foreign intelligence effort targeting Huang, a separate national security committee will oversee trade compliance, and Nvidia is now hiring a new chief compliance officer.

### 🚗 Tesla says new FSD is 25x safer

[↗ Primärquelle: digitaltrends.com](https://www.digitaltrends.com/cars/tesla-fsd-v15-rollout/)

- Tesla has started releasing Full Self-Driving v15, which updates its whole driving network and, the company says on X, handles safety-critical situations 25 times better than before.
- Tesla says the 25x figure refers to the critical intervention rate after an upgraded vision encoder was trained on millions of internet videos, and the update adds a live Reality View showing what FSD plans to do.
- The release improves detection of signs, potholes, animals, and speed cameras, slowing for cameras unless you cancel twice at one spot, and adds Bike Rack Mode, but it stays a supervised system.

### 🛑 OpenAI urges rival labs to cap AI training

[↗ Primärquelle: unite.ai](https://www.unite.ai/openai-proposes-shared-ai-development-limits-tied-to-safety-milestones/)

- OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki asked rival AI labs to agree on shared limits for frontier model training, warning that safety and monitoring research could fall behind if pretraining speeds up as soon as 2027.
- Pachocki published OpenAI's internal log-perplexity scores, a measure of how well a model predicts the next word, showing GPT-3.5 at about 0.99 and GPT-4 at 0.91, with new skills emerging below 0.8.
- He proposed that developers not cross perplexity-based thresholds until oversight research hits a clear milestone, such as a successor to chain-of-thought monitors, and jointly set evaluation norms, red-teaming, and transparency standards.

### 🧠 Meta AI chief says superintelligence is arriving

[↗ Primärquelle: nerds.xyz](https://nerds.xyz/2026/11/meta-ai-chief-superintelligence-warning/)

- Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, warned in a post on X that superintelligence is coming and said humanity should refuse any "handover" of control to AI, with the next year being a critical period.
- Wang pointed to a formal proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, a 167-year-old math problem about prime numbers, which Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge worked out with Claude and two Lean proof-checking groups confirmed as correct.
- His biggest worry is AI automating AI research itself, with labs using one model to design a better successor until humans signing off can no longer truly check the work, something he calls "recursive self-improvement."

### ⚠️ US intelligence chief warns of more tech outages

[↗ Primärquelle: cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/22/jay-clayton-tech-outages-faa-microsoft-thanksgiving.html)

- US intelligence chief Jay Clayton told Americans to expect "bumps in the road" and more tech outages as companies and the government upgrade their systems to handle the AI age, speaking on CNN's "State of the Union."
- The warning follows a nationwide ground stop a week ago that the FAA blamed on router upgrades flooding systems with data, plus a Microsoft Outlook outage the company tied to an earlier network capacity upgrade.
- Officials have brushed off claims the outages, which also slowed bank transactions, stemmed from a coordinated or AI cyberattack, with Bessent comparing the glitchy security patches banks are applying to a vaccine's temporary side effects.

### 🛡️ CrowdStrike buys Zscaler for $43.9B

[↗ Primärquelle: implicator.ai](https://www.implicator.ai/crowdstrike-agrees-acquire-zscaler-which-develops-network/)

- CrowdStrike has agreed to buy network security firm Zscaler in an all-stock deal valuing it at roughly $43.9 billion, pushing the endpoint security maker into cloud network protection, which both companies call cybersecurity's biggest market.
- Zscaler shareholders get 1.135 CrowdStrike shares each, worth about $260 per share, a 34% premium, and will own around 15.9% of the combined company, whose founder Jay Chaudhry keeps running the Zscaler business and joins CrowdStrike's board.
- CrowdStrike expects about $1 billion in extra yearly revenue and $500 million in cost savings, with roughly 8,000 Zscaler customers it can sell to, and plans to close the deal in the second half of its fiscal 2028.

items.body:
Gasoline prices have been trending downward, dropping about 75 cents per gallon [since](https://x.com/GasBuddyGuy/status/2122693671745392848) Sept. 24, though prices are still about 69 cents higher than this time a year ago.

In a social media post on Nov. 17, President Donald Trump wrongly [suggested](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117634065135557984) there was a political motivation behind the falling prices to hurt Republicans in the midterms. “Biggest drop in gasoline in 18 years,” Trump wrote. “Notice that they waited until after the ‘Election?’”

We reached out to the White House to find out whom the president meant by “they,” but we did not get a response.

For the drop in prices, the president’s post [cited](https://tradersunion.com/news/market-voices/show/4212469-us-gasoline-prices-drop/) a Bloomberg columnist who [posted](https://x.com/JavierBlas/status/2120848679309553987) on Nov. 12 that the previous two days were the largest one-day drops in retail gasoline prices in 18 years.

[Patrick De Haan](https://patrickdehaan.com/), the head of petroleum analysis for the fuel-price tracking service GasBuddy, said that while those days did not represent the largest one-day drops in 18 years according to GasBuddy data, the decline was nonetheless “substantial.”

However, the average retail price of gasoline had been steadily falling for more than a month before the Nov. 3 midterms. Indeed, the day before the election, Trump [posted](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117548803071800973) to social media, “Oil Prices are DROPPING LIKE A ROCK.” Oil prices are connected to gasoline prices because crude oil is the main component in gasoline.

In a press conference on Nov. 20, [Trump said](https://www.c-span.org/clip/white-house-event/user-clip-trump-on-crude-oil-prices/5211284), “Crude oil prices have plummeted right since the end of the election. I wonder how that happened. Crude oil is down 20% since the start of November, and now it’s down to close to $80 a barrel. … It was a very big drop. Too bad we didn’t have that in front of the election, but that’s the way it goes.” In fact, as Trump’s post on Nov. 2 mentioned, the price of crude oil dropped from $110 a barrel on Oct. 19 to $100 the day before the election, according to the [Energy Information Administration](https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/prices/table.php?show_by=12_series&period=D&table_key=PET_PRI_SPT_S1_D). It was at around $87 a barrel on Nov. 19.

“The crude oil market began to ‘clean up’ early in the third quarter, and a lack of new US or Israeli initiatives in the Middle East has helped soften prices,” said Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil. “Even before that happened, crude prices normalized thanks to more crude from non-Middle Eastern sources, some modest global demand destruction, and the puzzling lack of Chinese buying that has been in the background for eight months.”

Lower prices are also a seasonal phenomenon, he said.

“The last 45-60 days of any year tend to bring inventory buildups for gasoline and diesel and we are now in the midst of that process,” Kloza said. “People drive less, refineries run hard, and it is typical for gas prices to bottom between Thanksgiving and the Epiphany” in early January.

What’s new this year, he said, is “the wildcard of extraordinary profits for refiners making diesel and jet fuel.” Profits for those fuels are so large, he said, it is allowing refineries to make gasoline at a loss.

“So we are in a rendezvous with much cheaper prices,” Kloza said. “It has nothing to do with executive action but everything to do with history as well as the economics created by stunning profits for diesel and jet fuel. Simply put, gasoline in much of the country is a ‘loss leader’ for the entire refined barrel.”

He expects prices to drop further, he said, because the markup for gasoline is currently much higher than normal.

De Haan from GasBuddy agreed there is no “nefarious” political manipulation of prices.

“There’s no they. It’s just the market,” De Haan said.

“There’s no conspiracy,” he said.” It’s simply just that instead of solving the problem earlier, the president elected to not really address it permanently, and there’s a lot of back and forth on this. I mean, Trump before the election had suggested that he was not looking to escalate the situation with Iran.” And then after the election, he said that “he didn’t see a need for a deal with Iran. So he’s kind of virtue signaling both ways, and the market is just caught in this confusion of what’s going to happen.”

Gasoline prices jumped between Labor Day, which was Sept. 7, and mid-September, De Haan said, largely due to refining issues in the U.S. interior. “Power outages at a Chicagoland refinery in early September started that huge surge, which then pulled in states in the Midwest in the Corn Belt” that also saw surges. “And then as those refining issues started to get sorted out, prices plateaued on Sept. 24th, and then they started to decline as those refining issues started to work their way out.”

De Haan said the falling prices since late September are a combination of seasonal factors and the resolution of the refining issues. He also credits the U.S. military’s efforts in helping to shepherd oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

“In addition, we also saw oil prices drop pretty precipitously in October as more oil was flowing through the Strait, and because in part the president hinted that he’s not looking for escalations between the U.S. and Iran,” De Haan said. “I mean that’s definitely part of it.”

As for seasonal factors, De Haan said demand declines every fall.

“Going back to the election in 2012, every election has seen gas prices drop in the 30-day run-up to it because it has nothing to do with the election, it has nothing to do with politics,” De Haan said. “It has everything to do with the fact that Americans drive less progressively as temperatures get cooler. We have made the switch back to winter gasoline. That happens in mid-September.”

“Oil and gas prices are a function of a couple of dozen different levers,” De Haan said. “The president’s got a fairly small lever when it comes to pushing prices down, but arguably this time around, because his policy created a lever that pulled prices up [with the war in Iran], he would be able to pull that lever back down if he wanted to. But he didn’t really do that.”

De Haan also expects prices to continue to come down in the short term.

A customer uses a credit card to pay at the pump at a gas station in Los Angeles on Oct. 30. Photo by David Swanson / AFP via Getty Images.

items.title: Warum reicht Laserlicht allein für die Weltraumkommunikation nicht aus?
items.subtitle: Schnelle Daten aus dem All: Laser können in wenigen Minuten riesige Datenmengen vom Erdorbit zur Erde übertragen.
items.feedText: Doch einer neuen Analyse zufolge sind nicht mehr die erreichbaren Datenraten das Hauptproblem, sondern die Zuverlässigkeit der optischen Verbindungen und die Kosten für ein wetterunabhängigeres Netz von Bodenstationen. Pasadena (U.S.A.). Ob hochauflösende Bilder der Erdoberfläche oder Messdaten von Raumsonden: Für die Übertragung großer Datenmengen wird zunehmend mit Laserlicht experimentiert. Solche optischen Verbindungen können erheblich mehr Informationen pro Sekunde transportieren als herkömmliche Funkverbin…
items.body:
**Schnelle Daten aus dem All: Laser können in wenigen Minuten riesige Datenmengen vom Erdorbit zur Erde übertragen. Doch einer neuen Analyse zufolge sind nicht mehr die erreichbaren Datenraten das Hauptproblem, sondern die Zuverlässigkeit der optischen Verbindungen und die Kosten für ein wetterunabhängigeres Netz von Bodenstationen.**

**Pasadena (U.S.A.).** Ob hochauflösende Bilder der Erdoberfläche oder Messdaten von Raumsonden: Für die Übertragung großer Datenmengen wird zunehmend mit Laserlicht experimentiert. Solche optischen Verbindungen können erheblich mehr Informationen pro Sekunde transportieren als herkömmliche Funkverbindungen.

Was inzwischen möglich ist, demonstrierte das Weltraumexperiment TeraByte InfraRed Delivery (TBIRD) im Jahr 2023. Innerhalb von nur fünf Minuten gelangten bei einem Satellitenüberflug 4,8 Terabyte an Daten fehlerfrei zur Erde. Die Übertragungsrate erreichte dabei bis zu 200 Gigabit pro Sekunde.

### Der Flaschenhals liegt am Boden

Der Physiker Dr. Slava G. Turyshev vom Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) hat nun öffentliche Missionsdaten ausgewertet und mithilfe von Modellen analysiert, unter welchen Bedingungen solche Übertragungen zuverlässig und wirtschaftlich wären. Die Arbeit liegt bisher als noch nicht fachbegutachteter Preprint vor.

Eine besondere Herausforderung ist die Erdatmosphäre. Denn ähnlich wie beim Funkeln der Sterne führen Luftturbulenzen dazu, dass sich die Lichtsignale eines Satelliten auf ihrem Weg zur Bodenstation verzerren. Abhilfe schaffen unter anderem verformbare Spiegel, die solche Störungen durch schnelle Anpassungen ihrer Oberfläche ausgleichen.

Doch gegen dichte Wolken hilft auch diese adaptive Optik nicht. Wird der Laserstrahl durch eine Wolkendecke blockiert, kann das optische Signal die Bodenstation nicht mehr in ausreichender Stärke erreichen.

### Ausweichstationen statt stärkerer Laser

Eine Lösung sind weit voneinander entfernte Empfangsstationen. Wie viel das bringen kann, verdeutlicht eine 2025 veröffentlichte Untersuchung eines geplanten Netzes in Australien und Neuseeland: Mit drei Stationen lag die modellierte Ausfallwahrscheinlichkeit bei 6,4 Prozent, mit acht Stationen hingegen bei nur 0,02 Prozent.

Allerdings muss die Zahl der Stationen nicht automatisch ihrer Wirkung entsprechen. Denn große Wolkenfelder oder zeitlich ähnliche Überflugfenster können die Ausweichmöglichkeiten mehrerer Standorte gleichzeitig einschränken.

### Mehr Verlässlichkeit hat ihren Preis

Eine solche Absicherung kostet Geld. Für seine Beispielrechnung setzt Turyshev pro Bodenstation jährliche Fixkosten von zwei Millionen US-Dollar, zehn Gigabit pro Sekunde, eine halbe Stunde geplanter täglicher Kontaktzeit und 70 Prozent Gesamteffizienz einschließlich wetterbedingter Verluste an.

Demnach entfallen bei einer einzigen Station rund 3.500 US-Dollar an Fixkosten auf jedes übertragene Terabyte. Finanziert eine Mission allein acht unabhängig verfügbare Stationen für dieselbe zu übertragende Datenmenge, steigen diese modellierten Kosten auf rund 18.000 US-Dollar pro Terabyte. Das sind keine realen Marktpreise.

Wirtschaftlicher könnte es werden, wenn sich mehrere Missionen die Infrastruktur teilen. Dafür müssen optische Kommunikationssysteme unterschiedlicher Anbieter kompatibel sein und die gemeinsam genutzten Stationen ausreichend ausgelastet werden.

### Funk bleibt als Rückversicherung wichtig

Bis 2030 erscheint Turyshev daher ein hybrides System aus Laser- und Funkverbindungen am sinnvollsten. Laser könnten vor allem große, zwischenspeicherbare Datenmengen übertragen, während Funkverbindungen beispielsweise die Übermittlung zeitkritischer Steuerbefehle auch bei Wolken unterstützen sollen.

**Quellen:**

- Forschungs-Preprint auf [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23711), doi: 10.48550/arXiv.2606.23711

items.body:
Auch in diesem Schuljahr veranstaltet die Föderation der Deutsch-Französischen Häuser den deutsch-französischen Geschichtswettbewerb EUSTORY-France. Der diesjährige Wettbewerb befasst sich mit dem Thema: « Klima- und Umweltschutz schreibt Geschichte. Engagement und Protest in Deutschland und Frankreich ». Er lädt Schüler*innen der 8. Klasse bis zum Abitur in Deutschland und Frankreich (4e bis zur Terminale) ein, sich mit dem vorgegebenen Thema auseinanderzusetzen und einen Beitrag zu verfassen – in Einzel- oder Gruppenarbeit oder idealerweise im deutsch-französischen Tandem.

**Klima- und Umweltschutz schreibt Geschichte. Engagement und Protest in Deutschland und Frankreich**

Menschen haben seit jeher ihre Umwelt beeinflusst. Aber beginnend mit der Industrialisierung im 18. Jh. ist das Ausmaß dieses Eingriffs ein anderes geworden: Maschinen, Fabriken und große Städte verändern nicht nur das Leben der Menschen – sondern auch die Natur. Die Folgen werden immer mehr spürbar. Vereinzelt werden Menschen laut, die fordern, dass sich etwas ändern muss. Sie machen auf Missstände aufmerksam, schließen sich mit Anderen zusammen, protestieren oder rütteln mit spektakulären Aktionen wach und schaffen es, Veränderungen herbeizuführen.

**Der Wettbewerb möchte es genauer wissen:**

Von ganz frühen Naturschutzinitiativen über erste Anti-Atomkraft-Proteste der 1970er Jahre und globale Klimadebatten seit den 1980er Jahren bis heute: Was hat Menschen in Deutschland und Frankreich zum Handeln gebracht? Was waren ihre Ängste und Hoffnungen? Welche Erzählungen und Konflikte prägten die Debatten innerhalb und außerhalb der Bewegungen? Und wer bestimmte mit – Menschen aus der Wissenschaft, der Politik oder der Zivilgesellschaft?

Welche Formen wählten sie für ihr Engagement? Was waren ihre Erfolge und Niederlagen? Wie ist es ihnen gelungen, in unseren Gesellschaften etwas zu verändern? Und wie kann aus der Idee Einzelner eine politische Entscheidung werden?

Der Wettbewerb lädt dazu ein, die Suche vor der Haustür zu beginnen, lokale Geschichte zu erforschen und in einen breiter gefassten, deutsch-französischen und europäischen Kontext zu setzen. Welche Rolle spielte internationale Vernetzung? Welche Gemeinsamkeiten und/oder Unterschiede gab es zwischen den deutschen und französischen Bewegungen?

Und genauso wichtig: Welche Menschen und Ereignisse aus der Vergangenheit machen heute Mut? Was lässt uns lernen für unsere Zukunft – und die der kommenden Generationen? Denn die Geschichte des Klima- und Umweltschutzes erzählt von Verantwortung, Engagement und Protest – und sie ist noch nicht zu Ende geschrieben.

Die besten Beiträge werden mit Preisen ausgezeichnet, die im Juli 2027 im Rahmen einer offiziellen Preisverleihung überreicht werden.

[Weitere Infos & Anmeldung](https://eustory.fr)

*Eine Meldung der EUSTORY-France.*

items.body:
The Wall Street Journal, “The Frantic White House Push to Get Jensen Huang Back” (gift link):

> What followed were a frantic 48 hours in which the president, the
> vice president and other top administration officials relayed
> Blanche’s assurances to board members as they rushed to rescue a
> leader Trump hadn’t even heard of when he began his second term.
> “The response from the market has been very positive,” Trump said
> in an interview with The Wall Street Journal Monday evening. “That
> really shows the decision was right.” Nvidia stock notched the
> largest one-day market cap gain on record for a U.S. company.

If the entire stock market and U.S. economy is held together by investor faith in Jensen Huang, it’s a bubble and it will burst.

> On Sunday afternoon, the board met for a marathon session
> and spent hours talking to Huang, people familiar with the
> matter said.
> Huang disclosed to the board additional affairs beyond the two
> that had been widely reported, but he was contrite about his
> behavior, people with knowledge of the discussion said.
> After conversations with Huang about the importance of candor and
> honesty, the board ultimately decided that having him return was
> the best path, the people said.

Yours truly, back on November 12, after Reuters found Huang’s third girlfriend (an executive assistant at Nvidia):

> What’s the over-under at? If it’s 4.5, I’ll take the over.

“Additional affairs beyond the two that had been widely reported” takes us to at least 4, but sounds like more than that.

items.subtitle: „Ted Lasso“ gehört seit 2020 zu den wichtigsten Aushängeschildern von Apple TV.

items.body:
**„Ted Lasso“ gehört seit 2020 zu den wichtigsten Aushängeschildern von Apple TV. Nach drei Staffeln schien die Geschichte um den gutmütigen Fußball-Coach eigentlich auserzählt. Im Sommer folgte dennoch das Comeback mit einer vierten Staffel. Wie es danach weitergeht, war allerdings lange offen. Nun bekennt der Streamingdienst Farbe.**

## Bestätigung nach wochenlangem Warten

Seit dem Finale der vierten Staffel am 07. Oktober hatte sich Apple nicht zur Zukunft der Serie geäußert. Am Montag kam dann die [offizielle Bestätigung:](https://www.apple.com/tv-pr/news/2026/11/apples-global-hit-juggernaut-ted-lasso-lands-season-five-renewal/) Ted Lasso kehrt für eine fünfte Staffel zurück. Apple feiert die Serie dabei als globales Phänomen und verweist auf Kritiker, die sie zu den beliebtesten Comedys des Jahrzehnts zählen. Konkrete Details bleiben aber aus. Einen Starttermin, die Zahl der Folgen oder Angaben zur Besetzung gibt es noch nicht. Auch Zuschauerzahlen nennt Apple nicht und spricht lediglich von einem Rekord-Debüt der vierten Staffel.

## Neuanfang mit den Lady Greyhounds

Die vierte Staffel lief vom 5. August bis zum 7. Oktober 2026 mit zehn Folgen. Zwischen ihr und dem Ende der dritten Staffel im Mai 2023 lagen damit gut drei Jahre. Inhaltlich schlug die Serie ein neues Kapitel auf. Ted kehrt nach Richmond zurück und übernimmt die Lady Greyhounds, ein Frauenteam aus der zweiten Liga.Vor der Kamera gab es dabei viele bekannte Gesichter. Neben Jason Sudeikis waren wieder Hannah Waddingham, Juno Temple, Brett Goldstein, Brendan Hunt und Jeremy Swift dabei. Dazu kamen Jude Mack, Faye Marsay, Rex Hayes, Aisling Sharkey, Abbie Hern und Grant Feely. Außerdem stieß Tanya Reynolds als Co-Trainerin Alice Chilton neu zum Ensemble und erntete viel Lob für ihre Rolle. Hinter den Kulissen bleibt vorerst alles beim Alten. Sudeikis steht weiterhin als Hauptdarsteller und ausführender Produzent an der Spitze. Die Resonanz auf die vierte Staffel fiel dennoch gemischt aus: Viele lobten den frischen Ansatz mit dem Frauenteam, andere vermissten die frühere Balance aus Humor und ernsten Momenten.

## Start frühestens Ende 2027

Ganz überraschend kommt die Verlängerung nicht. Schon im Sommer hatte Sudeikis gegenüber The Hollywood Reporter von einem Erzählbogen über drei Staffeln gesprochen. Im Oktober klang er in einem Podcast dagegen vorsichtiger. Weitermachen wolle er zwar, sicher sei er sich aber noch nicht. [Apfelpage berichtete](https://www.apfelpage.de/news/jason-sudeikis-weckt-hoffnungen-fuer-weitere-staffeln-von-ted-lasso/). Wann die neuen Folgen erscheinen, ist noch offen. Laut einem Bericht vom Sommer sollen die Dreharbeiten im Januar 2027 in London beginnen. Damit wäre ein Start frühestens Ende 2027 möglich. Als wahrscheinlicher gilt jedoch 2028. Die drei Jahre Wartezeit zwischen Staffel 3 und 4 dürften sich somit nicht wiederholen.

items.title: Agentic system personalizes physical controls to help users “DJ their art”
items.subtitle: In 2017, Apple removed the home button from its iPhones.
items.feedText: Users lost a convenient, tangible control — part of a larger shift to digital buttons, knobs, and sliders we also see in cars (like with radio presets and air conditioning) and kitchens (see smart fridges). items.body:
In 2017, Apple [removed the home button](https://apnews.com/article/ad9e1a52b5dc4d48bc55256a1124315b) from its iPhones. Users lost a convenient, tangible control — part of a larger shift to digital buttons, knobs, and sliders we also see in cars (like with radio presets and air conditioning) and kitchens (see smart fridges).

We can’t leave physical controls behind entirely, though. They tend to be more convenient and efficient — think of how you can use a physical gaming controller without looking at it — and, at times, more precise, like when you use a dial to get the volume just right. But tangible controls are typically preprogrammed to do a specific thing, minimizing their usefulness.

A new system called “[TangiMap](https://yunyi-zhu.github.io/tangimap/),” co-developed by an MIT graduate student and researcher at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), helps bring tangible control back to your software. The system personalizes the physical controls on everyday devices by mapping digital widgets onto tangible inputs, turning things like editing photos, animation, performing music, and creating 3D models into more dynamic and tactile experiences. Just as a DJ’s pads switch between triggering cues, loops, and samples, TangiMap gives a device’s controls entirely new roles.

But how, exactly? TangiMap relies on an AI agent, or semi-autonomous programs that “think” and complete well-defined tasks, to find and act on context about the software you’re using, your tendencies, and the device used to control that program. To gather the required context, the agent can draw on sources such as the program’s API (the rules that let programs talk to each other), an MCP server (a standard that connects AI agents to apps), or a screenshot interpreted by a vision-language model. Then, the agent uses a large language model to put all the info it's gathered into a file before mapping specific digital functions to physical controls.

“TangiMap builds on our broader vision of reprogramming common objects to be more dynamic,” says Yunyi Zhu ’20, MEng ’21, a doctoral student in the MIT Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and a CSAIL researcher whose advisor is MIT Associate Professor Stefanie Mueller. “Here, AI agents help us adapt physical controls to whatever we’re working on. We want to bring back physical controls so we can interact with our devices eyes-free, the way you adjust a car’s volume without looking away from the road. Physical controls also let you adjust several settings at once, like tweaking brightness and contrast together when editing an image, which is hard to do on a screen.”

The system helped the researchers turn a standard mixer into a photo-editing controller. That way, they could adjust color in Adobe Lightroom, with a complementary visualization of those controls displayed on their screen. The team did the same with sound-mixing software, so that performers can adjust their music in real-time with their own inputs to knobs and faders.

The researchers also reprogrammed a simpler mixer to work with the 3D modeling program Blender. Their interface included an area where users can type in a prompt, and once the model was generated, users could adjust features like shininess on a mixer using physical controls. Within Adobe’s Character Animator software, TangiMap connected specific expressions and movements to buttons on a control pad so users could animate (or “puppeteer”) a cartoon character live.

Zhu and co-author Chang Xiao, an assistant professor at Boston University, [presented their tool at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3830398.3830602) earlier this month.

Zhu and Xiao created a custom user interface (UI) for each application. While that adds another layer of personalization to the creative process, the team is hoping to create a more streamlined system that helps the designer to generate the UI for their device by taking a picture.

The researchers are also considering the physical aspects of user interactions. They want to use more ergonomic devices and also ensure that TangiMap accounts for where users position their hands when doing different tasks. For example, users typically hold a mixer differently when they’re using it to make music than, say, when playing a video game. You may want controls mapped closer or further apart, depending on what you’re doing.

Zhu is hoping to do a user study to get more feedback about TangiMap, and whether this kind of “smart DJing” could indeed improve those experiences. But the dynamic reprogramming she ultimately envisions is even more ambitious.

“The same way our phones and computers generalize to a range of tasks, we want other objects to be more intelligent,” she says. “I would like to build physical items that use an AI agent as a brain to decide what to reprogram into. They could understand what to transform into, given a specific situation.”

A chemical jar, for instance, could tell you if it’s sealed correctly when asked, and when you want to see what it’s typically used for, the container would instead display that information. While that kind of versatility and interactivity is a ways off, more powerful agents and more intricate fabrication pipelines could bring everyday objects to life.

Their work was supported, in part, by Google’s Gemini Academic Program Award.

items.body:
# Facharzttermin gegen Aufpreis: Was Deutschland von Griechenland lernen kann

KBV-Chef Gassen fordert Extra-Bezahlung für schnellere Termine. In Griechenland wäre das strafbar – und das System dort ist trotz weniger Geld oft effizienter.

Schnellere Facharzttermine für gesetzlich Versicherte soll es, geht es nach KBV-Chef Dr. Andreas Gassen gegen Extra-Bezahlung geben. Der Ärztefunktionär meint, dass die Mediziner so auf die Honorarkürzungen der Gesundheitsreform reagieren müssen. Die Meldung wurde in Griechenland mit besonders großem Interesse gelesen.

Ein Vergleich Deutschlands mit Griechenland und den übrigen EU-Staaten zeigt zudem, dass das Problem der deutschen Gesundheitspolitik nicht unbedingt mit noch mehr Geld und weiteren Leistungskürzungen gelöst werden kann. Eher erscheint es, als wäre "Effektivität" das gesuchte Zauberwort.

### 2010 hätte so eine Nachricht blankes Entsetzten ausgelöst

Bevor im Mai 2010 Griechenland mit dem Gang zum Internationalen Währungsfonds (IWF) faktisch den Staatsbankrott erklären musste, wurde das staatswirtschaftlich taumelnde Land von der deutschen Presse besonders gründlich durchleuchtet. Man entdeckte das " Fakelaki ", das Fachwort für einen kleinen, mit Geldscheinen gefüllten Umschlag.

Damit kam man im Griechenland vor der Krise unter anderen schneller an einen Termin im Krankenhaus, auf dem Bauamt oder man konnte bei entsprechender Bargeldfüllung leichter eine Führerscheinprüfung bestehen. Dass so ein Usus für jede Volkswirtschaft Gift ist, darüber waren sich alle – auch die Griechen – einig.

Umso mehr wundern sie sich nun, dass es in Deutschland Facharzttermine nur gegen " Grigorosimo " geben soll. Über den griechischen Sprachdienst der Deutschen Welle kam diese Nachricht an die griechischen Medien, welche begeistert das Wording der Überschrift übernahmen.

items.body:
Das Familienministerium streicht die Förderung für die Zentrale Anlaufstelle bei organisierter Frauenfeindlichkeit und Antifeminismus. Im Interview spricht Ans Hartmann vom Verein Lola für Demokratie über antifeministische Angriffe, die Unterstützung von Betroffenen und die Folgen des drohenden Endes.

Ein Umbau des Programms "Demokratie leben" sei nötig, findet Bundesfamilienministerin Karin Prien. – Alle Rechte vorbehalten: IMAGO / dts Nachrichtenagentur

Rechtsaußen-Kampagnen und Angriffe auf Menschen und Strukturen, die sich für eine offene und demokratische Gesellschaft einsetzen, nehmen zu. Eines der liebsten Steckenpferde der Neuen Rechten sind dabei alle Themen rund um Geschlechtergerechtigkeit, Gleichstellung und Feminismus. Ausgerechnet jetzt baut das Bundesfamilienministerium sein wichtigstes Programm „Demokratie leben“ um und streicht vielen etablierten Projekten die Förderung,

Die Kürzungen treffen [zahlreiche Organisationen](https://taz.de/Umbau-des-Programms-Demokratie-Leben/!6164747/), von HateAid bis zum [Nahost-Dialogprojekt](https://www.deutschlandfunk.de/foerder-aus-empoert-nahost-dialogprojekt-initiative-gegen-islamfeindlichkeit-und-konservative-denkfa-100.html) gegen Antisemitismus. Dabei hatte Bundesfamilienministerin Karin Prien eigentlich angekündigt, der Fokus verschiebe sich auf Projekte gegen Islamismus, Antisemitismus und „Hass im Internet“.

Vor wenigen Tagen hat auch der Verein Lola für Demokratie erfahren, dass es [nicht mehr weitergeht](https://www.lola-fuer-demokratie.de/2026/11/18/absage-von-demokratie-leben-foerderung-antifeminismus-nimmt-zu-staerkung-beratung-und-unterstuetzung-von-betroffenen-werden-gestrichen/). Der Verein bietet seit 2025 eine Anlaufstelle, die in Deutschland so einzigartig ist: die Zentrale Anlaufstelle bei organisierter Frauenfeindlichkeit und Antifeminismus (ZAFFA). Menschen, die ins Visier von antifeministischen Kampagnen geraten, können sich dorthin wenden und Hilfe bekommen. Parallel sammelt und dokumentiert der Verein solche Kampagnen.

Im November hat Lola für Demokratie erfahren, dass es ab Januar kein Geld mehr gibt. „Das betrifft unsere Existenz“, sagt Ans Hartmann, eine von drei Mitarbeitenden bei ZAFFA.

## „Wir wissen, wie solche Angriffe laufen“

**netzpolitik.org:** Was macht eure Anlaufstelle, und wer wendet sich an euch?

**Ans Hartmann:** Wir sind ein kleiner Verein aus Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Seit 2025 beraten wir Menschen und Organisationen, die von organisierter Frauenfeindlichkeit und Antifeminismus betroffen sind. Dazu gehören politisch aktive Frauen, Gleichstellungsbeauftragte, Frauenverbände, queere Organisationen oder Menschen aus der politischen Bildungsarbeit. Wir unterstützen bei Angriffen, entwickeln Sicherheits- und Schutzkonzepte und dokumentieren antifeministisch motivierte Vorfälle über die Meldestelle Antifeminismus. Wir arbeiten bundesweit auch mit Fachverbänden und Beratungsstellen zusammen. Unser Ansatz ist, auch Multiplikator*innen zu stärken, damit das Wissen in ihre Strukturen weitergetragen wird.

**netzpolitik.org:** Wie sieht diese Unterstützung konkret aus?

**Ans Hartmann:** Eine politische Bildnerin bietet etwa in einer Kommune Veranstaltungen zu sexualisierter Gewalt oder vielfältigen Lebensweisen an Schulen an. Ihr Name steht auf den Einladungen, daraufhin wird online gegen sie mobilisiert: Sie wird bedroht, ihre privaten Daten werden veröffentlicht. Und diese Mobilisierung passiert eben anhand bestimmter antifeministischer Narrative und Feindbilder.

Manchmal ist es auch eine Wissenschaftlerin oder eine Gleichstellungsbeauftragte, die wegen ihrer Arbeit zum Ziel einer Kampagne wird und dann bei uns landet. Besonders häufig sehen wir Mobilisierung gegen Menschen, die sich [intersektional positionieren](https://netzpolitik.org/2026/fachleute-fordern-das-fehlt-beim-schutz-vor-digitaler-gewalt/), etwa für rassismusbetroffene oder behinderte Frauen.

**netzpolitik.org:** Was tut ihr in so einer Situation?

Manchmal geht es erst mal um einen kollegialen Austausch. Wir wissen, wie solche Angriffe laufen und wie es sich anfühlt, in so einer Situation zu sein. Manchmal wird das mehr gebraucht als eine konkrete Beratung, wie man etwa juristisch gegen die Angriffe vorgehen kann, denn diese Expertise haben die Menschen selbst.

Wir können die antifeministischen Feindbilder und die Dynamiken hinter solchen Angriffen einordnen. Manchmal reicht es, gemeinsam die Lage einzuschätzen und Betroffene zu entlasten. Manchmal geht es [auch um digitale Sicherheit](https://netzpolitik.org/digitale-selbstverteidigung/), die Dokumentation von Angriffen oder ein zeitweises Monitoring rechtsextremer Telegram-Kanäle, damit Betroffene nicht selbst ständig nach neuen Drohungen suchen müssen. In längeren Prozessen entwickeln wir mit Organisationen auch Schutzkonzepte und klären, wer im Ernstfall informiert sein muss und verantwortlich ist. Dafür fehlen vielen Einrichtungen Zeit und Ressourcen.

## „Wir sehen einen Andrew-Tate-Effekt“

**netzpolitik.org:** Wie viele Anfragen bekommt ihr, wie groß ist der Bedarf?

**Ans Hartmann:** Wir haben allein im ersten Projektjahr mehr als 60 Fachakteur*innen beraten und mit Fortbildungen ungefähr 1.000 Menschen erreicht, überwiegend Multiplikator*innen. Etwa jede zweite bis dritte Anfrage können wir derzeit nicht bedienen. Wir arbeiten auch viel mit Opferberatungsstellen, mit den Beratungsstellen für Betroffene von rechter, rassistischer, antisemitischer Gewalt zusammen.

Besonders Anfragen aus Schulen und der außerschulischen Bildung haben zugenommen. Wir sehen da [einen Andrew Tate-Effekt](https://netzpolitik.org/2024/breakpoint-variante-alpha-eine-epidemie-toxischer-maennlichkeit/). Lehrkräfte und Bildungseinrichtungen erleben antifeministische Mobilisierung und Gewalt, sie finden dafür aber nur wenige spezialisierte Anlaufstellen. Der wachsende Bedarf liegt sicher auch an einer größeren Aufmerksamkeit für das Thema Antifeminismus – aber ebenso daran, dass die Menschen und ihre Arbeitsfelder tatsächlich angegriffen werden und ihre Arbeit zunehmend rechtfertigen müssen.

**netzpolitik.org:** Antifeminismus ist ein wichtiger Teil der Ideologie der Neuen Rechten. Warum ist Antifeminismus als politische Strategie so attraktiv?

### The Spectator:

[The dangerous fantasy of GTA VI](https://spectator.com/article/the-dangerous-fantasy-of-gta-vi/?edition=us)

Yesterday I shared some thoughts about the newly released *Grand Theft Auto VI*. Reprinted in The Spectator.

### The Best Sleep Upgrade I’ve Ever Had:

I’ve now had some time with the new **Eight Sleep** Pod 6.

The biggest upgrade is that the Pod has gotten much better at figuring out what your body needs without you having to make your own adjustments. This new version has 18 sensors, up from two in the previous model. These sensors track things like heart rate, breathing, HRV, and sleep patterns, then work with Autopilot to adjust the Pod’s temperature as you sleep through the night.

One improvement I particularly like is that you can adjust the temperature using actual, physical buttons on the side of the Pod itself. This is a massive improvement. If you wake up too warm or too cold, you don’t have to grab your phone in the middle of the night.

The heating and cooling are also about 20 percent faster than before. And the redesigned hub is now noticeably smaller and can now fit under the bed.

I appreciate that these upgrades are mostly invisible. We don’t need more technology requiring our attention. Most of us prefer technology that works in the background and makes our lives better.

That is what the new **Eight Sleep** Pod 6 does.

items.subtitle: One of the key parts of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) decision finding Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya was the inclu…
items.feedText: The ICJ’s Gambia v Myanmar decision represents a much more comprehensive understanding of what genocide encompasses than in some (or even much) of the past jurisprudence, including its own. In the cases brought against Serbia in the ICJ, the Court only found that what occurred in Srebrenica constituted genocide, in keeping with the findings of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia.
