items.body:
One of the key parts of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) [decision](https://www.icj-cij.org/case/178/judgments) finding Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya was the inclusion of sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) in the Court’s reasoning.

The ICJ’s *Gambia v Myanmar* decision represents a much more comprehensive understanding of what genocide encompasses than in some (or even much) of the past jurisprudence, including its own. In the cases brought [against Serbia](https://www.icj-cij.org/case/118) in the ICJ, the Court only found that what occurred in [Srebrenica constituted genocide](https://www.icj-cij.org/case/91), in keeping with the findings of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. *Gambia v Myanmar* goes beyond the focus on genocide as killing, engaging substantially with other genocidal crimes – including SGBV.

The judgment addressed two types of sexual and gender-based violence, particularly [against women](https://verfassungsblog.de/gambia-v-myanmar-violence-women/), that were part of this case: rape (and sexual violence), and imposition of measures intended to prevent births. These crimes were comprehensively recognised by the ICJ as an integral part of the genocide against the Rohingya, as specific crimes and as evidence of genocidal intent.

## A Dearth of Attention to Sexual and Gender-Based Violence in Genocide Before International Courts

There has generally been insufficient attention paid by [international courts](https://doi.org/10.1080/13642987.2017.1360006) and tribunals to sexual and gender-based violence against women in the context of international crimes, but particularly so for the crime of genocide. [Over the years,](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejil/chaf024) there have been advances, but gaps remain, despite feminist scholars and practitioners framing [sexual and gender-based violence](https://access.heinonline.com/HOL/P?h=hein.journals/hwlj17&i=13) as [part of](https://www.globaljusticecenter.net/beyond-killing-gender-genocide-and-obligations-under-international-law/) the genocide process, [including the Rohingya genocide](https://doi.org/10.1080/14623528.2026.2759582).

It was only at the push of [feminist advocates](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1154259)and then-judge Navi Pillay (incidentally, an ad hoc judge on the bench for *Gambia v Myanmar* ) that [rape featured](https://access.heinonline.com/HOL/P?h=hein.journals/cjtl44&i=948) as part of the [Akayesu case](https://www.refworld.org/jurisprudence/caselaw/ictr/1998/19275) in the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR).

However, few other ICTR cases resulted in convictions for sexual violence, and that Tribunal’s subsequent treatment of sexual violence has [been criticised](https://doi.org/10.1163/15718123-01304002). In the ICTY, there was no finding of genocide other than the gendered killing of boys and men at Srebrenica, despite the extensive and systematic sexual and gender-based violence against Bosnian girls and women, including [rape camps](https://access.heinonline.com/HOL/P?h=hein.journals/hgejcejl2&i=162). Such violence was recognised in convictions for war crimes and crimes against humanity. Thus, while the case law contributed to the [development of the definition of rape](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejil/chy043) and other forms of sexual violence, there was no engagement with the idea of sexual violence as genocide even though such sexual violence has had [long-term impacts](https://www.routledge.com/Rape-Sexual-Violence-and-Transitional-Justice-Challenges-Lessons-from-Bosnia-Herzegovina/Clark/p/book/9780367191788) on Bosnian women.

## Rape and Sexual Violence

[Rape](https://www.hrw.org/report/2017/11/16/all-my-body-was-pain/sexual-violence-against-rohingya-women-and-girls-burma), including gang rape, was a [ubiquitous part](https://www.ohchr.org/en/hr-bodies/hrc/myanmar-ffm/sexualviolence) of [the violence](https://doi.org/10.1080/13642987.2021.1931136) against the Rohingya, directed predominantly against girls and women. The Court would have been remiss if rape had not formed a significant part of its ruling, and the Court blatantly found “extensive acts of rape and other forms of violence” were committed by Myanmar’s security forces, with rape and gang rape “a notable and recurrent feature of the violence” (para. 254).

At no point was the definition of rape discussed; the Court simply took its reference to rape as a given, which demonstrates the acceptance of this crime in the context of international crimes. The Court also determined that the exact number of victims is difficult to establish due to stigma, but noted *at least* 1,834 victims were listed in one report (paras. 258, 335). However, the Court held that “it need not set out the precise extent of the injuries suffered or make a conclusive finding on the number of victims” to find that serious physical or mental harm occurred. This is an appropriate finding, given that it is impossible to have an exact number of victims of sexual violence, and it is generally assumed that the number of victims is always higher than any figure that may be produced.

[Rapes](https://www.fortifyrights.org/mya-inv-rep-2017-11-15/) were committed with particular brutality, usually in public, often gang rapes, in front of family members, and frequently including mutilation. The “extreme physical brutality” of the rapes was acknowledged, as was the rape of pregnant women, and the fact that such violence was also committed with mutilation of the victims (including breasts and genitalia) (paras. 255-6). There are [also reports](https://www.womensrefugeecommission.org/research-resources/its-happening-to-our-men-as-well/) of sexual violence against boys and men (mentioned in paras. 254, 260, 369).

The Court also included sexual violence as a component of its discussion on attacks on children. Here, the judges specifically positioned children as victims of sexual violence. The judgment draws attention to several individual cases, with girls as young as 9 raped (para. 260).

The decision considered rape within the context of [Article II(b)](https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/convention-prevention-and-punishment-crime-genocide) causing serious bodily or mental harm, acts under which must be intentional. The Court drew from several intervening states’ submissions that “the harm resulting from sexual and gender-based violence is ‘almost universally’ » serious « by its nature” (para. 324). It confirmed its previous finding in the Serbia cases that rape and SGBV can constitute the *actus reus* of genocide under Article II(b). It confirmed that the widespread rape and sexual violence committed by Myanmar’s security forces “resulted in serious physical harm” (para. 329).

…

items.body: Protein domain annotation underlies large-scale functional inference and is commonly performed by scanning sequences against libraries of profile hidden Markov models (profile HMMs). We describe PSALM, a protein domain annotation method that combines (i) a pretrained protein language model (ESM-2) with (ii) a per-residue domain-state classifier and (iii) a structured probabilistic decoder that produces a single, non-overlapping set of domain calls with explicit boundaries and scores. On a benchmark of 76.9M protein sequences with 107M annotated domains, PSALM attains a domain-detection sensitivity-specificity tradeoff comparable to HMMER. We characterize sequence and residue-level coverage on UniProtKB, observing higher coverage for HMMER at stringent expected false positive counts (E-values) and higher coverage for PSALM at relaxed E-values. We release code for data processing, training, and inference, along with the model weights and datasets used for training, validation, and benchmarking.

- [Colophon](https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/23/grasshoppers-v-ants/#bragsheet): All the rest.

## The Debt Trap (permalink)

[↗ Primärquelle: pluralistic.net](https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/23/grasshoppers-v-ants/#)

Smoking is very stupid. I was a smoker for 17 years, from ages 13-30. I was very stupid to start smoking. That stupidity only came into sharper focus a few years ago, when I got a cancer diagnosis (don't worry, I am now cancer-free):

[https://pluralistic.net/2024/11/05/carcinoma-angels/#squeaky-nail](https://pluralistic.net/2024/11/05/carcinoma-angels/#squeaky-nail)

In my defense, I'll point out that I was just a kid when I started, but also, smoking belongs to a class of pernicious problems whose insidiousness is rooted in the distance between their causes and effects:

[https://pluralistic.net/2021/06/03/i-quit/](https://pluralistic.net/2021/06/03/i-quit/)

I've often said that if a little tumor had sprouted immediately after I took my first puff, I never would have taken a second one. Now that I've actually had the experience of being told that I have a tumor, I can say *definitively* that I would not have taken that second puff. An economist would tell you that I was engaged in "hyperbolic discounting": underpricing a future cost and overvaluing a present pleasure:

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_discounting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_discounting)

But I don't think that tells the whole story. Sure, I was engaged in hyperbolic discounting, but *why* was I doing that? What was it about smoking (as opposed to, say, French-kissing light-sockets) that led me to apply a hyperbolic discount to the costs of smoking? I say it was the attenuated relationship between cause and effect. It's not just that we undervalue the price of smoking: it's that we struggle to arrive at a correct price for smoking in the moment, because the intellectual knowledge of cancer statistics is in no way comparable to the visceral experience of a cancer diagnosis. Estimating the "cost" (emotional, physiological, monetary) of a cancer diagnosis is *hard*, especially if you're young and have had the good fortune of a life untouched by close contact with agonizing illness and death.

The point I'm making is that the discount isn't just hyperbolic, it's hyperbolic *because* it relies so much upon guesswork, without comparable experiences to anchor your estimate.

What's more, it's this same *attenuated causality* (in which cause is separated from effect by so much time and space) that allowed the tobacco industry to sow so much profitable doubt about the connection between smoking and cancer. Sure, *some* of the policymakers who let Big Tobacco off the hook were doubtlessly in their pocket, reliant on campaign contributions or beholden to a party that was in some queasy, cozy relationship with these death merchants. But the reason Big Tobacco was able ( *is* able) to get away with killing us for so many decades is that you don't get a tumor with each puff.

I believe that *most* of the policymakers who reasoned their way into doubting the connection between smoking and cancer were ensnared by this attenuated causality. They might have had low morals and low intellect, but the factor that made them such easy marks for Big Tobacco's death-hustlers was this wide, long gap between cause and effect.

This cuts both ways: if you're a policymaker of low intellect and morals, you can rig your policies to put their consequences a long way off in the future, which might give you time to escape to a lucrative private-sector career with the industrial interests who benefited from your chicanery. Or (if you're a Mitch McConnell-adjacent flesh-eating ghoul who plans to die only after centuries in office, chin red and slick with the heartblood of the innocent), you can put so much time and space between your fuckery and the ruin it brings that the voting public fails to connect your actions with the consequences. After all, no one ever lost money betting against the American public's object permanence.

For example, Trump's Big Bill was designed to make its deepest cuts – to Medicaid, rural hospitals, the increased tax-load on workers to advantage their bosses – *after* the midterm elections. The cynical reasoning isn't hard to follow: We'll just tell voters that all the bad things they've been told about the coming cuts are Fake News, and then, after the cuts arrive, blame their post-midterm misery on Biden, communists, trans people, immigrants, and the phases of the moon.

This cheap trick may be deplorable, but you should also save some anger for politicians who enact *good* policies but refuse to take account of this principle. Take Biden's 2021 plan to lower prescription drug prices. This started off as a rule that would end the longstanding, outrageous policy that bans Medicare/Medicaid from negotiating with pharma companies. Yes, you read that right: when Uncle Sucker buys drugs from Big Pharma, the government just asks the pharma companies how much public money they'd like, and then the USA writes the companies a check for whatever sum they name, no questions asked. That's why the US pays 300% more than any other advanced nation for its drugs.

…

items.title: What the End of Anonymous Writing Means for Academia
items.subtitle: A reader who asked to remain anonymous (seriously) pointed me to an article about the impending end of anonymous writing.
items.feedText:

Given a single text and a simple zero-shot prompt (no web access, tools, candidate lists, or writing samples), frontier models can answer “who wrote this?” at three increasingly specific levels: (1) whether an AI or human wrote it, (2) if an AI, which lab, and (3) if a human, often exactly who. Th…
items.body:
A reader who asked to remain anonymous (seriously) pointed me to an [article](https://www.theargumentmag.com/p/say-goodbye-to-anonymous-posting?) about the impending end of anonymous writing.

Large language models are getting increasingly good at identifying the authors of human-written text. In a preprint, “[Frontier models need only one text to unmask its human or AI author](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26216),” a team of authors claim that:

> Given a single text and a [simple zero-shot prompt](https://github.com/denizbt/unmasking_authors/blob/main/prompts/RQ3/holistic.txt) (no web access, tools, candidate lists, or writing samples), frontier models can answer “who wrote this?” at three increasingly specific levels: (1) whether an AI or human wrote it, (2) if an AI, which lab, and (3) if a human, often exactly who.

The authors asked LLMs to provide the identity of different kinds of often-anonymous writing, such as peer reviews and internet comments.

Their findings:

> The best-performing model we test is Claude Fable 5.2, which names the reviewer of 56% of private peer reviews and the username behind 31% of recent Reddit comments.

It appears that your writing is more likely to be outed as yours if some previous writing of yours was in an LLM’s training data, or if you a lot of your writing is available online. And once a model becomes familiar with you, your writing is very likely to be identified as yours:

> Even when a text is brand new, a model can identify its writer from what it learned about them elsewhere; i.e., once that knowledge is in the weights, the writer cannot do anything about it. This leaves people with the largest public footprints, such as active social media users or established authors, permanently exposed, since paraphrasing the text does not completely remove the deanonymization risk. Moreover, the set of vulnerable writers expands as models improve… Maintaining anonymity is especially important for peer review. Our private lab review data comes from only six writers, but a study across thousands of private peer reviews is underway.

Having an AI disguise your writing style by paraphrasing your writing does diminish its recognizability somewhat, but not entirely, the researchers report.

One commenter on the paper, Kelsey Piper, [writes](https://www.theargumentmag.com/p/say-goodbye-to-anonymous-posting?), “We’re witnessing a total erosion of the ability to write anonymously online,” though “the process is still incomplete. Not everyone should consider themselves deanonymized yet. But the erosion is happening.”

Regarding peer review, she writes:

> [T]he institution of anonymous peer review does not look like it will hold up any longer. The space of possible reviewers for a given academic article review in a particular discipline is pretty small; stylistic tics are sufficient to confidently distinguish between them.

Suppose the LLMs get quite a bit better at identifying the authors of anonymous text. What would that mean for the future of peer review? Well, while some reviewers have regularly opted to forgo anonymity, that is typically a privilege exercised by the relatively senior and secure members of the profession. I wouldn’t expect many more to join their ranks. Nor would I expect academia to be content relying on the forbearance of, say, curious authors or grant judges, to preserve anonymity.

There are [alternatives to peer review](https://dailynous.com/2022/02/07/why-a-crowd-sourced-peer-review-system-would-be-good-for-philosophy-guest-post/). Will the erosion of anonymity push more branches of academia to embrace these alternatives?

Or will it be a reason to use AIs even more in academia, say, as peer reviewers? After all, recently [one set of researchers found that](https://gking.harvard.edu/files/peerless.pdf):

> AI-generated article reviews are now better, by every measure we could construct, than reviews written by well-compensated human experts and judged to be of unusually high quality by journal editors and authors.

The study was performed on quantitative social science papers, not philosophy papers, but of course this technology is only a few years old; who knows how it might develop, and how rapidly.

Discussion welcome.

**UPDATE:** Shen-yi Liao [provided](https://bsky.app/profile/liao.shen-yi.org/post/3n32y4m2mgs2v) a direct link to [the prompt the researchers used](https://github.com/denizbt/unmasking_authors/blob/main/prompts/RQ3/holistic.txt). Try it on an unpublished piece of your writing. I gave ChatGPT [the prompt and the introductory section of an unpublished talk I wrote](https://chatgpt.com/s/p_6b05bf5973a08191aa93b52e7a43d0ed) a couple of years back and it identified me as the author with.62 confidence. You can read its report [↗ chatgpt.com](https://chatgpt.com/s/t_6b05bff752448191821da26c86cb9f2b). I fed it a referee report I wrote and it returned my name with.55 confidence.

items.body:
# Die Alltäglichkeit organisierter Gewalt

Elisabeth Pönisch | Rezension | 24.11.2026

## Die Alltäglichkeit organisierter Gewalt

## Rezension zu „Gewalt erleiden. Eine Soziologie organisierter sexualisierter und ritueller Gewalt“ von Tabea Koepp

Tabea Koepp: Gewalt erleiden. Eine Soziologie organisierter sexualisierter und ritueller Gewalt Deutschland Hamburg 2026: Hamburger Edition 352 S., 40,00 EUR ISBN 978-3-987-22006-7

Über organisierte sexualisierte Gewalt zu lesen, kann schwer auszuhalten sein. Die Schilderungen des Erlebten hinterlassen eine Beklemmung, die sich auch durch wissenschaftliche Einordnung nicht einfach auflösen lässt. Diese Gewalt wissenschaftlich zu erforschen und darüber zu schreiben, stellt eine besondere Herausforderung dar. Tabea Koepp nimmt diese in ihrer Studie Gewalt erleiden. Eine Soziologie organisierter sexualisierter und ritueller Gewalt an und rückt dabei die Erfahrungen der Betroffenen ins Zentrum. Ihr Ausgangspunkt ist eine Sprachlosigkeit, die das Begreifen des Erlebten betrifft. Im Anschluss an Carolin Emcke beschreibt Koepp, wie schwierig es sein kann, Gewalterfahrungen zu verstehen und sprachlich auszudrücken. Auch für sie selbst war zunächst vieles „schwer in Worte zu fassen“ (S. 7). Ihr gelingt es, diese Schwierigkeit analytisch fruchtbar zu machen, indem sie die Sprachlosigkeit selbst zum Gegenstand ihrer Untersuchung macht. Besonders überzeugend ist ihre Auseinandersetzung mit der vermeintlichen Unvorstellbarkeit von Gewalt. „Was dabei übersehen wird […]: Diese ‚Unvorstellbarkeit‘ von Gewalt ist ein Privileg“ (S. 15), schreibt Koepp in Anlehnung an Hannah C. Rosenblatt. Der Satz trifft einen entscheidenden Punkt: Was Außenstehenden unvorstellbar erscheint, kann für andere alltägliche Wirklichkeit sein. Koepp zeigt, wie wichtig es ist, auch schwer vermittelbare Erfahrungen zur Sprache zu bringen und ihnen Gehör zu schenken. Ihre Studie macht deutlich, weshalb diese Auseinandersetzung notwendig ist: Sie trägt dazu bei, die gesellschaftlichen Bedingungen zu verstehen, unter denen Gewalt unsichtbar bleibt, und sie hilft, die Betroffenen mit ihren Erfahrungen nicht allein zu lassen.

Hinzu kommt eine weitere Herausforderung: Koepp beschreibt, wie sehr ihre Forschung von der Erwartung begleitet war, sich in der öffentlichen Debatte um sogenannte rituelle Gewalt zu positionieren und die Wahl ihres Untersuchungsgegenstandes zu rechtfertigen. Dieser Rechtfertigungs- und Positionierungsdruck wäre seinerseits eine soziologische Untersuchung wert. Für die Auseinandersetzung mit ihrer Studie sollte jedoch entscheidend sein, welche Fragen sie stellt, wie sie diese untersucht und zu welchen Erkenntnissen sie gelangt. Eine Rezension muss ihren wissenschaftlichen Beitrag diskutieren, ohne die Bewertung des Buches auf eine Stellungnahme der Autorin zur öffentlichen Kontroverse zu verengen. Der vorliegende Text bespricht Koepps Arbeit deshalb als gewaltsoziologische Untersuchung und misst sie an ihrem wissenschaftlichen Anspruch. Im Mittelpunkt steht, was die Studie zum Verständnis von Gewalt beiträgt, wie sie ihre Erkenntnisse gewinnt und wie weit diese tragen.

## Rituelle Gewalt verstehen

Viele Bücher beanspruchen, eine Soziologie von etwas zu entwickeln. So auch die 2026 in der Hamburger Edition erschienene Studie von Tabea Koepp. Ihr geht es um eine

> „Soziologie der Gewalt, die nicht den Tätern und ihren Handlungen, sondern der Perspektive der Gewalterleidenden und ihren Verletzungserfahrungen folgt und nachzeichnen kann, wie andauernde (kollektive) Gewalt als soziale, zwischenmenschliche Erfahrung erlebt und erlitten wird“ (S. 9).

Während ihrer Forschung sei sie „immer wieder von der Normalität und Alltäglichkeit überrascht“ worden, „mit der sich die Gewalt in das Erleben (und Leben) der Betroffenen einzufügen schien“ (S. 8). Damit ist das zentrale Problem benannt: Wie lässt sich Gewalt verstehen, wenn sie für diejenigen, die sie erleiden, keine klar abgrenzbare Unterbrechung ihres Alltags darstellt? Wenn sich vielmehr „um die Gewalt herum über Jahre hinweg eine Lebenswelt baut, die so vieles mehr ist als die Gewalt“ (S. 9)?

Im Mittelpunkt stehen Menschen, die als Kinder bereits in Gewaltverhältnissen aufgewachsen sind. Koepps Forschungsgegenstand sind auf Dauer angelegte, klandestine, also gegenüber der Außenwelt verborgene Gewaltgemeinschaften, in die organisierte sexualisierte Gewalt weltanschaulich eingebettet ist. Die Autorin fragt, wie diese Gemeinschaften fortbestehen und ihre Gewalt verbergen können. Der Zugang erfolgt vor allem über rückblickende Interviews. Die Analyse rekonstruiert die untersuchten Gewaltverhältnisse aus den Erzählungen und Deutungen der Befragten. Wie prägt die Gewalt die Erfahrungen und Beziehungen von Betroffenen und wie entstehen neben Verletzung und Abhängigkeit auch Zugehörigkeit, Bindung und Orientierung? Die Perspektive überzeugt vor allem deshalb, weil sie eine verbreitete Vorstellung infrage stellt: dass Gewalt dort beginnt, wo das gewöhnliche soziale Miteinander aufhört. Koepp untersucht stattdessen, wie beides ineinandergreift und Gewalt in Beziehungen eingebunden ist, die über die einzelne Gewaltsituation hinaus bestehen.

Dafür ist zunächst zu klären, was Koepp unter ritueller Gewalt versteht. Sie ist eine „Variante von in Gruppen organisierter sexualisierter Gewalt, die sich primär durch die weltanschauliche Einbettung der Gewalt von anderen Gewaltformen unterscheidet“ (S. 10). Die begriffliche Unterscheidung hat analytische Konsequenzen. Sie richtet den Blick auf die Funktion der Weltanschauung innerhalb sozialer Ausbeutungsverhältnisse. Das ist wichtig, weil die Konzentration auf vermeintlich außergewöhnliche Rituale verdecken kann, welche Interessen innerhalb solcher Gruppen verfolgt werden. Koepp verweist ausdrücklich auf Machtinteressen sowie sadistische und kommerzielle Interessen (S. 11). Die Weltanschauung dient der Rechtfertigung der Gewalt und prägt zugleich die Deutungen, mit denen die Beteiligten das Geschehen und ihre eigene Stellung darin verstehen (S. 11).

## Theorie und Methodik

Koepp bewegt sich in einem Forschungsfeld, das sie als jung, umkämpft und empirisch unzureichend erschlossen beschreibt (S. 31). Der öffentlichen und medialen Aufmerksamkeit steht eine bislang begrenzte wissenschaftliche Auseinandersetzung gegenüber. Die deutschsprachigen Untersuchungen sind demnach überwiegend quantitativ ausgerichtet und folgen psychologischen oder psychiatrischen Perspektiven (S. 36). Ihr qualitativer, ausdrücklich soziologischer Zugang erweitert dieses Feld. Die von ihr gewählte explorative Herangehensweise erscheint angemessen: In einem wenig konsolidierten Forschungsfeld müssen zunächst Zugänge erschlossen, Begriffe präzisiert und Zusammenhänge am empirischen Material herausgearbeitet werden.

> In einer „gewaltaffizierten Lebenswelt“ (S. 279) prägt Gewalt auch alltägliche Gewohnheiten, Beziehungen und Erwartungen, die über die unmittelbare Gewaltsituation hinausreichen.

items.body:
[Janet Flanner-Solita Solano papers](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/95507085/), Library of Congress. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Georges_Gurdjieff.JPG).

My first mistake was to draw a connection. The flyers appeared all at once over the telephone poles of my neighborhood in the East Bay, with contact info provided on the kind of tear-away strips more typical of a HELP WANTED or FOR SALE notice, only here the subject read: AN INTRODUCTORY DISCUSSION: G. I. GURDJIEFF. The accompanying copy spoke of spiritual methods and cosmic scale; the words seemed to promise some tremendous synthesis between part and whole, spirit and matter, individual and collective. More prosaically, they advertised a series of public meetings to take place in Berkeley. My second mistake, I think, was to write an email expressing interest.

Where had I heard the name Gurdjieff? The question took me several minutes of standing in front of the poster to answer. I must have missed the crossing signal before remembering with a start that the life’s work of the Russian-born mystic, teacher, sacred choreographer, and occasional composer of piano music [George Ivanovich Gurdjieff](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2020/10/22/the-lesbian-partnership-that-changed-literature/) had—for me at least—everything to do with a small, neglected corner in the [short fiction](https://www.theparisreview.org/authors/4476/joy-williams) of [Joy Williams](https://www.theparisreview.org/authors/4476/joy-williams).

Photograph by Drew Dickerson.

“Gurdjieff in the Sunshine State” appears in Williams’s 1990 book *Escapes,* but is among the very few stories not to make it into her nearly comprehensive collection *The Visiting Privilege*, published twenty-five years later. I have never understood the logic behind its exclusion any more than I can claim to understand the story itself—in which G. astral projects to Florida, where, as a specter, he observes a roller rink, drinks a Tab, and chats briefly with what may be the ghost of Katherine Mansfield. By virtue of being disincluded from Williams’s collected work, this story of an esotericist feels in turn to have become itself esoteric, tucked away and little read. Even Williams’s own mentions of the story seemed charged with the force of mystery. “There is a Gurdjieff story in Escapes,” she wrote to her editor, the late Gary Fisketjon, in 2011. “I was going to write a whole mess of these stories on Gurdjieff but haven’t, you’re probably happy to know.”

The historical Gurdjieff was no stranger to hermetic situations. He traveled widely during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. In the course of his itinerary between the Mediterranean and southwest Asia, he absorbed the teachings that would result in his syncretistic blend of Sufi, Hindu, Zen, and Christian tendencies. But the articulation of his thought in a system and set of practices later known as the Fourth Way would come to be passed between generations, making Gurdjieff one of the most influential figures in what we today call the New Age Movement.

Some of this biographical picture was imparted at the first public meeting I attended in the auxiliary room of a Unitarian Universalists Fellowship Hall. For practical purposes the scene might have been lifted straight out of the fiction of Williams herself—from “The Country,” say, in which a group of denominationally wide-ranging seekers meet weekly “in one of the many, many rooms” of an Episcopal church to discuss the question: “Why Are We Here?”

I took my seat in a circle of folding chairs under a framed black-and-white portrait of Gurdjieff that someone had arrived early to hang. It was the first time I’d seen a picture of him. His eyes were enormous. Introductory talk proceeded gnomically. Most present seemed to have been steeped in one or another Gurdjieff-adjacent current. All were capable of trading words as tokens in a kind of code I had trouble grasping.

“I was brought here out of interest in the work of Maurice Nicoll.”

“Yes, well. Nicoll certainly had a lot to say, didn’t he? Maybe he ran out of things to say by the time of his fifth book. You should read Ouspensky.”

“I’m wary of Ouspensky. Remember what Gurdjieff told him: if you understood half of what you know, you’d be my teacher.”

Why were we there? Newcomers were encouraged to share our answers to this question. I owned up to my literary detective work in tracking down this reference of Williams’s, so marginal in her body of work as to be secretive. I also said that I wanted to enjoy a closer relationship to [God](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2013/06/03/3-stories-of-god/), which was true.

Motivations varied. One woman mentioned a near-death experience several months ago that convinced her of the need for greater spiritual attunement. Another spoke about how, after a childhood spent being told to shut up, she was now emboldened to want to find her voice. Someone else detailed a fairly fresh LSD episode before producing a decorative knife that he told us had been forged from the metal of an authentic meteorite. The ceremonial blade looked no shorter than six inches.

Georges Gurdjieff, 1930. [Time](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Time_-_1930.03.24_-_62_-_Georges_Gurdjieff.png), Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Time_-_1930.03.24_-_62_-_Georges_Gurdjieff.png).

*Experience* certainly struck me as a keyword in the group’s talk, in the sense of a spiritual experience’s spontaneous flash of insight that leaves one wholly changed. *Vibration*, too, was in frequent currency. *Self-observation*. *Self-knowledge. Self-remembering.* One first-time visitor’s chancing upon the term *wish* was met with a gasp. The wish, it seemed, was fundamental. The lights were dimmed. The scent of patchouli was strong. Boredom was my prevailing attitude—shot through at odd intervals with the numinous feeling that somehow anything at all might be possible.

Others seemed less impressed. An attendee identifying himself as a veteran of workshops in human development at the Esalen Institute complained, not without cause, that we’d certainly heard the name Gurdjieff plenty. But what did he teach in specific terms? What did he promise? We’d been told Gurdjieff had answers. I felt my own small disappointment with the session, mired in personal anecdote, without much in the way of a survey of Gurdjieff’s system.

“You’re right to ask,” said one man. “Gurdjieff works by allegory. He says of his writing in *All and Everything*: ‘I bury the bone so deep that the dogs have to scratch for it.’”

…

items.body:
*Updated at 6:54 a.m. ET on November 25, 2026*

Last summer, a Russian drone came crashing down in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, killing three people. Ukrainian engineers [examined](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/24/world/europe/russia-drones-autonomous-ai-kill-ukraine-war.html) the machine afterward and learned that it had been guided by minicomputers made by an American company. The Ukrainians then found the same minicomputers made by the same American company on a new missile that the Russians seemed to be testing in Ukraine.

The American company is the chipmaker Nvidia. When its Jetson Orin minicomputers started showing up inside AI-guided weapons designed to kill people in Ukraine, an Nvidia spokesperson issued a disclaimer. These were not military-grade products, he told *The New York Times*, but rather “consumer-grade products sold to students, developers and start-ups.” Nor, the company declared, does it sell the equipment directly to Russia. But it’s not hard to work out where Russia got this technology: The circuit boards inside the inspected drones and missiles were stamped Made in China. More sophisticated products, including the advanced AI chips that the Trump administration allowed Nvidia to sell to China, could eventually make their way along the same route to the Ukrainian front line. Some Chinese companies are [reportedly offering](https://wirescreen.ai/insights/the-malaysia-hong-kong-russia-chip-pipeline) restricted chips to Russian customers already.

The evolving scandal surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has many facets. It is a sex scandal, a spy scandal, and a corruption scandal. President Trump’s holdings of Nvidia stock, estimated at up to 370,000 shares, [rose](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/donald-trump-nvidia-stock-jensen-huang-stock-market) by perhaps $15 million after Huang was reinstated; Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial firm controlled by the sons of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, has [business ties](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/politics/trump-lutnick-ai-chips-nvidia-cantor-fitzgerald.html) with Southeast Asian companies that work with China and rely on Nvidia chips too. But this is also a special kind of national-security scandal: An American company, enabled by a greedy American president, has been selling what could become lethal technology, not just to China, but to the entire autocratic world.

*[[From the October 2026 issue: MAGA is making the world safe for corruption](https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/2026/10/maga-foreign-policy/688352/?utm_source=feed)]*

If anyone in the Trump administration understands what is at stake, they haven’t yet spoken up. Trump himself is earning too much to care. Besides, he likes and admires Vladimir Putin, whom he calls a “friend,” and he appears to be in awe of Xi Jinping; he is learning fast from both of them. He shares some of their instincts: the same dislike of the language of democracy and human rights, disdain for the rule of law, a belief that the powerful should never be held accountable. His intervention to have Jensen Huang reinstated, though extraordinary in American history, would have been an ordinary event in Russia or China, where the head of state regularly makes or breaks the fortunes of individual companies for political or personal gain.

That’s not the kind of government Americans were voting for a mere three weeks ago. But Trump isn’t very interested in what the voters want either, or in what might be good for them in the long term, or in what might keep them and their allies safe in the next decade. National security, to Trump, is an abstraction. Only money, and the captivating feeling of personal power, is real.

items.body:
The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation won a crucial victory against the Trump administration in court on Tuesday in a case challenging the president’s right to sell early access to his social media posts on Truth Social.

The ruling by Judge J. Paul Oetken in the Southern District of New York allows both organizations to seek limited discovery, offering a chance to peel back the layers on the president’s scheme to enrich himself through his public office. The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation can request records from the president’s private media company on both the operation of its six-figure early-access model and whether other media companies have purchased a subscription.

Truth Social is owned and operated by Trump Media & Technology Group, a company in which the president holds the largest stake in a trust controlled by [his son, Donald Trump Jr.](https://s3.amazonaws.com/sec.irpass.cc/2660/0001474506-24-000291.pdf) The early-access model, known as Truth API, requires subscribers to pay $60,000 to $100,000 a month. The service offers a first look at Trump’s posts — where, as the White House has [acknowledged](https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=1621912962326576), he often makes official policy announcements.

The lawsuit argues that the premium service violates the First Amendment rights of the public and the media to enjoy equal access to official government information. According to the lawsuit, Trump has published about 11,000 posts or reposts on Truth Social since returning to office.

[Related The Intercept Sues Trump for Selling Premium Access to Truth Social Announcements](https://theintercept.com/2026/08/12/trump-media-truthsocial-premium-first-amendment/)

The ruling will allow the plaintiffs “to get some answers about how this scheme works,” said Nikhel Sus, chief counsel at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, who is representing the plaintiffs. The subscription service, he added, was “rolled out with minimal transparency as to how the actual functionality works and who has been subscribing to the service thus far.”

In October, The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation requested a preliminary injunction arguing that the president should be barred from posting on his personal platform, Truth Social, as long as the premium service is in effect.

Oetken has not ruled on the preliminary injunction. But his decision on Tuesday is a “positive step forward,” Sus said. “The court didn’t explicitly say that it thinks our claims have merit, but the fact that it ordered discovery, we think, indicates that the court doesn’t think our complaint is non-meritorious because otherwise it wouldn’t have granted discovery.”

David Bralow, The Intercept’s chief legal officer, agreed.

“We are grateful that the Court is allowing us to proceed with uncovering the nature of the scheme that violates our First Amendment rights,” Bralow wrote in a statement. “By continuing to allow President Trump to exclusively post official government announcements on Truth Social’s API, the President and the other defendants continue to provide preferential access to those who pay up to $100,000 a month to increase Mr. Trump’s personal wealth.”

Despite the initial victory, Sus noted, the court still has not ruled on the government’s motion to dismiss the case, nor the initial motion for a preliminary injunction. “So we still have to wait and see,” he said.

items.title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists
items.subtitle: Positrons are the antimatter counterpart of an electron.
items.feedText: Physicists trapped a positron and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero. Positron is suspended in a wall-free trap, safely separated from ordinary matter. Team will conduct most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter. Any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.

items.title: Marie Curie Became the First Woman to Win a Nobel Prize, the First Person to Win Twice, and the Only Person in History to Win in Two Different Sciences

items.feedText: Cornell historian of science Margaret Rossiter coined the term “The Matilda Effect” to describe sexist bias in the sciences. items.body:
For most of scientific history, women who made contributions to various fields have been sidelined or ignored in favor of male colleagues, who reaped fame, professional recognition, and cash rewards that come with prestigious prizes like the Nobel. Cornell historian of science [Margaret Rossiter](https://sts.cornell.edu/margaret-rossiter) coined[the term “The Matilda Effect”](https://www.openculture.com/2025/12/matilda-effect.html) to describe sexist bias in the sciences. Rossiter’s work and popular reappraisals like book-turned-film *[Hidden Figures](https://amzn.to/2HTG1jS) * have inspired other women in academia to search for forgotten female scientists, and to find them, literally, [in footnotes](https://www.openculture.com/2019/02/womens-hidden-contributions-to-modern-science-get-revealed-by-new-study.html).

When systematic discrimination limits opportunities for any group, those who do receive recognition, the exceptions to the rule, must often be truly exceptional to succeed. There has been little doubt, both in her lifetime and in the many decades afterward, that Marie Curie was such a person. Although forced to study science in secret at a clandestine “[Floating University](https://www.openculture.com/2016/07/marie-curie-attended-a-secret-underground-flying-university-when-poland-blocked-her-other-women-from-advancing-their-education.html)” in her native Poland—since the universities refused to admit women—Curie (born Marie Salomea Sklodowska in 1867) would achieve such renown in her field that she was awarded not one, but two Nobel Prizes.

Curie and her husband Pierre shared the[Nobel Prize](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1903/summary/) [in Physics](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1903/summary/) with Antoine Henri Becquerel, discoverer of radioactivity, in 1903. The second prize, in Chemistry, was hers alone in 1911, “in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements radium and polonium, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element.” Curie was not only the first woman to win a Nobel, but she was also the first person to win twice, and the only person to win in two different sciences.

These are but a handful of achievements in a string of firsts for Curie: denied positions in Poland, she earned a Ph.D. in France, awarded the degree in 1903 by the [Sorbonne](https://www.sorbonne-universite.fr/en/university/history-and-heritage/history), the same year she won her first Nobel. “Her examiners,” notes the site [Famous Scientists](https://www.famousscientists.org/marie-curie/), “were of the view that she had made the greatest contribution to science ever found in a Ph.D. thesis.” Three years later, after Pierre was killed in an accident, Marie was offered his professorship and became the first female professor at the University of Paris.

Curie succeeded not in the absence of, but in spite of the sexist obstacles placed in her path at nearly every stage in her career. After she received her doctorate, the Curies were invited to the Royal Institution in London. Only Pierre was permitted to speak. That same year, the Nobel Committee decided to honor only her husband and Becquerel. The Academy relented when Pierre protested. Curie fell victim to a wave of xenophobia and anti-Semitism (though she was not Jewish) that swept through France in the 1900s, most famously in the so-called “Dreyfus Affair.”

In 1911, the year of her second Nobel, Curie was passed over for membership in the [French Academy of Sciences](https://www.academie-sciences.fr/en/). It would take another 51 years before the first woman, [Marguerite Perey,](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marguerite_Perey) a former doctoral student of Curie, would be elected to that body. That same year, Curie was persecuted relentlessly by the French press, the public, and her scientific rivals after it was revealed that she had had a brief affair with physicist Paul Langevin, one of Pierre Curie’s former students.

But no matter how many men in positions of power wanted to deter Curie, there always seemed to be more [influential scientists](https://www.openculture.com/2017/12/read-the-dont-let-the-bastards-get-you-down-letter-that-albert-einstein-sent-to-marie-curie-during-a-time-of-personal-crisis-1911.html) and politicians who recognized the supreme value of her work and the need to help her continue it. After her second Nobel Prize, her native country finally recognized her with the offer to direct her own laboratory in Warsaw. Curie turned it down to focus on directing the Curie Laboratory in the Radium Institute of the University of Paris, which she founded in 1914, a major achievement and, again, only a small part of her legacy.

Curie is known, of course, foremost for her exceptional scientific work, but also for opening doors for women in science all over the world, though much of that door-opening may only have happened decades after her death in 1934, and much of it hasn’t happened at all yet. Incidentally, in the following year, the Curies’ daughter Irène Joliot-Curie and her husband Frédéric Joliot-Curie were jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Since then, only seven other women have claimed that honor, and [only five women, including Marie Curie, have won the Prize in physics](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/are-the-nobel-prizes-missing-female-scientists/?redirect=1), out of 230 winners total.

There may be nothing yet like gender parity in the sciences, but those who know where to look can find the names of dozens of women scientists running women-owned companies, women-founded research institutes and academic departments, and, like the famous Curies, making [major contributions to chemistry](https://www.thoughtco.com/famous-women-in-chemistry-609453). Perhaps not long from now, many of those exceptional scientists will be as well-known and widely celebrated as Marie Curie.

Note: An earlier version of this post appeared on our site in 2019.

items.body:
Slap fighting is the world’s newest combat sport. Built for short attention spans and super-viral moments, it’s aiming for global dominance. No flinching

In the days before Power Slap 22, in Belgrade, Serbia, in late July, the organisers of the world’s newest combat sport were taking no chances. At the Crowne Plaza hotel, where competitors were booked to stay, those facing off had been separated by floor, lest any unauthorised violence took place.

It turned out there was little need. The night before the main event, contestants mingled amiably in the lobby and bar. The atmosphere was more specialist sales conference than brewing barroom brawl. In the lobby, I joined Louis “Razor” Robinson, and Ryan “the Punisher” Kenny. “We’re all friends in slap,” Robinson said, earnestly, by way of a greeting. Robinson, a Brit from Stalybridge, Greater Manchester, is 30, stout, intense. Kenny, a Canadian, is 34, lofty, laid back.

items.body:
arXiv:2611.31329v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Attribute reduction in incomplete information systems is difficult because missing values break the equivalence-class structure of rough set theory. We propose the Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Set (COFRS) model. Each object is described by its set of present attributes. The similarity of two objects is a weighted overlap on the attributes present in both, divided by the fixed number of attributes |A| instead of the size of their union, so missing values are penalised globally and are not matched as wildcards. From this similarity we define a soft dependency degree based on weighted granule consistency, and we search for reducts by greedy backward elimination in O(|U|^2 |A|^2) time. We show that the relation is symmetric and non-reflexive, that the dependency degree is not monotone, and we give a sufficient condition under which monotonicity holds. On 11 UCI benchmarks with missing rates from 0.15% to 20.46%, COFRS gives the smallest reducts on average (4.1 attributes, against 5.0-11.2 for Tolerance-RS, a range-threshold variant Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and the min-aggregation variant COFRS-min). The difference is significant against Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and COFRS-min (Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon p<0.01) but not against Tolerance-RS (p=0.56), and it is small against the Jensen-Shen selector (adjusted p=0.084). At equal reduct size, COFRS selects more informative attributes than random subsets. With a kNN classifier the methods do not differ significantly in accuracy, F1 or G-mean; with an RBF-SVM they do, and COFRS ranks last. The gain is therefore compactness, not predictive accuracy.

sourceReferences.title: Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Sets for Incomplete Data
sourceReferences.author: Trung Hieu Vuong, Van Thien Nguyen, Nhu Son Nguyen, Thanh Dai Tran

items.body: Background: Generative AI (GenAI) tools are increasingly used for health information and emotional support, yet little is known about their use for mental health by university students, a population with high digital literacy and elevated mental health need. Objective: To estimate the prevalence of GenAI use for mental health support among respondents to a survey at a single UK university and to identify demographic and well-being characteristics associated with use. Methods: Cross-sectional online survey of students at a large UK university. The primary outcome was self-reported GenAI use for mental health support in the past 6 months. Well-being was assessed using the Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale. Associations were examined using multivariable modified Poisson regression to estimate adjusted prevalence ratios. Results: Of 22,207 students invited, 2020 responded (response rate 9.1%). Among respondents, 25.0% (n=503) reported GenAI use for mental health support in the past 6 months. The most common reasons were advice when emotionally distressed (n=380, 19.3%), insights into mental health (n=256, 12.7%), and using GenAI as a personal therapist or coach (n=173, 8.6%); 2.7% (n=54) reported using GenAI to seek support when experiencing thoughts of self-harm. Use was more common among students aged 26-29 years, those identifying as Asian, students reporting a declared disability, students enrolled in management programs, and those with lower well-being. Conclusions: Among respondents at a UK university, approximately one in four reported using GenAI for mental health support. Use was concentrated among students reporting poorer well-being and disability, suggesting that GenAI may function as an informal help-seeking pathway. Universities and health services should anticipate GenAI as a help-seeking pathway and ensure appropriate guidance, integration with existing services, and safeguards to support safe and equitable use.

items.body: AI and multiomics can describe therapeutic cell and extracellular-vesicle (EV) products and the postischemic environment, but a molecular signature matters only if it changes a defined development or treatment decision. Existing reviews address stroke single-cell and spatial biology, AI in stem-cell multiomics, or AI-enabled regenerative engineering. This critical narrative review connects those topics through three decisions: whether a finished product has reproducible activity, which host conditions permit that activity, and whether a patient gains benefit attributable to treatment. We compare integration methods by their assumptions for paired, unpaired and mosaic data; distinguish Geneformer, scGPT, scFoundation and universal cell embeddings by input encoding and learning objective; and examine why larger pretraining has not produced consistent gains over simpler baselines. A worked EV-potency task specifies candidate functional labels, independent training units, controls and external validation. Representative stroke studies are mapped from molecular description through experimentally tested mechanisms to prediction of unseen product lots and controlled clinical benefit. The reviewed stroke and adjacent cerebrovascular literature includes AI-assisted molecular prioritization, computational graft-host analysis and automated behavior quantification, but does not establish an externally validated AI predictor of finished-product potency or treatment-attributable patient benefit. Cross-scale virtual-cell and heterogeneous protein representations offer transferable methods, not validated ischemic-repair models. The framework identifies the experiments needed to turn molecular associations into decisions with measurable biological value.

items.body: The relative influence of developmental bias and natural selection on evolutionary outcomes remains a central, unresolved question in evolutionary biology. Here, we combine large-scale phylogenetic trees with herbarium data to confirm that, across the evolutionary history of angiosperms, transitions from complex to simple leaf shapes have occurred at a significantly higher rate than the reverse. To investigate whether this directional trend reflects an underlying developmental bias, we simulate evolutionary transitions by introducing random mutations into a well-established computational model of leaf development. Despite excluding selection, the transition rates produced by the model closely align with those observed in the phylogenetic data. This agreement indicates that a strong developmental bias, reflecting the relative ease with which gene regulatory networks generate simple over complex leaves, has played a major role in shaping the evolution of leaf morphology. Our findings echo recent work showing that similar biases towards simplicity influence the evolution of molecular structures, including RNA secondary structures and protein quaternary assemblies. Together, these results suggest that a developmental bias favouring simplicity may be a widespread and general feature of evolutionary systems.

items.body: A glimpse lasting only a few milliseconds can convey meaningful information about a face, but how the brain transforms such minimal input into stable representations of facial expression and conscious experience remains unclear. Across two experiments using ultra-brief face presentations, we combined hierarchical psychophysical modelling, multivariate EEG decoding, and information-theoretic measures to characterise this transformation. Extending previously reported findings, hierarchical modelling quantified distinct exposure-dependent trajectories for intact-face localisation and expression identification, providing a behavioural calibration of weak, intermediate, and stronger perceptual evidence. The critical neural transition occurred between 4.4 and 6.2 ms. At 4.4 ms, expression sensitivity was behaviourally detectable, but neural expression patterns did not reliably generalise to faces excluded from classifier training. At 6.2 ms, previously observed emotion-related ERP differences were accompanied by expression representations that generalised across faces and locally detectable emotion information during the early posterior negativity (EPN) interval. Subjective clarity tracked location-related neural evidence more consistently than expression-specific evidence, indicating that awareness did not simply mirror the emerging expression representation. The degree to which early centroparietal activity statistically predicted later occipital activity differed between emotional and neutral faces as exposure increased, indicating that the relationship between successive neural responses was reorganised. Thus, a few additional milliseconds of visual input did not merely strengthen facial-expression processing; they transformed weak evidence that did not reliably generalise across faces into more stable, generalisable, behaviourally relevant, and distributed neural information.

We have had many words for heretics over the epochs — rebels, radicals, freethinkers — but they have always been the ones to dislodge humanity from the stagnation of the status quo, to illuminate our blind spots, dismantle our unexamined biases, and jolt us out of ou…
items.body:
### “If we are to be true and worthy heretics, we need not only new heads, but new hearts, and, most of all, that new emotional imagination… begotten of enlarged sympathies and a more sensitive habit of feeling.”

**UPDATE 2025: This book is now [back in print](https://www.amazon.com/Alpha-Omega-Jane-Ellen-Harrison/dp/1961341417/?tag=braipick-20) as the third title in [Marginalian Editions](https://www.themarginalian.org/editions/). When the Inquisition persecuted Galileo for advancing the rude truth that Earth is not the center of the universe, the charge against him was heresy — the same charge on which Joan of Arc was burned at the stake for her crusade for political reform. We have had many words for heretics over the epochs — rebels, radicals, freethinkers — but they have always been the ones to dislodge humanity from the stagnation of the status quo, to illuminate our blind spots, dismantle our unexamined biases, and jolt us out of our herd mentality. Without those devoted to seeing reality more clearly and possibility more wildly, we would still live in a world haunted by superstition and governed by dogma. The power and dignity of this most courageous human mindset is what the pioneering classicist Jane Ellen Harrison** (September 9, 1850–April 15, 1928), who brought the culture of Ancient Greece to the modern world, explores in her magnificent essay “Heresy and Humanity,” found in [Alpha and Omega](https://www.amazon.com/Alpha-Omega-Jane-Ellen-Harrison/dp/1961341417/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](https://www.worldcat.org/title/769418)) — the out-of-print essay collection that gave us Harrison on [the art of growing older](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/09/10/jane-ellen-harrison-crabbed-age-and-youth-alpha-and-omega/), published just as humanity was being dehumanized by its first World War.

Jane Ellen Harrison

Harrison writes:

> The word “heretic” has still about it an emotional thrill — a glow reflected, it may be, from the fires at Smithfield, the ardours of those who were burnt at the stake for the love of an idea.
> Heresy, the Greek hairesis, was from the outset an eager, living word. The taking of a city, its expugnatio, is a hairesis; the choosing of a lot in life or an opinion, its electio, is a hairesis; always in the word hairesis there is this reaching out to grasp, this studious, zealous pursuit — always something personal, even passionate… To be a heretic today is almost a human obligation.

In a sentiment Bertrand Russell would echo in [timeless manifesto for freedom of thought](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/05/18/bertrand-russell-free-thought-propaganda-doubt/), Harrison adds:

> The gist of heresy is free personal choice in act, and specifically in thought — the rejection of traditional faiths and customs.

Art by Olivier Tallec from [Louis I, King of the Sheep](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/10/14/louis-i-king-of-the-sheep-olivier-tallec/)

A century and a half after Emerson inveighed that [“masses are rude, lame, unmade, pernicious in their demands and influence,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/05/04/emerson-masses/) she considers what makes heresy so difficult yet so necessary to the health of society:

> All traditional views are held with such tenacity, such almost ferocity, because they belong to the class of views induced, not by individual experience, still less by reason, but by collective, or, as it is sometimes called “herd,” suggestion. This used to be called “faith.” The belief so held may or may not be true; collective suggestion is not in the least necessarily collective hallucination. Mere collective suggestions — that is the interesting point — have the quality of obviousness; they do not issue from the individual, but seem imposed from outside, and ineluctable; they have all the inevitableness of instinctive opinion… Hence they are held with an intensity of emotion far beyond any reasoned conviction. To doubt them is felt to be at once idiocy and irreverence. Inquiry into their rational bases is naturally, and in a sense rightly, resented, because they are not rationally based, though they may be rationally supported. It is by convictions such as this that a society of the homogenous kind — a society based on and held together by uniformity — lives and thrives. To attack them is to cripple and endanger its inmost life.

Observing that the development of science is what pivoted heresy from damnable to desirable in society, Harrison contrasts sensemaking by empiricism with sensemaking by authority:

> Science classifies, draws ever clearer distinctions; herd-suggestion is always in a haze. Herd-suggestion is all for tradition, authority; science has for its very essence the exercise of free thought. So long as we will not take the trouble to know exactly and intimately, we may not — must not — choose… We must follow custom; we must accept the mandates of [those] who enforce tradition.
> […]
> Science opens wide the doors that turned so slowly on tradition’s hinges, and opens them on clean, quiet places where we breathe larger air… It is well to remember our debt to science — our inward and spiritual as well as material debt.

Art by [Rockwell Kent](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/02/15/rockwell-kent-wilderness/), 1919. (Available as [a print](https://society6.com/product/the-star-lighter-by-rockwell-kent-1919_print?curator=brainpicker) and as [stationery cards](https://society6.com/brainpicker/cards?sort=new?curator=brainpicker).)

And yet, Harrison argues, the heretic needs more than science — the heretic needs humanity. She writes:

> Science broke the binding spell of herd-suggestion. For that great boon let us now and ever bless and praise her holy name. She cleared the collective haze, she drew sharp distinctions, appealing to individual actual experience, to individual powers of reasoning. But by neither individual sense — perception nor ratiocination alone do we live. Our keenest emotional life is through the herd, and hence it was that, at the close of the last century, the flame of scientific hope, the glory of scientific individualism that had blazed so brightly, somehow died down and left a strange chill. Man rose up from the banquet of reason and law unfed. He hungered half unconsciously for the herd. It seemed an impasse: on the one side orthodoxy, tradition, authority, practical slavery; on the other science, individual freedom, reason, and an aching loneliness.
> […]
> We live now just at the transition moment; we have broken with the old, we have not quite adjusted ourselves to the new. It is not so much the breaking with the old faiths that makes us restless as the living in a new social structure.

Art by Olivier Tallec from [Louis I, King of the Sheep](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/10/14/louis-i-king-of-the-sheep-olivier-tallec/)

…

items.body:
Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job.

Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension, CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there.

Xue “Alice” Dong

Employer

Colorado State University Extension in Logan County

Title

Extension regional specialist

Member grade

Senior member

Alma maters

Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products.

Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business.

She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside.

“We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in.

Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and theU.N.’s International Telecommunication Union, and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC), and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP).

She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture.

An early love of design and problem-solving

Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors.

As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs.

That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings.

“I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says.

She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career.

She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education.

She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016.

That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020.

From outreach to extension work

After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College, in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator.

She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water.

She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain, helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park.

In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns.

She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds.

Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System, a nationwide network run by land-grant universities, schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states.

The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture, managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties.

The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program, which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship.

Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person.

She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says.

“We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says.

items.body:
## Re-Design

Wer den Kuketz-Blog in den vergangenen Wochen regelmäßig besucht hat, dürfte es bemerkt haben: Hier hat sich einiges verändert. Was ursprünglich mit ein paar kleineren Anpassungen begann, ist schließlich zu einer umfassenden Überarbeitung des gesamten WordPress-Themes geworden. Sowohl auf dem Smartphone als auch auf dem Tablet und Desktop präsentiert sich der Blog nun in einem neuen Gewand.

Dabei ging es mir nicht einfach darum, alles etwas moderner oder schicker aussehen zu lassen. Im Mittelpunkt stand die Frage, wie sich die vielen Inhalte übersichtlicher, angenehmer und möglichst ohne unnötige Ablenkung darstellen lassen.

## Weniger Ballast, mehr Übersicht

Die [Startseite](https://www.kuketz-blog.de/) wurde grundlegend neu gestaltet. Kurzbeiträge und ausführliche Artikel sind nun deutlicher voneinander getrennt und werden in einer übersichtlichen Kachelansicht präsentiert. Auch die Navigation, die Suche, die Darstellung einzelner Beiträge und zahlreiche kleinere Elemente wurden überarbeitet. Wer lieber chronologisch stöbert, findet sämtliche Veröffentlichungen weiterhin in der [Sitemap](https://www.kuketz-blog.de/sitemap/).

Auf größeren Bildschirmen ist die bisherige Seitenleiste verschwunden. Stattdessen bekommen die Inhalte mehr Raum. Auf mobilen Geräten wurde die Darstellung ebenfalls umfassend angepasst. Alles soll besser zusammenpassen und unabhängig von der Bildschirmgröße ein möglichst einheitliches Erscheinungsbild bieten.

Auch unter der Haube hat sich einiges getan. Zahlreiche Altlasten wurden entfernt, bestehende Funktionen vereinfacht und der Code aufgeräumt. An einem Grundsatz halte ich dabei weiterhin fest: Das Theme kommt ohne JavaScript aus. Für eine gut funktionierende Webseite braucht es schließlich nicht für jede Kleinigkeit ein zusätzliches Skript.

## Über Geschmack lässt sich streiten

Natürlich ist mir bewusst, dass ein neues Design nicht jedem gefallen wird. Manche mochten die bisherige Darstellung, andere werden sich erst an die neue Aufteilung gewöhnen müssen. Das ist völlig in Ordnung. Gestaltung ist immer auch Geschmackssache, und Veränderungen brauchen manchmal etwas Zeit.

Mir war vor allem wichtig, dass der Blog seinen Charakter behält. Er soll kein überladenes Nachrichtenportal werden, sondern ein Ort, an dem Inhalte im Mittelpunkt stehen. Mit möglichst wenig Ablenkung, einer klaren Struktur und einer angenehmen Lesbarkeit.

Ob mir das gelungen ist, müsst letztlich ihr entscheiden.

## Fertig – aber Feedback ist willkommen

Die Überarbeitung ist inzwischen abgeschlossen. Das neue Design steht und ich bin mit dem Ergebnis zufrieden. Trotzdem kann sich bei einer so umfangreichen Umgestaltung natürlich irgendwo noch ein kleiner Fehler eingeschlichen haben. Gerade unterschiedliche Browser, Geräte und Bildschirmgrößen bringen manchmal Überraschungen mit sich.

Deshalb freue ich mich über eure Rückmeldungen. Was gefällt euch? Was könnte besser sein? Und falls euch Darstellungsfehler oder andere Probleme auffallen, gebt mir gerne über die [Kontaktseite](https://www.kuketz-blog.de/kontakt/) Bescheid. Besonders hilfreich sind konkrete Hinweise, möglichst mit einem Screenshot.

Auch kritische Rückmeldungen sind ausdrücklich willkommen. Schließlich soll der Blog nicht nur mir gefallen, sondern vor allem für euch gut funktionieren.

Eines bleibt bei aller Veränderung unverändert: Der Kuketz-Blog steht weiterhin für unabhängige, kritische und möglichst verständliche Beiträge rund um IT-Sicherheit, Datenschutz und digitale Selbstbestimmung.

Die Verpackung ist neu. Der Anspruch bleibt derselbe.

Viel Freude beim Lesen und Stöbern!

👇

kuketz-blog.de wird vollständig durch Spenden unserer Leser getragen. [Unterstütze](https://www.kuketz-blog.de/unterstuetzen/) auch du unsere Arbeit und werde Teil dieser großartigen Community! ❤️
