items.body:
# GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

November 24, 2026

## GPT‑6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

## Key findings:

- Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.
- An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take.
- In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing.
- The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules.
In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models , we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools.

Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.

Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical.

Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements.

Our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs.

Points farther from the center indicate better performance. Newer generations of models improved on many of the 14 protein tasks tested.

## A closer look at our models’ protein designs

We ran computational tests of whether the GPT‑6 models series could design small proteins to bind given targets, build proteins around specified structural features, predict protein structures and molecular interactions, and rank how sequence changes affect properties such as stability and binding. Our latest models performed comparably to or better than specialized models on most tasks, although predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness.

The models’ written reasoning and code offer clues to how they approach these tasks. They draw on mathematics, physics, chemistry, and coding alongside knowledge of recurring patterns in protein sequences and structures. For example, when designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction.

The model’s written reasoning and code show it drawing on math, physics, chemistry and biology to design a protein intended to attach to IL-7Rα. It examines the target’s surface, arranges five coiled sections into a protein shape, and checks how the two proteins could fit together.

With our research partner, Onava ⁠ (opens in a new window) , we also tested the models’ structure and sequence designs in the lab. First, Onava made small proteins based on three-dimensional structures designed by a pre-released version of GPT‑6.2. Specialized models supplied amino acid sequences and helped select candidates for testing. For each of the five targets we chose, at least one protein showed evidence of binding in the lab. In separate experiments, GPT‑6.2 designed new amino acid sequences for existing minibinders and antibodies. Following candidate selection with specialized models, many of the redesigned proteins also showed evidence of binding to the same targets as the originals.

## Laboratory Experiment 1: Designing small proteins that bind to a target

Our first laboratory experiment tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design small proteins that would bind to their intended targets. We compared computational measurements of quality against RFdiffusion, a specialized model for protein design, and found that GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs scored slightly lower while our latest internal models scored higher. For the lab experiment, we made proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs and measured how strongly they bound to their targets.

We gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models.

To turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins we could test in the lab, we needed amino acid sequences that would fold into the proposed structures. We used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design. Other specialized protein models helped us select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target.

…

items.body:
# The Real Nvidia Scandal

## The Real Nvidia Scandal

## How China Exploited a Massive Loophole in U.S. National Security—and How Congress Can Close It

### Emily Kilcrease and Vivek Chilukuri

Emily Kilcrease is Senior Fellow and Director of the Energy, Economics, and Security Program at the Center for a New American Security. From 2019 to 2021, first in the Trump administration and then in the Biden administration, she was Deputy Assistant U.S. Trade Representative for Investment.

Vivek Chilukuri is Senior Fellow and Director of the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a New American Security. He previously served as Legislative Director to Senator Michael Bennet and as a policy adviser at the U.S. Department of State.

- More by Emily Kilcrease
- More by Vivek Chilukuri
### The Real Nvidia Scandal

How China Exploited a Massive Loophole in U.S. National Security—and How Congress Can Close It

Emily Kilcrease and Vivek Chilukuri

- Share in email
- Share on Facebook
- Share on X
- Share on LinkedIn
- Copy Link Copied Article link: https://www.foreignaffairs.com/china/real-nvidia-scandal-kilcrease-chilukuri https://www.foreignaffairs.com/china/real-nvidia-scandal-kilcrease-chilukuri Copy

The reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia this week added another twist to a scandal that has transfixed Washington and Silicon Valley. The stakes go beyond the swings of the stock market or the salacious details about Huang’s affairs, including with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed and a potential Chinese asset. At its core, the scandal has exposed something that matters far more than any one man or company: American export-control policy remains riddled with loopholes, hobbled by incapacity and infighting, and divorced from clear strategy. Unless Washington fixes this, it risks imperiling the United States’ hard-won advantage in artificial intelligence.

This export policy failure is more than the sum of specific deficiencies. It stems from the Trump administration’s broader posture on China. Washington has embraced unfettered AI acceleration at the same time as it has struck a more accommodating stance toward Beijing. That combination set the stage for the explosive Megaspeed scandal—and perhaps others that have yet to emerge. As a result, China has been able to access an alarming number of advanced chips that have enabled it to narrow the AI gap with the United States and power its AI-driven military modernization. According to the AI research institute Epoch AI, up to a third of China’s AI computing power may come from smuggled chips. China’s top AI models are now just months behind the U.S. frontier. The narrow gap reflects China’s genuine innovation and access to abundant energy resources as well as its relentless efforts to circumvent U.S. controls.

Huang’s return to Nvidia at the behest of President Donald Trump suggests that both the company and the White House seem utterly uninterested in keeping powerful AI chips from China. It will instead fall to Congress to ensure that the United States leverages its compute advantage and maintains its AI edge. The midterm elections and mounting bipartisan concerns over the Megaspeed debacle give Congress new momentum to correct course. Its near-term agenda should include closing known loopholes that played a key role in allowing Megaspeed to supply advanced chips to China, stepping up enforcement of existing controls, and strengthening oversight of the administration’s export-control decisions.

Over the medium term, Congress must also tackle the broader question of how to balance the strategic benefits of exporting U.S. technology to build the world’s AI infrastructure with robust controls to prevent its leakage to China. The long-standing debate over which American AI chips and capabilities Washington should permit to diffuse globally and under what conditions has finally boiled over into the mainstream—and, in a perverse way, the national security community can thank Alice Huang for forcing the issue.

The issue before Congress, however, is much broader than addressing the specifics of the Nvidia scandal. Congress must also contend with the underlying impulses driving the administration’s China policy and install guardrails to avoid the erosion of U.S. export controls. This means that after Congress passes near-term bills to mop up the Megaspeed mess, it must then take the reins on setting long-term export-control strategy.

### UNFORCED ERRORS

Congress cannot stand by idly as AI blazes forward. OpenAI’s top model can now perform professional tasks as well as or better than humans 85 percent of the time, up from just 14 percent in 2024. The time an AI model can independently work on a task is doubling every four months. Last week, a researcher at Anthropic announced that AI helped him untangle the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous problems in pure mathematics.

As capabilities have grown, so have risks. Frontier models can now complete simulated cyberattacks on networks on their own, and hackers are using AI models to partially automate their attacks. In the July incident involving the AI platform Hugging Face, rogue AI agents escaped their testing environment and plotted to evade human oversight, underscoring the difficulty of aligning model behavior with human intent. The growing power of AI and the risks from misuse or loss of control make U.S. leadership a national security imperative.

At its core, the U.S.-Chinese AI competition boils down to which country can deploy the best chips in the highest quantities to train and adopt advanced AI models. The Biden administration’s controls slowed Chinese AI developers by leaving them with fewer, worse chips. Nvidia’s top Blackwell chips are nearly seven times better than Huawei’s Ascend equivalents. By the end of 2026, Huawei will likely have produced less than four percent of the compute that Nvidia will have over the same time. As the founder and CEO of DeepSeek, one of China’s top AI companies, admitted in 2024, “Our problem has never been money—it’s the embargo on high-end chips.”

items.title: Putin neben riesigem Cai Qi: Das Foto ist verfälscht
items.subtitle: Ein X-Bild lässt den chinesischen Funktionär Cai Qi riesig neben Putin erscheinen.
items.feedText: Kostenlos · der tägliche Mimikama-Newsletter Die wichtigsten Faktenchecks und Meldungen des Vortags – jeden Morgen kostenlos und unabhängig vom Social-Media-Algorithmus. Weitere Analysen zu diesem Thema: → Bild- und Kontext-Fakes erkennen – Gesamtüberblick Den Faktencheck per Artikellink teilen oder das 4:5-Faktenbild als PNG herunterladen. Die Netzwerke öffnen einen Beitrag mit dem Link zum Artikel .
items.body:
# Putin und Cai Qi: Foto verfälscht den Größenunterschied

- Die Behauptung Das auf X verbreitete Foto zeige den wirklichen Größenunterschied zwischen Putin und Cai Qi. China habe seinen körperlich größten Funktionär absichtlich zum Empfang geschickt, um Putin bloßzustellen. Falsch Das verbreitete Bild verfälscht den Größenunterschied zwischen Putin und Cai Qi. Eine gezielte Bloßstellung und Cai Qis angeblicher Größenrekord sind unbelegt. 💬 Wie werden echte Bilder gezielt falsch eingeordnet? Antworten finden Sie im Leitfaden Bild- und Kontext-Fakes . Das auf X verbreitete Foto von Wladimir Putin neben einem riesig wirkenden Cai Qi ist verfälscht. Cai ist tatsächlich größer als Putin, doch die Vergleichsaufnahmen zeigen einen deutlich geringeren Abstand. Unbelegt ist auch die Behauptung, China habe ihn wegen seiner Körpergröße ausgewählt, um Putin bloßzustellen. Der X-Account RS Archer behauptet, China habe eigens das körperlich größte Mitglied seiner Parteiführung zum Flughafen geschickt. Das beigefügte Bild zeigt Cai und Putin auf einem roten Teppich vor einem Flugzeug und lässt Cai übermäßig groß erscheinen. Der beanstandete X-Beitrag übertreibt den Größenunterschied. Screenshot: X / Nutzerübermittlung. Der Bildvergleich zeigt den Unterschied Auf der Vergleichsaufnahme reicht Putins Kopf deutlich höher in Richtung von Cais Gesicht. Außerdem hält Putin einen Arm vor dem Oberkörper, während im verbreiteten Bild beide Arme nach unten zeigen. Eine weitere, als Getty-Aufnahme ausgewiesene Abbildung zeigt ebenfalls einen geringeren Größenunterschied. Die verglichene Kremlaufnahme ist als Screenshot bei Lead Stories dokumentiert; die Kremlseite selbst war beim Abruf nicht erreichbar. Lead Stories und What the Fact ordnen das verbreitete Bild als KI-verändert beziehungsweise KI-erzeugt ein. Auch unser zusätzlicher Detektortest stuft das Bild mit einem Wert von 99,8 Prozent als wahrscheinlich KI-generiert ein. Das ist ein weiterer Hinweis auf KI-Bearbeitung, aber keine gemessene Sicherheit über die tatsächliche Herstellung. Der Bildvergleich zeigt die verfälschte Darstellung; welches Werkzeug dafür verwendet wurde, bleibt offen. Mimikamas zusätzlicher Detektortest: Das Werkzeug zeigt 99,8 Prozent für ein wahrscheinlich KI-generiertes Bild an. Der Wert ist eine technische Einschätzung und allein kein Beweis für die Herstellung. Screenshot: Mimikama. Ein echter Empfang belegt keine Demütigungsabsicht Cai Qi empfing Putin tatsächlich am Flughafen von Shenzhen zum APEC-Treffen. Das bestätigt die Meldung der chinesischen Nachrichtenagentur Xinhua . Cai gehört dem Ständigen Ausschuss des Politbüros an. Dass er der körperlich größte Parteifunktionär sei oder gerade deshalb ausgewählt wurde, ist durch die geprüften Quellen nicht belegt. Die Ankunft war am 18. November 2026 nach chinesischer Ortszeit. Laut South China Morning Post landete Putin kurz nach 2 Uhr früh. In Moskau und Wien war es da noch der 17. November, den Lead Stories nennt. Die Zeitverschiebung kann diese Abweichung erklären; ausdrücklich erläutert wird sie dort nicht. Bei solchen Bildern lohnt sich der Vergleich mit weiteren Aufnahmen desselben Termins. Eine sichtbare Körpergröße lässt sich prüfen. Eine politische Absicht hinter der Auswahl der Empfangsperson braucht einen eigenen Beleg. Quellen FAKTENCHECK What the Fact Did China send its tallest official to greet Putin at Shenzhen airport? 20. November 2026 FAKTENCHECK Lead Stories Fact Check: FAKE Photo Shows Huge Height Difference Between Vladimir Putin And Chinese Official — Image Is AI-Altered 19. November 2026 MEDIUM South China Morning Post Putin gets high-level airport welcome in Shenzhen as he arrives for Apec 18. November 2026 BEHÖRDE Xinhua / South Putin arrives in Shenzhen for APEC meeting 18. November 2026

items.title: beer.drv.drv.drv

items.feedText: Have you heard about dynamic derivations ? They are an experimental-feature in Nix that lets a derivation produce other derivations as its output. This lets you dynamically create your build graph, instead of having to know it all at evaluation time. It’s Nix’s answer to try and match the build speed of other build systems like Bazel or buck2 . There is not much written about dynamic derivations, and the documentation is sparse. I have written a few posts about them, so I sometimes get questions about them.
items.body:
# beer.drv.drv.drv

Have you heard about dynamic derivations ?

They are an experimental-feature in Nix that lets a derivation produce other derivations as its output. Why ? This lets you dynamically create your build graph, instead of having to know it all at evaluation time. It’s Nix’s answer to try and match the build speed of other build systems like Bazel or buck2 .

There is not much written about dynamic derivations, and the documentation is sparse. I have written a few posts about them, so I sometimes get questions about them.

Recently, I got a DM from Evan Porter over LinkedIn , the ultimate bug triaging network, about whether it is possible to query the deriver of a dynamic derivation to get the initial derivation.

> For dynamic derivations let’s say I have a .drv.drv file. This file outputs a derivation. Is it usually possible to query deriver the output derivation to obtain the initial derivation?

They had tried it and got this:

$ nix-store --query --deriver \ $ ( nix-store --query --deriver ./result ) unknown-deriver That should work. 🤨 Every path a build registers carries a deriver , the .drv that produced it, and a .drv that came out of a build is still a path a build registered.

When I tried it, it worked. 🤷

You will need extra-experimental-features = dynamic-derivations ca-derivations recursive-nix in your nix.conf to drive the samples in this post.

$ nix build -f default.nix \ --print-out-paths /nix/store/v4hkwn8y4m083gsap6523c0m5r985ygr-result $ nix-store --query --deriver \ /nix/store/v4hkwn8y4m083gsap6523c0m5r985ygr-result /nix/store/6pniymfhwcyrmkns0np7ap1argjziqq2-result.drv $ nix-store --query --deriver \ /nix/store/6pniymfhwcyrmkns0np7ap1argjziqq2-result.drv /nix/store/m5x261fv29jkn0rvznqj2fzkaql01xiy-result.drv.drv Turns out, there is a case where you do get unknown-deriver if you set __contentAddressed = true on the producer. If the producer is content-addressed, its output path is not known until after the build, and Nix does not fill in the deriver of a path that already exists. I filed NixOS/nix#16823 .

The question though made me wonder how far back you can walk the chain of dynamic derivations. I had to try it. 😈

Let’s pick a fun example to see how far we can go. Here is a derivation that imitates the classic song 99 bottles of beer by producing a chain of derivations, each one outputting the next verse. 1 1 The builder writes the next derivation by hand in ATerm , so there is no recursive Nix and no nix-instantiate involved.

export PATH = $busybox /bin # A content-addressed derivation does not know its output path, so its # "out" variable holds this placeholder and Nix swaps in the real path at # build time. It is "/" + nix32(sha256("nix-output:out")), the same for # every derivation with an output named "out". OUT_PLACEHOLDER = /1rz4g4znpzjwh1xymhjpm42vipw92pr73vdgl6xs1hycac8kf2n9 bottles () { case $1 in 0 ) echo "no more bottles" ;; 1 ) echo "1 bottle" ;; * ) echo " $1 bottles" ;; esac } # The last derivation in the chain writes the punchline instead of a .drv. if [ " $n " -eq 0 ] ; then echo "No more bottles of beer on the wall, no more bottles of beer." > &2 echo "Go to the store and buy some more." > $out exit 0 fi next = $(( n - 1 )) echo " $( bottles $n ) of beer on the wall, $( bottles $n ) of beer." > &2 echo "Take one down, pass it around, $( bottles $next ) of beer on the wall." > &2 # Input sources must be sorted. srcs = $( printf '"%s"\n' " $busybox " " $script " | sort | paste -sd , - ) # Write the derivation for the next verse. A .drv is a single line of # ATerm, so strip the spaces and newlines that are only here for reading. # Nix takes a derivation's name from its store path, so the next name is # ours minus one ".drv". tr -d ' \n' > $out << EOF Derive( [("out", "", "text:sha256", "")], [], [ $srcs ], " $system ", " $busybox /bin/sh", [" $script "], [ ("builder", " $busybox /bin/sh"), ("busybox", " $busybox "), ("n", " $next "), ("name", " ${ name %.drv } "), ("out", " $OUT_PLACEHOLDER "), ("outputHashAlgo", "sha256"), ("outputHashMode", "text"), ("script", " $script "), ("system", " $system ") ] ) EOF Tip A derivation whose output is a .drv must set outputHashMode = "text" .

In our example we are using a content-addressed derivation, but the same idea works with an input-addressed one, but it’s more work to compute the output path in the shell, unless you are using nix-instantiate to do it for you with recursive Nix.

The Nix side builds the first derivation and then follows builtins.outputOf once per bottle.

let pkgs = import ( fetchTarball { url = "https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/archive/6dadaf4375be35033e1c84395adbd53ff5fded96.tar.gz" ; }) { }; inherit ( pkgs ) lib ; # maximum bottles of beer on the wall, # 50 is the most that fits in a store path!? bottles = 50 ; top = derivation { name = "beer" + lib . concatStrings ( lib . replicate bottles ".drv" ); system = builtins . currentSystem ; builder = " ${ pkgs . busybox } /bin/sh" ; args = [ ./bottles.sh ]; script = ./bottles.sh ; busybox = pkgs . busybox ; n = bottles ; __contentAddressed = true ; outputHashMode = "text" ; outputHashAlgo = "sha256" ; }; in # Follow the chain of outputs down to the last derivation. lib . foldl ' ( drv : _ : builtins . outputOf drv "out" ) top . outPath ( lib . range 1 bottles ) While working through this example, I hit a bug in Nix that made me set __contentAddressed = true on the top derivation. That is not necessary for a derivation that outputs a .drv , but it works around the bug. I filed NixOS/nix#16830 .

You might notice that we limit the number of beers to 50. Why 50 and not 99?

Well, 50 is the most that fits in a store path.

error: path '…-beer.drv.drv.drv…' is not a valid store path: name 'beer.drv.drv.drv…' must be no longer than 211 characters The maximum length of a store path is 211 characters . A derivation’s store path must include the .drv suffix, and every .drv in a chain adds four characters. The top derivation is named beer and if you add 51 .drv s we get 208 characters. No room for any more beer. 🍻

> Aside b + 4 n ≤ 211 ⇒ n = ⌊ 211 − b 4 ⌋ Even with a name of length 1, b = 1 , we get a theoretical limit of n = 52 .

Let’s build sing it.

…

items.body:
Mark Gurman, [reporting for Bloomberg today](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-19/apple-s-iphone-camera-and-photos-software-chief-jon-mccormack-leaves-company?accessToken=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzb3VyY2UiOiJTdWJzY3JpYmVyR2lmdGVkQXJ0aWNsZSIsImlhdCI6MTc5NTEwOTM1MSwiZXhwIjoxNzk1NzE0MTUxLCJhcnRpY2xlSWQiOiJUT1IzMlJUOU5KTTUwMCIsImJjb25uZWN0SWQiOiJDNEVEQ0FFMUZBMDU0MEJFQTI0QTlGMjExQzFFOTA4MCJ9.aeSQbn794aHs3B5ecmfYGppiDoPtcY_FXRHn7Hbe76Y) (gift link):

> Jon McCormack retired at the end of October after more than eight
> years at the company, according to people with knowledge of the
> matter. He oversaw the Camera and Photos apps and the underlying
> technology that determines how users capture, view and edit their
> pictures and video.
> Apple hasn’t named a new vice president to take over McCormack’s
> exact role. Instead, his former deputies are assuming his
> responsibilities under another executive, said the people, who
> asked not to be identified while discussing internal moves. An
> Apple spokesperson declined to comment.
> His work included the redesigned selfie camera introduced with the
> iPhone 17 lineup last year.

I’ve met McCormack a few times. He frequently led media briefings for new iPhone camera features. He was always thoughtful, insightful, and fair. Like, sometimes his demonstrations would involve comparisons between photos of the same subjects and scenes captured on iPhones and ones captured with flagship Android phones. The photos were *all* good. It was never “ *Here are some beautiful images captured on iPhones and some dogshit ones from a Samsung and OnePlus* ”. The differences were often subtle. He’d even make the case for why someone might prefer the Android ones. But he could explain why Apple — and he personally — preferred the ones from the iPhone. Not just how the iPhone camera captures and processes images, but why. He also knew when to let the images speak for themselves.

McCormack was deeply informed at a technical level. He reported directly to Craig Federighi and that level of engineering acumen showed. I can’t recall any question being too technical for him to have a ready answer. One of the best iPhone camera innovations in recent years is the redesigned [Center Stage selfie camera](https://support.apple.com/guide/iphone/take-a-selfie-iph1b88429a6/ios) introduced with the iPhone 17 (and Air) lineup last year. The square sensor is hardware, and McCormack was a software VP, but the feature exemplifies the way hardware and software are developed in tandem at Apple. McCormack was [the public face for that feature](https://www.businessworld.in/article/exclusive-jon-mccormack-on-how-apple-reinvented-the-selfie-for-the-iphone-17-575523) — and internally, pushed to make it happen. That square sensor is bigger, which means (a) it’s more expensive; and (b) it takes up more space internally. Both of those require winning hard-fought arguments inside Apple in order to ship. The bottom line is that it helps iPhone users take better photos of themselves — and [according to McCormack himself](https://www.instagram.com/helloapple/reel/Daiat9bNtiF/), over 1 billion selfies are taken with iPhones *every day*. The influence Apple’s Camera team has on the daily lives of *billions* of people is significant; McCormack understood that.

But what really struck me about McCormack, right from the start, is that he is clearly a serious photographer himself. That’s perhaps understating it. He recently published a book of his own nature and travel photography: *[Patterns: Art of the Natural World](https://jonmccormack.com/book/)*. He [discussed the book in an hour-long interview](https://www.linkedin.com/in/chenpamela/) with his Apple colleague Pamela Chen, whose [job title](https://www.linkedin.com/in/chenpamela/) is one of the coolest I’ve ever heard: Chief Aesthetics Scientist. (Chen, unsurprisingly, is also [a talented photographer](https://www.instagram.com/chenpamela/).)

Gurman:

> His departure comes at a time when Apple is navigating a
> fundamental shift in photography. Competitors such as Alphabet
> Inc.’s Google and Samsung Electronics Co. have increasingly
> embraced generative AI features that allow users to make
> substantial changes to images. That has blurred the distinction
> between capturing a real moment and creating an artificial one.

Two years ago [in his iPhone 16 Pro review](https://www.theverge.com/24247538/apple-iphone-16-pro-review), returning to his repeated theme of “What is a photo?”, Nilay Patel quoted, at length, the answer he got from McCormack. I, in turn, [quoted Patel quoting McCormack](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2024/09/23/nilay-patel-iphone-16-pro-review), and added:

> McCormack’s response is genuinely thoughtful, and resonates deeply
> with my own personal take. But it’s worth noting that Apple is the
> conservative company when it comes to generative AI and
> photography — and yet they’re still shipping Clean Up. I’m not
> complaining about Clean Up’s existence. I’ve already used it
> personally. I’m just saying that even Apple’s stance involves
> significant use of generative AI.

This year, Apple added [“extend” and “reframe”](https://support.apple.com/guide/iphone/clean-up-extend-and-reframe-photos-xy0grrlxue5w/ios) alongside Clean Up. I don’t love either of those features simply because I don’t like how they change the meaning of “What is a photo?”, but I don’t *hate* them either. We can’t put the generative AI genie back in the bottle. Apple, still, is the conservative company in the generative AI phone photography space.

Jon McCormack had a knack for shepherding good new features *into* the Camera app. But also, based on conversations I’ve had with multiple people who worked with him at Apple, McCormack was *great* at keeping stupid ideas *out* of the Camera app. Good new features that ship get more recognition than stupid new features that never ship — but the latter, I would argue, is the rarer and more important management skill. It’s far more important to keep stupid ideas out of any app than it is to add good new features. McCormack was the protector of the Camera app. Under his leadership, it remains focused on the craft and art of photography.

Lastly, everyone I know who worked with him loves the guy. McCormack was the perfect guy for an essential job, and he leaves big shoes to fill.

items.body:
We moderns tell ourselves that while the ancients were transparently and strongly dominated by elites, we hold our leaders far more accountable, such as via law, media, and democracy. But we allow our elites many easy ways to use money or political connections to gain far more favorable treatment from media and law. And we use democracy much more to fight each other via coalition politics than to hold leaders accountable. That is, we much more submit to the leaders we vote for, than we defy the leaders we don’t.

Consider 18 ways we now block holding our leaders accountable:

- We make [blackmail](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/checkmate-on-blackmailhtml) illegal, so they are less penalized for misbehavior.
- We don’t arrange to try to secretly and randomly bribe officials.
- We don’t expect leaders to post bonds they forfeit if not keep promises.
- We mostly pick leaders on recommendation of other leaders.
- We rarely collect track records re their performance outcomes, or predictions.
- We rarely use prediction/decision markets to check leader prediction/decisions.
- We let firms pick their own auditors, and audits are rarely randomized.
- Evaluators usually can’t see leader decision internal records.
- Old leaders are not given regular tests re dementia.
- We don’t much protect or reward whistleblowers.
- Leader evaluations are rarely blinded.
- 360 reviews are rare and toothless.
- Only for-profit leaders have much cash performance incentives.
- We give police, prosecutors, and govt officials have legal immunity.
- Police internal affairs reports to police chief, not mayor.
- Firms use poison pills to block takeovers, and we vilify short sellers.
- Golden parachutes and option price resetting cushion CEO losses.
- We let CEOs pick who is on their boards.

Many excuses are offered for each of these patterns, but the obvious explanation here is that we are far more like the ancients than we like to think. We are eager to submit to the powerful, and show them our fealty, and are wary of endorsing positions by which we might seem to challenge or defy their power.

This is a big problem with two of my solutions to cultural drift, which require at least some of our groups to adopt much more competent forms of governance, forms that induce leaders to actually achieve identified goals. Our world now far less achieves most of the goals we give our leaders, due to our using pretty bad governance mechanisms. But we each prefer that to risking our seeming less loyal to our elites.

items.body:
# Kommentar: Vanessa Emde und die Berliner Linke – dieser Ausschluss war überfällig - Meinung - SZ.de

Vanessa Emde nach der Fraktionssitzung. Christian Mang/REUTERS Es ist richtig, dass die Partei, die künftig die Regierende Bürgermeisterin stellen will, diese Abgeordnete aus ihrer Fraktion ausschließt. Zu diesem Kraftakt darf man gratulieren - und noch einen Wunsch äußern.

D ie Linkspartei im Berliner Abgeordnetenhaus hat Schluss gemacht mit Vanessa Emde. Das ist nicht schön, aber es ist richtig. Die Abgeordnete, die seit Monaten ihre Parteifreunde auf Trab hält und sich immer weiter verzettelt hat in Provokationen zum Nahost -Konflikt, ist am Dienstagabend aus der Fraktion ausgeschlossen worden. Ein Kraftakt war das für ihre Partei, vor allem aber eine Demonstration. Die Linke will Berlin regieren, zusammen mit Grünen und SPD. Wenn das überhaupt gelingen kann, dann nur auf Basis eines unmissverständlichen Signals: Mit Judenhass gezündelt wird nicht in der Stadt.

Regierungsbildung in Berlin : Ende für Emde – Linksfraktion schließt Abgeordnete aus Auf dem Weg zur ersten Linken-Bürgermeisterin in Berlin kann Elif Eralp einen wichtigen Erfolg verbuchen. Die wegen ihrer radikalen Positionen umstrittene Abgeordnete Emde fliegt aus der Fraktion.

items.body:
Hello everyone,

I’m delighted to announce the release of Silver Bough, the third album from my wyrd folk / medieval ambient / experimental Celtic music project Glamourie:

Since the previous album whose production process was described in a topic entitled Otherworldly music for futuristic Middle-Ages, my set-up has slightly changed. I have switched from processing effects in series to processing them in parallel, which has allowed me to preserve the sound of the acoustic instruments I use (hammered dulcimer, flutes, percussions) in a much drier form. I’ve also had a bit of fun with some subtle feedback loops in the effects, which add a bit of shimmer and movement to the sound.

I continued my exploration of modal scales, which I was able to expand upon with the arrival of a C-tuned low whistle, and I read many more medieval texts and anthropological publications, which enriched my knowledge base in terms of themes and scholarly allusions to Celtic folklore and Arthurian mythology.

For the first time as part of this project, I also collaborated with an Irish singer who came to record her vocals for a contemporary arrangement of an old sean-nós about fairies.

This is a real clip of Democratic New York City Assemblyman Jordan Wright, who reportedly told the New York Post that he is "obviously" human.
items.body:
# Real video of NYC lawmaker Jordan Wright's eye roll fuels lizard conspiracy theory

About this rating

Conspiracy theorists claimed the video served as evidence that "lizard people" walk among us. Wright reportedly told the New York Post that he's "obviously" a human.

A video circulating online appears to show a man rolling his eyes in a so-called "reptilian" fashion while standing behind New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani during a news conference.

The clip, which was posted on X , Facebook and other platforms, reignited a decades-old conspiracy theory claiming shape-shifting reptilians secretly hold positions of power, which Snopes has previously reported on.

Snopes readers wrote in to ask if the video was real or generated using artificial intelligence.

This is a real clip of Democratic New York City Assemblyman Jordan Wright, who reportedly told the New York Post that he is "obviously" human.

Wright's eye roll is visible in multiple credible livestreams of the news conference in question, which Mamdani held on Nov. 20 to announce a plan to shutter Rikers Island, the city's largest jail, by 2032.

For example, Wright's eye roll is visible at the timestamp 1:51 in a YouTube livestream posted by the official New York City mayor's office account, whereas USA Today's livestream shows the eye roll at 1:54 .

There's no evidence that the livestreams in question were enhanced using AI, nor would there be any reason to do so.

According to the New York Post, Wright said he has "no idea what was going on in that video."

"Obviously I'm a human being, and my humanity can be seen through my legislation like the $4 million for the WE ACT environmental justice center in Harlem," he reportedly told the Post. "I can't speak to any reptiles or aliens."

We reached out to Wright, who assumed office in the New York State Assembly in January 2025, to verify that he spoke to the Post and await a response.

## Background on reptilian conspiracy theories

As we previously reported , the "reptilian" conspiracy theory was popularized in the modern era by David Icke, a British man who is barred from holding events in countries like the Netherlands and Germany over antisemitic conspiracy theories.

According to the UK anti-fascist advocacy group HOPE not hate , " the 'reptilian theory' is just one element of the hugely convoluted narrative Icke has developed over his long career" that promotes longstanding antisemitic tropes.

In the United States, officials have previously examined whether the conspiracy theory was a possible motive for the Nashville Christmas Day 2020 bomber.

There is, of course, no evidence that a secret race of reptilians controls the world.

items.body:
# Tech Giants Are Effectively Ungovernable. Here’s How to Change That.

## Tech Giants Are Effectively Ungovernable. Here’s How to Change That.

## The return of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang exposes a dangerous gap in corporate oversight.

American business has minted a new brand of executive: the CEO who is too big to fire. On Nov. 17, Nvidia’s board declared that it had accepted the resignation of Jensen Huang, felled by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy and a romance with one of the executive’s own subordinates. Six days later, Huang was back, restored after a unanimous vote by the same board. Nvidia’s shares soared. Many investors celebrated the return of the leather-jacketed founder credited with making the company the engine of the artificial intelligence revolution.

Three years earlier, OpenAI’s board had dismissed Sam Altman, citing a lack of candor with directors. Five days later, Altman returned, and most of the directors responsible for his removal were out.

American business has minted a new brand of executive: the CEO who is too big to fire. On Nov. 17, Nvidia’s board declared that it had accepted the resignation of Jensen Huang, felled by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy and a romance with one of the executive’s own subordinates. Six days later, Huang was back, restored after a unanimous vote by the same board. Nvidia’s shares soared. Many investors celebrated the return of the leather-jacketed founder credited with making the company the engine of the artificial intelligence revolution.

Three years earlier, OpenAI’s board had dismissed Sam Altman, citing a lack of candor with directors. Five days later, Altman returned, and most of the directors responsible for his removal were out.

In both cases, directors discovered that formal authority to remove a chief executive does not mean the power to do so in practice. The episodes exposed a three-pronged weakness in corporate governance: the challenge of maverick founders, the extraordinary complexity of AI, and the growing dependence of the U.S. economy and national security on a handful of companies at the technological frontier.

Both Altman and Huang have personas, know-how, and market-moving power that made them unfireable. Yet if the boards of the country’s most consequential technology firms cannot exercise ultimate authority over management, these companies are effectively ungovernable. This reveals a major gap in corporate stewardship, underscoring the imperative of robust regulation to ensure that the vulnerabilities of powerful U.S. companies do not become fatal weaknesses for the country’s democracy and society writ large.

The iconic corporate founder is a hallmark of U.S. business culture. Henry Ford and Andrew Carnegie shaped society-altering industries around their personalities and distinctive working styles. Steve Jobs provides the most celebrated historic example of this type of figure in tech. Forced out of Apple in 1985, Jobs returned in 1997 when the company was in steep decline. His track record of inventiveness helped win back employees, customers, investors, and developers. He also persuaded Bill Gates to invest $150 million in Apple and commit to developing Microsoft software for Macintosh computers, building an ecosystem whose fortunes were intertwined with his own and that has dominated the market for decades.

These bold founders may have as much in common with an artist or creator than they do with fellow CEOs. A great architect or film director works with large teams but puts an unmistakable stamp on their work. Although a studio or tradition can continue after its originator dies or departs, investors, collaborators, and audiences do not always stay on.

This analogy helps explain why succession at frontier technology companies is so fraught. Investors bet on a founder’s judgment about technologies whose commercial potential is unproven. Engineers are inspired by a particular visionary. Customers and business partners invest in the future that the founder promises. As these forces rally, they reify perceptions of an individual’s genius, which attracts still more talent and capital. Confidence becomes self-perpetuating.

Such devotion is measurable. Huang topped Glassdoor’s 2026 ranking of CEOs with a 99 percent approval rating among employee reviewers. Thousands of employees reportedly signed a letter seeking his reinstatement this month. His reportedly cruel behavior toward certain employees seemingly did little to puncture that aura.

OpenAI’s 2023 crisis demonstrated the power of such fealty. After its board fired Altman, more than 95 percent of the company’s employees signed a letter threatening to resign unless he came back. Microsoft, OpenAI’s largest commercial partner, rolled out a red carpet to Altman, promising to allow him to rebuild his team there. Faced with losing the workforce that was OpenAI’s principal asset, the board folded. The employees, investors, and commercial partners whose confidence had helped make Altman successful overpowered those charged with supervising him.

These examples do not prove that founders are irreplaceable. Apple’s revenues more than doubled during the early years of John Sculley’s post-Jobs tenure in the 1980s; more recently, the company has thrived under Tim Cook since Jobs’s death. When Uber’s Travis Kalanick was forced out in 2017, investors worried about losing the transportation innovator’s aggressive founder. His successor, Dara Khosrowshahi, now presides over a company that generated $193 billion in gross bookings and $10 billion in free cash flow in 2025.

Board members are a little like grandparents. They admire and care about the baby, comforted that the parent—the CEO—does the daily grind. When the parent disappears, the board is left holding a crying, demanding infant. Sedate quarterly meetings suddenly turn into frantic round-the-clock Zooms. Having lost the one person who they trusted to raise the child, boards want nothing more than to once again pass the progeny into capable hands.

…

items.body:
Did the German news website NiUS publish a video reporting 113 infant deaths in cold Lower Saxony maternity wards due to low gas storage levels? No, that's not true: This is a made-up news story falsely presented with the "NiUS Live" logo of a real news outlet. A search of the NiUS website did not return any results matching the topic of this story.

The claim appeared in [a post](https://x.com/ColoursOfWorld1/status/2125498691188662394) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125170318/https://x.com/ColoursOfWorld1/status/2125498691188662394) ) by the @ColoursOfWorld1 account on X on Nov. 25, 2026, with a video 1 minute, 17 seconds long bearing the logo *NiUS Live*. The post caption read:

> 113 infant deaths in Lower Saxony. Delivery rooms at 13°C. Care homes at 11°C. Gas storage: Rehden at 22.6%, Wolfersberg at 0%. Merz says: "We're growing again." The cost of this "growth" is paid in lives. [#EnergyCrisis](https://x.com/hashtag/EnergyCrisis?src=hashtag_click) [#Merz](https://x.com/hashtag/Merz?src=hashtag_click)

This is what a screenshot of the video in the post looked like at the time of publication:

*(Image source: post by @ColoursOfWorld1 on X.)*

The text in the screenshot above reads:

> Wer trägt die Schuld am Tod von Babys in Geburtskliniken?

Google translated this:

> Who is to blame for the deaths of babies in maternity wards?

Lead Stories searched [Google News](https://news.google.com/search?q=113%20S%C3%A4uglingstode%20in%20Niedersachsen&hl=en-US&gl=US&ceid=US%3Aen) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125172414/https://news.google.com/search?q=113%20S%C3%A4uglingstode%20in%20Niedersachsen&hl=en-US&gl=US&ceid=US%3Aen) ) and [Yahoo News](https://search.yahoo.com/news/search;_ylt=A2RRt2akGQdr7gIAM3XQtDMD;_?fr=uh3_news_web&fr2=sb-top&p=113+S%C3%A4uglingstode+in+Niedersachsen.+) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125182143/https://search.yahoo.com/news/search;_ylt=A2RRt2akGQdr7gIAM3XQtDMD;_?fr=uh3_news_web&fr2=sb-top&p=113+S%C3%A4uglingstode+in+Niedersachsen.+) ) for the German phrase "113 Säuglingstode in Niedersachsen" (113 infant deaths in Lower Saxony). There were no relevant results returned. Lead Stories also searched the website of nius.de for the number [113](https://nius.de/search?term=113) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125170718/https://nius.de/search?term=113) ) and the [headline phrase](https://nius.de/search?term=Wer+trägt+die+Schuld+am+Tod+von+Babys+in+Geburtskliniken), "Wer trägt die Schuld am Tod von Babys in Geburtskliniken" (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125192304/https://nius.de/search?term=Wer%20tr%C3%A4gt%20die%20Schuld%20am%20Tod%20von%20Babys%20in%20Geburtskliniken) ) -- there were no results for either search. Lead Stories used the [advanced search](https://x.com/search?q=Wer%20tr%C3%A4gt%20die%20Schuld%20am%20Tod%20von%20Babys%20in%20Geburtskliniken%20(from%3Aniusde_)&f=top&src=typed_query) function on X to see if the headline had been posted by NiUS: "Wer trägt die Schuld am Tod von Babys in Geburtskliniken (from:niusde_)".

There were no relevant results at the time of publication (pictured below).

*(Image source: Advanced search on X.)*

The Gnida Project, a research group that tracks what it describes as Russian-backed disinformation campaigns, has attributed this fake news story to Storm-1516 (embedded below). In a Nov. 25, 2026, [post on X](https://x.com/gnidaproject/status/2125548431468835260) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261125172702/https://x.com/gnidaproject/status/2125548431468835260) ) they wrote:

> The latest Storm-1516 disinformation campaign is targeting Germany. The campaign promotes a false narrative that hospitals in Germany are not receiving enough heating in relation to the alleged low gas storage levels.

> The latest Storm-1516 disinformation campaign is targeting Germany. The campaign promotes a false narrative that hospitals in Germany are not receiving enough heating in relation to the alleged low gas storage levels.
> -- gnida project (@gnidaproject) [November 25, 2026](https://x.com/gnidaproject/status/2125548431468835260?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

Lead Stories reached out to NiUS for comment and will update this article if a reply is received.

items.body:
A flurry of hyperactive and melodic percussion establishes the unmistakable rhythmic vocabulary of Nyege Nyege Tapes before a burst of laughter rounds off the 33-second introduction to *3OK*, a fitting elevator pitch into the record’s unruly, exuberant world. Yet beneath the apparent chaos lies an intricate rhythmic architecture, bringing together **Zoë Mc Pherson**‘s deconstructed club experiments,**Jay Mitta**‘s breakneck Tanzanian singeli and**DJ Diaki** ‘s electro-balani.

Born out of extended improvisational sessions at Nyege Nyege’s Kampala studios in 2022 and aboard Hamburg’s former fishing vessel MS Stubnitz in 2023, *3OK* takes its title from the three musicians’ shared expression of approval, a simple “OK” bridging the absence of a common spoken language. Their spontaneous exchanges, sometimes stretching to an hour and constantly changing tempo, subsequently became the raw material for Mc Pherson’s painstaking reconstruction. The intricate breakbeat manipulations of [States of Fugue](https://sfx-space.bandcamp.com/album/states-of-fugue-sf02) and [Pitch Blender](https://sfx-space.bandcamp.com/album/pitch-blender-sf04) meet the frenetic momentum of Mitta’s [Tatizo Pesa](https://nyegenyegetapes.bandcamp.com/album/tatizo-pesa) and the increasingly elaborate production of his recent [Kazi Kwanza](https://nyegenyegetapes.bandcamp.com/album/kazi-kwanza). Rather than smoothing out their differences, Mc Pherson finds ways of making them coexist.

On “222”, recurring, reverb-drenched motifs open up pockets of space within the frantic percussion, creating overlapping planes of sound. “Singeli on TV” develops this spatial play further, its circular patterns and submerged electronic textures seeming to rotate at different depths. The six-minute “Stubnitz” is the record’s most sustained excursion into rhythmic delirium, its relentless momentum gradually acquiring an almost trance-like intensity. “Drill”, meanwhile, introduces an almost symphonic quality, its densely layered electronic gestures suggesting instrumental sections competing and converging amid the rhythmic onslaught.

Throughout, pitched figures double as percussion while drum patterns acquire melodic contours, the different elements becoming almost impossible to disentangle. There is also a distinctly cartoonish humour to the music, with rubbery synthesizers, exaggerated pitches and abrupt interruptions. Yet much of this playfulness was already present in the original sessions. Mc Pherson’s intervention was less about adding further absurdity than giving the material a sense of dramatic progression, allowing particular motifs to emerge from the relentless flux.

The closing “Orchestra”, featuring DJ Diaki, has something of an afterparty atmosphere. Its interlocking motifs and playful exchanges feel less like a grand finale than the musicians continuing to bounce ideas off one another after the main event, restoring something of the spontaneous camaraderie from which the project emerged.

[Jingxin Wang](https://www.instagram.com/wjx_hasnoenglishname/)‘s artwork, depicting three psychedelic eyes with intersecting orbits, offers a fitting visual analogy. Each musician retains a distinct perspective, yet their trajectories continually overlap, collide and realign. For all its escalating tempos, abrasive textures and irrepressible humour, *3OK* never loses its sense of collective purpose. There is order in this chaos, even if it rarely stays still long enough to reveal itself.

To find out how the combo came together I approched **Zoë Mc Pherson** directly.

**3OK began with jams with Jay Mitta and DJ Diaki, which you later took away and developed into the finished album. How did you approach that material in the studio — what made you decide that a particular spontaneous exchange should remain recognisable, while another could be cut up, reorganised or transformed completely?**

Oh my, this is a very good question, actually! This process took a lot of thought, and a lot of time too, and I’m really happy with where it ended up.

I wanted the essence of our encounter to come through, but I also wanted to share finished material: tracks that could become a mini album. I thought a lot about the musical balance between our parts, and about the match that brought Jay and me together for the residency: the Singeli / Jay side and the bass / breaks / Zoë side. Diaki comes in on the intro with his voice, and on the last track with several of his recognizable pads. I kept the jam sessions with the three of us for side B of the tape, since they have a more live feel.

I also thought about each person’s role and involvement. We were in different positions, with different privileges too: living in Africa or in Europe, being a man or a non-binary person, knowing more or less about the music industry. That made the project even more interesting to me.

When we jammed, we were all equally involved. Afterwards, Diaki and Jay felt the rough jam recordings already worked as finished tracks, and they trusted me to finish the work the way I envisioned it. It took me a moment to step into that role, because I cared about keeping everyone’s involvement balanced. I checked with them several times, and they were happy to let me run with it Honestly, I get it, it was a lot of work!

The jams kept changing BPM, so I couldn’t just chop and edit quickly, and the recordings were mono, so I had to give them more weight. I edited everything, replayed melodies with other synths and extracted parts, and the jams became my inspiration material. They were 20-minute to one-hour pieces that changed every couple of bars, full of precious memories of us playing together.

I didn’t want to make a Zoë Mc Pherson EP. I wanted everyone’s engagement to be present while bringing my own vision forward. So I followed the sounds I loved most: nostalgic, sad EDM synths and hyperactive, almost glitching rhythms that are clownesque and dark at the same time. I think it’s a really original match of music. I haven’t heard anything like it before, and I don’t think anyone has.

I was lucky to have friends in the studio, most of whom had seen us perform in the main room at Berghain during CTM Festival. Kasimyn (Gabber Modus Operandi and Hulubalang), DJ Scotch Egg and my friend Darin listened with me and helped me carve the tracks down and bring our different roles to the front.

Side A is the produced version. Side B includes a snippet of a live set, so listeners can hear where the music came from and nerd out on how this sound evolved. I’m proud of it!

**You, Jay and Diaki didn’t share a common spoken language during the original sessions, and the title comes from the three “OKs” that signalled everyone was happy with what was happening. How did that affect the way you listened and responded to each other, and did the absence of verbal discussion allow things to happen that might otherwise have been talked out of existence?**

…

items.title: Did Democrats blow it in Florida?
items.subtitle: Angie Nixon speaking at a rally in Kissimmee, Florida.
items.feedText: Joe Raedle/Getty Images. Eight years ago, Democrats retook the U.S. House, netting 41 seats and winning the national popular vote by 8.6 points in a textbook blue wave. But despite the rosy national environment, Republican Rick Scott narrowly defeated incumbent Democratic Senator Bill Nelson in Florida. In hindsight, that victory, on the heels of Donald Trump’s 2016 win in the state, was the harbinger of a death spiral for Florida Democrats that had begun years earlier. When I wrote about the Sunshine State back…
items.body:
Angie Nixon speaking at a rally in Kissimmee, Florida. Joe Raedle/Getty Images.

Eight years ago, Democrats retook the U.S. House, [netting 41 seats and winning the national popular vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_elections) by 8.6 points in a textbook blue wave. But despite the rosy national environment, Republican [Rick Scott narrowly defeated incumbent Democratic Senator Bill Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_Senate_election_in_Florida) in Florida. In hindsight, that victory, on the heels of Donald Trump’s 2016 win in the state, was the harbinger of a [death spiral for Florida Democrats](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida) that had begun years earlier.

When I [wrote about the Sunshine State back in February](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida), the consensus from both prediction markets and the experts I spoke with was that Democrats were highly unlikely to win the state in 2026. After a decade of losses and underinvestment, it looked like it could take another ten years for Democrats to turn Florida purple again. The short-term goal of the Florida Democratic Party (FDP) was less “win the 2026 Senate race” and more “[get out of the](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida) *[superminority](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida)* [in the state legislature](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida).”

But back then, no one knew that [2026 would be a blue tsunami](https://www.natesilver.net/p/after-an-extraordinary-wave-what) where Democrats would win the national popular vote by 13 points and net *nine* Senate seats.1 And yet they still lost both statewide races in Florida. Almost immediately, people started posting [post-election recriminations](https://x.com/hollyotterbein/status/2117796466551066896) that if Democrats had spent more in Florida, they could have pulled off at least one win.

So did Democrats blow a golden opportunity in Florida? Or is the state still too tough a target? That question should weigh on the party because in two short years, [Ashley Moody will be up for re-election](https://www.natesilver.net/p/an-extremely-unofficial-first-look).

[↗ natesilver.net](https://www.natesilver.net/p/did-democrats-blow-it-in-florida)

Release: datasette-charts 0.2a0

I introduced this new charting plugin for Datasette yesterday. Today it's gained integration with Datasette Agent, so now you can ask chat for a chart and it will create one for you using the same underlying chart suggestion and generation tools.

Here's a demo video, recorded on agent.datasette.io where you can sign in with GitHub to try the plugin yourself:

items.title: The Physics Wall Facing Orbital AI Data Centers
items.subtitle: Basing entire business plans on back-of-the-envelope calculations might not seem like the best idea.
items.feedText: However, according to a new paper available in preprint on arXiv by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, that is precisely what the companies touting orbital AI data centers are doing. While on paper, the math looks good, the physical constraints of actually utilizing all the processing power and free energy of the Sun that orbit provides is prohibitive in a number of ways - and it will be a long time before we have the technology to truly capitalize on the advantages of space-based AI.

items.feedText:
However all these are outshone by today’s twin title stories…

Jensen Huang is back. Eleven days after announcing his resignation, Nvidia announced his return as CEO, president and member of the Board of Directors. View post on X ↗

The board voted unanimously after more meetings with Jensen on Sunday and said it received input from senior U.S. officials (aka the Treasury Secretary and the President dialing into the board meeting). Colette Kress remains CFO, the independent directors’ investigation continues,…
items.body:
Congrats to Sierra on [tripling](https://x.com/sierraplatform/status/2124832956795539842?a=LMwTZcXTCy6VIdPRUb0&s=46) last year’s [$10B valuation](https://x.com/SierraPlatform/status/1963654362384724388), and to [Z.ai](http://z.ai/) for releasing [GLM 5.4](https://z.ai/blog/glm-5.4), their first looped transformer following Thinking Machine’s much smaller [Inkling Mini 2](https://x.com/miramurati/status/2123872534970208421) from last week. However all these are outshone by today’s twin title stories…

**Jensen Huang is**[back](https://x.com/aburducky/status/2124924846266277988/video/1?a=6-tbBZhGNaBzRNGkqhk&s=46)**.** Eleven days after [announcing his resignation](https://latent.space/p/ainews-jensen-huang-resigns-after-33-years-leading-nvidia/), Nvidia [announced](https://investor.nvidia.com/news/press-release-details/2026/NVIDIA-Board-Reinstates-Jensen-Huang-as-President-CEO-and-Board-Director/default.aspx) his return as CEO, president and member of the Board of Directors.

[View post on X ↗](https://x.com/alecqfong/status/2124938191761555517)

The board voted unanimously after [more meetings with Jensen on Sunday](https://x.com/lookner/status/2125067095113154824) and said it received input from senior U.S. officials (aka [the Treasury Secretary](https://x.com/CGasparino/status/2124899810314437062) and [the President dialing into the board meeting](https://x.com/rogoswami/status/2124881764535464261?a=wUcGlCxi-wvs1ZrGiJw&s=46)). Colette Kress remains CFO, the independent directors’ investigation continues, and Jensen’s Senate hearing is still due in 8 days. Nvidia also formed a board committee for national security and export control.

As [Matt Levine points out](https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/newsletters/2026-11-23/jensen-s-candor-is-satisfactory-now?accessToken=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzb3VyY2UiOiJTdWJzY3JpYmVyR2lmdGVkQXJ0aWNsZSIsImlhdCI6MTc5NTQ3NDYxNSwiZXhwIjoxNzk2MDc5NDE1LCJhcnRpY2xlSWQiOiJUT1lWVEtSMjRVODkwMCIsImJjb25uZWN0SWQiOiI5MjgxRkY1M0M2N0Q0Qzg5QUQxNUQyMDNGMjlEOEEyRiJ9.xJ5NMXrrwB70YTBP2MCG1blRaX5XHxD7S0fAVzCB7Vw), with the firing AND the rehiring by this board with involvement from the government, the investigators are now being put in a position of having had the outcome somewhat predetermined for them, because both have demonstrated that they did not need to wait for any further evidence to come to light.

**OpenAI put its pretraining loss curve on the record.** In [Perplexity and Intelligence](https://openai.com/index/perplexity-and-intelligence/), Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki plotted base-model log-perplexity back to GPT-3.5 (on their [internal held-out coding dataset](https://openai.com/index/perplexity-and-intelligence/#citation-top-3)… which has [notable caveats](https://x.com/ziv_ravid/status/2124685987402182737)):

[View post on X ↗](https://x.com/merettm/status/2124549218995949967)

Think of it as how surprised the model is by the next token on a held-out dataset. Lower is better. GPT-3.5 was around 0.99 and GPT-4 around 0.91. When OpenAI put a model around 0.76 (GPT6 Astra) to work on open math problems, [hundreds of frontier math problems started falling quickly](https://latent.space/p/ainews-quasi-riemann-hypothesis-openai/). Pachocki extrapolates that another jump in capabilities could come around 0.68–0.70.

This is all in context of [pacing the frontier](https://latent.space/p/ainews-fearing-rsi-openai-anthropic/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv). Pachocki proposes that labs agree on a first limit to development and spell out what would let them cross it, such as a successor to chain-of-thought monitoring. Microsoft’s [Mustafa Suleyman](https://x.com/mustafasuleyman/status/2124663594449318173) gave the first win by cosigning and joining in, running MAI-2 Base on OpenAI’s evaluation set and reporting 0.819. We’d need at least a couple more top labs to join this effort for it to gather steam as a real self-regulatory limit, most notably of course, Anthropic.

**

If your data is growing faster than planned, you need storage that grows with your business, feeds flash and GPUs with terabit-scale throughput, and doesn’t charge egress.

Backblaze B2 has delivered capacity tier storage for twenty years, manages more than six exabytes, and is trusted by leading neoclouds, labs, and gen AI companies.

Growth shouldn’t be something you sweat. We’ve got room for whatever you’re building.

items.title: Green light for Starmind: SpaceX gets approval to deploy 1 million AI satellites
items.subtitle: Earth orbit could get a lot more crowded in the coming years.

"This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said today (Nov. 25) in a statement announcing the approval. items.body:
Earth orbit could get a lot more crowded in the coming years.

The U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) just granted [SpaceX](https://www.space.com/18853-spacex.html) approval to deploy one million of its [Starmind](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/another-star-is-born-spacex-names-ai-megaconstellation-starmind) AI data-center satellites in orbit.

"This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said today (Nov. 25) in a [statement](https://x.com/BrendanCarrFCC/status/2125623026918002860) announcing the approval.

AI has become central to SpaceX's business plans and identity over the past year or so. For example, the company has said that it's eyeing a ["total addressable market" of $28.5 trillion](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/usd1-77-trillion-spacex-is-about-to-become-the-7th-most-valuable-american-company) over the long haul — and nearly $23 trillion of that is in "enterprise AI applications."

Starmind is key to those lofty ambitions. SpaceX founder and CEO [Elon Musk](https://www.space.com/18849-elon-musk.html) believes that the future of AI compute is in space, where energy (from [the sun](https://www.space.com/58-the-sun-formation-facts-and-characteristics.html)) is unlimited and there are no land-owning neighbors to lodge NIMBY complaints.

SpaceX aims to launch the first of its Starmind satellites in the third quarter of 2027. The spacecraft will fly on the company's fully reusable [Starship](https://www.space.com/spacex-starship-super-heavy.html) megarocket, which has deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen [Starlink](https://www.space.com/spacex-starlink-satellites.html) satellites on its [most recent two test flights](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/spacex-starship-flight-15-chopsticks-double-catch-super-heavy-ship).

Those 52 spacecraft are the vanguard of another enormous constellation: Musk has said that the next-gen Starlink network will eventually consists of about [100,000 satellites](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/satellites/spacex-wants-to-launch-100-000-starlink-satellites-to-orbit).

The planned numbers for Starlink and Starmind are truly mind-boggling. To put them into perspective: Since the dawn of the space age in 1957, humanity has launched a total of just 28,000 satellites, give or take a few hundred. And the biggest constellation ever operated to date, the current iteration of Starlink, consists of about 11,000 spacecraft.

These coming buildouts will require an enormous number of launches. Starship can carry a maximum of 60 V3 Starlink satellites per launch, for instance, so it will take about 1,700 liftoffs just to assemble that network (and more to maintain it, as the operational life of each satellite is expected to be about five years).

Putting so many satellites into orbit also raises the risks of collisions. SpaceX has proven to be extremely proficient in this regard with its current Starlink satellites, which can detect and avoid potential collisions autonomously. But more [evasive maneuvers](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/satellites/every-spacex-starlink-satellite-has-to-dodge-a-collision-almost-weekly-and-experts-fear-the-worst) will be required as space gets more and more crowded.

SpaceX isn't the only company that aims to operate data centers in space; [Cowboy Space](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/cowboy-space-unveils-big-iron-rocket-to-launch-20-000-ai-data-centers), Starcloud, [Blue Origin](https://www.space.com/19584-blue-origin-quiet-plans-for-spaceships.html) and Google, among other companies, have voiced similar ambitions. [Starcloud](https://www.space.com/technology/nvidia-gpu-heads-to-space-starcloud-1) and [Google](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/satellites/spacex-google-project-suncatcher-ai-satellite-transporter-18-mission), in fact, have already launched AI pathfinder satellites.

"Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America's leadership in SI," Carr said in the same statement. ("SI" stands for super intelligence, the Trump administration's preferred term for AI.)

"By moving compute capacity beyond [Earth](https://www.space.com/54-earth-history-composition-and-atmosphere.html), SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment," Carr added. "This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home."

items.body:
AI forecasters now equal or beat top human performance at traditional forecasting questions (eg [ForecastBench](https://forecastingresearch.substack.com/p/ai-models-have-likely-reached-parity), the [Metaculus Cup](https://www.economist.com/science-and-technology/2026/09/16/artificial-intelligence-now-beats-some-of-the-best-human-forecasters)).

These are usually specialized AIs with forecasting harnesses, created by forecasting startups (eg [FutureSearch](https://futuresearch.ai/), [Mantic](https://mantic.com/), [Preseen](https://preseen.com/)), but foundation models like ChatGPT and Claude are only about six months behind the specialized models, so by the end of the year they’ll match top humans too.

In the past, the options for getting top-human-level forecasts were slim and inconvenient. You could hire a team of superforecasters to work on the problem, but this would cost thousands of dollars and take weeks. Or you could check prediction markets (or Metaculus), but they only have a small sample of general-interest questions and are constantly trying to screw you over by gaming resolution criteria.

The rise of AI forecasters solves these problems more cleanly and comprehensively than almost anyone thought possible just a year ago. The “science of forecasting”, which only recently felt like trying to pick the least-bad of various bad options, now faces tasks more like “what kind of magnifying glass should we use to inspect our giant novelty lottery check as we confirm that it’s real?” and “how do we spend our winnings?”

Specifically: AI forecasters now equal or beat top human performance at traditional forecasting questions. We need to learn how this success decays as we move to different types of non-traditional forecasting questions.

I recently got to talk to some people at the [Forecasting Research Institute](https://forecastingresearch.org/), one of the leaders in this field. Here’s my impression of the remaining challenges:

**1: Can AI do conditional forecasts?**

A traditional forecasting question asks something like: will the Democrats win the next election?

A conditional forecasting question is more like: *if* the Democrats win the next election, how will that affect the chances of a stock market crash?

Conditional forecasting questions are more exciting than traditional ones because they directly speak to policy outcomes. If we defund the police, how will that affect crime rates (compared to the counterfactual where we hold police funding constant)? If we mandate COVID vaccinations, how will that affect COVID mortality and myocarditis mortality (compared to the counterfactual where vaccines are voluntary / banned)?

Prediction markets have been slow to experiment with these, partly because of annoying logistical issues (you have to refund people’s money if the condition doesn’t come true) and partly because they entice fewer customers than new forms of degenerate sports gambling. AI forecasters don’t have this problem; you can ask an AI forecaster any of those questions above right now, and the big companies ([FutureSearch](https://futuresearch.ai/docs/forecast-conditional-scenarios/), [Preseen](https://blog.preseen.com/p/predicting-science-and-technology), [Mantic](https://blog.mantic.com/p/friday-forecasts-2)) have it as an explicit feature.

What remains is to prove that AI forecasters’ great performance on traditional questions carries over to conditional questions. About a year ago, FRI tested this and found that it didn’t - the AIs of the time did significantly worse on conditional questions. It seemed like some kind of weird misunderstanding where the AI didn’t entirely understand the concept.

Will this flip like a switch? At some point, the AI is smart enough to fully grasp conditionals, and it becomes exactly as good at conditional forecasting as the regular type? The experts I talked to thought no - as it gets smarter, its conditional forecasting ability will improve gradually. Where is it now? The experts weren’t willing to hazard a guess on whether it was better or worse than the average smart human, although they did think it was still worse than top superforecasters. They’re working on a benchmarking experiment that should give us a better measure of this in a few months.

**2: Can AI do truly causal forecasts?**

There’s a known flaw in standard conditional forecasting. When we ask “if the Democrats win the next election, will the economy go down?”, what we really want to know is a causal question - does voting for Democrats hurt the economy?

But that’s not what we asked. Suppose we’re wondering this in 2025, so we ask “If the Democrats win in 2026, is the economy more likely to be bad in 2027?” But maybe the Democrats will win in 2026 because there’s a already a bad economy (eg the Republican president implements tariffs and declares war on Iran, raising prices and making him historically unpopular), and then that bad economy continues into 2027. So the answer to the question “If the Democrats win in 2026, is the economy more likely to be bad in 2027?” is yes, but we still don’t know whether voting for Democrats in 2026 is good or bad for the economy.

Prediction markets can’t answer this question, because they can only be used to predict observable events that let us give payouts to successful gamblers. Might AI superforecasters succeed where the markets fail? Could you just prompt them with “please answer the unobservable causal question, instead of the easily-resolved conditional one”?

The experts I talked to weren’t excited about that particular prompt, but they did point out that a causal forecast is basically a combination of conditional forecasts. That is, if your original conditional forecast implicitly considered the four different combinations of two variables - that is:

- p(Democrats win & economy good)
- p(Democrats win & economy bad)
- p(Republicans win & economy good)
- p(Republicans win & economy bad)

…then things like “the previous economy was good” or “we’re at war with Iran” are just more variables you can add to the stew. It would be crazy to ask humans to forecast 2^10 branches so you could combine ten variables, but for AIs that could just mean a bit higher API spend. If you capture enough relevant variables in your “conditional” forecast, and find that the economy is still worse when the only one you’ve changed is whether or not the Democrats win, that’s a causal forecast. At least one company already tries something like this, though there are no studies of how well it works.

items.body:
# This Well-Known Butterfly is Actually Three Species in Disguise - Nautilus

## This Well-Known Butterfly is Actually Three Species in Disguise

A new discovery after 250 years

3:00 PM CST on November 23, 2026

Sometimes discovering a new species is a question of looking a little bit closer at wildlife we already know all about—which is how the Colobura cryptica butterfly has been identified in the tropical rainforests of Central and South America.

Butterflies of the Colobura genus are found all over these areas, and for more than 250 years, C. cryptica has been hiding in plain sight as the Colobura dirce species. In 2001, researchers realized that C. dirce populations actually included a second, distinct species, which was formally named Colobura annulata in 2001. Now, we have a third.

Read more: “ What a Massive Butterfly Count Reveals ”

It was caterpillars being studied in Venezuela that offered a big clue: They lacked the pale body markings seen on the other two species. As adults, these butterflies are harder to tell apart (what are known as cryptic species), but the differences in the caterpillar patterns prompted researchers to take a fresh look at 670 specimens stored in museums.

Alongside DNA analysis of those collected in the field, as well as careful comparisons of the wings of adults, the third species emerged. “It’s crazy to think about,” study author Anisha Sapkota said in a statement . “These butterflies look almost exactly the same and are found in the exact same place at the same time.”

In adult butterflies, C. cryptica is tricky to spot even for experts. All that tells it apart physically is the uniformity of the width of a gray band along the wing, and how well the wings reflect ultraviolet radiation. As disguises go, it’s pretty effective. The genetic comparisons were definitive though, and so, the new species is official—the end result of some careful caterpillar observations.

Now that researchers are aware of all three species, they can start to look at how their distributions and habits vary across Central and South America. The study authors think that even though there’s a lot of overlap in where these species live, that vertical stratification may have played a role in their isolation and eventual speciation. C. cryptica and C. annulata are usually found in forest canopies, while C. dirce more typically live in the undergrowth.

Another open question is how the butterflies recognize mates of the same species, with such minor physical differences. It’s possible that UV coloration is involved here too. UV-reflecting scales are relatively common across moths and butterflies.

Whatever the case, they’re certainly three of a kind.
