# USA: US-Gericht spricht Huawei wegen Betrugs schuldig

Huawei: Der chinesische Technologiekonzern wurde vor Gericht schuldig gesprochen. Foto: IMAGO/ZUMA Wire New York. Der chinesische Technologiekonzern Huawei ist in den USA in einem jahrelangen Strafverfahren schuldig gesprochen worden. Eine Jury in Brooklyn befand das Unternehmen am Dienstag in zehn von zwölf Anklagepunkten für schuldig, darunter Bankbetrug, Verstöße gegen Sanktionen und Diebstahl von Geschäftsgeheimnissen.

Die Vorwürfe entbehrten jeder rechtlichen Grundlage, teilte Huawei mit. Man werde rechtliche Schritte einleiten, um die eigenen Rechte zu schützen. Vom Vorwurf der Bildung einer kriminellen Vereinigung sprachen die Geschworenen den Netzwerkausrüster frei.

Die Anklage warf Huawei vor, Banken wie HSBC über Geschäfte im Iran getäuscht zu haben. Meldungen der Nachrichtenagentur Reuters aus den Jahren 2012 und 2013 hatten maßgeblich dazu beigetragen, diese Aktivitäten aufzudecken. Den Geschworenen lag zudem eine Erklärung der Huawei-Finanzchefin Meng Wanzhou vor, in der sie illegale Iran-Geschäfte eingeräumt hatte.

Das Gericht sah es ferner als erwiesen an, dass Huawei über zwei Jahrzehnte hinweg Technologien von US-Firmen wie Cisco und T-Mobile gestohlen hat. Die Verteidigung wies dies zurück: Die Anklage habe sich lediglich unzusammenhängende Vorfälle herausgepickt. Der Erfolg von Huawei beruhe auf eigener Forschung.

## Crazy Tube Circuits Rapture – Das Wichtigste in Kürze

- Was für ein Verzerrer ist der Rapture? Der Rapture ist ein Amp-in-a-Box-Overdrive-Pedal und liefert Zerrgrade vom leichten Clean-Boost bis in den Medium-Gain-Bereich.
- Was hat der Rapture mit dem Triptychon zu tun? Der Rapture entspricht der Drive-Sektion des Triptychon und wurde um einen schaltbaren Gain-Boost- sowie eine zusätzliche Clipping-Option erweitert.
- Was sagt der Test? Der Rapture macht dem Attribut „Amp-in-a-Box“ alle Ehre und überzeugt als vielseitiger Verzerrer mit herausragender Ansprache und Dynamik.

## Was steckt drin? Aufbau und Features

Der Rapture sitzt in einem goldenen Gehäuse mit den Maßen (B × H × T) 65 × 47 × 110 mm und bringt schlanke 216 Gramm auf die Waage. In Bezug auf die Bedienelemente präsentiert sich das Pedal als klassischer 3-Knob-Overdrive mit Potis für die Ausgangslautstärke (Master), den Grad der Verzerrung (Gain) und den Anteil der hohen Frequenzen (Tone).

Zusätzlich gibt es zwei Wahlschalter zum Aktivieren einer zweiten Gain-Stufe (More) und einer alternativen Clipping-Variante (Mod). In Betrieb genommen wird der Rapture über einen Soft-Switch-Fußschalter (True-Bypass) und kann mit einem Standard-Netzteil zwischen 9 V und 18 V (mind. 50 mA) betrieben werden. Über das Halten des Fußschalters ist es zudem möglich, den Power-Up-Status nach erfolgter Stromzufuhr festzulegen.

items.title: The Cauldron and the Making of the Modern Middle East
items.subtitle:
Calder Walton in Harvard Kennedy Center Belfer Center Website:

Simon Sebag Montefiore is one of Britain’s finest historians—a national treasure.

items.body:
Calder Walton in *Harvard Kennedy Center Belfer Center Website:*

**Simon Sebag Montefiore** is one of Britain’s finest historians—a national treasure. In [The Cauldron](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/803078/the-cauldron-by-simon-sebag-montefiore/), he tackles a subject that lesser historians would not attempt: the making of the modern Middle East in all its bewildering complexity. The region is too large for a single national story, too diverse for a civilisational shorthand and too politically charged for comfortable detachment. Its history is usually broken into manageable pieces: the end of the Ottoman Empire, the creation of Israel, Arab nationalism, oil, political Islam and American intervention. Montefiore attempts something far more ambitious. In one sweeping narrative, he carries the reader from Morocco to Iran and from the capture of Riyadh in 1902 to the wars of 2026. The result is a remarkable feat: panoramic without becoming bloodless, learned without losing narrative momentum, and passionate without surrendering to partisanship.

More [↗ belfercenter.org](https://www.belfercenter.org/research-analysis/book-review-cauldron-and-making-modern-middle-east).

items.body:
ICIJ’s [China Capital](https://www.icij.org/investigations/china-capital/) investigation revealed how the London units of the world’s largest bank, the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC), routinely financed companies to push Beijing’s geopolitical agenda, sometimes flouting their own compliance rules in the process.

ICIJ, in collaboration with 23 media partners, obtained 4.8 million internal documents leaked from ICBC London, including loan application forms, due diligence reports, know-your-client documents and internal email exchanges.

To better understand ICBC’s London operations, the ICIJ data team dissected more than 200 loan agreements and amendments dated from 2010 to 2024. ICIJ found that ICBC London partnered with at least one other Chinese state-owned commercial bank in more than half of the agreements and amendments reviewed. Among the Chinese lenders, Bank of China stands out as the main Chinese partner of ICBC London: They joined forces in 102 agreements.

ICIJ’s analysis shows that the London units of the Chinese banking giant usually partnered with other Chinese and international banks on loan agreements often worth hundreds of millions of dollars—or more. ICIJ identified 36 loan agreements and amendments for which half or more of the money was provided by Chinese lenders. In 16 of those cases, the financial commitments were entirely from Chinese banks.

ICBC documents prepared as part of the due diligence process on the bank’s clients show how the bank at times downplayed compliance problems or otherwise justified continued business with clients it had classified as high risk, an ICIJ review found. In Zambia, ICBC played a role in exacerbating the country’s debt burden, creating dependency on Chinese loans and contributing to years-long difficulties for Zambians. In the U.K., ICBC bank officers disregarded legal risks faced in a U.S. court by one of their Chinese clients so the bank could finance the company’s acquisition of a British competitor and consolidate its market share.

The case studies below reveal the inner workings of a bank balancing the advancement of the agenda of the Chinese party-state with its own global commercial ambitions.

## Ignoring Red Lights

01

In May 2024, ICBC’s high-risk client list included the financing arm of global fuel trader and distributor Puma Energy, along with a major shareholder Trafigura Pte. Ltd., a trading giant registered and headquartered in Singapore with major trading operations in Switzerland, and two other Trafigura entities. Despite ICBC's concerns about Puma and Trafigura dating back to at least 2015, ICIJ identified 19 syndicated credit facility agreements involving Puma and Trafigura, between 2015 and 2024, with a combined value of $38.7 billion. ICBC's London entities committed a total of $1.4 billion across those facilities. In 2015, ICBC escalated its due diligence of Puma’s financing vehicle, Puma International Financing; in its May 2015 Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) report, it rated the company’s bribery risk as high. At the time, Puma's shareholders included Angola's state-owned oil company Sonangol and Cochan Holdings LLC, an investment company founded and chaired by Angolan presidential adviser Leopoldino Fragoso do Nascimento. The report acknowledged extensive adverse media coverage alleging bribery and corruption involving senior Angolan officials, including then-President José Eduardo dos Santos and his children, as well as Sonangol, Cochan and Nascimento. Still, ICBC characterized much of the adverse reporting as “rumour based and unfounded” and continued the relationship, subject to enhanced monitoring. In February 2020, ICBC’s EDD report again identified allegations centered on Nascimento’s close ties to former President dos Santos and speculation in media reports and elsewhere that he had used political connections to acquire a stake in Puma Energy while serving as a public official. The report also noted that Nascimento had faced investigations into alleged corruption, conflicts of interest and money laundering in several countries. Yet ICBC cited reasons for discounting the risks, noting that Nascimento did “not appear to have been convicted” of wrongdoing. In December 2021, the U.S. Treasury sanctioned Nascimento and Cochan, saying Nascimento and another Angolan official had embezzled billions from the Angolan government. In 2025, an Angolan court convicted Nascimento of fraud, document forgery, money laundering and influence peddling. Likewise, ICBC's October 2019 Enhanced Due Diligence report came after a highly public Brazilian corruption investigation into allegations that commodity traders, including Trafigura, had bribed employees of Petrobras, Brazil’s state-owned and state-controlled oil company. A month earlier, Reuters reported allegations that senior Trafigura executives Mike Wainwright and José Larocca knew about the bribes. But ICBC's EDD report referred only to "two high-ranking executives” at Trafigura, without identifying them, despite separately listing both men as key controllers of Trafigura. Wainwright's adverse-media assessment was marked "No." ICBC continued the relationship, citing Trafigura's status as a longstanding "strategic client," the participation of major international banks in syndicated loans, its compliance controls and the absence of suspicious activity detected by ICBC. In 2024, Trafigura Beheer B.V., the Dutch-registered former parent company of the Trafigura Group, pleaded guilty in the U.S. to conspiring to violate U.S. anti-bribery laws in a scheme that ran from approximately 2003 to 2014. The companies also reached a settlement agreement with Brazilian authorities. Read responses Responses Trafigura: In response to ICIJ's questions, a Trafigura spokesperson said lender due diligence was a normal part of doing business and that the company cooperated with lenders' reviews, supported by its public financial and sustainability disclosures. Regarding the Petrobras bribery case, the spokesperson referred to Trafigura's 2024 statement announcing the resolution of the U.S. investigation, in which the company said the misconduct involved former employees or agents and was inconsistent with its principles and code of conduct. The statement said U.S. authorities had recognized improvements to Trafigura's anti-corruption compliance procedures. Puma: didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. Nascimento: didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. Angolan government: didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. Cochan: ICIJ could not successfully contact Cochan for comment. Sonangol: Didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. A legal representative for Mike Wainwright didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. José Larocca: didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. ICBC: Didn’t respond to ICIJ’s request for comment. Main borrowers Puma International Financing S.A., Trafigura Group Pte. Ltd., Trafigura Pte.

items.title: An Alarming Spike in Ectopic Pregnancy Deaths Was Hiding in Plain Sight in a Federal Dataset
items.subtitle: Ectopic pregnancy deaths have nearly doubled in the United States in recent years.
items.feedText:
Shawn Patrick Ouellette/Portland Portland Press Herald/Getty Images

For years, ProPublica has examined maternal health and the ongoing impacts of abortion bans since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. Data analysis has been central to that effort, offering a quantitative view into an area that has long been underresearched, especially as studying the impact of abortion bans has become politicized and federal agencies have been gutted under the Trump administration. For example, last year my colleagues un…
items.body:
Ectopic pregnancy deaths have nearly doubled in the United States in recent years. Shawn Patrick Ouellette/Portland Portland Press Herald/Getty Images

For years, ProPublica has examined maternal health and the [ongoing impacts of abortion bans](https://www.propublica.org/series/life-of-the-mother) since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. Data analysis has been central to that effort, offering a quantitative view into an area that has long been underresearched, especially as studying the impact of [abortion bans has become politicized](https://www.propublica.org/article/abortion-bans-deaths-state-maternal-mortality-committees) and [federal agencies have been gutted](https://projects.propublica.org/federal-health-worker-cuts-rfk-trump-administration/) under the Trump administration.

For example, last year my colleagues [uncovered a dramatic rise](https://www.propublica.org/article/texas-abortion-ban-sepsis-maternal-mortality-analysis) in sepsis rates since Texas instituted its abortion ban, which carries the strictest penalties for healthcare providers. The [number of blood transfusions](https://www.propublica.org/article/texas-abortion-ban-miscarriage-blood-transfusions) during emergency room visits for first-trimester miscarriage spiked in the state as well.

Most recently, my colleagues Andrea Suozzo, Sophie Chou, Kavitha Surana and I [examined pregnancy-related deaths on a national level](https://www.propublica.org/article/ectopic-pregnancy-deaths-doubled-analysis). We turned our attention to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. The agency collects information from death certificates and publishes totals based on variables like location, demographics and cause of death. It’s a commonly used resource for journalists and academics who want to learn more about trends in mortality.

Deaths involving an ectopic pregnancy are presented as a rate within three-year intervals to meet data suppression thresholds. Source: ProPublica analysis of CDC WONDER multiple cause of death and natality data. Lucas Waldron/ProPublica

The increase was particularly stark in states that had banned abortion.

Deaths involving an ectopic pregnancy are grouped into three-year periods to meet data suppression thresholds. States with abortion bans that begin at six weeks of pregnancy or earlier are considered to have a strict ban. Source: ProPublica analysis of CDC WONDER multiple cause of death and natality data. Lucas Waldron/ProPublica

This was a significant and serious finding. And as far as we could tell, the fact that the number of women who died from ectopic pregnancies nearly doubled after abortion bans came into effect hadn’t been reported before.

A death from an ectopic pregnancy should be a “never event,” according to Dr. Alice Abernathy, an OB-GYN in Philadelphia. And yet, as we later confirmed, more than a dozen leaders in the field of maternal health were unaware of the spike. Neither state governments *nor* the federal government, whose own dataset we were using, had publicly identified this trend.

How could it be that seemingly no one was aware of this but us?

The answer, as it turns out, is multifold and begins with the nature of the condition itself. Ectopic pregnancies occur when an embryo fails to properly implant in the uterus and begins to develop elsewhere, most commonly inside a fallopian tube. The pregnancy grows until it causes the organ to rupture, triggering catastrophic bleeding.

It is a rare condition, estimated to impact up to 2% of pregnancies, but it is incredibly dangerous.

“I genuinely thought I was going to die,” said Kyleigh Thurman, whose right fallopian tube ruptured after she struggled to get ectopic care in Texas in 2023.

“There were a few times I asked my husband if I was going to die,” Leitaea Lowrimore of Oklahoma said in an ongoing lawsuit challenging an abortion ban, after being denied treatment for an ectopic pregnancy at multiple hospitals in February. “I kept thinking about our kids.”

Even before ectopic pregnancy deaths began rising, the condition was noted as the leading cause of death in the first trimester of pregnancy. Yet it has received little research attention. For example, the CDC doesn’t track how many ectopic pregnancies occur a year and doesn’t require healthcare providers to report them. The [most recent nationwide study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6983328/) we could find examined data only through 2013.

The U.S. doesn’t conduct national maternal mortality reviews in the same way as countries like the United Kingdom, which responded to a similar spike in the years after the COVID-19 pandemic by instituting changes to emergency services and promoting awareness of ectopic pregnancy symptoms. Instead, in our country, much of the work of investigating pregnancy-related deaths is left to state committees.

This creates a large potential knowledge gap. In individual states, the number of ectopic deaths is small and subject to a lot of variation, making it harder to spot a trend. After our story was published, we reached out to maternal mortality review committees in states with abortions bans; many of them responded that they didn’t identify an increase in ectopic deaths and that, despite the findings of our reporting, they had no plans to examine this issue further.

We realized the fact that nearly double the number of women are dying from ectopic pregnancies is visible at only the national level.

It is unclear why the CDC and other federal agencies across two administrations have failed to publicly respond to the increase in deaths despite having access to the same information ProPublica analyzed. We reached out to the CDC to ask what the agency has done to investigate or address this trend. It has epidemiologists who review death and birth records and has in the past done its own investigations and analyses. A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the CDC, didn’t provide a direct answer to that question but said the agency continues to track maternal mortality trends, investigate their causes and provide funding for research.

Maternal experts agree that the government’s capacity to respond to this trend has been significantly reduced as a result of the staffing cuts initiated by the Trump administration since the beginning of last year. The CDC’s Division of Reproductive Health, for example, lost most of its 100 employees, according to a lawsuit filed by more than a dozen states’ attorneys general last year.

This lack of awareness surrounding ectopic pregnancy deaths is imperiling women’s lives.

### Read More

[Ectopic Pregnancy Deaths Have Nearly Doubled. It’s Worse in States With Abortion Bans.](https://www.propublica.org/article/ectopic-pregnancy-deaths-doubled-analysis)

items.body:
Vernor Vinge is possibly my favorite science fiction author of all time.1 The Singularity, which he famously predicted would happen somewhere between 2005 and 2030, features heavily in most of [his stories](https://www.amazon.com/stores/Vernor-Vinge/author/B000APOW0E?ref=ap_rdr&shoppingPortalEnabled=true&ccs_id=8c9a5a85-687e-4609-8f62-c647a22cfbe5). It usually happens the same way: an Intelligence Explosion, of the type envisioned by [I.J. Good](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I._J._Good) — the smarter AI gets, the faster it’s able to make itself even smarter, meaning that AI becomes godlike nearly instantaneously once it reaches a certain threshold of capability.

Almost every discussion about AI safety that I hear in San Francisco or read in the tech blogosphere centers around this sort of event. The discussions are all about whether recursive self-improvement (RSI) is near, and whether we should “pace the frontier” — i.e., deliberately slow down or pause AI progress — to stop RSI from creating an intelligence explosion.

As I’ve listened to these arguments, I’ve grown increasingly skeptical that this is the right discussion we should be having. But before I explain why, let me quickly summarize the debate itself, to give an idea of what the arguments look like.

#### The intelligence explosion debate, in brief

In fact, I’ve published some pieces of that discussion on this blog. Back in September, Ramez Naam wrote a guest post arguing that an intelligence explosion is not imminent:

His basic arguments were:

- OpenAI data show that AI is still only able to automate short chunks of the AI research process.
- AI research is subject to diminishing returns, so that each increase in AI capability should buy less of a speedup in the pace of automated research.
- Diminishing returns also mean that accelerating AI progress will require exponentially more of other resources, such as compute and money.
- There’s no sign yet of an acceleration in the rate of AI progress.

In [a follow-up post](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/can-a-million-ai-agents-create-superintelligence), Ramez did a deeper dive on the topic of agent swarms, arguing that they’re not as effective as many people believe.

Theo Jaffee [echoed these arguments](https://x.com/theojaffee/status/2123231377177157992), noting that OpenAI’s data shows that AI hasn’t even been able to fully automate smaller research tasks yet:

Source: OpenAI via [Theo Jaffee](https://x.com/theojaffee/status/2123231377177157992)

Luis Garicano and Alex Imas also wrote a post downplaying the likelihood of an intelligence explosion:

[Silicon Continent Are we approaching an intelligence explosion? (Dear reader: this is an unusual post; it gets a bit technical. Alex and I are trying to do something hard here: look at the data and try to understand what they tell us about the intelligence explosion. There is math, Greek letters, and two models. So please bear with us, and if you are bored, apologies. We think it is worth making an exception here… Read more 12 days ago · 65 likes · 13 comments · Luis Garicano and Alex Imas](https://www.siliconcontinent.com/p/are-we-approaching-an-intelligence?utm_source=substack&utm_campaign=post_embed&utm_medium=web&embedding_publication_id=35345)

Their arguments are more economic in nature. They show that although AI progress has accelerated, it also shows diminishing returns in terms of research spending, meaning that every unit of progress has come with a higher price tag:

Source:[Garicano and Imas](https://www.siliconcontinent.com/p/are-we-approaching-an-intelligence)

They also estimate an economic model of RSI,2 and conclude that ideas in AI research are probably getting harder to find, reducing the likelihood of an intelligence explosion.

On the other side of the debate, we have [the recent METR report](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/) about Anthropic’s internal progress in automating AI research. The report uses Anthropic’s own internal measure of AI capability, AECI, rather than the better-known public ECI. It also relies on data that aren’t public, meaning that deciding how much of the report to believe requires a lot of guesswork and assumption-making. But the basic story METR tells is that Claude is already speeding up Anthropic’s research process by a lot:

> As we describe below, we were able to confidently determine that the acceleration [of AI progress in late 2025] was not due to an acceleration in the rate of growth of training compute…We guess that a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current…acceleration is due to AI.

Dwarkesh Patel, meanwhile, argues that AI research isn’t that different from math, and that the same factors that made AI suddenly go from useless to godlike at math will happen soon with AI’s own self-improvement:

[Dwarkesh Podcast The avalanche that hit math is coming for AI development Read more 12 days ago · 547 likes · 103 comments · Dwarkesh Patel](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/rsi?utm_source=substack&utm_campaign=post_embed&utm_medium=web&embedding_publication_id=35345)

He writes:

> It’s crazy how fast we went from, in 2023, “This model can’t reliably add four-digit numbers,” to…about a month ago, “Okay, it fucking [solved a Millennium Prize problem](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/) in 88 hours.”…
> AI research is actually surprisingly similar to the type of mathematical progress that current AIs are disproportionately good at: unlocking a ton of low-hanging fruit by applying a combination of incredible persistence and a superhuman capacity to connect ideas from lots of adjacent domains…In every domain where we can check answers and give AIs thousands of rounds of practice—for example, competitive programming contests, or well-scoped open math problems—they’ve gone from worse than most humans to better than the best humans within a few years…AI research has those same verifiable properties…
> Once AI is as good as the best humans at AI research, algorithmic progress will get radically faster…Today’s AIs already do work at about 10 times human speed. And automated researchers would also be working around the clock, nights and weekends included. As a result, each individual automated researcher will be cramming in roughly 50x more work every calendar week than a human researcher can do…During the intelligence explosion, automated engineers will build tens of thousands of times more [reinforcement learning] training environments than we have currently.

So that’s the debate. Basically, it depends on whether ideas get harder to find faster than AI gets better at finding ideas, and only time will tell which one wins.

But as I said, while this debate is intellectually interesting, I’m not sure how much it matters.

#### How useful is this debate?

items.body:
NASA announced Monday that NASA+ content has found its first theatrical home at The Greenbelt Cinema in Greenbelt, Maryland, expanding the agency’s reach across major viewing platforms and bringing space even closer to home.

“The National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958 calls us to share our story of space exploration with the broadest possible audience, and our partners help us accomplish that,” said Rebecca Sirmons, general manager of NASA+ at the agency’s Headquarters in Washington. “Artemis II captured the imagination of the Artemis generation, but we are just getting started. With Artemis III on the horizon and our sights set on building humanity’s first Moon Base, this is only the beginning of our story being told, and we’ll continue sharing transparent, engaging content every step of the way.”

NASA and The Greenbelt Cinema will kick off their partnership with screenings of the NASA+ original documentary “The Europa Concept,” which follows NASA’s journey to investigate the science driving future exploration of Europa, Jupiter’s icy moon. Dates for screenings will be announced soon on NASA.gov.

Future programming may include other NASA+ original content, in-person live streaming events of NASA’s Artemis missions, including the first crewed mission to the Moon under the Artemis program, additional Europa content, and more. NASA+ also will remain available for free, with no ads, through the NASA app and on the agency’s [website](https://plus.nasa.gov/).

Earlier this year during its [Ignition](https://www.nasa.gov/ignition/) event, NASA outlined a bold path forward for the agency, including increasing the cadence of [Artemis](https://www.nasa.gov/artemis) missions to the lunar surface, and building the first [Moon Base](https://www.nasa.gov/moonbase), among other agency priorities. Partnerships like this one help NASA maximize engagement with communities around the world by making the agency’s missions and educational content available to viewers on their preferred devices and channels.

For more information about NASA missions, visit:

**[https://www.nasa.gov](https://www.nasa.gov)**

items.body:
WhatsApp arbeitet an einer neuen Möglichkeit, Unterhaltungen etwas lebendiger zu gestalten. Künftig lassen sich animierte Sticker mit Ton versehen und direkt innerhalb eines Chats abspielen. Die Funktion wird bereits an erste Nutzer der iPhone-Beta verteilt. Gleichzeitig erweitert die Tagesschau ihr Angebot innerhalb des Messengers um einen eigenen Kanal für Nachrichten in Einfacher Sprache.

## Eigene Sticker mit Ton erstellen

Wie [WABetaInfo berichtet](https://wabetainfo.com/whatsapp-is-rolling-out-sticker-messages-with-audio-on-ios/), unterstützt die aktuelle WhatsApp-Testversion 26.46.10.70 für iOS sogenannte Sound-Sticker. Dabei handelt es sich um animierte Sticker, die zusätzlich eine kurze Tonspur enthalten.

Eigene Sound-Sticker lassen sich direkt im Sticker-Editor erstellen. Dazu wird zunächst ein Video aus der Fotomediathek ausgewählt, das WhatsApp automatisch in einen animierten Sticker umwandelt. Über eine neue Schaltfläche kann anschließend ein passender Ton hinzugefügt werden.

Zur Auswahl stehen der Originalton des Videos, verschiedene vorgefertigte Geräusche sowie eigene Aufnahmen. Auch Audiodateien aus der Dateien-App lassen sich verwenden. Wer möchte, kann direkt im Editor eine kurze Sprachnachricht aufnehmen.

## Wiedergabe erst nach Antippen

Damit Gruppenchats nicht plötzlich zur Geräuschkulisse werden, spielen die Sticker ihren Ton nicht automatisch ab. Stattdessen erscheint ein kleines Lautsprechersymbol, über das die Wiedergabe gestartet werden kann. Der Ton wird anschließend dreimal wiederholt.

Die Neuerung ist zunächst für ausgewählte Betatester verfügbar. Vereinzelt soll sie bereits in der regulären App-Store-Version auftauchen. Wann WhatsApp die Funktion für alle Nutzer freischaltet, ist noch offen. Schon bisher konnten Anwender [eigene Sticker aus Fotos erstellen](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/whatsapp-schaltet-neue-formatier-optionen-fuer-alle-nutzer-frei-230439/).

## Tagesschau startet Kanal in Einfacher Sprache

Abseits der neuen Sticker gibt es auch Neuigkeiten bei den WhatsApp-Kanälen. Die ARD bietet ihre „Tagesschau in Einfacher Sprache“ ab sofort über einen [eigenen WhatsApp-Kanal](https://www.tagesschau.de/ard-angebote-in-leichter-und-einfacher-sprache) an. Damit erweitert der Sender sein seit 2024 bestehendes Nachrichtenangebot.

Von Montag bis Freitag veröffentlicht die Redaktion von ARD-aktuell dort Texte zu ausgewählten Nachrichten sowie einen Link zur vollständigen Sendung. Regelmäßig wird außerdem auf weitere Nachrichtenangebote in Leichter und Einfacher Sprache hingewiesen.

Das Format richtet sich unter anderem an Menschen mit Schwierigkeiten beim Lesen oder Lernen, Menschen mit kognitiven Einschränkungen sowie Personen, die Deutsch lernen. Kurze Sätze und verständliche Begriffe sollen den Zugang zu aktuellen Nachrichten erleichtern.

Parallel hat die ARD eine neue Übersichtsseite eingerichtet, auf der sämtliche entsprechenden Nachrichtenangebote gebündelt werden. Wer dem neuen Kanal folgt und die Glocke aktiviert, kann sich über neue Beiträge benachrichtigen lassen.

[★ iPhone-Ticker bei Google bevorzugen ★](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=iphone-ticker.de)

Der Beitrag [WhatsApp: Sticker bekommen Ton, Tagesschau startet neuen Kanal](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/whatsapp-sticker-bekommen-ton-tagesschau-startet-neuen-kanal-291402/) Wurde zuerst auf [iphone-ticker.de](https://www.iphone-ticker.de) veröffentlicht.

items.body:
Josie Ford

**[Feedback](https://www.newscientist.com/topic/feedback)** is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more

Reader Jenny Ozanne writes to tell us of a horrific incident that befell her partner. He had bought [Audrey Niffenegger’s novel](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2594474-theres-two-ways-of-doing-time-travel-right-says-audrey-niffenegger/) *The Time Traveler’s Wife* as a CD audiobook, to listen to on long car journeys.

“After a while, he complained that the plot was completely impossible to follow,” writes Jenny. “It was only when I checked his player that I realized he had accidentally set the CD to ‘shuffle’. “

Jenny raises two points, which Feedback heartily endorses: “I’m still not sure what’s more impressive: the story’s ability to survive total chronological chaos, or the fact that he listened to three random chapters before suspecting anything was wrong.”

Feedback would suggest that *The Time Traveler’s Wife* might be the ideal novel to experience on shuffle, since the narrative is heavily non-linear. The main character hops uncontrollably back and forth through history. This led us to wonder: would any similarly chrono-displaced stories survive the experience of being played on shuffle, or even be improved by it?

We wondered, for instance, about David Mitchell’s *Cloud Atlas*. This has six stories set in different periods, including a future in which human clones are used as cheap labour, and a more distant future in which everything has gone a bit *Mad Max*. The stories are linked by characters in later timelines reading about the earlier ones, and by subtle coincidences. What would it be like on shuffle?

However, after careful reflection, we realised there is only one correct answer to this, and that is Shane Carruth’s 2004 film *Primer*, which tells the story of two tech bros who invent a time machine in their garage. At first, they use it to go back in time and make money on the stock exchange, only to become caught up in an escalating web of betrayal and deception as they endlessly rewrite their lives.

*Primer* is so overcomplicated, so mind-wreckingly confusing, that some poor soul once went so far as to draw a diagram trying to convey its timeline. [Posted on Reddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/movies/comments/1wxpfc/detailed_explanationtimeline_of_shane_carruths/) by u/Clawz114, the diagram looks like a cross between a metro map and a flowchart of the inner workings of a chemical factory. It is therefore possible that playing the scenes in random order might actually cause the film to make more sense.

## The scent of success

It’s that time of year when many of us are thinking, “Oh blimey, I need to buy everyone presents” and then having a meltdown when we can’t think of anything. The last refuge of the true gift scoundrel is, of course, the scented candle. This item might as well come with a note saying, “Sorry, I couldn’t think of anything”.

Readers looking to step up their scented candle game may wish to investigate [JD + Kate Industries](https://jdandkateindustries.com/), which is run by a pair of humour writers with a sideline in themed scented candles. They have taken these tedious items to new and different places.

For instance, consider the Late Bronze Age Collapse scented candle, which “commemorates everyone’s favorite late 13th century [BC] widespread societal collapse”. Happily, it doesn’t smell of violence and decay, but rather of “burning cedar”, since “Lebanese cedar was a popular building material in the Late Bronze Age”.

Those with more contemporary tastes may wish to consider the AI scented candle, which has a little sculpture of a data centre on the top, “surrounded by a post-apocalyptic, bombed-out city”. What does it smell of, you ask? “Diesel generator exhaust fumes”.

Finally, those nostalgic for the headier days of space exploration might appreciate the Apollo 11 scented candle. Disappointingly, this doesn’t smell of moon dust, which, as we understand it, basically smells of burning because it reacts with oxygen on contact. Instead, its scent mimics “a certain powdered orange drink mix often associated with the space program, but that was not brought on Apollo 11. The astronauts brought a generic, grapefruit-flavored powdered drink mix instead, because they selfishly did not consider us and our desire to market candles.”

Feedback has no idea if these candles are any good, but we enjoyed JD + Kate’s website a lot.

## By the letter

Let us foray once again into the wonderful world of scientific acronyms. First, two reader claims that, for reasons that will become obvious, we cannot verify.

Michael Berkson tells us: “As a solicitor my late wife was involved in development of insurance for doctors. The firm had to tell the client that they needed to choose a better name. Their original choice was Professional Indemnity Support Scheme.” Michael says the clients were open to replacing “scheme” with “service”, which helps not at all.

Likewise, Jim Taylor asserts that he was once confronted with a military programme intended to ensure that spare parts would always be available for key equipment. It was called the Contractor Repair Advanced Provisioning System.

Finally, a story we can confirm is true because we looked it up. Reader Geraldine Beare is an indexer, which is one of those jobs that we often forget about but would swiftly notice if it wasn’t done. “I am at present indexing a book on goats,” says Geraldine. Through this assignment she has learned the acronym “OMAGOD”, which she recommends saying “quickly, or perhaps in a vaguely Scottish accent”. It actually stands for ovine mouth and gum obscure disease.

**Got a story for Feedback?**

*You can send stories to Feedback by email at feedback@newscientist.com. Please include your home address. This week’s and past Feedbacks can be [seen on our website](https://www.newscientist.com/article-type/feedback/).*

items.body:
On a foggy September morning in 1877, Eugene Victor Debs adjusted his suit collar and set out for the Indiana State House. Just shy of twenty-two years old, he’d been a member of his labor union, the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen, for barely two and a half years. But today he would deliver the opening address to its national convention.

Horse-drawn wagons and carriages rolled through the downtown streets of Indianapolis, clacking on the cobblestones and kicking up gravel as paved stretches came to an end. Lavishly ornamented cast-iron buildings mingled with simple brick structures; steam whistles sounded from the railroad tracks bound for the teeming Union Depot, the first in the country to bring all train traffic to a central hub. City leaders were thinking longterm here. Meatpacking was the city’s other big industry, Kingan and Company’s mammoth plant one of the largest in the world, its state-of-the-art chilling system allowing year-round production in these days before refrigeration.

Theirs was grimy, dangerous work.

Indianapolis wasn’t Chicago or St. Louis, Midwestern metropolises with populations in the hundreds of thousands, but its 75,000 inhabitants painted a smaller-scale picture of a rapidly industrializing America. With all the corresponding possibilities and cruelties. The boom-and-bust of capitalism had gone bust four years before in the so-called Panic of 1873, an economic disaster nearly as severe as the Great Depression of the 1930s—and joblessness persisted in Indianapolis, as elsewhere. Workers terrified of being laid off grudgingly accepted wage cuts. Politicians responded to calls for a public jobs program with creative new punishments instead: fines for begging, a proposed workhouse “where all persons incapable of paying fines” would be forced to smash stones to pave more city streets.

Soon, Gene Debs would have seen the Indiana State House come into view. A white wooden fence edged the tree-lined lawn—the trunks like matchsticks, branches draped with green leaves holding on despite the imminent change in seasons. The dome of the state capitol rose above, a grand if crumbling structure of blue limestone and gray stuccoed columns patterned on the Greek Parthenon. Debs—amiable and outgoing, a bit over six feet tall, with a slim but solid build—entered the capitol and mounted the stairs to the House of Representatives’ chamber on the upper floor, which the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen was borrowing for the convention. He greeted his fellow delegates, who had exchanged their soot-stained work clothes for suits and ties.

Theirs was grimy, dangerous work. Firemen shoveled the coal that powered steam engines into the locomotive’s firebox, which was prone to explosion. Every month the firemen’s magazine carried grim news of widowed wives, orphaned children, maimed railroaders. Train derailments and collisions were ubiquitous. Railroad workers made up the bulk of workplace injuries in Gilded Age America: by one count 56 percent of the broken ribs, 50 percent of broken arms, 41 percent of broken legs, 71 percent of severed arms, and all of the amputated legs.

Nearly one in four trainmen could expect to die on the job if he worked for thirty years; only coal mining was as lethal. The work was well paid by the standards of the day, with veteran engineers often able to own their own home, but shifts were long and irregular, running anywhere from twelve to twenty-four hours, or longer. “It is no uncommon thing,” one railroader said, “for an engineer to go for nearly a week without sleep except in snatches on the road or waiting on a branch or engine house.” Workers lived close to the railyards, knowing that at a moment’s notice they could be gone for days or weeks. The imperatives of their employers, rather than their own individual wants or collective needs, governed workers’ lives.

Not that Debs begrudged the railroad companies. If the work was too dangerous or too demanding, the hours too long or the bosses too harsh, it was up to railroad workers to prove themselves worthy of more respect. If they could do so—if they could renounce strikes and hard-drinking and rebelliousness, if they could live out the brotherhood’s motto of “benevo-lence, sobriety, industry”—then the companies would treat them with the dignity they deserved and pay them a decent wage. He was sure of it.

The story of Eugene V. Debs’s life is the story of one man’s radicalization—and of the country he helped radicalize in turn.

That summer, as far as Debs was concerned, rail workers had done the opposite.

Exhausted by four dragging years of economic depression, railroaders had struck by the tens of thousands, from the East Coast to the Corn Belt, inspiring hundreds of thousands of other workers to join them on strike. It was the first walkout of its size in United States history. The government treated it as an insurrection. President Rutherford B. Hayes sent in federal troops and militias, who shot down protesters, which triggered violence and widespread destruction of railroad property—torched locomotives, smoldering roundhouses, train tracks turned into twisted hulks of metal. The question at the heart of the Great Upheaval, as it came to be called, was whether the nation’s industrial development would benefit the workers who stoked the engines and ran the cotton looms and mined the coal, or whether it would anoint a new class of economic barons who’d monopolize the country’s wealth and power. “It is wrong to call this a strike,” one newspaper announced. “It is a labor revolution.”

And that’s exactly what Eugene Debs—a fresh-faced twenty-one years old, idealistic and respectable—did not want. After all, those same railroad companies that workers struck against had granted the brotherhood’s delegates free transport to their national convention. What better sign of the rail lines’ goodwill? What stronger proof of the benefits of currying favor with employers?

And so when Debs rose to address his fellow delegates that September morning—nerves surely buzzing, as he’d only just been asked to fill in—out came the words of a young man playing the part of an elder statesman. “I would impress upon the minds of this assemblage of firemen,” he said, “the necessity of reflecting with due consideration upon the duties we are about to fulfill.”

He turned philosophical. “A railroad,” he mused, “is the architect of progress, and by its magic power the uncultivated inhabitant is lifted from the shades of ignorance and idleness.” Could protest too be an architect of progress? On this, Debs—future labor agitator, future democratic socialist—was unequivocal:

The question has often been asked: Does the Brotherhood encourage strikers? To this question we most emphatically answer: No, Brotherhood. To disregard the laws which govern our land? To destroy the last vestige of order? To stain our hands with the crimson blood of our fellow beings? We again say, No, a thousand times No.

…

items.title: the spectacle of entry: how concept car designers set entire bodies in motion
items.subtitle:
the moving architecture of the concept car

When Pininfarina presented its Ferrari 512S Modulo at the 1970 Geneva Motor Show, the Italian design…
items.feedText: The wheels were partially hidden beneath a white body, the roof barely rose above the hood, and the continuous black band of glazing gave little indication of how someone might get inside. To enter Paolo Martin’s futuristic concept car, the entire canopy had to slide forward. The Modulo belongs to a radical period in automotive design when coachbuilders began to rethink the simple act of entering a car. items.body:
## the moving architecture of the concept car

When Pininfarina presented its **[Ferrari](https://www.designboom.com/tag/ferrari/) 512S Modulo** at the 1970 Geneva Motor Show, the Italian design team brought a vision of the [automobile](https://www.designboom.com/tag/car-design/) with almost all its familiar elements erased. The wheels were partially hidden beneath a white body, the roof barely rose above the hood, and the continuous black band of glazing gave little indication of how someone might get inside. To enter Paolo Martin’s futuristic [concept car](https://www.designboom.com/tag/car-concept/), the entire canopy had to slide forward.

The Modulo belongs to a radical period in automotive design when coachbuilders began to rethink the simple act of entering a car. With the freedom afforded by experimental prototypes, designers could do away with typical doors and set in motion much larger portions of the body. A windshield could become an entrance, and a roof could lift away to expose the entire cabin.

Read on as we revisit a series of these experiments from the 1960s through the end of the century. While much of the discussion around automotive design concerns the appearance of speed, these cars reveal some of their most dynamic qualities while standing perfectly still.

1970 Ferrari 512S Modulo concept

1970 Ferrari 512S Modulo concept

## car designers made the door disappear

Seven years before the Modulo made its debut, a young Giorgetto Giugiaro had explored the possibilities of a continuous automotive shell with the **[Chevrolet](https://www.designboom.com/tag/chevrolet/) Corvair Testudo**. Designed at Bertone and presented in Geneva in 1963, the car had a distinctly organic profile. Its name, the Latin word for tortoise, alluded to the rounded body beneath which much of the mechanical equipment was concealed. The glass windshield and roof formed part of a single assembly that pivoted forward to expose the two seats.

The Testudo emerged at a time when the futuristic imagery of aviation and space exploration had entered the vocabulary of industrial design. The aircraft canopy offered an alternative to the upright door inherited from the horse-drawn carriage, and its application to the automobile gave designers greater freedom over the shape of the passenger compartment. The legendary designer could draw an uninterrupted line along the flank of his car because the point of entry had been moved elsewhere.

Paolo Martin took Giugiaro’s idea to an extreme with the **Ferrari Modulo** in 1970. Built on the chassis of a Ferrari 512S racing car, the concept was composed of two broad, almost horizontal volumes separated by a fine red line. The glazed upper enclosure sat within this geometry like the retractable roof of a building. In photographs of the Modulo with its canopy open, the familiar proportions of the car give way to an unexpected arrangement of overlapping planes.

1963 Chevrolet Corvair Testudo | image courtesy Carrozzeria Bertone

1963 Chevrolet Corvair Testudo | image courtesy Carrozzeria Bertone

## marcello gandini and the theater of arrival

At Bertone, Marcello Gandini approached the question of entry from an entirely different direction. His copper-colored **Lancia Stratos Zero**, unveiled at the 1970 Turin Motor Show, stood just 84 centimeters (33 inches) tall. Its sharply angled profile was partly the product of an exercise within the design studio to see how low a car could possibly be built.

There is a small black rectangle at the base of the Stratos Zero’s windshield, which could easily be mistaken for a decorative detail. It is actually a rubber mat designed to accommodate the feet of someone stepping onto the bodywork. Beneath the Lancia badge is a concealed handle that releases the hinged windshield, while a hydraulic linkage connects the movement of the glass to that of the steering column.

Where most cars are approached from the side, the Stratos Zero asks its occupants to walk directly toward its nose, step onto its sloping surface, and lower themselves into the reclining seats. Gandini effectively designed a sequence of arrival around the geometry of the wedge. The exterior bodywork takes on some of the functions of a building’s entrance, right down to its little doorstep.

1970 Lancia Stratos HF Zero | image courtesy [Petersen Automotive Museum](https://petersen.org/pages/petersen-vehicle/1970-lancia-stratos-hf-zero)

1970 Lancia Stratos HF Zero | image courtesy Petersen Automotive Museum

## when the car moved to receive the human body

While Italian coachbuilders experimented with increasingly extreme proportions, designers at General Motors were developing cars whose interiors could physically accommodate the movements of their occupants.

At the 1967 New York Auto Show, Chevrolet introduced its **Astro I**, an aerodynamic research vehicle designed by Larry Shinoda under the direction of Bill Mitchell. The red fiberglass body stood only 90 centimeters (35.5 inches) high, and a large section of its upper body hinged upward from the rear. Inside, the seats rose with the canopy.

1967 Chevrolet Astro I | image © GM

1967 Chevrolet Astro I | image © GM

## a dynamic and responsive interior

Two years later, on the other side of the world, General Motors’ Australian division introduced the metallic orange **Holden Hurricane**. Its hydraulically operated canopy pivoted forward over the front wheels, while the two seats rose and tilted toward the opening. The steering column moved out of the way. Once the occupants had climbed aboard, the seats descended into a reclining driving position and the roof closed above them.

The Hurricane is particularly interesting from an architectural standpoint because the interior arrangement changes according to how the space is being used. There is one position for entering the car and another for traveling in it. At a time when much of the automotive industry’s experimentation with aerodynamics called for increasingly low bodies, Holden considered how a mechanical interior might reconcile those proportions with the human form.

1969 Holden Hurricane | image © GM

1969 Holden Hurricane | image © GM

## the automobile as a glass pavilion

Another line of experimentation emerged through the extensive use of glass. In 1967, Marcello Gandini designed the four-seat **[Lamborghini](https://www.designboom.com/tag/lamborghini/) Marzal** at Bertone, with enormous gullwing doors whose glazing extended well below the occupants’ shoulders. Silver leather covered the seats, and hexagonal geometric motifs appeared throughout the interior. With the doors raised, nearly the entire side of the passenger compartment was exposed.

items.body:
[Adobe](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/adobe/) has rolled out its Creative Agent across the Creative Cloud, providing users with agentic workflows across its platforms to give creatives "more time for their craft".

Unveiled at the Adobe MAX conference in Miami Beach on 10 November, the update spans the brand’s flagship Creative Cloud tools.

The updates were unveiled at the Adobe MAX conference

[Photoshop](https://www.adobe.com/products/photoshop.html) now features generative restyle and relight, [Premiere](https://www.adobe.com/products/premiere.html) has a new colour mode, and [InDesign](https://www.adobe.com/products/indesign.html) now supports co-editing (beta).

Adobe is also bringing the Creative Agent to [Firefly](https://news.adobe.com/news/2026/11/adobe-firefly-expands) – its AI creative studio – through the [Firefly AI Assistant, which is currently in beta](https://www.adobe.com/products/firefly/features/ai-assistant.html).

Users can direct the assistant in plain language, with Adobe stating it has already been used for everything from batch retouching portraits to turning product shots into short-form social videos.

The aim is to help creators take on projects that may previously have required more time, resources or technical complexity.

Adobe has also launched [Firefly Design](https://www.adobe.com/products/firefly/features/design.html) in beta, a single workspace that combines raster and vector graphics with motion, 3D and print design.

Available as part of Creative Cloud, Firefly Design allows designers to build, review, and hand over projects without leaving the platform.

The conference took place at Miami Beach on 10 November

Topaz Labs, now part of Adobe, has released two new image-enhancement models, Wonder 4 and Image HDR, which are sold separately through Topaz.

Adobe said the Creative Cloud updates respond to the way creatives are increasingly working – juggling more formats, apps and mediums while being asked to turn projects around faster.

The brand's latest approach aims to tackle this by bringing "AI assistance and collaboration directly into the Adobe tools they rely on".

Deepa Subramaniam, vice president of product marketing for Creative Cloud at Adobe, said the aim is to protect what makes a creative’s work distinctive.

“The ideas, taste, style and vision that creative professionals bring to their work are what make their work stand out,” said Subramaniam.

“Our latest Creative Cloud innovations transform our trusted creative tools into agentic, intelligent workflows that give pros the precision, control and flexibility to explore their ideas, streamline their work and stay focused on the creative decisions that make their work uniquely theirs.”

The updates aim to help creators take on more complex projects

The Creative Agent – which Adobe describes as a creative partner – now powers AI Assistants (currently in beta) across Premiere, [Illustrator](https://www.adobe.com/products/illustrator.html), InDesign, [After Effects](https://www.adobe.com/products/aftereffects.html) and [Frame.io](https://frame.io/). In Photoshop, the assistant is available only in the Photoshop beta app.

The agent handles multi-step tasks behind the scenes, letting professionals delegate work and increase their creative velocity while remaining "in the director’s chair".

In Premiere, the agent now supports new capabilities, including applying an effect to every clip in a sequence, tracking a masked subject through a frame, and adjusting colour and exposure across a whole sequence at once.

Adobe is also previewing local MCP integrations, which allow external AI agents to connect with its software.

Adobe is also bringing the Creative Agent to Firefly

The integrations will let users instruct third-party agents of their choice to work inside Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere and After Effects, editing project files directly on their own computer.

Layers, vectors and sequences stay fully editable throughout the process, so users can "step in at any moment to refine the work by hand". The local MCP integrations will be available in private beta in early 2027.

If a user’s chosen third-party agent is also connected to other MCP-capable tools, such as Google Drive or Slack, it can bring them into the same workflow. For example, it could pull in a brief from Google Docs, work on the project using Adobe’s tools and share the result with colleagues in Slack.

Adobe has also added several updates that give Firefly users more say over how the AI assistant works. Creatives are now able to save their preferred formats, colours, brand guidelines, characters and products to be applied consistently in future projects.

A new plan mode lets users review, edit and approve the agent’s plan before it starts, or leave the agent to run on its own. Adobe explained that creators remain in control, "guiding the work and making creative decisions as their projects evolve".

Users can also choose which AI model the agent works with, or let the agent select the best fit for the task.

The workflows will give creatives "more time for their craft"

In [Firefly Boards](https://www.adobe.com/products/firefly/features/boards.html), the agent can help develop mood boards, storyboards and concepts through conversation as they take shape in real time, “guided by human taste and direction".

Adobe also introduced a preview of always-on agents to carry out routine jobs, such as sorting new files or preparing content for different platforms, “even when the customer steps away".

Firefly’s video, design and image editors have also been updated, with the aim of taking projects from initial idea to finished work in a single workflow.

Among the other additions are a gallery of ready-made, [quick actions](https://firefly.adobe.com/quick-actions), [visual boards](https://firefly.adobe.com/boards), and [node-bases workflows](https://www.adobe.com/products/firefly/features/graph.html) through Firefly Graph (beta), which lets users build repeatable workflows of their own.

Adobe's examples include turning a video storyboard into a finished cut and, in Firefly Design, carrying a brand identity from initial concept through client review within a single design workspace.

To learn more about the updates, visit Adobe’s [website](https://www.adobe.com/uk/products/firefly/).

items.body:
Built in 1840, this one-room School House served as the educational center for all of the first to eighth grade children in the Hockanum area, later serving only up to sixth grade. This was one of several school houses serving small neighborhood communities around Hadley.

A 1647 Massachusetts law required all towns with 50 or more families to hire a teacher to instruct their children in reading and writing. Parents and students contributed to their school in the form of money, goods, supplies, and chores.

These were one-room schoolhouses, on land that was usually donated. Most schools had one book, the "New England Primer," that was used to teach the alphabet, syllables, and prayer.

The last class to go through this school was in 1933. By then, it was more economical to bus students to the center of town than to keep the neighborhood school houses open.

Along with the outhouse next to it, the Hockanum School House was, and still is, taken care of by the Hockanum community.

## Basquiat’s Paintings Reveal Hidden Images Under UV Light in New Miami Exhibition

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/jean-michel-basquiat-a-hidden-world/)

> View this post on Instagram
> [A post shared by Jean-Michel Basquiat: King Pleasure© (@basquiatkingpleasure)](https://www.instagram.com/p/DA0tZ2yxbRG/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

In a focused exhibition for [Art Week Miami](https://mymodernmet.com/design-miami-2026-preview/), a previously unseen side of [Jean-Michel Basquiat’s artwork](https://mymodernmet.com/basquiat-figures-signs-symbols-miami-pamm/) is finally coming to light in *Basquiat. A Hidden World*. The show highlights Basquiat’s use of ultraviolet (UV) materials, bringing together four of his paintings that contain hidden images and markings invisible to the naked eye. The exhibition offers a new look at Basquiat’s creative process, revealing that there may be more to some of his most recognizable works than meets the eye.

Opening Nov. 29 at the Institute of Contemporary Art (ICA) Miami, the exhibition is the first dedicated specifically to Basquiat’s use of UV materials. With the help of specialized lighting, visitors will be able to see a completely different side of paintings that, under normal lighting, appear much simpler.

One of the most striking examples is *Emblem*, a painting from 1984. Under normal light, the painting features a largely white background with scattered figures and markings. However, when illuminated with UV light, the canvas is transformed, revealing a vibrant collection of hidden drawings, words, and symbols. Among them is the phrase “invisible men,” which the exhibition’s catalogue connects to the underrepresentation and erasure of Black people in art.

Interestingly enough, Basquiat was already known for his tendency to paint over or partially erase parts of his work, often leaving traces of what had been there before. “I scratch out and erase but never so much that they don’t know what was there. My version of pentimento,” the artist once said. *Pentimento* is a term used to describe earlier layers of a painting that become visible beneath the final image. With his use of UV materials, Basquiat took this practice a step further, creating entire layers that could only be seen under certain lighting conditions.

Other works featured in the exhibition include *Untitled (Orange Sports Figure)* from 1982, which contains Basquiat’s signature and date in invisible ink, as well as *Cash crop* and *O.M.R.A.V.S.*, both completed in 1984. Together, the four paintings offer a closer look at how the artist experimented with different materials and played with the idea of what should be seen and what should remain hidden.

The exhibition is also working with art conservator Suzanne Siano to study the paintings and better understand the materials Basquiat used. These findings will be documented in an accompanying catalogue, offering further insight into an aspect of his work that has remained hidden for decades.

Curated by Dieter Buchhart and Anna Karina Hofbauer, *Basquiat. A Hidden World* will be on view at ICA Miami’s Expansion Space in the Design District through Feb. 15, 2027. For an artist whose work has been studied and celebrated for decades, the exhibition raises an interesting question: How much of Basquiat’s art have we really been seeing all this time?

## Previously unseen paintings by Jean-Michel Basquiat are coming to Art Week Miami in Basquiat. A Hidden World.

Every month, we share opportunities for artists and designers, including open calls, grants, fellowships, and residencies. Make sure you never miss out by joining our monthly [Opportunities Newsletter](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/newsletter/opportunities/).

**[Fall $1,800 Innovate Grants for Art + Photo](https://innovateartistgrants.org)** **Featured**
Innovate Grant awards two $1,800 grants each quarter to one visual artist and one photographer. Nine honorable mentions in each category are also featured on the Innovate Grant platform and join a growing creative community of esteemed artists. Applicants must be 18 years and older, and all media and genres are accepted. All applicants retain the right to the work they submit.
**Deadline: 11:59 p.m. PST on December 15, 2026.**

**[Bryson County Retreat](https://www.brysoncountyretreat.org/)** **Featured**
Practicing artists of any background and at any stage of their career are encouraged to apply for a 2027 residency at Bryson County Retreat. Residency periods can be flexible, but month-long stays are suggested. Bryson County is designed to provide ample living and working space and inspirational settings where an artist may work free from the distractions and responsibilities of day-to-day life. The program includes free lodging near tannic dark water lakes, sprawling live oaks, and drooping Spanish moss at the headwaters of the Santa Fe River in north central Florida.
**Deadline: Rolling.**

**Open Calls**

**[Wildlife Photographer of the Year](https://www.nhm.ac.uk/wildlife-photographer-of-the-year/competition.html)** *(International)*
Alongside its conservation message, this prestigious global competition is hosted by London’s Natural History Museum to champion the work of photographers, whether professional or amateur, young or older, or using top-of-the-range equipment or smartphones. Photographers are eligible for myriad awards, with a Grand Title prize of £15,000. The entry fee is £35 (free for Young WPY contest).
**Deadline: 11:30 p.m. GMT on December 3, 2026.**

**[Responsa Foundation Open Call for Textile Art](https://responsafoundation.com/2026/10/13/this-memory-competition/)** *(International)*
The Responsa Foundation champions projects that create meaningful social impact and foster public engagement. The organization is seeking textile artists to submit work for *This Memory,* a group exhibition taking place from September 22 to October 3, 2027, at Burgh House in Hampstead.
**Deadline: December 4, 2026.**

**[Open Call for Public Art Proposals in Moab](https://www.moabarts.org/public-art-application)** (Utah, National)
Moab Arts is accepting proposals for 2027 public art projects. Proposals are welcome for sculpture, murals, three crosswalks, and sticker designs but may include other ideas for different media or locations around the city. Preference is given to local and regional artists.
**Deadline: 11:59 p.m. MST on December 6, 2026.**

**[Material Works Art Award 2026](https://pci.jotform.com/form/262185636090156)** *(International)*
Material Works supports artists through one-time $2,500 awards in exchange for original pieces added to its growing contemporary art collection. The award recognizes artistic excellence and aims to promote career advancement through increasing visibility and exposure. There is a €40 application fee.
**Deadline: December 6, 2026, or when the first 300 artworks submitted, whichever comes first.**

**[Call for Mail Art](https://www.hivebookarts.org/exhibitions/call-for-mail-art)** *(International)*
Hive Center for the Book Arts in Evanston, Illinois, welcomes mail art for the exhibition *love|mark*, which runs from January 1 to February 27. All submissions must arrive at at the center by December 15 for inclusion in the show.
**Deadline:** **December 15, 2026.**

**[Sony Future Filmmaker Awards](https://www.sonyfuturefilmmakerawards.com/)** *(International)*
The Sony Future Filmmaker Awards is a major program providing opportunities for creators and filmmakers. The shortlisted filmmakers are flown to Sony Pictures Studios in Culver City, California, to attend an awards ceremony and an industry immersion program. Categories include fiction, nonfiction, animation, immersive, student, and vertical format.

items.body:
Continuing their series on how our brains find the right paths, Aatish Bhatia and Arkarup Banerjee show the learning process through “sparks” that stand in as simplified versions of brains [moving through a space of possible brains](https://aatishb.com/myriad/how-brains-learn/).

> It’s worth taking a moment to appreciate how surprising this is — given enough tries, the same learning process turned every novice into an expert light seeker.
> Of the myriad possible arrangements of this spark’s brain, only a tiny fraction generate the behavior that we want. There are far more ways to fail than to succeed.
> And yet, you’ve just witnessed a small miracle. The spark navigated this labyrinth of dead ends and rewired its brain to find the light, guided by nothing but reward and punishment.

items.body:
## Improving on a timeless recipe

The bezier curve is a staple of CAD and computer graphics. Like Bic pens, the design is decades old and they're everywhere. You'll often find them as the default or only choice in various illustration and animation tools.

Conceived by [Paul de Casteljau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_de_Casteljau) in 1959, and refined by [Pierre Bézier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Bézier) in the 1960s at Renault, the enduring appeal of the bezier curve lies in its simplicity. While more sophisticated curves have been invented, and [new ones continue to be proposed](https://linebender.org/blog/hyperbezier/), these are limited to specific domains, like high-precision CAD or road design. In general use, the bezier stubbornly refuses to be dethroned, despite its shortcomings.

Hence bezier curves are a piece of legacy tech we appear to be stuck with. As a software engineer, my question then is: can we make beziers better without invalidating all the tech built on and with them?

The answer is yes.

[↗ wallup.net](https://wallup.net/renault-4cv-classic-cars-french-73/)

## Lerp-a-derp

Drawing a bezier curve is a surprisingly simple and linear process:

*Tip: All the diagrams in this post are fully interactive.*

Given a series of control points, we connect them with lines. We then run along those lines simultaneously, to produce new points, which can be connected again. This process is repeated until we are left with a single point, which lies on the curve.

This construction makes beziers far more regular than they might first appear.

The linear interpolations (aka *lerps* ) can be summarized into a single compact formula, e.g. for 4 control points $ \left(A, B, C, D\right) $:

$$ \gamma \left( t \right) = A \cdot \left(1 - t\right)^3 + B \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right)^2 t + C \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right) t^2 + D \cdot t^3 $$

The rule is simple: descending powers of $\left(1 - t\right)$, ascending powers of $t$, with coefficients taken from the n'th row of Pascal's triangle:

$$
\ {ccccccccccccc}
&&&&&& 1 \\
&&&&& 1 && 1 \\
&&&& 1 && 2 && 1 \\
&&& 1 && 3 && 3 && 1 \\
&& 1 && 4 && 6 && 4 && 1 \\
&1 && 5 && 10 && 10 && 5 && 1 \\
... &&&&&&... &&&&&&... \\
\ $$

For curves in 2D and 3D, the formula is applied to the individual X, Y or Z coordinates.

While beziers can be constructed for any number of control points, the common practice is to only use cubic beziers with 4 control points. This is because the curve is only guaranteed to cross through the first and last control point, which makes higher degree beziers more difficult to shape.

Larger curves are instead constructed by joining together multiple cubic bezier segments, with the tangents lined up to create a segmented curve that appears smooth:

This is the cubic bezier *spline*, as commonly understood. The precision "pen tool" in most drawing apps then consists of drawing and editing the control points, rather than drawing curves directly.

## A Lie Told Everywhere

Pen tools typically have a few different modes for the control points:

Intuitively these represent various degrees of smoothness. Symmetric tangents are offered as the smoothest option, with some qualities of smoothness being lost as you relax the constraints.

In reality this is **completely wrong**, and this is easy to demonstrate.

Bezier curves can be split exactly, by reading off the new control points from the interpolation diagram:

The left and right segments are 100% identical to the original curve, and always join up perfectly at the seam. Yet the tangents in the middle will be asymmetric except for one split near the middle. This can be confirmed using a *curvature comb* which represents the (inverse) radius of curvature at every point:

The curvature comb remains continuous, with no jumps.

This means that whether or not adjacent tangents are of equal length, i.e. symmetric, is completely irrelevant. Attempting to draw smooth and intuitive bezier curves this way is a fool's errand.

A simple way to improve this is to treat the tangents as relative rather than absolute. e.g. We can make them proportional to the distance between the start and end of each segment:

This spline is easier to edit, because as you move each curve point around, the adjacent segments naturally flex to get out of the way. There are far fewer cusps created this way. Editing the tangents remains the same.

However if we plot curvature again, we can tell this isn't a great solution:

Scaling tangents proportionally doesn't guarantee that curvature is preserved as you edit, nor does curvature remain continuous from one segment to the next.

This also shows that offering users a curvature comb visualization as a "helpful tool" is really quite *mean*: adjusting the curvature on one end will also affect the other side, requiring repeated adjustments back and forth until it's close enough.

## Handle Carefully

A much more effective strategy is to work with curvature directly.

While this is a difficult problem in general, it turns out there are some surprising relationships here, which we can observe directly:

Consider the curvature at the start of segment $A-B-C-D$. This is affected only by the positions of $A$, $B$ and $C$. Point $D$ can be moved freely if it's detached from $C$.

Furthermore, because the tangent $A-B$ is horizontal, only the vertical position of $C$ matters. This is a result of the underlying linear interpolations, which end up cancelling out a lot of terms in the formulas.

The curvature at $A$ is therefor only affected by the length of $A-B$, and the perpendicular distance from $C$ to $A-B$. The same applies to $D$ on the other side with $C-D$ and $B$.

This isn't very useful by itself though. When we move a curve point ($A$ or $D$), typically the adjacent control point ($B$ or $C$) is moved as well to preserve the tangent. And when we turn a symmetric or asymmetric tangent, the adjacent tangent in the next segment is turned by the same angle, altering the curvature on that side.

Still, this shows that preserving curvature is not by itself a crazy idea and can be done simply by scaling the tangents appropriately. The rules would be simple:

- When we move a curve point, we have to preserve the start and end curvature in the adjacent segments
- When we move a tangent, we have to preserve the curvature on the opposite end of the current segment, as well as on both sides of the adjacent segment

This ought to produce an editing experience where the curve actually respects your intent. Except not quite:

Moving curve points works great, but when turning a tangent, the length of that tangent is itself a poor representation of the user's intent. Small changes can cause huge shifts in curvature, which can cause the curve to jump around and explode unexpectedly as it tries to find a matching solution.

Hence it's better to work with curvature handles instead, where the length corresponds directly to curvature:

items.body:
## fabrizio giugiaro introduces his copper-bodied peralta D

Italian automotive designer Fabrizio Giugiaro and his studio GFG Style unveil the Peralta D, a one-off [supercar](https://www.designboom.com/tag/car-design/) with bodywork made entirely from hand-hammered [copper](https://www.designboom.com/tag/copper-architecture/). Presented at the Pastejé Automotive Invitational in Mexico in October 2026, the Maserati-based grand tourer revisits the angular automotive design language that the designer’s father, Giorgetto Giugiaro, helped establish in the 1960s and 1970s.

The car has the appearance of a solid piece of polished metal, even across its expansive windshield and roof. A specially treated mirrored glass canopy takes on the reddish tones of the copper below, and the distinction between the two materials nearly disappears when the car is viewed in profile.

The project follows GFG Style’s 2025 Peralta S, a sports car sculpted from mirror-polished aluminum and inspired by Giorgetto Giugiaro’s 1971 Maserati Boomerang. Both vehicles were commissioned by Mexican collector Carlos Peralta. While the earlier model was dedicated to his sons, the latest takes its name from his daughters, with the letter D also referring to donne, the Italian word for women.

Fabrizio Giugiaro’s Peralta D features a hand-hammered copper body | images courtesy GFG Style

## GFG style shapes the bodywork by hand

The warm color of the Peralta D comes directly from the metal itself. The [design team](https://www.gfgstyle.it/) at GFG Style works sheets of copper by hand to achieve the broad, uninterrupted surfaces of the body, whose low nose and sharply defined edges recall the wedge-shaped concept cars of half a century ago.

Beneath the copper skin, a carbon fiber structure supports the bodywork, while an aluminum chassis and mechanical components draw from the Maserati GranTurismo. The dark, geometric wheels reference designs from the 1970s and sit almost entirely within the contours of the body.

Much of the functional hardware disappears into the exterior. Narrow blades of light extend across the nose and tail, while diamond-patterned aluminum grilles conceal additional lighting elements within their geometry. Even the carbon fiber aerodynamic components are tucked into the body.

the entire glass canopy lifts upward and forward to open the cabin

## a moving glass canopy replaces conventional car doors

Perhaps the most unusual aspect of the Peralta D becomes apparent when its occupants step inside. In place of conventional car doors, [designer](https://www.giorgettofabriziogiugiaro.it/) Fabrizio Giugiaro develops a system in which the entire canopy lifts upward and forward in one motion. Smaller gullwing sections can open independently along either side.

Access to the second row of seats introduces another moving element to the architecture of the car. Two additional panels rise from the rear bodywork in a configuration that recalls the split engine cover of the 1967 De Tomaso Mangusta, designed by Giorgetto Giugiaro. Here, Fabrizio adapts his father’s idea to accommodate passengers.

With all of these elements raised, the seemingly solid copper volume opens up into a series of thin metallic planes. It is a particularly expressive evolution of the moving dome that distinguished the Peralta S, this time adapted to the proportions and practical demands of a four-seat grand tourer.

independently opening gullwing panels are integrated into the canopy

## copper extends into the interior of the supercar

Inside the Peralta D, the reddish metallic finish continues across the leather upholstery, with genuine copper thread sewn into the seams. Dark, perforated Alcantara interrupts the otherwise continuous material palette.

The dashboard is organized symmetrically around the center console. Opposite the driver’s instrument display, a second screen sits above a concealed vanity compartment with an illuminated mirror. Between the rear seats, a retractable refrigerator houses a champagne bottle alongside four copper drinking glasses.

More than fifty years after Giorgetto Giugiaro experimented with the geometric possibilities of the automobile through his Maserati Boomerang, the Peralta D explores that same design language through the malleability of a different metal. Its futuristic appearance owes much to the work of traditional metalworkers and the painstaking process of shaping each surface by hand.

the angular silhouette recalls the futuristic wedge cars of the 1970s

a thin red light traces the perimeter of the copper tail

metallic leather upholstery echoes the exterior bodywork

the symmetrical dashboard features dedicated displays for the driver and passenger

the four-seat grand tourer transforms its silhouette through its movable panels
